A few days ago, I watched CTT's YouTube channel and discovered that Hugo + GitHub or Hugo + Netlify are also great options for building a blog. Considering that Blogger's editing mode really isn't that modern, and my hard work trying to switch over to Markdown syntax, starting with this post I plan to move this unread blog of mine from Blogger to GitHub—and take the opportunity to learn the trendy Git way of managing my blog.

The new blog requires the following tools: Hugo - A tool for generating static websites, available on Linux, Windows, macOS, FreeBSD, etc.—a pure CLI tool. Github - Arguably Microsoft's most generous service. We mainly use it because we can create our own projects for free and easily upload and manage them using git commands. Remarkable or Typora or other Markdown editors - Mainly for comfortably editing .md files as the body of blog posts, which is also my primary reason for switching. git - An ultra-powerful tool that basically comes pre-installed on Linux by default; if you're on Windows, you'll need to install it separately. Surprisingly, not many tools are needed, though since I'm not familiar with it, I had to look up quite a lot of references. Actually, there are plenty of resources out there—just search Google for hugo tutorial and tons of results pop up.
Since I mostly sneak in blog writing during work hours, my main machine runs Manjaro. Anyway, let's install Hugo first: sudo pacman -S hugo

Here I recommend following chanmitsu55's approach. First, you'll need a GitHub account—it's free, just sign up with an email. Once registered, please create two repositories: A repo with the same name as your site; in my case, Blog. A repo named <username>github.io. First, clone the repo with the same name as your local base directory: git clone https://github.com/<username>/Blog.git

Next, create a new site. This step basically only needs to be done the first time: hugo new site _blog cp -p -f -R _blog/* Blog/ cd Blog git submodule add -b master https://github.com/<username>/<username>.github.io.git public The reason for copying it over first is that the Fuji theme I use is attached as a submodule, and you can't add a submodule outside a git directory. Also, the reason for attaching public before Hugo generates the site is that otherwise you'd have to run rm -rf public later to attach it anyway, so you might as well attach it before anything is generated.
documents.s: Creating the Site Body, Copying to the Local Working Directory & Mounting the Public Submodule

documents.t: Now we have a basic web framework. Next, let's install a theme so it actually looks like something. I'm pretty minimalist, so I picked a simple theme, Fuji, though you can install whichever one you like. cd ~/Blog git submodule add https://github.com/amzrk2/hugo-theme-fuji.git themes/fuji That installs the theme. Next, let's do some simple configuration for it: cp themes/fuji/exampleSite/config.toml ./ cp -R themes/fuji/exampleSite/content/archives ./content/ cp -R themes/fuji/exampleSite/content/search ./content/ The important part of this step is taking config.toml from exampleSite to modify; the other two are because I only plan to keep the Archives and Search menus, so I copied them over. Next, edit config.toml: vim config.toml There are a few main items to change: #這個是定義你的主頁網址,請跟你的設定一致 baseURL = "https://Kiwi0093.github.io" #這個是你的網頁主要Title title = "中年大叔的自言自語" #這個是定義你網頁的主題 theme = "fuji" [params] #這個是作者的名字 author = "Kiwi.L" #這個是網頁的副標 subTitle = "對應老年癡呆與記憶衰退的筆記" [taxonomies] #這是定義Tag會使用tags來進行分類 tag = "tags" [menu] #這個定義的是導向哪邊而非簡單的link [[menu.nav]] #這個定義了右邊連結的Home name = "Home" #連線是相對位置*/*對應的是*./content* url = "/" #這個定義了排序 weight = 1 [[menu.nav]] name = "Archives" url = "/archives/" weight = 2 [[menu.nav]] name = "Search" url = "/search/" weight = 3 #這個定義的是簡單的link [[menu.link]] #這個是你想要表現的字串 name = "R2d Blog" #這個是他的連結 url = "https://roidintw.kaienroid.com/" #這個一樣是排序 weight = 1

With that set up, the basic website framework is ready. Next, let's write a simple post: cd ~/Blog hugo new post/what-ever-you-like-to-name.md Then open this file with your favorite editor and you will see: #這個---不要動 --- #這個是這個文件的主題會出現在Post的標題上 title: "what-ever-you-like-to-name" #這個是時間戳記 date: 2020-07-06 #這是標記是否為草稿,寫好要正式發出去的文章把這行去掉 draft: true #增加tag的寫法 tags: [ "A-tag", "B-tag", "C-tag" ] #這個---不要動 --- Edit the section above as the header of your file, and then write your blog content directly below using Markdown syntax. At this point, the core essentials are done; next comes generating the site and putting it on GitHub.
documents.s: Creating and Writing a New Post

documents.t: Before pushing it live, please generate the site and preview it locally to make sure it looks the way you want: cd ~/Blog hugo && hugo server Remember to follow the prompt to view it locally and see if anything else needs adjusting; if not, it's time to push it to GitHub!

For this part, it's easy to forget the manual commit message part in the official recommended script, so here I'm using [chanmitsu55]'s version, which basically just appends the update timestamp at the end: #!/bin/bash echo -e "\033[0;32mDeploying updates to GitHub...\033[0m" # Build the project.我們已經在config.toml裡定義了theme所以簡單的hugo就夠了 hugo # Go To Public folder cd public # Add changes to git. git add . # Commit changes. msg="rebuilding site `date`" if [ $# -eq 1 ] then msg="$1" fi git commit -m "$msg" # Push source and build repos. git push origin master # Come Back up to the Project Root cd .. # Commit source repository changes git add . git commit -m "$msg" git push I don't like making it an executable directly, so I put the above contents in deploy.sh and run it with: sh ./deploy.sh During the process, it will ask for your GitHub username and password twice—once for pushing Blog and once for Public—don't mistype them.

What if you also want to edit on other machines? Basically, you just need the following command to pull everything down from scratch: git clone --recursive https://github.com/<username>/Blog.git On machines that already have an existing git folder, you can just write new updates, because git push/pull compare diffs. Files that aren't updated won't be uploaded (of course, if you're paranoid and have unlimited bandwidth, you can re-clone every time). That way, we can ensure our data is basically all stored on GitHub.

documents.t: The biggest reason I use Arch Linux instead of FreeBSD—which I have used for many years—as the primary Gateway for a network environment is the V2Ray + iptables combo for bypassing the firewall (looking at V2Ray alone, FreeBSD can actually install it too, but it doesn't have iptables). Almost every guide I saw online used this exact combination. Since I'm not a true expert either, I just went with the flow and picked a Linux distro that looked pleasing to use. Some might ask why I didn't just use Ubuntu like the guides—all I can say is that I still have a bit of tsundere pride.... Actually, I originally wanted to go even more extreme and use Gentoo, but remembering the painful past where just installing the system took me three days (because of tons of compiling, though my machine back then wasn't powerful enough either), I settled for the next best thing and switched to Arch Linux, which installs almost everything via binaries.

Basically, the biggest expectation is to build a network environment similar to home in Taiwan without needing to do anything extra. Based on this, a large NAT internal network and bypassing the firewall right at the Gateway side are the most basic of the basic requirements.
A piece of server hardware capable of running VMware ESXi A Wireless AP that meets the network requirements

VMware ESXi 5.5 or 5.0 - (Mainly because of the client, though you can actually use the latest version) or other types of VMs such as Xen, etc. Archlinux install Image - This is the main protagonist, like MS-06F RX-78 to the original Gundam vSphere Client - This is the client used to control VMware ESXi Now VMware has renamed ESXi to vSphere Hypervisor, which has more features, though I'm not sure about its pricing and haven't actually used it myself, so I'm just leaving it here for reference. If I have the chance to set up a new VMware server in the future, I might give it a try.

Out of respect, I'm still listing all the documents I referenced when writing this earlier: Arch Wiki - The very detailed Arch Wiki has documentation for almost all Arch Linux configurations, and many pages have Chinese translations, which is super useful. Archlinux Install Guide - This is the official Chinese installation guide, considered the most fundamental reference for installation, and is actually part of the Arch Wiki. Miro's Blog - These Arch Linux installation notes are very well written. Another reference webpage disappeared for some reason when I was organizing this... so I won't list it anymore, though I'm still very grateful for the predecessors' efforts and sharing.

Because I am a lazy bum mainly use this to install a Gateway, I need to avoid looking things up left and right during installation as much as possible. Even though I listed a bunch of key installation points earlier, in the end it still comes down to using simple installation scripts to handle the setup for me under poor network conditions, keeping everything as simple as possible.

Because the Arch installation process involves chroot, one script cannot finish all actions in a single run, and I'm not skilled enough to automatically run another script inside chroot at the same time, so the scripts are entered manually in two stages. The first script after booting: zsh <(curl -L -s http://my_home.or.any.vps/arch-install-before-chroot.sh) It will automatically run up to chroot and stop, and then you use the second dose: zsh <(curl -L -s http://my_home.or.any.vps/arch-install--after-chroot.sh) Put bluntly, the way these two scripts run is by using the curl command to let the shell directly execute scripts hosted on another web server. This is a relatively convenient approach for running scripts in a Live environment, but it requires preparing a web server to host the scripts in advance and worrying about sensitive security issues inside the scripts—so it's not a foolproof method. Therefore, my approach is to customize the scripts and store them somewhere private first, upload them to a VPS or another server when needed, and delete them right after running. This is a bit more troublesome.

ASCII color definitions are as follows: Color Code Color Code Black 0;30 Dark Gray 1;30 Red 0;31 Light Red 1;31 Green 0;32 Light Green 1;32 Brown/Orange 0;33 Yellow 1;33 Blue 0;34 Light Blue 1;34 Purple 0;35 Light Purple 1;35 Cyan 0;36 Light Cyan 1;36 Light Gray 0;37 White 1;37 If needed, you can change the display colors in the scripts below according to your personal preference.

Some basic explanations of what's inside the scripts: echo -e "<what ever you like>" This syntax is for strings you want to display on the screen while running the script; typing it as above will output <what ever you like>. 變數=XYZ ${變數} This syntax pairs with the variable definitions at the very top—whenever something is used repeatedly, this saves typing. Below, I mainly set the colors as variables, so as long as you don't want rainbow text, you only need to change it right here. Update 7/12: I changed the non-generic parts into interactive inputs, so this script can later be placed on GitHub for anyone who needs it to use directly. arch-install-before-chroot.sh​ #------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- #(從Iso boot後直到完成change root內所有安裝/調整動作) #------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- #!/bin/zsh #Parmeter Define COLOR='\033[1;35m' NC='\033[0m' #start ntp echo -e "${COLOR}Starting NTP Service${NC}" timedatectl set-ntp true echo -e "${COLOR}Finished.${NC}" #Modify Mirrorlist to setting country echo -e "${COLOR}Starting Modify mirrorlist to China servers${NC}" echo -n "${COLOR}Please Enter which Country you like(ie. United_State or China)${NC}" read COUNTRY sed -i '/Score/{/$COUNTRY/!{n;s/^/#/}}' /etc/pacman.d/mirrorlist echo -e "${COLOR}Finished.${NC}" #Fdisk echo -e "${COLOR}Partition your HDD please create 1 data as sda1 and 1 swap as sda2${NC}" fdisk /dev/sda echo -e "${COLOR}Finished.${NC}" #Format echo -e "${COLOR}Format /dev/sda1 as EXT4 format${NC}" mkfs.ext4 /dev/sda1 echo -e "${COLOR}Finished.${NC}" echo -e "${COLOR}Format /dev/sda2 as Linux Swap${NC}" mkswap /dev/sda2 echo -e "${COLOR}Finished.${NC}" echo -e "${COLOR}Mount /dev/sda1 to /mnt${NC}" mount /dev/sda1 /mnt echo -e "${COLOR}Finished.${NC}" echo -e "${COLOR}Mount Swap${NC}" swapon /dev/sda2 echo -e "${COLOR}Finished.${NC}" #Install echo "${COLOR}Starting Install Archlinux into /mnt${NC}" pacstrap /mnt base vim zsh curl echo -e "${COLOR}Finished.${NC}" #fstab echo "${COLOR}Starting Gernerate fstab${NC}" genfstab -U -p /mnt >> /mnt/etc/fstab echo -e "${COLOR}Finished.${NC}" #Copy Zsh echo "${COLOR}Starting Copy ZSH setting file to new Archlinux${NC}" cp -Rv /etc/zsh /mnt/etc/ echo -e "${COLOR}Finished.${NC}" # Change root echo -e "${COLOR}Change root to new Archlinux${NC}" arch-chroot /mnt /bin/zsh #------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ #(以下是什麼都弄完了只剩下重開機) #------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ echo -e "${COLOR}Finished Installation, will reboot, Good luck${NC}" # Reboot echo -e "${COLOR}Rebooting...${NC}" reboot Basically, other than possibly adjusting the partitioning options, there's really nothing you need to touch in this script. Since I only use this machine as a Gateway on a VM, there's naturally no need to make the partitioning complicated. If you have other needs, you can refer to the official installation guide to adjust the partitioning layout as desired. The default partitioning layout is: /dev/sda1為主要資料 /dev/sda2為Swap arch-install-after-chroot.sh​ This can be considered the main installation script. There are many things in it that need to be modified and configured in advance, and I've tried my best to turn them into variables at the very top. #------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ #(所有動作都是在change root內完成的) #------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- #!/bin/zsh #Parameter Define COLOR='\033[1;34m' NC='\033[0m' #update package echo -e "${COLOR}Start Pacman Update${NC}" pacman -Syuu echo -e "$COLOR}Finished.${NC}" #locale-gen to add en_US & zh_TW echo -e "${COLOR}Setting local file${NC}" echo "en_US.UTF-8 UTF-8" >> /etc/locale.gen echo "zh_TW.UTF-8 UTF-8" >> /etc/locale.gen echo -e "#{COLOR}Generate locale.conf${NC}" locale-gen echo -e "${COLOR}Setting locale.conf${NC}" echo LANG=en_US.UTF-8 > /etc/locale.conf export LANG=en_US.UTF-8 echo -e "$COLOR}Finished.${NC}" #change Timezone to CTS(Taipei) echo -e "${COLOR}Change Time Zone to Asia/Taipei & Set Hardware time${NC}" ln -sf /usr/share/zoneinfo/Asia/Taipei /etc/localtime hwclock --systohc --utc echo -e "$COLOR}Finished.${NC}" #Network echo -e "${COLOR}Setting 'Gateway' as hostname${NC}" echo Gateway > /etc/hostname echo "127.0.0.1 localhost Gateway" >> /etc/hosts echo -e "${COLOR}Finished.${NC}" echo -e "${COLOR}Define your NIC by Mac address${NC}" echo -n "${COLOR}Please Enter your MAC address for your outside NIC${NC}" read OUTSIDE echo 'SUBSYSTEM=="net", ACTION=="add", ATTR{address}=="$OUTSIDE", NAME="EXT0"' > /etc/udev/rules.d/10-network.rules echo -n "${COLOR}Please Enter your MAC address for your inside NIC${NC}" read INSIDE echo 'SUBSYSTEM=="net", ACTION=="add", ATTR{address}=="$INSIDE", NAME="INT0"' >> /etc/udev/rules.d/10-network.rules echo -e "${COLOR}Finished.${NC}" echo -e "${COLOR}Define your PPPOE Setting${NC}" echo "Description='EXT0 PPPOE SETTING'" > /etc/netctl/EXT0.service echo "Interface=EXT0" >> /etc/netctl/EXT0.service echo "Connection=pppoe" >> /etc/netctl/EXT0.service echo -n "${COLOR}Please Enter your PPPOE acount:${NC}" read ISP echo "User='${ISP}'" >> /etc/netctl/EXT0.service echo -n "${COLOR}Please Enter your PPPOE password${NC}" read ISPPW echo "Password='${ISPPW}'" >> /etc/netctl/EXT0.service echo "ConnectionMode='persist'" >> /etc/netctl/EXT0.service echo "UsePeerDNS=false" >> /etc/netctl/EXT0.service echo -e "${COLOR}Enable EXT0{NC}" netctl enable EXT0.service echo -e "${COLOR}Finished.${NC}" echo -e "${COLOR}Define your Private Gateway IP for INT0${NC}" echo "Description='INT0 IP SETTING'" > /etc/netctl/INT0.service echo "Interface=INT0" >> /etc/netctl/INT0.service echo "Connection=ethernet" >> /etc/netctl/INT0.service echo "IP=static" >> /etc/netctl/INT0.service echo -n "${COLOR}Please Enter your Gateway IP address:${NC}" read GATEWAYIP echo "Address=('${GATEWAYIP}/24')" >> /etc/netctl/INT0.service echo -e "${COLOR}Enable INT0${NC}" netctl enable INT0.service echo -e "${COLOR}Finished.${NC}" #Initramfs echo -e "${COLOR}Initramfs your Linux${NC}" mkinitcpio -p linux echo -e "${COLOR}Finished.${NC}" #Root Password echo -e "${COLOR}Set your root password${NC}" passwd chsh -s /bin/zsh echo -e "${COLOR}Finished.${NC}" #add User echo -e "${COLOR}Add user account:${NC}" echo -n "$What ID you want:${NC}" read YOURID useradd -m -g root -s /bin/zsh ${YOURID} passwd ${YOURID} echo -e "${COLOR}Finished.${NC}" echo -e "${COLOR}Add $YOURID into sudo list${NC}" pacman -Syu sudo echo "$YOURID ALL=(ALL) ALL" >> /etc/sudoers #install Tools echo -e "${COLOR}Install Packages Microcode/Bootloader - grub/dnsutils/open-vm- tools/v2ray${NC}" pacman -Sy intel-ucode grub dnsutils open-vm-tools v2ray screen echo -e "${COLOR}Finished.${NC}" #install Bootloader echo -e "${COLOR}Install grub Boot Loader into /dev/sda1${NC}" grub-install --target=i386-pc /dev/sda1 grub-mkconfig -o /boot/grub/grub.cfg echo -e "${COLOR}Finished.${NC}" #V2ray config.json get echo -e "${COLOR}Fetch V2ray config.json and replace${NC}" echo -n "${COLOR}Please Enter where you put the file:${NC}" read link echo -n "${COLOR}Please Enter the file name:${NC}" read conffile wget $Link/$conffile mv -f ./$conffile /etc/v2ray/config.json echo -e "${COLOR}Finished.${NC}" #Set Nat echo -e "${COLOR}Open package fowrading${NC}" echo "net.ipv4.ip_forward=1" > /etc/sysctl/30-ipforward.conf echo -e "${COLOR}Finished.${NC}" echo -e "${COLOR}Create Iptable start script${NC}" echo -n "${COLOR}Please Enter your V2ray Server IP:${NC}" read VPSIP echo "#Re-direction TCP" > /etc/iptables/iptable.sh echo "iptables -t nat -N V2RAY" >> /etc/iptables/iptable.sh echo "iptables -t nat -A V2RAY -d 0.0.0.0/8 -j RETURN" >> /etc/iptables/iptable.sh echo "iptables -t nat -A V2RAY -d 10.0.0.0/8 -j RETURN" >> /etc/iptables/iptable.sh echo "iptables -t nat -A V2RAY -d 127.0.0.0/8 -j RETURN" >> /etc/iptables/iptable.sh echo "iptables -t nat -A V2RAY -d 169.254.0.0/16 -j RETURN" >> /etc/iptables/iptable.sh echo "iptables -t nat -A V2RAY -d 172.16.0.0/12-j RETURN" >> /etc/iptables/iptable.sh echo "iptables -t nat -A V2RAY -d 192.168.0.0/16 -j RETURN" >> /etc/iptables/iptable.sh echo "iptables -t nat -A V2RAY -d 224.0.0.0/4 -j RETURN" >> /etc/iptables/iptable.sh echo "iptables -t nat -A V2RAY -d 240.0.0.0/4 -j RETURN" >> /etc/iptables/iptable.sh echo "iptables -t nat -A V2RAY -d ${VPSIP} -j RETURN" >> /etc/iptables/iptable.sh echo "iptables -t nat -A V2RAY -p tcp -j REDIRECT --to-ports 12345" >> /etc/iptables/iptable.sh echo "iptables -t nat -A PREROUTING -p tcp -j V2RAY" >> /etc/iptables/iptable.sh echo " " >> /etc/iptables/iptable.sh echo "#Natd" >> /etc/iptables/iptable.sh echo "iptables -t nat -A POSTROUTING -s 192.168/16 -j MASQUERADE" >> /etc/iptables/iptable.sh chmod 750 /etc/iptables/iptable.sh echo -e "${COLOR}Finished.${NC}" echo -e "${COLOR}Create Systemd Service${NC}" echo "[Unit] > /etc/systemd/system/iptables.service echo "Description=iptables rules for V2Ray Daemon >> /etc/systemd/system/iptables.service echo " " >> /etc/systemd/system/iptables.service echo "[Service]" >> /etc/systemd/system/iptables.service echo "ExecStart=/bin/sh /etc/iptables/iptable.sh" >> /etc/systemd/system/iptables.service echo " " >> /etc/systemd/system/iptables.service echo "[Install]" >> /etc/systemd/system/iptables.service echo "WantedBy=multi-user.target" >> /etc/systemd/system/iptables.service systemctl enable iptables.service echo -e "${COLOR}Finished.${NC}" #Finished install sync sync sync exit This script makes the following assumptions: This machine has an Intel CPU V2Ray's config.json is already written in advance and uses the DNS feature of V2Ray 4.20, allowing you to skip installing and configuring Dnsmasq (making it much cleaner)

In the original blog I wrote two posts about automating this Gateway installation, and I've actually used and tested it several times in real life. You can basically take this script, adjust the variables, and use it directly.

V2Ray—this is arguably the main reason I started writing this blog, because it is a specialized skill only needed when living inside the Great Firewall. Generally, technical documentation is in English, yet ironically, documentation related to bypassing internet censorship is almost exclusively in Simplified Chinese... Because this area of knowledge is quite niche, I felt inspired to record the methods and results I researched so I wouldn't have to look everything up from scratch every time—and, if possible, automate these steps to reduce the effort required. Originally, the article under this title was meant to consolidate everything up to the "update IV" version of VPS V2Ray Server setup and configuration. However, thinking about it carefully, I hadn't really covered the finer configuration details (since the V2Ray official website explains them very clearly, and once I have a working config I rarely rewrite it from scratch and mostly just reuse it). So I'll include a bit about the configuration here as well, though the official website's documentation is still better.
documents.s: Escaping the GFW - V2Ray Server Setup Summary

documents.t: Even though many people rent VPS instances for general purposes, specializing one solely for bypassing the firewall is probably something only netizens behind the GFW do, so you can find plenty of reviews online. Personally, since I've always thought online freedom should be a given, I tend to be stingy when choosing a VPS—picking the cheapest, barely-usable option. In practice, I just pick the lowest price available; machine performance doesn't matter (though KVM does)... Anynode - This is my main machine. I'm on the $20 USD/year plan with 500 GB of monthly traffic, which is more than enough as a primary VPS for personal use. Hostenos - A cheap and generous option at $21 USD for two years, with unlimited traffic and only a 100M speed cap. Very suitable if you want to generously share with others or burn through bandwidth without worrying about traffic limits (though 500 GB for one person is practically unlimited anyway...). Bandwagonhost - BandwagonHost is actually a very convenient choice. Their early VPS offerings already came with a one-click ShadowSocks installation service, and recently they also launched Just my socks. Though a bit off-topic, anyone who doesn't want to set things up themselves can consider this option to save hassle.

Since we're picking cheap VPS hosts, it's naturally unrealistic to run anything with a GUI or Windows—we can only run a pure CLI OS. Among them, the easiest to get started with is probably FreeBSDLinux. Everyone has their own preferences, so just pick one whose commands you're comfortable with from what your VPS provider offers. Because of my own preferences, I mostly choose distros that use the apt package manager, such as Ubuntu or Debian. However, after being converted by Arch, I've become especially fond of rolling-release systems (even though for server stability it really should be the other way around). So here I'll use Debian as the baseline. For those using a different distro... please mentally translate the commands yourselves.

You'll need this if you plan to use WebSocket+TLS+Web for obfuscation. Strictly speaking, you also need to apply for an SSL certificate, but Caddy can handle the SSL part for you, making it very simple. You just need to prepare a domain—either a free one or a purchased one will do.

You only need this if you plan to add another layer of obfuscation on top of WebSocket+TLS+Web, betting that the firewall won't block all routes to your VPS web port. The principle is using CDN forwarding to bypass blocks and keep the connection alive, mainly betting that a company as large as Cloudflare won't have all its IPs blocked. Of course, if you don't like Cloudflare, you can use another CDN, though Cloudflare's free tier is quite tempting. Finally, the more obfuscation layers you add, the slower the connection speed becomes—there's no way around that. You'll need to balance speed and reliability according to your own needs.

Browser - Needed to perform initial VPS setup via the web control panel. PuTTY or Linux Terminal - Simply put, an SSH client you're comfortable with. vi, vim, or any editor you like - There will be a lot of file editing, and since we almost never download files to edit in a GUI environment, it's best to use a CLI text editor. I personally prefer the vi family...

freenom - A place where you can get a free domain. New V2Ray Plain-Language Guide - Essentially the official V2Ray documentation site; the content is simple and easy to understand. Caddy Documentation - The official Caddy V2 documentation page. Compared to V1, it has much more detailed config file and CLI documentation. The only thing Caddy V2 lacks compared to V1 is that automatic install script. Blog - sprov Na Shu Yang Guang 233boy

In your browser's VPS management panel, select your preferred Linux distro and install the OS. I chose Debian. Once installed, configure your SSH (via web terminal or whatever method is available). Log into your VPS using your preferred SSH client. Change your password for future login management: passwd Update the system: #Debain or Ubuntu sudo apt update && apt upgrade #Archlinux sudo pacman -Syu Install the required programs - Vim, V2Ray, Caddy: #Debain or Ubuntu sudo apt install vim bash <(curl -L -s https://install.direct/go.sh) echo "deb [trusted=yes] https://apt.fury.io/caddy/ /" | sudo tee -a /etc/apt/sources.list.d/caddy-fury.list sudo apt update sudo apt install caddy #Archlinux sudo pacman -Sy yay yay -Sy vim v2ray caddy2 When I wrote the original blog post, Caddy hadn't officially transitioned to Caddy2 yet, but since the Caddy official site announced that Caddy V1 is now under limited support, updating to V2 was only a matter of time. Arch definitely looks cleaner and neater (pure personal bias).

#!bash #變數定義 COLOR='\033[1;35m' NC='\033[0m' echo -e "${COLOR}Update Ubuntu System${NC}" apt-get -y update apt-get -y upgrade echo -e "${COLOR}Install V2ray${NC}" bash <(curl -L -s https://install.direct/go.sh) echo -e "${COLOR}Set Auto Monthy Update V2ray${NC}" echo '59 3 1 * * root bash <(curl -L -s https://install.direct/go.sh)' >> /etc/crontab echo -e "${COLOR}Install BBR${NC}" bash <(curl -L -s https://github.com/teddysun/across/raw/master/bbr.sh) echo -e "${COLOR}Install Caddy${NC}" wget "https://github.com/caddyserver/caddy/releases/download/v2.1.1/caddy_2.1.1_linux_amd64.deb" dpkg -i ./caddy_2.1.1_linux_amd64.deb" echo -e "${COLOR}Setup Caddy${NC}" mkdir /etc/caddy chown -R root:www-data /etc/caddy mkdir /etc/ssl/caddy chown -R www-data:root /etc/ssl/caddy chmod 0770 /etc/ssl/caddy mkdir /var/www chown www-data:www-data /var/www ufw allow http ufw allow https apt install libcap2-bin setcap cap_net_bind_service=+ep /usr/local/bin/caddy echo '

Before using this, you need to install and configure sudo. I'll fold this step into the Arch Linux installation script later; the method is as follows: pacman -Syu sudo echo ALL=(ALL) ALL >> /etc/sudoers This script must be run as root. Midway through, it will ask you to enter a non-root account—the one you added to sudoers. It's only this troublesome because Arch Linux doesn't allow running yay as root. #!bash #變數定義 COLOR='\033[1;35m' NC='\033[0m' echo -e "${COLOR}Update Arclinux System${NC}" pacman -Syu echo -e "${COLOR}Install yay for Archlinux${NC}" git clone https://aur.archlinux.org/yay.git cd yay makepkg -si echo -e "${COLOR}Need None Root account to run yay${NC}" echo -n "Please Enter your none root account" read YOURID su $YOURID echo -e "${COLOR}Install V2ray, Caddy2${NC}" yay -Syu v2ray caddy2 exit echo -e "${COLOR}Install BBR${NC}" bash <(curl -L -s https://github.com/teddysun/across/raw/master/bbr.sh) echo -e "${COLOR}Setup Caddy${NC}" mkdir /etc/caddy chown -R root:http /etc/caddy mkdir /etc/ssl/caddy chown -R http:root /etc/ssl/caddy chmod 0770 /etc/ssl/caddy mkdir /var/www chown http:http /var/www curl -s https://raw.githubusercontent.com/mholt/caddy/master/dist/init/linux-systemd/caddy.service -o /etc/systemd/system/caddy.service systemctl daemon-reload systemctl enable caddy.service ufw allow http ufw allow https setcap cap_net_bind_service=+ep /usr/local/bin/caddy echo '

Honestly, V2Ray is a great piece of software. Fundamentally, it is a framework rather than just a single communication protocol. Even though its configuration is relatively complex, once you understand how it works, even if VMess stops working later on, another useful protocol like VMess2 will likely be wrapped into the V2Ray framework so you can keep using it. Currently, as a network traffic routing tool, V2Ray already includes the following capabilities: Intercepting all local UDP port 53 packets and forwarding them to a specific IP and port to implement DNS functionality. Routing all traffic entering a certain port via a chosen protocol to a designated IP machine to act as a proxy (a "ladder"). Even if you don't use it as a proxy ladder, V2Ray could also serve as a firewall for your home network—for example, preventing kids from accessing sites they shouldn't visit (though you can just do that directly with a firewall without going to all this trouble). For V2Ray configuration details, you can refer to the New V2Ray Plain-Language Guide. It is very detailed and practical—you can basically just copy it, tweak a few values, and start using it. In the current environment, it is recommended to use WebSocket+TLS+Web paired with a CDN like Cloudflare. There are plenty of tutorials online for reference.

Comparing Caddy v2 installation methods, using yay on Arch-based distros is still much simpler. On Debian/Ubuntu-based systems, following the official instructions didn't allow installing via apt properly at the time, so I ended up installing via the .deb package from GitHub. The downside is having to update the package version in the auto-install script whenever a new release comes out. Another difference is that on Arch-based systems the config file is /etc/caddy/caddy.conf, whereas when installed via .deb it remains /etc/caddy/Caddyfile. Keep this in mind during later use so you don't run into issues.

This configuration file is adapted directly from the New V2Ray Plain-Language Guide: # Caddy v2 (recommended) <mydomain.me> { log { output file /etc/caddy/caddy.log } tls { protocols tls1.2 tls1.3 ciphers TLS_ECDHE_ECDSA_WITH_AES_256_GCM_SHA384 TLS_ECDHE_ECDSA_WITH_CHACHA20_POLY1305_SHA256 curves x25519 } @v2ray_websocket { path /<your_path> header Connection *Upgrade* header Upgrade websocket } reverse_proxy @v2ray_websocket localhost:<your_port_Number> } Replace <mydomain.me> with your domain without <>. Replace <your_path> with your V2Ray WebSocket path without <>. Replace <your_port_Number> with your V2Ray port number without <>. You can copy everything else as-is. Strictly speaking, since I only just adopted Caddy v2 while writing this post, I'm not too familiar with its config format myself—I recommend checking the Caddy Documentation.

This is a Qt-based GUI for V2Ray. You generally use it together with V2ray-Core. V2ray-Core updates frequently, though it usually maintains compatibility with the previous three versions, so it's rarely an issue. Windows​ choco upgrade qv2ray v2ray -y This single line installs everything—just open it and configure your settings. Linux (Arch Linux / Manjaro)​ yay -Syu qv2ray v2ray And that's it for installation. Linux (Others)​ There is an AppImage file on the official GitHub releases page that you can download and run directly. macOS​ I can't afford one so I don't know, though there's a .dmg file on the official GitHub releases page—you should just be able to download and install it directly. For related instructions, please refer to the Official Qv2ray Documentation.

Just tap to install. For those who can't access Google Play, you'll have to find a way to get the APK—for instance, you can set up a V2Ray proxy on Windows and have your phone/tablet connect through it to install. As for phones without Google Play Services... we'll save that topic for another day if the opportunity arises. For usage instructions, check out this guide written by a GFW-bypass expert.

As long as you don't use a Mainland China Apple Store account, you should be able to buy this app directly on the App Store (yes, it's the only paid one here, though iPhone users usually don't mind spending a few bucks). For friends in China who have no other choice, you can only use this unorthodox workaround rely on kind-hearted folks. However, third-party sharing methods easily lead to other installation issues that I'm not an expert at troubleshooting. You'll have to figure those out on your own, fellow seekers of the Way...

In conclusion, the most effective method is physically crossing the firewall, though even now I still haven't managed to do that myself. So this post serves as a reference for anyone who needs it (and mostly as my own notes). Hopefully one day the contents of this post become obsolete because they're no longer needed—not because we lost the technical cat-and-mouse game...

Ever since this uncle switched to using GitHub + Markdown syntax to write blog posts, my efficiency has definitely improved a lot. However, because I wasn't familiar enough with Git commands, I did a lot of really dumb things (like nuking my own repo and starting over from scratch multiple times). Things like not knowing how to handle diverged branches when pushing—stuff that looks hilariously stupid to experienced Git veterans. So I decided to spend a short post writing down the Git commands I actually use, along with turning the commands I frequently run for this blog into scripts for future use.
documents.s: An Uncle's Ramblings - Basic Git Usage & Essential Tools for Blogging

documents.t: Basically, my workflow is very simple—I just write on different machines and can't finish a post in one sitting, so I need a way to seamlessly pick up where I left off across machines (when I say "multiple locations," it's really just the office and my dorm). A machine that can run Git — for me, that's basically Manjaro running on my work PC and a Manjaro VM inside Windows in my room. Typora + PicGo — since Typora is cross-platform, there's zero issue there. A GitHub account — based on what I learned in the previous post, you need one repo for the whole site, one repo to serve the public web pages, and another repo to act as an image host. Later on, I'll probably create one more repo to store reusable general-purpose scripts. In short, as long as I'm somewhere with Git, Typora, and an internet connection, I can write.
First, you need to install Typora (I used to write with Remarkable, but after getting hooked on Typora, I switched completely).

We can use Chocolatey to install it, which is super convenient: choco upgrade typora -y I know the standard syntax is choco install, but choco upgrade not only upgrades existing packages, it also installs ones that aren't installed yet... so just using this one command is super convenient.

yay -Syu typora Typora is currently still in the AUR, so you need to install it using yay. On a side note, although Typora supports a lot of Markdown diagramming syntax, the Hugo theme I picked doesn't support it—so once Hugo generates the static site, those diagrams won't show up. To some extent, rather than trying to render diagrams directly with Markdown syntax, it's simpler to just draw an image and upload it to your image host.

On Typora regardless of platform, you can go to: File-->Preferences...-->Image and select PicGo-Core under Image Uploader It will automatically install PicGo. As for the config file, although the official docs tell you to run: picgo set uploader to configure it interactively, PicGo installed this way is buried in a hard-to-find path, and when using GitHub as an image host, even the interactive setup configures it wrong... It's much easier to just click Open Config File and paste in a modified version of the config below. PicGo Config File for GitHub​ { "picBed": { "current": "github", "github": { "repo": "<github_User_name/Repo_Name>", "branch": "master", "token": "<your Github Token>", "path": "<your path under your Repo>", "customUrl": "" } }, "picgoPlugins": {} } <github_User_name/Repo_Name> - Fill in your username/repository name <your Github Token> - Your GitHub Token for accessing the GitHub API <your path under your Repo> - Optional subfolder path inside your repo Basically, this plugin is super powerful: it can upload your local images directly to your image host and automatically rewrite the link to point to the hosted URL, making it effortless to include and manage images in blog posts. One catch is that files with the same name cannot be overwritten, so if an upload fails, check whether there's a filename collision and rename it.
TW git book ihower's Git Classroom

git clone - Download an entire Git repo from scratch where nothing exists yet git clone --recursive https://github.com/<user_name>/<repo_name>.git Because using GitHub for a blog in this setup involves more than one submodule inside a single Git repo, you need to add the --recursive flag to make sure submodules are downloaded as well. git config - Used to configure the Git environment; adding the --global flag applies settings globally git config --global pull.ff only Since I write everything myself, branches shouldn't diverge in general; this specifies that merges should only proceed in fast-forward mode. git config --global user.name "<github_account>" This line defines your Git account name. git config --global user.email "<your_Email_address>" This defines your email address. git branch - Used to create or list branches; for my use case, it's mainly to check whether any messy branches exist that might cause update issues git branch This lets you see which branches you have. For details, check out the Taiwan Git Book. git checkout - Used to switch branches git checkout <repo_you_want> Switches the current branch to <repo_you_want>. git pull - Fetch and sync from remote git pull Syncs from origin/master, equivalent to git fetch + git merge origin/master. git push - The opposite of git pull git push origin/master Pushing from local up to origin/master is the primary command for publishing and uploading.
#!/bin/bash echo -e "\033[0;32mSync your Local git folder with github\033[0m" #pull data from github git pull #update theme git submodule update --remote --merge
documents.s: Auto-Download to Sync Local with Remote Repo First (Reduces Branch Conflicts)

documents.t: #!/bin/bash echo -e "\033[0;32mDeploying updates to GitHub...\033[0m" # Build the project. hugo # Go To Public folder cd public # Add changes to git. git add . # Commit changes. msg="rebuilding site `date`" if [ $# -eq 1 ] then msg="$1" fi git commit -m "$msg" # Push source and build repos. git push origin master # Come Back up to the Project Root cd .. # Commit source repository changes git add . git commit -m "$msg" git push
documents.s: Auto-Upload Website Updates and Back Up Source Files

documents.t: Git is a very powerful version control tool—paired with generous platforms, it becomes an unbeatable combo.

After years of using computers, the software I rely on has gradually changed over time. Looking back at the posts I wrote earlier about installing and using Manjaro or Linux gaming, I started thinking about writing a hodgepodge consolidated post to document the software I'm currently using—or have used for years without getting tired of—along with my preferred setup methods, as a reference for anyone interested.
documents.s: Uncle's Ramblings - Windows & Linux Tool Inventory

documents.t: Starting this year, I've gradually gotten used to working across multiple platforms (mainly Windows and Linux desktops), so when choosing software, I try to prioritize the following characteristics: Freeware or Open-Source software Cross-platform support Ideally able to sync with each other, so switching platforms or devices doesn't interrupt my workflow Able to operate without depending on an internet connection Basically, these points help me avoid pirated software as much as possible and reduce reliance on web apps (such as tons of Chrome extensions).

Typora - Windows & Linux​ Windows #Powershell as Administrator with Chocolatey choco upgrade typora -y Linux(Manjaro) #None root account & yay installed yay -S typora You only realize how amazingly good this is once you've used it. As I mentioned in another post (Updated 2026-11-27: another post), it can also integrate with GitHub as an image host to automatically upload images. Once you get used to the hotkeys, writing blog posts with it is super productive—definitely a Markdown editor worth recommending. By the way, as a quick note, if you want to embed a YouTube video in Markdown, do it like this: 基本語法 [![alt text](http://example.com/exampl.png)](http://example.com/link "title") 封面的圖 http://img.youtube.com/vi/{video-id}/0.jpg 所以範例就是 [![Audi R8](http://img.youtube.com/vi/KOxbO0EI4MA/0.jpg)](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=KOxbO0EI4MA "Audi R8") Here, KOxbO0EI4MA is the Video ID, which you can find from the video URL—though playlists don't have cover thumbnails.

Notepad++ - Windows & Linux​ Windows #Powershell as Administrator with Chocolatey choco upgrade notepadplusplus -y This editor is pretty handy on Windows. I mainly use it to edit HOI4 files (a prime example of slacking off from real work). Unfortunately, it's Windows-only; you can install it via choco, download and run the installer, or even run it as a portable app.

Notion - Browser based​ Windows & Linux & macOS & any device with a browser Use your favorite browser and click here. iOS Search for Notion on the App Store. Android Ever since Notion changed its free-tier block limit to unlimited, it instantly became an absolute powerhouse. For anyone in the habit of taking notes, it's basically a must-sign-up (though I switched my note-taking style to blogging, so I don't use it much myself). Fun fact: I actually wanted to learn Markdown only after watching Notion promo videos—that shows just how tempting it is to use. Here's a related YouTube playlist link too; friends behind the Great Firewall can just pretend they didn't see it. Note: YouTube Video - Hold Ctrl + Left Click to open in new window

K-lite codepack - Windows​ Windows #Powershell as Administrator with Chocolatey choco upgrade k-litecodecpackfull -y or choco upgrade k-litecodecpackmega -y or choco upgrade k-litecodecpackbasic -y VLC - Windows & Linux​ Windows #Powershell as Administrator with Chocolatey choco upgrade vlc -y Linux(Manjaro) Built-in; on other distros you can easily install it with your package manager, or even through a GUI software center.

foobar2000 - Windows​ Windows #Powershell as Administrator with Chocolatey choco upgrade foobar2000 -y For this program, though, I actually recommend not using the installer version—use the portable version instead. The main reason is that with the installed version you have to tweak the UI every time, and honestly its software updates aren't really necessary since almost all its codecs rely on plugins, and those plugins barely ever update... When using it, remember to pair it with the Lame MP3 Encoder so you can easily convert and organize your music.

Steam - Windows & Linux​ Windows #Powershell as Administrator with Chocolatey choco upgrade steam -y Linux(Manjaro) Pre-installed out of the box—no special tweaks needed. This can only be called a godsend, especially on Linux where it is hands-down the single most important piece of gaming software. Now that I'm older, instead of spending time and energy hunting down random ISOs or sketchy repacks online, it's much more practical and hassle-free to just whip out the credit card during a sale. With games in your Steam library, not only can you wait until you want to play to install them, you can also verify file integrity to restore a heavily modded/broken game right back to a working state. Paired with Steam Workshop and Nexus Mods, the PC gaming experience and satisfaction (yeah, I'm a modder + cheat lover, deal with it) are sky-high. On top of that, Steam now has new features like Steam Link and Remote Play Together, which run smoothly on Linux too—a great choice for Linux users following the teachings of AMD who want to stream games. GOG Galaxy - Windows​ Windows #Powershell as Administrator with Chocolatey choco upgrade goggalaxy -y This is GOG's version of a Steam game download/install manager. GOG's biggest selling point is being DRM-free. Most casual players might not notice much difference, but simply put, the copy protection isn't as strict, making it super convenient for playing old games (it's literally called Good Old Games, after all). Lutris - Linux​ Linux(Manjaro) sudo pacman -Sy lutris Although Lutris is also an awesome tool—since it gathers tons of game install scripts written by community wizards and automates them (though I haven't personally succeeded in running any games with it yet)—because a lot of it is built on Wine (yes, all sorts of different Wine versions and configurations), you have to get your hardware setup right beforehand. And when running it, in classic Linux fashion, you still need to keep an eye out for how to troubleshoot issues if something goes wrong. Here is a simple Manjaro Lutris Install Guide. To sum up the key takeaways: If you use Linux, buy an AMD CPU & GPU—Nvidia will make you question your life choices. If your game is on Steam, just use Steam, kid. Gaming is supposed to be fun; don't torture yourself over non-game headaches.

Moonlight - Steam - Windows & Linux & macOS & Android & iOS​ At the very bottom of the link above, there are clean and complete installation links, so I'll save some words here. This is basically a third-party Nvidia Shield client-and-server architecture. The recommended way to use it is: Great as this is, it has a few limitations: It can only discover servers on the same subnet. If you want to connect and play from outside your network, you need to poke holes in your gateway you can set it up via the Moonlight Internet Hosting Tool. Because it's streaming, one server can only accept one client connection at a time, and whatever you do on the client happens directly on the server—to some extent, it can even work as a remote desktop. The server is basically limited to Nvidia GPUs, as rendering relies on Nvidia GeForce Experience's native streaming capability. The upside, though, is that host setup is super simple. Just like in the architecture diagram, if I ever lose my mind and decide to switch all my work consoles over to Linux in the future, this would be ideal for setting up a dedicated Windows gaming server tucked away in some corner without a monitor attached. Paired with WOL (Wake-on-LAN), you can power it on only when you want to game and shut it down remotely when you're done—saving power and taking up no desk space. You can even hook it up to a TV box to play on a big-screen TV. If only in the future this could work more like X Window— instead of sending over the whole rendered screen, outputting directly to the client so one server could let multiple clients run different things, that would be amazing (keep dreaming). PS: AMD also made AMD Link which should be able to do something similar, I just haven't tried it yet.

Brave Browser - Windows & Linux & Android Windows installation #Powershell as Administrator with Chocolatey choco upgrade brave -y Of course, you can also go the old-fashioned route, download it from the official site, and double-click to install—though I think letting a package manager handle updates fits modern tastes a bit better. Linux(Manjaro) installation sudo pacman -Syu brave Android installation This browser is highly compatible with Google Chrome (since it's built on Chromium, after all). Its sync method doesn't use account-based sign-in; instead, it uses a passphrase string as a Sync Code to sync data. So far, there haven't been any special settings worth mentioning.

Putty - Windows & Linux​ Windows installation Use the Portable version Portable Version Install via Chocolatey #Powershell as Administrator with Chocolatey choco upgrade putty -y Linux(Manjaro) installation sudo pacman -Syu putty On Windows, not having PuTTY is painful because there aren't many good SSH clients. On Linux, however, the built-in terminal or Terminator (installed later) works great, so aside from socket features or private key compatibility, there isn't really much reason to use PuTTY. JuiceSSH - Android​ Even though touchscreen keyboards on Android are universally painful for CLI work, having a client on hand for emergencies is still pretty useful in a pinch.

Filezilla - Windows & Linux​ Windows #Powershell as Administrator with Chocolatey choco upgrade filezilla -y Linux(Manjaro) yay -S filezilla These days I don't use FTP/SFTP nearly as much as back in college, but to some extent you still need an SFTP client. This one also supports PuTTY keys, so it's quite practical. Otherwise, the alternative is WinSCP, though in practice there isn't that big of a difference between the two.

Rambox - Windows & Linux​ Windows #Powershell as Administrator with Chocolatey choco upgrade Rambox -y Linux yay -S rambox This is actually quite handy. We live in the smartphone era, so most IM apps—like LINE, WeChat, Telegram, etc.—are mobile-first. Rambox is essentially a wrapper that brings all IM/mailboxes with web clients together in one place, saving your desktop from the clutter of having a dozen separate apps open. The downside is there's no LINE (since it doesn't have a web client).

Remmina - Linux​ Linux(Manjaro) yay -S remmina To use RDP, make sure to install: yay -S freerdp This is a great tool if you want to use RDP on Linux. I'm not a big fan of remote desktop apps like TeamViewer or VNC that rely on other proprietary/special protocols, so I prefer RDP (on Windows I just use the built-in RDP client). Apparently this can open an SSH tunnel directly without needing PuTTY, though I haven't successfully tried that myself. Teamviewer - Windows & Linux​ Windows #Powershell as Administrator with Chocolatey choco upgrade teamviewer -y Linux(Manjaro) yay -S teamviewer Honestly, this is a very powerful remote desktop tool—and precisely because it's too powerful, I don't really like it. My biggest mental hurdle is that a machine sitting behind NAT, without any port forwarding configured on the NAT gateway, can still be connected to using just a code or account. Its NAT traversal and connectivity are insanely strong... which is why I'm a bit hesitant to use it.

qv2ray - Windows & Linux​ Windows #Powershell as Administrator with Chocolatey choco upgrade qv2ray -y Linux(Manjaro) yay -S qv2ray Needs to be used together with V2ray-Core. It's basically just a GUI frontend for V2ray-Core, works smoothly and is easy to use. Short description, but a very important "ladder" (proxy tool).

Orchis - Windows​ Windows This program has been with me for a very long time. Basically, you can only download it from its website—a very classic Japanese-style approach. Gnome Pie - Linux​ Linux(Manjaro) yay -S gnome-pie This is what I ended up with while looking for a Linux alternative to Orchis. In actual use, it feels pretty nice.

Chocolatey - Windows​ Windows #Powershell as Administrator with Chocolatey Set-ExecutionPolicy Bypass -Scope Process -Force; [System.Net.ServicePointManager]::SecurityProtocol = [System.Net.ServicePointManager]::SecurityProtocol -bor 3072; iex ((New-Object System.Net.WebClient).DownloadString('https://chocolatey.org/install.ps1')) This is super useful, provided your internet connection cooperates. yay - Archlinux & Manjaro​ Linux(Manjaro) sudo pacman -S yay In Manjaro, yay can be installed directly with the command above, whereas on Arch Linux that won't work—you have to install it via git.

Windows Terminal - Windows​ Windows #Powershell as Administrator with Chocolatey choco upgrade microsoft-windows-terminal -y This is easily Microsoft's best terminal app—the old cmd and PowerShell don't even come close. If you have WSL installed, you can open a Linux terminal right inside it, which is super convenient. Terminator - Linux Linux(Manjaro) yay -S terminator Honestly, I don't have high demands for a Linux console—basic features are plenty for me—but after seeing Chris Titus recommend it as his favorite, I decided to jump on the bandwagon.

VMware Workstation - Windows & Linux​ Windows #Powershell as Administrator with Chocolatey choco upgrade vmware-workstation -y Linux(Manjaro) yay -S vmware-workstation VMware—the reigning king of virtual machine environments in my heart. Simple yet powerful VMs; I even run VMware ESXi on my server. The fact that it can be installed via Chocolatey on Windows was also a major reason I leaned completely into using Chocolatey. The day before yesterday, I picked up another cheap VPS from RackNerd's Thanksgiving sale—getting two years of usage for around 18 USD.

I mainly bought this one to test out VLESS configuration and usage, so as soon as I got it, I went straight to setting up VLESS. As usual, the detailed installation notes will go into the Wiki, so I won't specifically go into the installation and setup details here—let's just talk about my initial impressions.

Even though I know VLESS was created because VMess has issues that make it 100% detectable, the "ladders" (proxies) I currently have all use the WS+TLS architecture, so they aren't actually that risky (and if that's considered risky, wouldn't VLESS be just as risky?). So it wasn't strictly necessary to switch to VLESS. Still, after seeing some recommendations from Chinese users saying VLESS performs much better (since removing all the encryption and authentication from the original VMess should theoretically make it faster), I couldn't resist... (a classic example of impulse buying).

When using VMess+WS+TLS, to save myself the trouble, I basically always recommended using Caddy to handle the WS+TLS part. However, with VLESS, because TLS has to be wrapped inside V2Ray itself, you need to specify the path to the SSL key. That turns Caddy's convenient automatic SSL certificate handling into a bit of an issue (actually it shouldn't really be a problem—it's just that because it's automatic, you still have to track down where it stores its keys and verify it yourself). On top of that, Caddy v2's configuration file became more complex compared to v1, and I'm not as familiar with its configuration logic and documentation as I am with Nginx or Apache (at the end of the day, it still comes down to my own limitations...).

Because Caddy was no longer needed, thanks to my bizarre habit, I naturally wanted to reinstall the entire OS instead of just uninstalling packages (I guess to some extent this is a bad habit spoiled by VMs—whenever I'm too lazy to make big changes, I just reinstall). So at first I started working on the Arch Linux machine at home that runs my backup V2Ray. Since I was also rewriting my Arch Linux automated install script recently, I got carried away and started debugging the script while reinstalling the system at the same time (speaking of which, I have to say it's really annoying that the installation process changed slightly again, forcing me to rewrite core parts of the script...). So the day before yesterday, most of my time was spent tweaking the script and reinstalling the OS... Later, when I got the RackNerd VPS, I took the opportunity to deploy directly on it. These VPS providers basically only offer Debian/Ubuntu or CentOS-based distros, and none of the Arch Linux I like to use... After looking at some tutorials online, I felt using Arch Linux might actually be simpler—at the very least, pacman can handle the installation without needing to run an external script, and you don't need to edit crontab for auto-updates (speaking of which, auto-updates on my other VPSes basically all broke because the install script path changed).

Because V2Ray can handle the WS+TLS part by itself, I initially thought naively that I wouldn't need to install Nginx or Apache during setup. However, thinking about it afterward, it's still easier to handle SSL keys with Certbot if a web server is installed, so I installed one anyway... Overall, though, the fact that once V2Ray is configured you can run WebSocket without even starting Nginx/Apache is pretty convenient—it saves you from configuring an extra web server. That said, in the end you probably still need to set up the web server anyway, otherwise its fallback won't work properly. You can see this trend aligns with the V2Ray team's vision: from the beginning, V2Ray never intended to be just a SOCKS server. What they want is more like a comprehensive, extensible network management Swiss Army knife—with DNS, routing tables, communication protocols, encryption, and so on. If one day it includes a full web server module rather than just WS functionality, I probably wouldn't be surprised at all. Right now it's set up with VLESS+WS+TLS in the most minimal way following a template. Once the XTLS licensing issue is sorted out later, I might also try VLESS+XTLS to see if it's really as powerful as people say (everyone says it's as fast as running unencrypted...).

Gateway V2ray client​ Yep, I switched my room's Gateway over to the VPS running VLESS+WS+TLS. It seems to work pretty normally. As for speed, it's probably bottlenecked by China Unicom's terrible network, so I can't tell at all whether it got faster... (so basically, my original goal wasn't achieved at all—well, comparing speed and efficiency without a decent network route is kind of a joke anyway, right??) Right now I'm basically doing stability testing to see if there are any surprises over the next few days (hopefully pleasant ones, not scary ones). Linux Client - QV2Ray+V2ray​ Because my Linux Desktop (the one I'm writing this blog post on right now) runs Manjaro, installing V2Ray is super easy, which makes me very grateful to the Arch team. As for how it feels to use... well, I can only say I only tried it for a short moment before stopping, mainly because there's currently no WiFi at the office to connect to (so this post probably won't be published on time on the day I wrote it). However, it seemed to perform about the same as the Gateway—no noticeable difference, probably still bottlenecked by the network route. Android Client - V2RayNG​ Since there aren't many clients that support VLESS yet, I had no choice but to newly install V2RayNG on my phone. I have to say, it feels more stable and nicer to use than BifrostV—honestly, this app is the main reason I wanted to write this post (wait, so everything before this was just filler?!). Pros (Very Subjective)​ QR code / barcode compatible with QV2Ray First, this app supports the same barcode format as Qv2ray, which follows the "standard specification." Compared to BifrostV, which uses its own proprietary format, this is much more convenient to use. That said, it's not that BifrostV was being stubborn, rather that there wasn't a clearly defined V2Ray link barcode standard earlier—but either way, being able to use the same barcode format is definitely much nicer. No ads, and a GUI to my taste Although I'm not completely opposed to free apps having ads, having a clean app without unnecessary ads really makes you feel happy. Maybe it's because the Shadowsocks app left such a good impression on me earlier—its clean GUI style, responsiveness, and being the first app that let me reliably climb over the wall—that I have a really high affinity for V2RayNG's interface, which looks a lot like shadowsocks. Fast response and high stability When I first switched to BifrostV for V2Ray, I often felt its responsiveness and stability weren't as good as shadowsocks—it would frequently hang upon opening, or randomly disconnect mid-session, and things like that. At the time, though, I felt there wasn't any other alternative that covered so many protocols, so I just put up with it—until I switched to V2RayNG for VLESS, and everything changed... It brought back that feeling of using shadowsocks again. Though honestly, since I rarely wander around outside, I don't actually rely on proxy apps on my phone or tablet all that heavily—and once I'm back in my room, the WiFi is already behind a Gateway that handles the proxy, so I basically don't need to proxy again on the device... Cons​ DNS issues I'm not sure whether it's a VLESS issue or a V2RayNG issue, but it doesn't handle DNS poisoning very well. With the exact same settings, connecting to VMess+WS+TLS works completely fine, but as soon as I connect to VLESS+WS+TLS, DNS errors occur and I can't connect. After randomly trying things out, only the following settings worked properly: Domain Strategy - Either IPIfNonMatch or IPOnDemand works Predefined Rules - Bypass LAN and Mainland China Enable Local DNS - Must NOT be enabled Remote DNS - Change to Google's 8.8.8.8 That's how it is for now, though logically there shouldn't be an issue. Maybe once I figure out what's causing it later, I'll come back and update this.

In short, proxy-related tech is probably something that only people living in the Great Power the Celestial Empire ever bother learning. Just like my master said, "That's a very niche skill tree—among this group, probably only you who's stationed over there would put points into it." So I could only dig through online resources, pick up a little superficial knowledge, and embarrass myself by sharing it here. Fortunately, there are still plenty of resourceful folks in the Celestial Empire, so related info is still easy to find—well, yes... it's easy to find once you've scaled the wall and can use Google, whereas inside the wall you can't find a single article... So when it comes down to it, a "ladder" is really just something where you need a tool to get over the wall the first time. Once you have that, building any other ladder afterward is relatively easy... That said, building ladders is inherently a small act of defiance against the Celestial Empire's state apparatus—it requires constant updates and refinement. If you truly want a permanent solution once and for all, physically getting yourself out ("emigrating in person") is still the most practical option.

After getting talked into buying several new RackNerd VPSs over the last few days, I really got to practice installing V2ray 4.33 (as of today, I've set up four new ones plus two updates). However, besides the machines under my own name, looking at my DNS list in CF... there are still other people's machines under my DN that I really ought to help upgrade... Because the annoying part is:
So you have to upgrade the clients along with the server all at once, otherwise things easily end in tragedy...
documents.s: Not every 4.3x client is compatible with a 4.2x server

documents.t: Honestly, given my usual lazy habits, it's just a VPS with nothing important on it anyway... backing up the contents of V2Ray's config.json and just hitting reinstall to start fresh would probably save more effort... Still, since there are VPSs I can't just reinstall at will, let's do the complicated upgrade method instead.... Why don't I copy the technical stuff over to the Wiki? Why would I put a one-off task that you can forget as soon as it's done into a Wiki??

Put simply, the workflow is: Stop and disable the service in systemd Use rm to wipe out the previously installed binaries and related files Use mv to move the config file from the old default /etc/v2ray/ to /usr/local/etc/v2ray/. As for why they changed the path? I guess maybe they were charmed by FreeBSD they wanted to separate v2ray configs from the system's main config directory Install using the new script (if you don't want to change the default path, you'd have to manually edit the script, which makes putting it in crontab a pain~~) Enable v2ray.service Start V2ray.service and call it a day If you want to switch to VLESS, you just add the v2ray account configuration, handle the certbot keys (or generate keys another way, though I don't know how yet), and finally update config.json. The detailed steps are pretty clearly documented in the official documentation. If your server runs Arch Linux....​ Then all it takes is one line: pacman -Syu And your V2ray upgrades to the latest version.... zero drama.. super effortless.... I really hate how VPS providers never offer Arch as a default OS option... so annoying.

As for clients, honestly the one I use most heavily is V2ray on Arch Linux—best compatibility (since it's the exact same binary as the server) and high stability. Still, as mentioned before, other clients need to be considered too. Android​ Lately I've really taken a liking to V2RayNG, though it's also the only client I ran into where the 4.33 core couldn't connect to a 4.23 server.... Between the previous release (1.33) and the newly updated version, there's a real difference in VLESS support and speed. In the future, whenever the server's V2Ray-Core gets upgraded, we might have to upgrade this immediately too for things to stay smooth..... (I hope it won't be like that...) Windows​ Since I use QV2Ray + V2Ray-Core on Linux Desktop, it works smoothly with no issues. On Windows, I have to switch to something else just use QV2ray as well... (this thing is cross-platform.. works on Windows/Linux/macOS). Download links: QV2Ray, paired with V2Ray-Core. iOS​ Folks in the China region, just go find a kind-hearted soul's US region account to borrow....

documents.t: First of all, this blog post is not a technical supplement, but a pure ranting deep palace resentful wife article. Friends hoping to find valuable information here are kindly advised to turn left and head to Wiki (Updated 2026-11-27: Wiki) which might actually be helpful to you.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com is blocked I really want to curse... Putting things on GitHub was supposed to ensure that the Great Firewall the Celestial Empire wouldn't target GitHub, making it very convenient to use, but alas... the Celestial Empire still delivered a DNS pollution strike.. truly frustrating. pacstrap /mnt base did not install the kernel Looking at the new Archlinux Installation Guide, it says running mkinitcpio is not needed, which is true, but it didn't mention that running pacstrap wouldn't conveniently install the kernel package along with it, so mkinitcpio naturally wouldn't run, and grub-mkconfig wouldn't build the boot menu either... and booting turns into a tragedy.... Correction: Well, I was just being blind. The latest Installation Guide explicitly requires: pacstrap /mnt base linux linux-firmware This was my own foolishness.. but I'm still going to complain anyway... netctl became something that needs to be installed separately Actually, I forgot whether it needed separate installation before. Although I love Arch, thinking about it carefully, I actually love Manjaro.... As a lifelong chubby guy, after being hospitalized for high blood pressure earlier this year, and thinking about my wife and kids, I figured I really ought to take losing weight seriously to prolong my life. After searching online for weight-loss methods, I found that over the past year or two, a ton of people have been promoting intermittent fasting for weight loss.

Intermittent fasting involves strategically eating properly during the eating window and consuming zero calories during the fasting window, letting insulin rest while glucagon kicks in to break down fat.

In my own case, after getting discharged from the hospital, I practiced a very-low-calorie diet, a low-carb diet, and 16/8 intermittent fasting. I once brought my weight down from 112.7 kg to 98 kg, and at the time it looked like it would keep dropping steadily.. However, I came back to Taiwan for a vacation, and between hotel quarantine / foodpanda / and the not-so-desperate efforts of the mom who spent nearly thirty years raising me into this body shape, my weight started rebounding rapidly. Then... I returned to Taiwan once again for the birth of my daughter, and my weight went right back up to 109 kg and stubbornly refused to budge. I've basically been doing 16/8 intermittent fasting consistently, but maybe my physical condition really isn't great, and I eat too much during the eating window, so it's been hard to see sustained, effective fat loss. That's why I recently switched to the much more aggressive 23/1 intermittent fasting. On day one, it started dropping—from 109.6 kg → 107.8 kg. Of course, day one isn't reliable, so I plan to monitor it for at least a week to see how it goes.

So far, intermittent fasting seems to be the most effective method I've tried. The main challenge going forward will be figuring out how to integrate it seamlessly into daily life—after all, the last time I broke my streak was due to a drastic change in lifestyle (was quarantine the main culprit for gaining weight?? Or was gorging myself during quarantine the main culprit??)

Due to family reasons, I ended my expat life wandering in Suzhou and returned to Taiwan to settle down and live a quiet life.

Lately I've basically been a couch potato. After returning to Taiwan and facing the baptism of raising kids, I basically have zero time to spend tons of hours playing with new toys like before (actually, it's also because at work I have to work seriously instead of writing blog posts on the clock like I used to....).

Since I'm back in Taiwan, my focus naturally shifted from wall-hopping "scientific internet access" back in Suzhou to focusing purely on the services themselves without having to worry about the network environment. Consequently, the server OS naturally switched back from Arch Linux—which is friendly to bypass tools—to FreeBSD, which I've used for ages but was a nightmare to deal with over on the mainland. Server OS​ There's still a bit of a transition period, though when reinstalling I noticed it really is way easier to set up than Arch. Just boot from the disc, pick the items you want to install, and basically without needing to use your brain at all, you can finish the installation in no time. Then just drop the old server's config files back in: /etc/rc.conf /usr/local/etc/screenrc /etc/csh.cshrc /etc/pf.conf /etc/ipfw.conf Put them back and reboot.... done.... seriously way too easy. ESXi​ Due to certain issues (yep, those twice-a-week power outages), one of my ESXi servers died... Fortunately, because that machine had ESXi installed on a USB drive, I was able to reinstall it and get it back up and running very quickly. This time I chose to switch from ESXi 5.1 to the ESXi 6.5U2 custom ISO for HPE (since my Gen8 can only run up to the 6.5 pre-Gen9 ISO). The best part after switching is that I finally don't need to install a separate client anymore. Since I've been working from home lately, I can spend a bit of time pretending to work while actually messing around with some fun toys. So I went ahead and tidied up my home server even further (previously it was just an emergency recovery; now it's entertainment disguised as expansion).
documents.s: A Few Recent Updates: tmux, Nextcloud

documents.t: Honestly, I discovered this thing while watching YouTube (see how slacker I am—I had to browse YouTube just to learn tmux exists). Now it has become part of my standard setup (replacing screen). This thing supports powerline, though it's pretty pointless since powerline only really works in an X environment (at least I haven't found a way for the console to render the relevant fonts properly). Still, even saying that, its features are slightly stronger than screen, so I've started transitioning over to tmux.

This one is a bit of reheating old leftovers... I actually played with it back when I was in Suzhou, though it wasn't very usable at the time (honestly, it hasn't gotten much better now either...). However, this time I did find Nextcloud Apps rather interesting. Nextcloud Music​ The basic feature of this app is that you can play music in a Nextcloud folder directly from a web browser, and after building it into a media library, you can stream it out as well. Paired with Subsonic-series apps (like Ultrasonic), it can stream playback and even supports album covers and such—making it a media server you can use even without Emby. (Though if this turns out to be the only useful feature left, I'll probably still go find another streaming server to use.) Nextcloud Deck​ This is a Kanban/Deck app. Truth be told, I only use it because there isn't really a Google alternative (actually, I just wanted a free Milanote to use...).

This isn't unfamiliar either, though honestly I never spent time properly using Docker because I've always just spun up VMs directly on VMware ESXi, rarely running multiple Docker containers on a single machine. But Docker is getting more and more convenient these days—for many things you can just grab an image and spin it up, saving the hassle of installation and configuration. Webtop​ Honestly, this is something that looks cool and sounds cool, yet when it comes to actually using it I really can't think of a use case.... Put simply, it lets you run a desktop environment remotely through a browser. Currently it supports Alpine/Ubuntu with Xfce/KDE/MATE/IceWM/i3/Openbox (no Manjaro, which I like... =-=!!). Sounds pretty nice, right? Wait—if you already have a browser to use, that means you're already in a GUI environment, and you're opening another DE inside it... Aside from setting it up so a locked-down company computer can escape through a browser to breathe the air of freedom, I really can't think of what else it's good for.
Basically, working from home gets pretty boring—you can't play games, and you can't focus on work either, so you get bored enough to go look for other distractions to try out.

Ever since returning to Taiwan, the ongoing maintenance and upgrades for my home servers haven't stopped, and it's finally time to upgrade ESXi on the main server...
This upgrade mainly referenced Master's experience. Though he lived dangerously and ran it without entering maintenance mode—I at least entered maintenance mode before executing it.

First, log into your My VMware account and look for the VMware vSphere Hypervisor download. Although 6.X currently has 6.7 out, all I saw were ISOs, so I just downloaded the 6.5 VMware vSphere Hypervisor (ESXi) Offline Bundle. It's a zip file; once downloaded, just drop it into ESXi's datastore.
This part is easy: connect to ESXi using the existing client and select Maintenance Mode.
Use PuTTY to SSH into your ESXi host: ls /vmfs/volume/ You'll see your datastore, and the ZIP file you just uploaded will be inside.
esxcli software sources profile list -d /vmfs/volumes/$(your_volume)/$(your_file.zip) This lets you see its profile image.

esxcli software profile update -d /vmfs/volumes/$(your_volume)/$(your_file.zip) -p $(profile-image) It will start installing a bunch of VIBs and then prompt for a reboot (this part is annoying because its shell wouldn't accept reboot or shutdown commands, so I went to the client UI and clicked Reboot Host).
Log in through the web interface instead, remember to exit Maintenance Mode, and then power back on whichever VMs need to be running.

The main reason for this wave of upgrades is that I want to start migrating several services at home from standalone Linux VMs to running Docker directly on Photon OS, which saves both disk space and machine performance. Second, it also cuts down on the Linux installation steps and tuning required just to run a service. So there are several areas I'll need to spend time learning next: Using Photon OS Configuring multiple IPs on Photon OS Changing the shell and installing/tuning related tools on Photon OS (after all this, I still end up jumping from Arch to Photon OS) Docker usage Basic syntax Practical ways to leverage Docker Which services I actually want to consolidate and run at home

Actually, that last question is the biggest one. I set up Nextcloud recently, but it feels pretty underwhelming—not sure I'll get much use out of it. I thought about setting up Airsonic for music streaming, yet I don't feel much motivation for it (mainly because while Nextcloud Music works, it feels sluggish right away). Or maybe setting up Emby (also feels unnecessary since most of the time I just go straight to streaming platforms). Setting up Calibre-web sounds a bit more promising, though that also involves organizing a huge pile of e-books... just thinking about it makes me tired...
