Anynode, which I rented back when I was still in Suzhou, seems to have been sold, so I got an email notifying me that the service was being migrated to BuyVM. After two or three days of tinkering, I finally got the new VPS service up and running today...

Plan Page For an unmetered-bandwidth VPS, $2.00USD a month—or only $19.67USD if paid annually—is a really generous price, and they even offer a Luxembourg server outside DMCA jurisdiction. On top of that, they also offer an attachable Block Storage service: for a little extra each month, you get a pretty sizable amount of capacity to use. If you want to do... whatever with it, it's definitely pretty handy. As for speed, honestly I have no idea, since I'm no longer physically on a network in the Celestial Empirethe neighbor across the strait to test it myself, so I can only ask friends still over there to help test. Still, if someone wants to host their own site but lacks the hardware and bandwidth, it's worth considering—for under $5 USD a month you get plenty of storage to work with.

This VPS finally shows some real effort: instead of the SolusVM interface, it actually looks like the real deal, and the machine itself allows installing Windows or custom ISOs. That said, I tried Arch Linux and it didn't seem to boot very smoothly, so I just went with the default Debian option. The control panel is called Stallion, and it looks much classier than the management panels used by previous budget VPS providers. Hopefully this turns out to be a solid provider across every metric.

Now for the main point: because Anynode was sold, the way they handled the migration to BuyVM was pretty interesting. Instead of directly giving me two ready-to-use VPS instances (yes, I had two Anynode VPSes under my name), they prorated the remaining time on both instances at BuyVM's current rates and refunded it into my credit account. My two old Anynode boxes were valid until November this year, and originally cost only $21 USD each for two years—the remaining balance converted to a total of $28.05USD, which actually works out to a pretty sweet deal.

Since coming back, without any real use for them, that whole pile of VPSes I held has indeed been slowly withering away—expiring or going unrenewed. Still, this week I did go through and tidy up the machines that are still alive. I originally wanted to run things with Docker, though looking closely, those VPSes seem to be OpenVZ or KVM, so I'm not sure if Docker will run into issues.

documents.t: I installed Docker on the VPS without knowing what to do with it, so the very first container I ran was portainer-agent. Pairing it with my existing host dashboard, I found it actually works! Even without running k8s or docker-swarm, you can add nodes to manage (though the price is having to install portainer-agent).

Since I put the setup steps on the Wiki, I'll just ramble a bit here. My impression is that using portaner-ce + portainer-agent together with its Stacks feature is really nice—you don't need to drop into the console to run docker-compose commands. For anyone who doesn't insist on doing everything via CLI, I think it's genuinely convenient (especially since Stacks can be migrated or duplicated to other machines).

The main reason I installed this thing was that I originally wanted to expose various web services through multiple layers, and writing Nginx configs by hand felt annoying, so I installed it. After using it for a while, though, I noticed that Nginx location rules are tedious to configure and break easily, so I gradually started thinking I might as well just attach a Virtual Host for every single service. After all, this thing can request SSL certificates too, and not doing it that way would feel like letting down the me who paid for a domain name...being needlessly fussy. I originally thought about setting one up on the VPS as well, then looked at my V2ray config file and suddenly felt too lazy... forget it....

Still, messing around with this made me realize a problem. Right now, this habit of mapping a bunch of random services directly to the host IP works fine behind a private network, but on a directly exposed VPS it feels pretty sketchy. Even though nothing serious is running on it, I still don't like leaving the front door wide open like that. Later on, I should really get into the habit of configuring Docker networks properly and keeping things tucked inside the internal Docker network as much as possible.

Although I no longer need scientific internet accesscircumventing the GFW, aka a "ladder" after leaving China, a bunch of services at home are still behind NAT, so setting up a VPN to connect back home is pretty normal.

Yes, I didn't pick V2ray—which I knew inside and out in China—and instead went with WireGuard, which has direct support in the Linux Kernel. Here's why: Outside of China, there's no need for obfuscated connections WireGuard is now directly supported by the Linux Kernel WireGuard is simpler to configure (well... once you understand it, yeah, it really is) However, because this protocol explicitly tells everyone "I'm a VPN," naturally, no matter how smoothly it runs in Taiwan, you can't use it as a ladder to climb the GFW. If you want to bypass censorship, you're still better off sticking with something obfuscated like V2ray.
As usual, I put the detailed technical steps on my Wiki (Updated 2026-11-27: WireGuard Wiki)—go take a look yourself.

The first thing I tried running was Wireguard Manager with a Web UI. Using Docker, it spun up painlessly, but... it didn't work... (Yeah, I spent an entire afternoon on a nice-looking interface whose core functionality simply didn't work...)

Later I gave up on that and just used WireGuard directly. I have to admit, I initially thought it would be a hassle, but once I actually used it I found the image provided by linuxserver.io is genuinely great—you just specify how many peers you want in docker-compose.yml from the start and it creates them all cleanly without fuss. Adding more peers to docker-compose.yml later also appends them automatically.
Honestly, Android setup is super easy—you literally just scan a QR code. Linux setup, on the other hand, is relatively troublesome; every single parameter has to match for it to work.

After moving back to Taiwan, sharing files with friends in China like I used to became more troublesome and difficult... so I thought about using a forum + cloud drive approach for sharing.

Actually, a cloud drive alone is enough for sharing files, but constantly passing download links back and forth over mobile IM apps—especially when not everyone is in the same chat group (or even using different IM platforms)— is really a hassle. So I wanted to set up a place to post links. If everything were shared solely by me, I could probably just write something like a blog to list them out. Unfortunately, the main people doing the sharing aren't really that geeky.... So I figured I'd set up a simple platform, and after shopping around I picked phpBB to run a forum for it. (Pretty much the same idea as places like Light Novel Kingdom or 3DM.)

Why choose phpBB? Good question. Actually I didn't really pick it carefully—mostly it's because back in college I set up a very old version of phpBB, though back then my conclusion was that it felt less convenient than a traditional BBS (because it was slow). Later on, though, these PHP-based forums popped up everywhere and the software got comparatively better. Then why didn't I pick Discuz, which dominated the Greater China region? Even though there are tons of comparisons online with fans on both sides, the real reason for choosing it is way simpler than all that.. Because phpBB has a Docker image you can spin up effortlessly~~~ Yes, all of it comes from my lazy desire to solve everything with Docker—that simple, that unpretentious of a reason. As usual, the detailed setup steps will go into the Wiki.

Speaking of this, it's honestly a bit awkward. Nowadays there are plenty of free cloud drives available, yet sharing across Taiwan and China narrows the choices down a lot. The ones commonly used in Taiwan either require a VPN to reach from China or are painfully slow. The ones commonly used in China generally offer huge space and fast speeds inside China, but the account registration process makes anyone in Taiwan want to back out immediately. Later, while downloading novels, I stumbled upon one where registration only needs an email, gives 500GB of free space, requires no login to download, and has decent speeds in both China and Taiwan: Chengtong Netdisk (ctfile) No idea how long this thing will last either, anyway that's how free hosting goes—everyone just uses it while it works, and if it dies we'll find another one.

Yesterday I excitedly received the server RAM brought back to Taiwan via human courier(kind Uncle Wang's generous help), and immediately upgraded my flagship carrier(ESXi) to 32GB. Shikashi(However), tragedy struck just like that...

Actually, what happened is pretty simple: after my PhotonOS rebooted, I noticed the forum wouldn't start up properly. Looking closer, the Docker volume mapping had failed. On top of just rebooting, because the original config didn't have a restart policy set and it didn't come back up automatically after the reboot, my itchy fingers ran docker-compose up -d. And then Docker very smoothly went ahead and recreated the container for me.... And then all the data was gone and blown up.....
The post-mortem investigation result left me completely speechless, pasted below:
... volumes: - /var/lib/docker/volumes/phpbb/mariadb:/bitnami/mariadb' ...
... volumes: - /var/lib/docker/volumes/phpbb/mariadb:/bitnami/mariadb ... See it? All because of one single ' character....

Over the past few days there has actually been some material(crappy annoying incidents) I could write about for my Blog/Wiki, though maybe because work has been getting back on track lately, I just felt too lazy to write....

Embarrassing to admit... while I was at work(slacking on company time), I suddenly got asked: "How come there are no connection logs for you on the AD Server? Haven't you been coming into the office??" That's when it hit me: when I'm in the office, I really do have to behave and use the company's system to connect to the company intranet so I don't draw attention... Suddenly, the webtop/Remote Desktop setup I previously thought was pointless became super relevant.

Because of that, I spun up Linuxserver.io's webtop, only to discover.. even though it sounds great with two distros and multiple DEs to choose from, in actual use they all felt like complete crap(not very smooth to use), so I gave up on it pretty fast. Still, I noticed its approach was simply running Apache Guacamole to expose internal VNC/RDP sessions, so I naively thought.. I'll set one up myself too....
Actually, it's not hard to set up—just write a docker-compose.yml and run it. Using it to connect to Windows via RDP afterward was pretty smooth, but my Manjaro turned into a tragedy..

Looking at tutorials, it seemed simple enough: just spin up TigerVNC, tweak a few things, and it should work... Then all I got was a completely black screen... Later I tried x0vncserver, which wasn't much better either.. so I gave up pretty quickly...

This one at least looked half-decent once running.. but it was super slow—even sluggish compared to a Windows VM with fewer resources allocated. Even though I'm keeping it alive for now.. I already want to nuke it... Using it like this, I might as well just connect via WireGuard and open an RDP client(turns out it's just as awful...)
I saw an awesome automated media-bingeing stack on some blog, so I wanted to build one myself... and then... and then everything blew up.

For some reason when I spun up Emby, its default network was 192.168.0.0/16, which collided directly with my internal network architecture... For a moment I freaked out thinking I had completely broken my pf config.... So I had to tear down a bunch of containers just to pinpoint where the issue was.... Afterward I went and learned how Docker container network configs are actually written.

This one really was.... Simply put, I was way too naive before... How could anything video-related possibly run smoothly on tiny RAM and a barely-there disk space?! The bottom line was my PhotonOS had too little RAM and not enough default disk, and then I botched the online disk expansion. So Saturday became a full reinstall....

Strictly speaking, this wasn't really an annoyance—it worked well as a test of how familiar I've become with PhotonOS and Docker over this period.... It only took me about an hour to get all the containers back up; the only irritating part was:

Even though I backed up the /etc/letsencrypt directory, the symlinks inside its live directory couldn't just be copied straight over with cp, so I ended up having to recreate the links one by one manually.. so painful...

I'll look into Manjaro's Xrdp/VNC later when I have time; as long as it works for now, that's good enough... The automated media stack is really powerful now that it's running, though the anime part barely works at the moment... which is annoying... Been slacking lately.. looks like I'll have plenty of stuff to write in the Wiki later....

Lately there's been a lot of commotion in my life, along with some shifts in my mindset, so I've been wanting to write something that, to readers, is pure rambling nonsense...

Because things are messy and all over the place, I'm going to tell this story using reverse chronology(jumping around randomly). Simply put, I'm not in a great mood—not only have there been some frustrations on the server side, a friend did something that made me want to roll my eyes and curse him out.. and after some time, I finally realized some psychological reactions triggered by changes in my workplace/life.... Still, I think I should be able to gradually adjust through self-growth and adaptation(binge-reading trashy novels/videos and other leisure).

This one is the simplest and easiest to fix, because it was purely caused by a lack of technical skill. The Manjaro system I've been running sneakily under the radar(blatantly, with zero fear) at work finally crashed starting from I/O errors because it's on a USB stick. Yesterday I was even dumb enough to stop yay -Syu midway because it was too slow, which resulted in a missing kernel and an unbootable mess... (I did manage to rescue it afterward, though). Meanwhile, the Manjaro xrdp setup I put together has performance so awful I have zero interest in using it.... (alright, alright, I'll figure something out soon~~) So my mood is just completely in the dumps....

I excitedly set up a phpBB thinking it'd be great for my circle to download stuff... Then I checked everyone's last login timestamp... Damn it—they literally registered just to humor me and never used it again.... Here I was diligently posting the stuff I grabbed.... F**k!! So jaded with the world~~
Since I'd be silenced if I spilled the details... all I can say is: Damn it~~ You haven't been a virgin for ages, what the hell are you doing~~
Alright, this is actually the main thing dominating my emotions lately.

A manager at a big company, with 20 underlings beneath me, handling upper management, subordinates, and external affairs effortlessly (even if some people thought I was a tactless jerk, I didn't give a damn). I had enough clout just by speaking up... and various odd jobs were handled by junior staff (work-related odd jobs, damn it!). Even though I enjoyed the convenience and POWER that came with the title~~ I loved saying, "I don't care about titles~~" (yeah, looking back now, total tsundere).
A one-person department—across the whole company, probably only the cleaning auntie has less say than me.... Have to do every single thing myself...

Since it was my own choice, I really have nothing to complain about, and not having to manage people really did relieve a lot of stress in certain areas, yet there's still a sense of letdown. So I started wondering: where does this feeling come from?? I think maybe it's just that after all these years, once I took off the environmental Buff that never truly belonged to me, it forced me to realize once again that I'm just an ordinary middle-aged otaku.... My abilities aren't any more outstanding than my peers; everything in the past was just good luck, not real skill... Probably all of that is why I feel empty and keep wanting to cling to past glories~~~ During a Roman triumph, someone had to stand behind the general constantly reminding him: "Remember you are mortal, not a god; this glory and feeling of omnipotence is only temporary..." The ancients were truly wise and pragmatic. I think I should reread The Story of the Romans—revisit the things that made me who I am before I ever put on that fake Buff... Maybe that way I can once again reaffirm my self-worth(that I'm just a dime-a-dozen ordinary otaku)

documents.t: Honestly, this is something that really caught my eye. Based on my previous tests with Chrome OS-based systems, they always felt very crippled—not only because they require Google services to function properly, but also because what they can do on their own is much more limited... However, this approach of using LXC to run Linux opens up a lot more possibilities (or rather, tinkerability). That said, it defaults to Debian, which I am not that fond of(don't really know how to use), and that kind of kills the mood for me. But now there's a way to swap what's inside to Arch Linux, which is genuinely exciting.
Honestly, the famously comprehensive Arch Wiki also has a related guide as follows: Arch Linux for Chrome OS device

Lately I don't know if I've been enjoying auto-downloading shows a bit too much, because my family keeps complaining that the home internet died.
Not much else to explain, really—the home gateway died, and checking it showed:
Looking it up online, the general reason is that the PF state entries overflowed, so PF stopped working.

I had asked my master about this before, and his approach was using crontab to schedule a daily reboot at a fixed time, taking advantage of that mechanism to also let FreeBSD auto-update. Being a good disciple, of course I copied that approach—that's the ticket~~(shikashi~~)—but yesterday afternoon it broke again not long after rebooting.

Alright, this was actually already in the PF config file I copied from my master ages ago. The reason my master needed periodic reboots was also because this table would overflow (which shows just how many people randomly brute-forcing SSH(assholes) there are). Then I took a closer look and realized I hadn't even installed sshguard..... So forget the blocklist table growing big enough to overflow—I didn't even have a ban table set up at all, which is why it blew up even faster....

Honestly, I don't even know whether using this thing has any impact, though in my heart I lean toward "no impact"—after all, I used to go all-out downloading stuff with other P2P tools before and never saw it blow up..
Simply put, I can only keep monitoring... and see whether the current countermeasures actually work.

Actually, I thought of this concept a long time ago, just never had an actual need so I didn't set it up...(just lazy) Recently though, because I wanted to play Pathfinder:WoTR, I went ahead and set it up.

It's actually very simple: turn a Windows PC capable of gaming into something you can remotely stream and play on, so you can freely use any other console/device to play games without being tied down to your Gaming PC/laptop. There are plenty of guides and tutorials on how to do this—even Learn Linux TV has a tutorial... Video below: If you want to set it up, you can check out the video yourself.

Wake on Lan This is basically a feature every motherboard has nowadays—just Google how to use it in detail. On the client side, Android has APKs and Linux can use gwake; both are super simple. Nvidia Experiance This is mainly because I use an Nvidia card, so it's installed anyway. If you don't use an Nvidia card, I'd recommend Steam Link or Kino Console, though neither is as fast as pairing with Moonlight. Moonlight This is a really great client—fast, free, awesome, and available on every platform.

I thought before that with growing needs of all kinds, you'd end up needing lots of powerful devices: a fast tablet, a laptop beefy enough to game on, another lightweight portable laptop, a laptop that integrates well with work, and a whole bunch of others. Since the services at home had already been gradually virtualized and consolidated via VMs, and after introducing Docker and WireGuard the boundary between home and outside grew increasingly blurry—from the Windows P2P box on a VM starting 10 years ago to Guacamole + Manjaro not long ago—I've really been heading down the path of cloudifying my systems so the client device goes back to truly being a thin console that doesn't need high speed or high performance (though a decent NIC is still needed). Yet the most original and important function of a PC/laptop for me—Gaming—had still never been integrated... This test confirmed that as long as network conditions allow, even Gaming can be remoted along with everything else. Still, due to power consumption and other factors, I wouldn't recommend cramming it into a VM right from the start (even with PCI passthrough); leaving it powered on burning electricity when you're not gaming is just too wasteful.

The importance of Wake on Lan To put it bluntly, it's about saving power... Honestly, if you don't care about electricity bills or the fate of polar bears, you could leave your Gaming Server running 24/7... Auto Login This is actually really important because of Windows' quirks: if you don't actually log in after booting, Nvidia Shield won't start, so you won't be able to connect. And if you connect via RDP, it'll conflict and RDP doesn't actually log into the local desktop session... So without auto-login you'd need a console you can connect to—something like VNC or DWService (and you'll also need it when typing a PIN to pair a device, unless you just walk over to the machine locally, set it up, and leave). MSTSC.EXE You need to add this into Shield to launch directly as a substitute for Steam's Big Picture mode, otherwise you'll have to get a Fake HDMI dongle or actually plug in a monitor (mentioned in LLT). This is another Windows quirk... but adding MSTSC.EXE solves that problem (though it also turns it into a remote desktop where controllers aren't convenient for direct control).

Moonlight really is quite smooth—when the network is solid, it doesn't feel much different from playing locally, though when the network is bad it stutters badly... Also, as long as your network allows it, it's best not to set the streaming resolution lower than what the game itself is running at... because then it has to compress it down even further before sending it out... which actually introduces more latency.

Actually, the fundamentals of automated media tracking are all the same, just that it seemed some people needed a Windows-based setup so I wrote this earlier. Though compared to Windows-based setups, they probably prefer the HDD sneaker-net approach...
sleele's Blog

Regardless of which platform you use, it's mainly achieved by having the following tools divide up the work: jackett - Responsible for searching on Indexers and sending the results back. sonarr - This is the core component. After subscribing to the TV shows you want via TVDB, it sends commands to Jackett to look for torrents, then passes the found info to the downloader to download, and finally renames and organizes the downloaded files neatly (to match Emby's formatting requirements). radarr - Basically has the same functionality as sonarr, except this one specializes in movies. So just as it's recommended to run separate sonarr instances for TV shows and anime, for movies you run another radarr instance. qBittorrent - Basically a BitTorrent downloader; used mainly because sonarr can control its downloads directly through its WebUI interface. Emby - This one is actually optional; its real purpose is just to give your media library a pretty UI so any device can watch by account. Simply put, having it just makes things look a bit more high-end. Chinesesubfinder - A tool that automatically finds Chinese subtitles for you.

Since it automatically downloads to fill up your media library, there are mainly two things to satisfy: Plenty of storage space - Whether it's storage for the media library or temporary space for BT downloads, both eat up a lot of disk space. Especially for BT temp storage, if possible it's best to use a disposable HDD you don't mind wearing out to extend the lifespan of your media library drives. A host that can stay powered on long-term - This is also why most tutorials say to use NAS + Docker; after all, a NAS is definitely running 24/7, making it the best fit for this.

Once configured, you just add the TV shows or movies you want to subscribe to in the Sonarr/Radarr interface and leave it alone. Whatever is available on the Indexers will be automatically queued in the downloader, then you wait for it to finish downloading, it'll automatically rename the files, wait a bit more and it'll find and place the subtitles on its own, and then you'll see it show up on your Emby.

The biggest difference is that everything else on the Blog is installed via Docker. If you want to run this on Windows, you'll have to download the Windows versions of these tools (I've basically only used the Docker method myself, though I've confirmed all of these programs provide Windows builds, so there shouldn't be any issue). jackett sonarr radarr qBittorrent emby - Make sure it's the emby server edition Chinesesubfinder
documents.s: Differences from the Rest of the Blog

documents.t: I think Sleele's Blog explains it in great detail, so I won't repeat it. At most, in the next section I'll mention a few caveats I ran into during setup.

Profile​ In sonarr/radarr's profile settings, you define how high of a video resolution to grab. All I can say here is don't get greedy. At first I set it to maximum 4K quality, and a single movie turned out to be 70GB. Unless you have ridiculously huge storage, stay within your means—generally setting it around 1080p webrip puts a movie at roughly 2~5GB. indexer​ Generally I use RARBG for US TV shows and movies, and whatever else depending on mood. For anime I use DMHY, though friends in mainland China should double-check whether these indexers are blocked by the firewall—if so, remember to route the machine that Jackett connects from through a proxy/VPN. Manual Downloads​ I basically download anime manually, and Chinese dramas too (since these tools have weaker support for both). For manually downloaded files, just put them under the show/movie's main folder defined in sonarr/radarr and then use their manual import feature to import and organize them, and you're all set. Other​ The various components mentioned above can actually be split to run on separate independent machines, just remember that /download and /media must be directly controllable by sonarr/radarr. Beyond that, I suggest you give it a try first and come back to discuss if you run into any issues (even using TeamViewer to help troubleshoot is totally fine).

Actually, I haven't even reached Chapter 2 yet—after all, I only get to play in short bursts at night after the kids fall asleep, connecting to my GL-73 via Moonlight. Still, you can tell this installment feels much more like a complete game compared to the previous Pathfinder: Kingmaker. As for the story so far, even though it's a classic heroic tale, it's relatively dark... feels pretty great.

It's actually very useful, though it still has the following issues: Insufficient frame smoothness Needs MSTSC.EXE to simulate a desktop to work properly Colors sometimes look weird and require reconnecting First, regarding the frame smoothness issue: my test environment uses a 1Gb wired home network, configured at around 20M bitrate with 1080p 30fps, yet it still feels stuttery at times... Not sure where the bottleneck is. Next is desktop simulation: this is mainly because Steam Big Picture isn't very smooth, so I have to launch it this way. Honestly, I could also just launch the game directly, but since I need to do desktop tasks like browsing Nexus Mods, using the desktop directly is still more convenient (maybe in the future if I really stream from a TV box, I'll handle it differently). After listing the issues, I still have to praise it: even with Intel integrated graphics, it plays smoothly... (So far in testing, only VMs on ESXi can't run smoothly, because they lack basic VP9 or HEVC support...)

Okay, I admit the real reason my progress is so slow is that I keep restarting and heavily modding the game.... The mod selection isn't as rich as Kingmaker yet (though most of the essential ones are already out). However, there is something I already modded back in my Kingmaker days—making a follower with a mercenary's appearance (basically treating a humanoid as an animal companion). Because I wanted to self-host a Mail Server without touching my home server, I tested Traefik + V2ray... The results were pretty good.

This has probably been explained in many places already: Traefik is a great tool that automatically relies on Label definitions in Docker-compose.yml to automatically generate the corresponding Virtual Host for each container.

NPM is ultimately just a proxy—you still have to expose/map the container ports yourself. NPM's SSL certificates are stored in /etc/letscrypt just like Certbot, whereas Traefik stores them directly inside ACME.json in a different format. NPM is more intuitive to operate, while Traefik requires understanding Docker-compose.yml label definitions.

Honestly, it's quite nice. You don't need to define ports or anything like that—basically you just define your Hostname in docker-compose.yml and it automatically generates everything. It's very suitable for people who want a fully automated migration. Although there are also features like load balancing, I don't need them yet, so....
When using Traefik, you basically don't use your main domain directly; instead, you isolate every container by assigning subdomains.

A couple of days ago, my long-uncontacted master brought bad news: "G Suite is going to start charging money, run while you can~" For someone like me who has tons of accounts and bindings tied to the email address my master gave me, this was a bolt from the blue....
documents.s: The Tragedy Stemming from G Suite Going Paid~~

documents.t: Even though I have lots of bindings, the ones with the biggest stakes—banks—were actually the easiest to update (after all, those are tied to a natural person, so as long as the country doesn't change my national ID number, I'm not screwed). Rented VPS accounts are all pretty troublesome, though most of the servers won't be renewed anyway so it's not actually that bad (actually I just forgot to change those...), except....

I basically finished changing the account so I can bind a different email address, but in the process I messed up a huge bunch of corresponding SSL keys. The auto-update SSL key feature really is a double-edged sword—the moment DNS settings weren't configured properly, the domain's corresponding SSL key broke.... I have to wait anywhere from a week to three months for it to be released before I can use it again... =_=!! On top of that, I happened to discover that domains with the proxy feature enabled can't have too many layers or things break... Adding this to my to-do list for now.
This one is a tragedy that cannot be changed... Looks like I can only keep using it as long as I never forget the password.....
As an alternative, the only one I've found so far is this—an email service that supports custom domains, with up to 5 free mailboxes.... Who knows how long "free" will actually stay free though....

Anyway, while there's still a free option available, I'll use it first. If it really stops working, I'll just have to host my own Mail Server. Good thing setting one up with Docker nowadays is super convenient—as long as you have a server, that is....

Since it's a company computer, I had been holding back from messing around too much, thinking I'd just make do with WSL2+WSLg and not push my luck (though honestly that was already pushing it pretty far). But last weekend, when my itchy fingers decided to tidy up the ManjaroWSL instance I was using, I realized I couldn't reproduce that fully functional WSL setup I had just wiped out... and so I said bye-bye to WSL.
Calling it a "solution" sounds a bit heavy—it's really just a Manjaro KDE guest in VirtualBox @ Windows 10 host.

Actually, before settling on the final setup, I hesitated a lot between VirtualBox and VMware Workstation Player... To be honest, if it weren't a company machine where I had to be careful about licensing, I would have gone straight for VMware Workstation Pro.. Why didn't I pick QEMU? Well.... the answer is dead simple: I assumed performance on a Windows host would be terrible, so I skipped it without even testing.... In the end, VMware Player's features were just too bare-bones—it doesn't even have auto-resize.... so I reluctantly gave up on it.

Honestly I only have myself to blame for being stupid here... When removing WSL I was still half-hearted about it, so Hyper-V related components weren't cleanly uninstalled, and I ran into almost every weird symptom you'd normally see over a whole month: Like the guest OS randomly freezing, Linux failing to boot with multiple cores, or being super slow even when it worked.... In the end, turning off Windows's Virtual Machine Platform fixed everything... zero bullshit issues after that.

We're really lucky to live in this era—none of that manual post-install base tuning is needed anymore, everything comes preconfigured out of the box... Just remove what you don't want, install what you need, and you're ready to roll...

Even though everything looks great, I still have to complain about that Guest/Host shared folder feature. I guess it's not that they didn't want to make it good, there must be real limitations, because in short, if I put my Git repo inside that shared folder, all kinds of bizarre issues happen: git clone fails mysteriously, weird files under .git get locked by the host and can't be removed... or npm install fails because symlinks fail... Completely shattered my fancy dream of doing Git & Hexo on Linux while editing in Windows; now I just have to be good and do all of that inside Linux...
Need to test whether a multi-monitor setup can run one full-screen OS per monitor (if that works, it'd actually be pretty awesome).

Windows is best left for gaming (and work).... WSL, Microsoft's attempt at integrating Linux, really feels like a crippled piece of cannon fodder—can't run anything depending on systemd (I tried genie systemd and it was pretty awful too), plus resolv.conf has its own set of issues. In an era where Linux increasingly depends on systemd, I can only describe WSL as tasteless yet hard to throw away. And as for that flashy-looking WSLg—it's not terrible, but it's basically just VcXsrv wrapped in a Microsoft skin without any special Microsoft black magic...

Lately I've been tirelessly studious(bored out of my mind), so I picked Ansible back up again to study it after having touched it briefly and given up before.

As written in My Wiki (Updated 2026-11-27: Kiwi Wiki, Ansible entries are currently being organized), this is a handy server management tool from Red Hat. Using Python + SSH, it can run playbooks or commands from the management node on the client side to control and manage clients. Its biggest advantage is having many modules to verify client state (for example, whether a certain package is installed, etc.) in order to achieve configuration management across clients.

Basically, to connect smoothly you need to pair it with an SSH private key that doesn't require entering a passphrase each time. Execution speed isn't as fast as running a script directly. Unless there is a large amount of repetitive configuration, it won't be faster or easier to use than a general-purpose shell script.

Basically, you use inventory to manage the target hosts and action-definition.yml to define automated actions. This action-definition.yml can be a top-level playbook, the main tasks inside a role, or another action-definition.yml pulled into tasks via inculde_tasks. That way, when writing, you can build standalone objects piece by piece and then tie them all together in a top-level playbook with variables and conditionals—eventually achieving a generic server management framework (at which point you can go back to inventory to define different groups doing different things).

Halfway through writing this, I realized that for configuring servers, running a script is still much easier and more pleasant, and easier to modify too. However, for state management, this is way more convenient than scripts....

I've long had the habit of using calibre + the kindle app to read e-books freely provided by kind souls(freeloaded). A while ago, Amazon announced that the long-standing mobi format was being phased out in favor of epub...

I've always used calibre-web to manage(show off) the e-books I have on hand. After checking, thankfully the newer version supports this feature. So I happily swapped out the image... (Besides, the converter bundled with the image I used before isn't needed under the new rules anyway, and I never even used it back in the old version...

version: '3' services: calibre-web: image: lscr.io/linuxserver/calibre-web:latest container_name: calibre-web environment: - PUID=1000 - USE_CONFIG_DIR=true - OAUTHLIB_RELAX_TOKEN_SCOPE=1 - DOCKER_MODS=linuxserver/calibre-web:calibre volumes: - /Books/lib/location:/books - /var/lib/docker/volumes/calibre/config:/config labels: traefik.enable: true traefik.http.routers.calibre-web.rule: Host(`$Your_Domain`) traefik.http.routers.calibre-web.tls: true traefik.http.routers.calibre-web.tls.certresolver: myresolver restart: unless-stopped Yep, I switched to the more frequently updated image from linuxserver.io.
Only one format shows up for me because I already cleared out all the mobi files; otherwise there would be a dropdown menu to pick from.

Honestly, not needing two formats is great. Previously I had to convert downloaded books using desktop calibre and upload both formats to the server, taking up nearly double the storage.. Now it saves both effort and disk space. Killing two birds with one stone—very nice.
Actually, I don't really know what the difference is between mobi and epub... Still, unifying on a single format is definitely more convenient....

info This article was automatically translated by Google "Gemini". The author does not guarantee its accuracy or wording. info This article is reposted from the old blog archive. After playing around with Ansible for a few days, I have a few thoughts regarding personal use.

Honestly, Ansible really is a powerful tool, and it has a huge community quietly contributing behind it, so there are tons of playbook examples on GitHub you can reference and borrow from. Being able to test out my setup smoothly is really thanks to these two references: Ansible tutorial video series by Learn Linux TV This series explains things in great detail; anyone interested in Ansible should watch it first. GitHub - PauloPortugal/manjaro-playbook: Manjaro/Arch Linux Ansible provision playbook Since my main desktop is Manjaro, this repo was super helpful for me.

Even though Ansible is powerful and makes everything look awesome, it still has these limitations (for me): There is no interactive manual input during execution—everything has to be written out in advance. If you host it on a public Git server like GitHub, security concerns come up. Behavioral differences are defined via Host Vars, while non-repetitive actions are controlled by separate playbook sections. Combined with the point above, it doesn't feel great for initial server setup right after installation. It operates over an SSH account, so similarly, on a freshly installed machine without an account and corresponding SSH key set up yet, you can't use it right away.

Handle general initial setup through a shell script, keeping interactive prompt options so the script stays versatile. Paired with scripts, use Ansible mainly for highly repetitive, homogeneous tasks—for example, keeping all servers updated in sync, and version-controlling config files across all servers through Ansible (since Ansible is typically used alongside a Git server). Use Ansible to automatically provision environments that require complex setup—such as multiple desktops, or simplifying the work when reinstalling a desktop (while a script can do this too, scripts have a harder time managing version control for individual config files).

Taking a closer look at what I'm currently working on, aside from machines that aren't on the internal network where ansible comes in handy, pretty much everything else can already be handled with an internal Git server + shell script (to some extent, even the rsync + shell script approach I originally wanted would have been enough....).

Strictly speaking, this is the thing really worth writing about. It's basically an expanded version of the Arch Linux Automatic Install Script I wrote before, aiming to cram in all the Unix-like OSes I use myself. Currently (planned) scope covered: Manjaro Linux with Desktop for Console and VNC/RDP server KDE (90% complete) Xfce (0% complete) Gnome (0% complete) - considering whether to drop this Cinnamon (0% complete) Fedora Linux with Desktop for Console and VNC/RDP server (0%) Linux Mint with Desktop for Console and VNC/RDP server (0%) - considering whether to keep Arch Linux (0%) Photon OS (0%) FreeBSD (0%)

Basically, it's about writing an auto-detection script first that routes to the corresponding child script for configuration or installation. That diagram roughly captures the logic above. Right now the progress is basically that I've finished writing that initial selector script, and the core Manjaro part (mainly KDE) is done. The other DE sections will need fine-tuning after I actually install those editions.
This is probably the feature I used most while writing the script recently.. definitely spent quite some time studying how to write the conditions.

I introduced this feature pretty late in the process, and it's awesome... Basically, just like in other programming languages, you can split out modules you've already written (or highly repetitive code) into separate files and load them using source. Combined with function features I learned later, you can load everything first and only call the function when needed, and even pass additional arguments when calling it.

This started out as a fancier way to write scripts—originally intended for cosmetic stuff like banners or menus—but later I found you can load all kinds of random things through functions... so I started going wild with it....

The biggest discovery is that these two things can actually coexist and run together.... just install what needs to be installed and you're good to go.... In a Manjaro environment, you need tigervnc for the VNC server and xrdp for the RDP server. One caveat though: when connecting to xrdp, you must not pre-fill the username by default—it'll cause issues. You need to go in blank and type it afterward.

Previously I used Manjaro XFCE for VNC and Manjaro KDE for console. However, today I found GNOME really doesn't suit my taste, so I took a cue from Linux Mint and tried Cinnamon and found it's actually pretty okay—especially since you can back up the entire DE's settings with dconf dump /org/cinnamon > file.name... Maybe later I'll try switching my main DE from KDE over to Cinnamon, though since Manjaro Cinnamon isn't an Official edition, its Chinese localization and performance tuning aren't super polished... there's a good chance it'll take a lot of time to fine-tune....

I've actually accumulated quite a bit of material to write about during this period... but honestly out of sheer laziness I simplified it again and again... Once it's finished later, I'll break it apart and write it into the Wiki.

Back around the KDE 3.x era, I used it once because it looked pretty, and from then on I had a long-standing stereotype: KDE is a very resource-heavy desktop... Because back then I remember comparing it to Windows Vista/7... Indeed, KDE with all visual effects turned on was a very heavy DE.

The reason I'm bringing up Manjaro XFCE is that when I started seriously using a Linux Desktop, I started with Manjaro XFCE.. At first I didn't dare think about using the KDE Edition because I was afraid my VM couldn't handle it. Only later, when I had a physical machine capable of running it and wanted a prettier look... did I give the KDE edition a try.

Honestly, I was mentally prepared for the machine to run slower, only to find there didn't seem to be any difference... Though in terms of flashiness it doesn't look quite as wildly imaginative as GNOME (yes, KDE is a sensible, down-to-earth homemaker... ).

This goes back to my VNC machine. I switched through a few DEs (initially because I thought XFCE wasn't pretty enough) and found that every single one I switched to felt heavy... On top of that, xrdp-related configs mysteriously refused to run properly on XFCE (probably just because I hadn't written the config file right), plus Manjaro doesn't make installing lxqt very convenient... (Now that Manjaro Architect isn't supported by default anymore, it's pretty hard to install... non-prepackaged desktop environments.)

I love KDE... even though GNOME looks prettier and dresses up nicer. I love KDE... even though backing up desktop settings means having to cp a pile of files that look messy, with no dconf available. GNOME is a flashy, seductive siren.. Sure, it's glamorous and catches the eye, but KDE is the one you can actually settle down and live a good life with. (The above remarks represent personal impressions only, with no intention to mislead or disparage GNOME enthusiasts...)

Project URL - GitHub - 89luca89/distrobox Intro page - Distrobox: Try Multiple Linux Distributions via the Terminal Put simply, it uses Docker or Podman to spin up another Linux distribution and export apps from inside it to run on the host outside.
I personally tested it on Fedora 36 KDE Plasma Edition (unfortunately I deleted the entire VM without taking screenshots). It does work, though there are a few quirks:
Basically, whatever you're running on the host outside is what gets used inside. So... when I was on Wayland outside, ulauncher inside acted super weird...
Since it's built on docker/podman... how could the kernel possibly be different??

All that said, it's very likely I just haven't figured out the best way to use it yet. Even just having exported programs pick up external config files is already great—in fact, I'm not even sure why that machine had my Brave profile without Brave installed, yet when Brave launched from inside the container it actually loaded the host's config... awesome! (Though ulauncher died beyond repair.) Here are the basic commands: Out/In distrobox command usage Example Manual Link outside distrobox create -n name -i Docker image Create a distrobox container distrobox create -n Archlinux -i Archlinux Distrobox-create outside distrobox enter <name> into named container distrobox enter Archlinux Distrobox-enter outside distrobox list list all containers distrobox list Distrobox-llist outside distrobox rm <name> delete container distrobox rm Archlinux Distrobox-rm Outside distrobox upgrade <name> upgrade container distrobox upgrade Archlinux Distrobox-upgrade Inside distrobox-export -a <app Name> -ep <path to outside> export apps installed inside container to outside to use distrobox-export -a Brave -ep ~/.local/bin Distrobox-export

In all my examples, I used distrobox to spin up an Archlinux container and abuse the AUR. The main reason is that there's basically no need to run Fedora or Debian/Ubuntu on top of an Arch-based distro (apart from updates occasionally breaking things, Arch's software availability pretty much sweeps everything else...). There is one awkward catch though—rather than saying I'm already shaped like Archlinux, it's more accurate to say I'm shaped like Manjaro... Unfortunately manjaro fails to deliver—its official Docker image is terrible... nowhere near as good as Archlinux's...

I've been trying Fedora lately and it really does look like an awesome base OS—paired with the ability to install from the AUR, it would be practically unbeatable (if things were actually as simple as a fool like me imagines, anyway). Still, looking at its desktop style and customization options... I'll probably stay in the shape of Manjaro for quite a long time yet....

Though in practice it isn't actually that scary... It's mainly just because connecting to it requires a dedicated browser that it feels extra sneaky.... However, the desktop version of Brave that I use regularly actually has built-in Tor browsing... you just need to open a Private Window with Tor.... Personally, I'm not really a fan of tools that require installing extra software like that.... Telegram Bot​ Honestly this really caught me by surprise... it's awesome.... Just add its bot (@firstlibrarybot) in your Telegram and link your account (instructions are right on its registration page, just follow along). I picked up a Steam Deck—my first real toy in a long time since having kids... As for why it took me so long to write about it, all I can say is that it's just that awesome.... It let me experience a thrill I hadn't enjoyed in a long time — the satisfaction of actually beating a game.

Taking advantage of KOMODO's Asian distribution, I also bought a 512GB Steam Deck (even though I already have a 2230 1TB SSD on hand, I wasn't planning on modding it myself....). I'll skip the unboxing stuff since there are already tons of unboxing articles and videos online, and just share my own thoughts...

Before getting it, I honestly didn't expect to play games on it that often.... I figured I'd mess around with the hardware a bit and then it would end up collecting dust just like my PSP... Turns out I was wrong.... Coinciding with the Steam Winter Sale, I picked up a few games at a discount that were basically collection-tier picks for me: Octopath Traveler and Triangle Strategy.. Starting with these two games, I realized my late nights were completely inseparable from the Steam Deck.... (And as a result, I later bought Tactic Orge Reborn while it was still pricey.)

Valve actually put a lot of care into SteamOS, with many nifty built-in utilities. The few minor drawbacks are basically: The OS is read-only; installing new applications relies on flatpak. Valve's repository stability isn't great (though I haven't run into issues myself—probably an early-days thing). The jump from 3.0 --> 3.3.4 had huge changes. Personally, I think that's partly an Arch-based habit where updates bring big shifts; on the other hand, it shows Valve is actively improving their product. Insufficient battery life. The screen is only 1280x800, shy of 1080p (though on a screen this small, the difference isn't very noticeable). Too big and heavy (personally, it's fine in my own use). There are quite a few pros—or rather, standout traits—as well: Complete UI integration. Sure, a handheld should get this right, but looking at other Windows-based Chinese handhelds makes it feel miles ahead. Ability to lock FPS to reduce power draw; whether you cap it at 40fps makes a huge difference to battery life. Thoughtful tweaks like Night Mode. Desktop Mode is available. Honestly, Desktop Mode feels a bit awkward because casual players just gaming will barely ever need it, yet when you need to set up extra things, it becomes essential (though it's definitely best used with an external keyboard and mouse).

Steam Tinker Launch You basically just install it through ProtonUP-Qt, and it's a god-tier utility. You configure it in Steam's launch options much like Proton. Once set up, it launches this menu before the game starts, allowing you to link a custom program, or check tool -> cheat engine to automatically launch cheat engine after the game starts with the process already attached—you just load the CT file directly. The only slight flaw is that when launching Cheat Engine, the touch input area doesn't quite align with the actual screen display. ProtonUp-Qt An installer utility for Steam Proton and other plugins (like STL). You can install the flatpak version via Discover (or just download the AppImage). If you like, you can also install Proton-GE through it. Proton-GE A custom build of Proton with plenty of extra patches bundled in. Proton GE: How Does It Differ from Proton? (Gaming) | Linux Addicts Emudeck Thanks to the Steam Deck's excellent performance, it's great for running emulators. Emudeck is an all-in-one installer (yes, its job is strictly unified installation; the emulators themselves are still the individual standalone emulators). Out of all these tools, this is the only one I haven't installed yet (because my SD card hasn't arrived, so I don't have the storage space).

If your Steam library is full of mouse-and-keyboard-heavy PC games like AOE or HOI, then the Steam Deck isn't really for you. If you only play ultra-demanding AAA PC games, the Steam Deck isn't for you either. The Steam Deck is made for controller-friendly games with lighter loading demands, and it's ideal for people who only have fragmented pockets of time to game. As for whether you're familiar with or good at Linux, that has no serious bearing on using the device itself—at most, the better you know Linux, the more likely you are to tinker with or break SteamOS settings. Would I recommend the Steam Deck to others?? Honestly, for the same price (or just a tiny bit more), you can get a low-end gaming laptop... and even the lowest-end gaming laptop outperforms the Steam Deck by a mile... You might say, "But it has the dedicated SteamOS, which is awesome!" Well, if you install Manjaro without Game Mode, you can get something 87% similar to SteamOS—not to mention someone released HoloISO that can be installed on regular PC hardware (though I failed to install it in VirtualBox). So there's really no need to buy a Steam Deck just for its OS. After narrowing it down like that, the remaining target audience seems like a bunch of people with more money than sense.... (though I'm broke, so I shouldn't belong in that category). To me, this product is like Microsoft making the low-value Surface lineup just to teach laptop manufacturers how to design and build hardware suited for Windows 8/10 (honestly, running Windows on a Surface really was pretty pleasant—too bad I barely use Windows anymore). Valve has made real software and hardware contributions to Linux Gaming, and hopefully plenty of manufacturers will step up and compete to build even better products down the line.

So here's what happened: one day while I was slacking off at work, I suddenly noticed the storage pool on one of my home NAS boxes had vanished. Looking closer, the PCI-passthrough SATA expansion card had suddenly died...

Although rebooting ESXi would temporarily bring the expansion card back to life before it died again after a while, I acted decisively and immediately ordered a new SATA expansion card (and threw in some other stuff on PChome that cost more than the card itself). Currently still waiting for delivery.

Since I also have an idle Gen8 sitting at home, last night I tried harvesting parts from the Gen8 to see if I could fix it. Long story short, while it's also a 4-port card and the card itself works, its 1-to-4 breakout cable has issues (probably), so out of four drives it could only detect three.... still a fail in the end..
documents.s: Emergency Response II - The Idle Gen8

documents.t: Then I turned my attention to the active Gen8, thinking the idle card still had at least two working ports so swapping them might work.... Then I opened up the machine and realized how naive and silly I was... The SATA expansion card in that machine... is a 2-port card.... damn it!! (I really cut corners back then.)
documents.s: Emergency Response III - The Active Gen8

documents.t: What else can I do? Right now I can only shut down all services bound to the dead NAS... unplug power to the HDDs, and wait until the new card arrives at home.
My main NAS went down, and even after frantic troubleshooting I still had to shut it down.. Yet most of my family's reaction was:
Yeah, right, only I use it! I won't bother factoring in whether you guys use it or not when planning the next generation~~~
documents.s: Doesn't matter... we don't really use it anyway, only you do....

documents.t: Later I chatted with my mentor, which shattered quite a few of my existing assumptions: If you haven't bought vMotion, or don't want to switch to Proxmox VE, it's still better to consolidate VMs onto a single machine.. Thinking about it carefully, as long as you beef up the hardware on one VM host, there's really no need to spread ESXi across the other two Gen8s.. Running ESXi with only 16GB RAM is pretty useless anyway... Just use your Gen8 as a pure NAS.. That's actually true, because a Gen8 only has one PCIe slot, and eventually it'll need a 10Gb NIC.... I originally wanted to do iSCSI and whatnot, but switching back to a pure NAS means the OS basically just needs a USB stick, leaving all the hardware resources for the NAS. Ditch Raidz1 and just use ZFS mirror (formerly RAID 1) instead Right now HDD prices per GB for anything under 8TB are basically dirt cheap/not worth it, so the recommendation is to go straight for 16TB HDDs x2. Currently two 16TB drives cost around 19k NTD, so in a 4-bay machine you can gradually build two 16TB pools. Given my current situation and budget, this seems like the better option—after all, just rebuilding the 10Gb backbone, Wi-Fi, and buying a base server is already super expensive (almost 100k NTD). Trying to go all-in all at once right now would be stretching way too thin. As a commercial distribution (and one that charges money), using licensing and withholding direct access to source code to protect its commercial value is completely normal. SUSE's commercial edition (SLES) doesn't hand out Source code for direct downstream rebuilds either. Moreover, both of them have their own upstream open source editions: Red Hat SUSE Open Source Upstream Fedora / CentOS stream OpenSuSE Commercial Edition Red Hat Enterprise Linux SUSE Linux Enterprise The ones getting killed off right now are RHEL downstream clones. Thinking about it, it makes sense—the company developing it needs to make money, and developers need to put food on the table. As for all the "they broke promises they made before the company took off" drama, well—people get divorced even after getting married, and vows sworn before the gods get ignored all the time... As for SUSE and Oracle jumping out right now to ride the wave, I think they're mostly seizing the opportunity to kick Red Hat while the sentiment is hot, seeing if public opinion can sway some frustrated Red Hat users into switching to their own paid distros. Let's grab some popcorn and watch how this plays out.
Recently, NixOS suddenly blew up among Linux YouTubers for some reason, so I hopped on the bandwagon and gave it a try too.

Honestly, the moment I touched it, the shock was pretty similar to the first time I installed Gentoo, and my takeaway was pretty much the same—basically: Whoa~ this thing's special features are so cool~ I can do this, and I can do that too~~ Then, after cooling down and thinking about it: sure, you can use it, though it's quite a hassle, and you don't really have to use it either. There's no compelling reason that makes it strictly indispensable...

NixOS is basically a dedicated OS owned by a package manager... (a bit like Prussia in a certain era—other countries have an army, while Prussia was an army that had a country). The core of NixOS is the Nix package manager, so it can configure the entire system using a single (or multiple importable) .nix configuration file (well, in theory—user configs in ~/.config still behave like usual). And every time you update, add, or remove a package, it rebuilds system symlinks so each version is isolated, and you can even spin up separate profile dev environments without touching the host system. Sounds super cool and awesome, right?

Something that sounds this flashy is bound to have corresponding drawbacks that haven't been solved (equivalent exchange, after all). After playing around with it briefly, I noticed: To make permanent system changes, you have to edit /etc/nixos/configure.nix and run nixos-rebuild switch to update the whole system generation. The system itself has major release versions and channels. And to fully achieve the "one config file to rule them all" ideal, they introduced something called flake... making it even more convoluted. Honestly, going rolling-release from the start would have been simpler... Huge disk space requirements. While you can use nix-garbage-collection to delete generations outside a certain range, doing so kinda defeats the whole point of the rollback features its fans brag about—if you wipe all your snapshots, what are you supposed to roll back to??

It's pretty great for tinkering, or if you have a huge fleet of identical machines to deploy and manage—assuming you don't constantly tweak the system, or you have a dedicated test machine to dial in the config before applying it everywhere. As a daily-driver desktop OS, it's probably not ideal... Unless you really need multiple dev environments coexisting on one system without interfering with each other and you also deeply despise container tech like Docker...

Amazed by Archinstall, I'm considering switching from Manjaro to Archlinux. Let's start with my WSL and a VM in VirtualBox...
Link - GitHub - yuk7/ArchWSL Online Manual - How to Setup | ArchWSL official documentation

You need to initialize archlinux-keyring first to avoid issues: [root@wsl]$ pacman-key --init [root@wsl]$ pacman-key --populate [root@wsl]$ pacman -Sy archlinux-keyring [root@wsl]$ pacman -Syyu You need to create a regular user account (otherwise some GUI apps will have issues): # 定義wheel群組的User都可以sudo [root@wsl]$ echo "%wheel ALL=(ALL) ALL" > /etc/sudoers.d/wheel # 建立一個{username}帳號,並且屬於wheel群組 [root@wsl]$ useradd -m -G wheel -s /bin/bash `{username}` You need to set {username} as the default user—this operation must be done outside WSL: [User@Windows]$ Arch.exe config --default-user `{username}`

Basically you just boot from the ISO, pick your options in archinstall, and install directly. From testing it myself, if you need a desktop you can just choose its desktop profile. Looking at my own choice of KDE: It installs both Xorg & Wayland by default, and you can choose between them at the SDDM login screen. Currently Wayland support still isn't great—even ArchWiki recommends sticking with Xorg for now.

Recommended essential packages are as follows: Pkg Name Description git Aside from regular Git usage, installing AUR packages before yay is set up (including installing yay itself) relies on it. base-devel This is actually a package group containing compilers and related tools, needed if you compile packages yourself. virtualbox-guest-utils VirtualBox guest tools including special drivers, equivalent to VMware Tools. yay Anyone using an Arch-based distro knows what this is. Manjaro lets you install it directly with pacman, while on Arch you have to install it using the method below.
# 不能用root [user@archlinux]$ git clone https://aur.archlinux.org/yay-git.git [user@archlinux]$ cd yay-git [user@archlinux]$ makepkg -si

systemd services need to be enabled manually: systemd-resolved.service This is the systemd version of resolvconf, mainly needed by wireguard. systemctl enable --now systemd-resolved.service vboxservice.service This automatically loads components from virtualbox-guest-utils. systemctl enable --now vboxservice.service

From what I've seen so far, as long as you copy over some customization configs from Manjaro (or another distro you like, such as zsh-theme-powerlevel10k settings), Archlinux won't look plain at all. Installation has also become super easy. In daily use it's Arch-based, pretty much no different (compared to Manjaro). I'll probably need to observe it for a while longer before making a clearer comparison of pros and cons.

A little while ago I finally finished renovating and moving into my new place. Staying true to the spirit of hardware lifecycle upgrades(chasing shiny new toys), I replaced almost all the networking gear and servers at the new house, so naturally it's time to jot down some notes on the hardware swaps and setup changes.

ASUS TS110-E14 This is now my main ESXi Server, currently running the following VMs: FreeBSD 14-release x1: Gateway + Firewall Archlinux x1: DHCPd + DNS + UniFi Network Application PhotonOS 5 x3: Docker hosts for Containers XigmaNAS 13 With PCI passthrough x2: Server Backup and Temp HPE MicroServer Gen8 XigmaNAS 13: Main NAS for Media Center UniFi Switch Enterprise 8 PoE Main Switch Access Point U6 In-Wall Access Point U6 Pro (in transit)

Honestly, the main motivation here was just showing off... I figured I'd upgrade my new home's IT infrastructure to prosumer/semi-enterprise grade, and being able to push settings to APs from a single central controller seemed much more convenient. Plus I got burned by the TP-Link Deco X75 I bought for my parents' place earlier—a pricey Mesh AP that didn't even have a whitelist mode for MAC Address filtering... Originally I thought the apartment wasn't big so a single U6 In-Wall would cover everything, but unfortunately the placement wasn't great and the signal behind the TV wall ended up weak. So I bought a U6 Pro to fill in the dead zone.

This is an older box—I used to have two of them, but my parents' ASUS Server died (after ~10 years, it definitely earned its keep), so I had to move one back there to serve as their NAS. The remaining one got a 10GbE NIC + 16TB HDD x4 upgrade, turning it into a 48TB usable raidz1 NAS.
No surprises here—this is the ESXi Server, though setting up the foundational network environment was still quite a headache.

Sticking with old habits, I still went with the tried-and-true FreeBSD + pf + ipfw for the gateway. Network Architecture​ Initially I wanted to put everything on a single Class C subnet to keep things simple (which meant no DMZ isolation, though DMZ was basically half-baked in my hands anyway). Turns out I hit a NAT Loopback issue where internal hosts couldn't access my external-facing services, so I had to revert back to the original WAN+LAN+DMZ layout—after tweaking the pf rules, I fixed it by referring to this guide: # Nat Loopback no nat on $int_if proto tcp from $int_if to $int_net rdr on $int_if proto tcp from $int_net to $ext_ip port { 25, 165, 993 } -> 192.168.0.2 nat on $int_if proto tcp from $int_net to 192.168.0.2 port { 25, 165, 993 } -> $int_if So in the end, I still managed to consolidate everything back onto a single Class C subnet.

This turned out to be part of the big landmine of this build. My original plan was to just spin up both dnsmasq and UniFi Network Application in Docker containers and call it a day, and well... Dnsmasq​ It ran in Docker, sure, but because of IP subnetting and me not digging carefully into network mapping, the service appeared to be up while none of the clients could actually get DHCP or DNS working properly. After fighting with it forever, moving dnsmasq onto a standalone VM made everything work immediately without changing a single thing... UniFi Network Application​ This one was even more infuriating. Either the MongoDB version specified in the docs threw issues, or once MongoDB was sorted out, the controller refused to serve the web UI properly due to Java version mismatches... After wading through walls of documentation, I discovered that on Archlinux with yay installed, all you need is: yay -S unifi And then just make sure the JRE version is 17... One single command took care of everything...

Given the storage needs of the Docker backend and system backups, I mounted a ZFS Mirror NAS via NFS to the various servers for basic backups. Later on, I'll pair it with a self-hosted Git server for overall internal project management. Also, on my parents' old server I used to attach an HDD directly in ESXi as a TEMP drive for BT downloads and overflow storage, and during this migration I suffered horribly because certain VMs refused to boot without that HDD attached. So this time I mounted the Temp HDD inside XigmaNAS and exported it over NFS instead.

For whatever reason, my existing XigmaNAS VM just wouldn't add the Temp drive, so in the end I had to spin up an extra VM with dedicated PCI Passthrough hardware running a separate XigmaNAS instance solely for exporting Temp storage.
documents.s: XigmaNAS Refusing to Mount the Temp Drive

documents.t: As mentioned earlier, the cursed UniFi-Network-Application wouldn't behave properly in Docker... plus Dnsmasq didn't play nice either, so I ended up spinning up an extra VM.

My brain must have been eaten by something during the interior design phase, because the U6 In-Wall ended up in a terrible spot—facing away from two bedrooms and two bathrooms, leaving weak signal in all of them... So I had to add a U6 Pro, kicking off the UniFi asexual reproduction cycle ahead of schedule...

Living in a new home is wonderful, though the moving process itself is not... Getting new servers and redesigning the architecture is fun(?), whereas emergency-rescuing dying hardware and migrating mountains of data is definitely not... I'll update the wiki with the detailed config changes later on.

There's really nothing special to configure for this. I became irretrievably hooked on it....

Ansible is an automation tool developed by RedHat. Through Python and SSH, it achieves "one control machine rules them all". It's not like I hadn't tried it before, but back then I just thought Ansible was slow, complicated, and hard to understand.... So I messed around with some beginner stuff and gave up. This time, something suddenly clicked in my head, and as I kept writing, it started covering more and more ground.
Here are some references and videos for beginners who want to try using Ansible:
Ansible Community Documentation Ansible Community Documentation (CN) Ansible Authoritative Chinese Guide
Jay from Learn Linux TV offers lots of useful Linux tutorial videos (though mostly focused on the basics). Besides Ansible, you can also browse his other topic playlists.
Previously, I mainly got stuck on two things when using Ansible:

Loops in Ansible almost always go hand-in-hand with variables. If you don't know how to define the "{{ }}" Jinja2 variable syntax, you basically can't use loops. An Ansible playbook without loops becomes bloated—the more machines and repetitive tasks you have, the more verbose and sluggish it runs.
This is also a huge point. Just like with shell script, if you don't know how to use if ..else ..fi to check states, you won't get very far writing a shell script either....

Previously, I already liked Ansible's roles feature—after all, it lets you break down a huge playbook.yml into smaller, easier-to-write roles, reducing the writing burden and enabling reuse. However, roles are static: whatever you write there will definitely be called and executed. When combined with include_task and variable checks, though, you can inspect a node's properties (such as os_family to automatically detect the OS type) and dynamically load the corresponding task.yml. That expands the coverage of a single playbook.yml to almost every machine (especially for someone like me who likes using different distributions for different types of servers/workstations).

Ansible is a tool that's constantly evolving with tons of people diving deep into it, so there are still quite a few complex conditional checks and loop patterns I don't really understand (yeah... the kind where I don't even understand someone else's example...). So the playbook.yml I'm writing right now still looks pretty rough, and its efficiency isn't optimized to the max, though at least it works.... Then again, my shell script writing level is about the same... so I guess they're six of one, half a dozen of the other...

Right now, my domain's email uses Zoho's service, though honestly I don't have the greatest impression of it... Cloudflare actually lets you alias domain emails to Gmail; after some setup, besides receiving mail, you can also send mail using your own domain: HalisUnreal's Blog Configuring a Custom Domain Email on Gmail Using Cloudflare Sending and Receiving Custom Domain Email with Cloudflare + Gmail Later on, I might still consider migrating email too just to cut down on having too many service platforms. Anyway, since it can map to any Gmail account, I can just register a random Gmail account and map it there. That makes it easy to set up email addresses for family members as well.
Money is hard to earn, so it is more practical to spend a little effort organizing these essential expenses and keeping them to a minimum.

After updating qemu, the default WSL kernel turned out to lack TC module support, which set me down the path of no return: compiling my own Linux kernel...

Actually, the story is pretty much what the preface already said (so why am I still rambling?). A few extra details are below: My WSL runs on my company Windows machine, and my Local Administrator privileges were revoked. Plus, since I'm not in an R&D department, getting them back is basically hopeless, meaning I can't update the WSL version via wsl --update. Even if I could run wsl --update, I checked the WSL-Kernel source on GitHub and the default config doesn't have TC or QoS kernel support anyway... (Wait, so my first point above... yeah, it was purely complaining about having no permissions...) The WSL kernel doesn't support dynamically loading modules (in other words, the modporbe command is completely useless in WSL...), so there's no way to load TC/QoS dynamically. So... this old guy had no choice but to configure and compile the kernel himself to satisfy his needs.
I'll put those in my Wiki (Updated 2026-11-27: WSL Custom Kernel)—feel free to check it out if you're interested.

A long, long time ago, back when I used Gentoo, I configured and compiled a Linux kernel (how could you use Gentoo without doing it yourself??), but after that I never bothered doing it manually again (just like long, long ago when I was diligent enough to configure and compile my own FreeBSD kernel, whereas now I just use GENERIC). Honestly, this hands-on attempt looked intimidating at first, though in practice it wasn't bad at all... You just have to get used to the fact that for a WSL kernel, everything is either enabled or disabled—anything you want to use has to be built-in rather than built as a module. This is basically the same as early FreeBSD kernels, and conceptually different from how mainstream Linux kernels are used today. And under that model, the hard part—aside from the specific features you know for sure you need (like TC/QoS for this time, plus wireguard support which I use a lot)—is remembering which modules are essential for WSL itself. That's why every guide you see recommends running: zcat /proc/config.gz > .config or cat /proc/config.gz | gunzip > .config to dump the currently running WSL kernel config as your baseline, and then simply add whatever else you need on top. That approach simplifies away all the parts that would otherwise fry your brain. Finally... once everything is working properly, WSL is still a blast to use—especially when you're slacking off at the office on a company Windows PC you aren't allowed to wipe, WSL really is the salvation of us wage slaves...
