Modern terminals (such as iTerm2, Windows Terminal, Alacritty, and Kitty) support richer 256-color and RGB true color modes: 256-color mode: Foreground: \e[38;5;<0-255>m Background: \e[48;5;<0-255>m Example: echo -e "\e[38;5;208mThis is a nice orange\e[0m" 24-bit True Color (RGB): Foreground: \e[38;2;<R>;<G>;<B>m Background: \e[48;2;<R>;<G>;<B>m Example: echo -e "\e[38;2;255;100;0mCustom RGB coral color\e[0m"

Do not scatter hard-to-read \e[31m sequences throughout your shell scripts. Industry best practice is to define constant variables or wrap helper functions at the top of the script: #!/bin/bash # --- Define color variables --- C_RESET="\033[0m" C_BOLD="\033[1m" C_RED="\033[1;31m" C_GREEN="\033[1;32m" C_YELLOW="\033[1;33m" C_BLUE="\033[1;34m" C_CYAN="\033[1;36m" # --- Logging functions --- log_info() { printf "${C_BLUE}[INFO]${C_RESET} %s
" "$*" } log_success() { printf "${C_GREEN}[SUCCESS]${C_RESET} %s
" "$*" } log_warn() { printf "${C_YELLOW}[WARN]${C_RESET} %s
" "$*" } log_error() { printf "${C_RED}[ERROR]${C_RESET} %s
" "$*" >&2 } # --- Test calls --- log_info "Starting Docker Compose services..." log_warn "Remaining memory is below 512MB" log_success "Nextcloud backup completed successfully" log_error "Unable to connect to MariaDB database"

documents.t: Basic Definition: VAR_NAME="value" # Absolutely no spaces are allowed on either side of the equals sign echo "${VAR_NAME}" # It is recommended to always wrap variables in curly braces ${} to prevent boundary confusion Command Substitution: CURRENT_USER=$(whoami) BACKUP_DATE=$(date +%F) Variable Scope: Declared normally as local variables (restricted to the current process). Declared as environment variables using export VAR_NAME so they can be inherited by forked child processes.

Variable Name Meaning Description Behavior Analysis & Engineer Must-Know Details Practical Example $? Exit code of the last command 0 means execution succeeded; non-zero (e.g., 1, 2, 127, etc.) means execution failed or encountered an anomaly systemctl restart nginx [ $? -eq 0 ] && echo "OK" $$ Process ID (PID) of the current shell process Commonly used in scripts to create unique temporary file names and prevent concurrency conflicts TMP_FILE="/tmp/run_$$.tmp" $! PID of the last background program execution Captures the process ID just sent to the background with &, convenient for subsequent monitoring with wait python3 job.py & JOB_PID=$! $- Flags enabled in the current shell Displays current shell execution options (such as interactive mode flags like h, B, i, etc.) echo "$-" $0 File name or path of the current shell script The command path entered upon execution (such as ./deploy.sh or /opt/deploy.sh) SCRIPT_DIR=$(dirname "$0") $1 ~ $9 Positional Arguments Sequentially receives the first to ninth external parameters passed in (the tenth onward requires ${10}) ./backup.sh /data /mnt/nas # $1=/data, $2=/mnt/nas $# Total number of parameters passed to the script Commonly used at the beginning of scripts to validate whether the parameter count is sufficient [ $# -lt 2 ] && exit 1 $* Collection of all passed parameters (merged string) When wrapped in double quotes "$*", all parameters are concatenated into a single string using $IFS (defaulting to space): "$1 $2 $3" echo "All args: $*" $@ Collection of all passed parameters (independent array) Most commonly used in loops and forwarding. Double quotes "$@" keep each parameter as an independent string: "$1" "$2" "$3" for arg in "$@"; do ... done
documents.s: 2. Special Automatic Variables and Positional Parameters Quick Reference

documents.t: Variable Name Description Typical Use Case $BASH_ENV Path of the configuration file automatically loaded when a non-interactive shell starts Automated CI/CD scheduling environment injection $CDPATH Colon-separated search directory list when using the cd command Quickly switching deep directories $LINENO Code line number currently being executed Log tracking and debugging: echo "Error at line $LINENO" $LINES / $COLUMNS Height (number of rows) and width (number of columns) of the current terminal screen Terminal UI / progress bar width adaptive calculation $PPID Parent Process ID of the current process Checking who called this script $RANDOM Randomly generates an integer between 0 and 32767 Generating random passwords or random ports: PORT=$((10000 + RANDOM % 10000)) $SECONDS Cumulative seconds elapsed since script startup Calculating script elapsed time: echo "Elapsed time: ${SECONDS}s" $SHELL Absolute path of the user's default preferred shell Viewing the default shell (usually /bin/bash) $TMOUT Inactivity auto-logout time (unit: seconds) Security hardening: automatically disconnect terminal connection after specified idle seconds

In shell scripts, directly using unassigned variables can easily lead to unexpected behavior (or even disasters like accidental root directory deletion such as rm -rf /${DIR}). Using Bash's parameter expansion syntax allows you to safely and gracefully set default values or defensive exits: Syntax Format Condition Judgment Handling Behavior Practical Example ${var:-word} var is empty or unset Temporarily uses word as the return value, without changing the content of var itself PORT=${CUSTOM_PORT:-8080} (Defaults to 8080 when unspecified) ${var:=word} var is empty or unset Assigns word to var, then uses the new value ${DATABASE_NAME:=homelab} (Automatically defines and stores in variable when unset) ${var:?word} var is empty or unset Prints the word error message to stderr and immediately forcefully halts and terminates the program DIR=${1:?"Please provide the target directory path!"} (Aborts execution immediately if parameter is missing) ${var:+word} var is set and non-empty Temporarily replaces it with word; returns an empty value if empty (used for existence detection) [ -n "${DEBUG:+x}" ] && echo "Debug on" Tip: If the colon is omitted (e.g., ${var-word}), it triggers only when var is completely unset; adding the colon (${var:-word}) covers both cases where it is unset or set but has an empty string value "". Using the colon syntax is recommended for all daily scripts.
documents.s: 4. Handling Empty and Unset Variables (Parameter Expansion)

documents.t: The read command is used to pause in the terminal and read keyboard input from the user: # Basic usage echo -n "Please enter project name: " read PROJECT_NAME echo "You entered: ${PROJECT_NAME}" # Recommended modern single-line usage (combining -p prompt, -t timeout, -s password hiding) # 1. With prompt string (-p) read -p "Please enter database name: " DB_NAME # 2. Hidden password input (-s, prevents printing password to screen) read -sp "Please enter connection password: " DB_PASSWORD echo "" # Manually add a newline after password input # 3. Automatic timeout skip (-t, e.g., waiting 10 seconds) read -t 10 -p "Confirm to continue execution? (y/N): " CONFIRM CONFIRM=${CONFIRM:-N} # Defaults to N if no input before timeout

documents.t: After storing external command output into a variable, make sure to wrap comparisons defensively: #!/usr/bin/env bash # 1. Capture current executor identity CURRENT_USER=$(whoami) # 2. Safe conditional judgment (recommended [[ ]] structure, best compatibility and features) if [[ "${CURRENT_USER}" == "root" ]]; then echo "Success: Currently executing with root privileges" else echo "Warning: Must execute this script with root privileges (current user is: ${CURRENT_USER})" >&2 exit 1 fi # 3. Check critical path variables (defensive programming to avoid undefined accidental deletion) TARGET_DIR="${1:-}" # Strict validation to avoid rm -rf / if [[ -z "${TARGET_DIR}" ]]; then echo "Error: Cleanup directory not specified!" >&2 exit 1 fi echo "Cleaning up temporary folder: ${TARGET_DIR}..."

documents.s: Bash Loop Flow Control, Case Conditional Branching, and Interactive Menus

documents.t: Inside any loop structure (while, until, for), the primary instructions for controlling execution flow are: Keyword Core Behavior Typical Use Case break Exits the entire loop, immediately executing the line following the loop's done statement User completes menu operations or target file has been found continue Skips the current iteration, skipping remaining code and returning directly to the loop condition check Prompting user upon invalid input and retrying, or skipping temporary files exit Terminates the entire script process immediately, returning a specified exit status code to the parent process (default 0) User actively chooses to exit or an unrecoverable fatal error occurs
documents.s: 1. Core Concepts: Flow Control Jump Keywords

documents.t: For interactive menu scenarios, here is a standardized template featuring prompt strings (read -r -p) and case validation mechanisms: #!/usr/bin/env bash while true; do echo "==================================" echo " HomeLab Operations Management Menu" echo "==================================" echo " a) View Docker container status" echo " b) Restart Nextcloud service" echo " c) Run database backup" echo " q) Exit menu" echo "==================================" # -r prevents backslash escaping, -p displays prompt text read -r -p "Please enter an option [a-c, q]: " CHOICE case "${CHOICE}" in a|A) echo "--> Listing running containers..." docker ps --format "table {{.Names}}\t{{.Status}}\t{{.Ports}}" break # Exit menu after execution ;; b|B) echo "--> Restarting Nextcloud..." docker compose -f /opt/nextcloud/docker-compose.yml restart echo "Restart complete." continue # Return to the beginning of the menu ;; c|C) echo "--> Executing backup task..." /opt/scripts/backup.sh continue ;; q|Q) echo "Exiting program." exit 0 # Terminate script normally ;; *) echo "Error: Invalid option [${CHOICE}], please try again!" >&2 sleep 1 continue ;; esac done echo "Menu exited, proceeding with subsequent automation tasks..." Syntax Details Reminder: case supports multi-value matching: Using the pipe | allows capturing both uppercase and lowercase (e.g., a|A)). Each conditional branch block must end with double semicolons ;;, indicating the end of that branch. *) acts as a wildcard, matching any other characters not previously matched, serving as a default fallback branch.
documents.s: 2. Standard While + Case Interactive Menu Architecture

documents.t: Beyond building menus with case, the following three loops are most commonly used when processing data in daily scripts:
documents.s: 3. Three Classic Bash Loop Syntax Structures

documents.t: Suitable for scenarios with a clearly defined quantity of targets (such as batch inspecting multiple Docker Compose projects): # 1. Iterate over a list STACKS=("nextcloud" "bookstack" "gitea" "wireguard") for stack in "${STACKS[@]}"; do echo "Checking stack: ${stack}..." docker compose -f "/opt/${stack}/docker-compose.yml" ps done # 2. Numeric sequence (C-language style) for ((i=1; i<=5; i++)); do echo "Retry attempt ${i}..." done
documents.s: 3.1 For Loop (Fixed List / Array / Range Iteration)

documents.t: Frequently used for polling service health until a specific state is reached: # Wait for MariaDB container to fully start (Health Check polling) CONTAINER="gitea_db" while ! docker inspect --format='{{.State.Health.Status}}' "${CONTAINER}" 2>/dev/null | grep -q "healthy"; do echo "Waiting for ${CONTAINER} database initialization (checking every 2 seconds)..." sleep 2 done echo "${CONTAINER} is ready, starting main application!"
documents.s: 3.2 While Loop (Execute While Condition is True)

documents.t: When processing configuration files, host lists, or logs, never use for line in $(cat file) (which causes bugs due to space word-splitting). The standard writing practice is to use while IFS= read -r line: # Safely read host IP list line by line and perform ping tests HOSTS_FILE="/opt/network/hosts.txt" if [[ -f "${HOSTS_FILE}" ]]; then while IFS= read -r host || [[ -n "${host}" ]]; do # Skip empty lines and comment lines starting with # [[ -z "${host}" || "${host}" =~ ^# ]] && continue if ping -c 1 -W 1 "${host}" >/dev/null 2>&1; then echo "[OK] ${host} is reachable" else echo "[FAIL] ${host} is unreachable" >&2 fi done < "${HOSTS_FILE}" fi
documents.s: 3.3 Reading Files Line by Line (While Read Mode)

documents.t: If you only need to quickly present a numbered menu for users to pick from, Bash natively provides an extremely concise select structure, which automatically renders numbers and eliminates tedious manual formatting code: #!/usr/bin/env bash PS3="Please select the service number to maintain: " # Define prompt string SERVICES=("Nextcloud" "BookStack" "Gitea" "Exit") select srv in "${SERVICES[@]}"; do case "${srv}" in "Nextcloud") echo "Maintaining Nextcloud..." break ;; "BookStack") echo "Maintaining BookStack..." break ;; "Gitea") echo "Maintaining Gitea..." break ;; "Exit") echo "Program ended." exit 0 ;; *) echo "Invalid input, please enter a number between 1 and 4." ;; esac done
documents.s: 4. Advanced Tip: Built-in Select Menu Syntax
1. Core Implementation: Robust Arrow Key Menu Function (select_option)

documents.t: echo "Use [Up/Down Arrow Keys] to move, [Enter] to confirm selection:" echo MENU_ITEMS=("Start all Docker containers" "Stop Nextcloud service" "Execute database backup" "Exit script") # Call function and capture the selected index CHOICE_INDEX=$(select_option "${MENU_ITEMS[@]}") echo "----------------------------------------" echo "Selected item index: ${CHOICE_INDEX}" echo "Selected item content: ${MENU_ITEMS[CHOICE_INDEX]}" case "${CHOICE_INDEX}" in 0) echo "Starting containers..." ;; 1) echo "Stopping service..." ;; 2) echo "Starting backup execution..." ;; 3) echo "Exiting program."; exit 0 ;; esac Updated 2026-11-27 The select_option above outputs both the menu screen printf and the final index echo "$selected" to standard output (stdout). If used with command substitution like CHOICE_INDEX=$(select_option ...), the menu's ANSI control codes will be intercepted together by the variable and fail to display properly in the terminal. In practice, please redirect the menu drawing and cursor control inside the function to >&2 (stderr) or /dev/tty, keeping only the final echo "$selected" output to stdout; additionally, it is recommended to use trap '...' RETURN or restore INT TERM signal handling before the function ends to avoid overriding the main script's trap.
documents.s: 2. Basic Usage Example: Fixed Option Menu

documents.t: The original notes used DATE1=$(ls ... | sed -n '1p') to hardcode 5 variables, which produced blank lines when actual directories were fewer than 5. Standard Solution: Use mapfile (or readarray) to dynamically read existing directories into an array, and dynamically append an Exit option: #!/usr/bin/env bash BACKUP_DIR="/storage/backup" # 1. Check if directory exists if [[ ! -d "${BACKUP_DIR}" ]]; then echo "Error: Backup directory ${BACKUP_DIR} does not exist!" >&2 exit 1 fi # 2. Dynamically read all "subdirectory names" under the directory into an array # Method A: Use find (most precise, excludes regular files) mapfile -t BACKUP_LIST < <(find "${BACKUP_DIR}" -mindepth 1 -maxdepth 1 -type d -exec basename {} \; | sort -r) # 3. Check if there is backup data if [[ ${#BACKUP_LIST[@]} -eq 0 ]]; then echo "Notice: No backup directories available at present." exit 0 fi # 4. Dynamically append the "Exit" option at the end of the array BACKUP_LIST+=("Cancel and Exit") # 5. Render menu echo "Please select the backup snapshot directory to restore:" SELECTED_IDX=$(select_option "${BACKUP_LIST[@]}") # 6. Determine user selection LAST_IDX=$((${#BACKUP_LIST[@]} - 1)) if [[ "${SELECTED_IDX}" -eq "${LAST_IDX}" ]]; then echo "User cancelled operation, script exiting safely." exit 0 fi CHOSEN_BACKUP="${BACKUP_LIST[SELECTED_IDX]}" echo "--------------------------------------------------" echo "Successfully selected backup directory: ${CHOSEN_BACKUP}" echo "Full path: ${BACKUP_DIR}/${CHOSEN_BACKUP}" echo "Preparing restoration process..."
documents.s: 3. Solving Dynamic Directory Blank Line Pain Points: Combining Dynamic Arrays

documents.t: Item Traditional Hardcoded Approach Dynamic Array Best Practice Directory Capture DATE1=$(ls | sed -n '1p') mapfile -t LIST < <(find ... -type d) Blank Options Blank lines inevitably appear when directories are fewer than declared variables Renders as many lines as there are items in the array, zero blank lines Exception Exit (Ctrl+C) Cursor disappears, terminal does not echo text Add trap to restore stty echo and cursor upon interruption Cursor Overwrite Mechanism \E[6n relies on terminal absolute coordinates (prone to scrolling misprints) \033[NA relative line rollback paired with \033[2K to clear entire line
documents.s: 4. Key Technical Details and Pitfall Quick Reference

documents.t: ... | tr : , | sed -e 's/^/| /' -e 's/,/,| /g' -e 's/$/,|/' | column -t -s, tr : ,: Converts colon delimiters to commas. sed triple replacement: s/^/| /: Prepends | at the start of the line. s/,/,| /g: Replaces , with | while preserving commas as subsequent split points for column. s/$/,|/: Appends | at the end of the line. column -t -s,: Specifies , as the delimiter to align columns and consumes the commas.

Toolchain Redundancy: column natively supports custom input delimiters (-s) and output delimiters (-o), eliminating the need to detour through tr to convert to commas. Empty Field Collapse Issue: Traditional BSD/SysV versions of column encounter consecutive delimiters (such as empty GECOS fields like :: in /etc/passwd), default to merging multiple delimiters into one, causing subsequent columns to shift left. Missing Headers and Separators: Features only vertical side borders without true table headers or horizontal separator lines.
documents.s: Blind Spots and Potential Issues of the Original Approach

documents.t: The column utility built into modern Linux distributions (Photon OS, Ubuntu, Debian, Arch, etc., originating from the util-linux package) natively supports specifying input and output delimiters:
documents.s: 2. Modern Pure column Minimalist Solution (util-linux Modern Standard)

documents.t: Set the input delimiter directly to : and output delimiter to |: head -n 4 /etc/passwd | column -t -s ':' -o ' | ' Output Effect: root | x | 0 | 0 | | /root | /usr/bin/zsh bin | x | 1 | 1 | | / | /usr/bin/nologin daemon | x | 2 | 2 | | / | /usr/bin/nologin mail | x | 8 | 12 | | /var/spool/mail | /usr/bin/nologin

If complete | ... | borders are required, a single concise sed command pads the start and end: head -n 4 /etc/passwd | column -t -s ':' -o ' | ' | sed 's/^/| /; s/$/ |/' Output Effect: | root | x | 0 | 0 | | /root | /usr/bin/zsh | | bin | x | 1 | 1 | | / | /usr/bin/nologin | | daemon | x | 2 | 2 | | / | /usr/bin/nologin | | mail | x | 8 | 12 | | /var/spool/mail | /usr/bin/nologin | Key Parameter -n (Preventing Empty Field Collapse): If column on your system strips empty :: fields causing column misalignment, be sure to add the -n parameter (e.g., column -t -s ':' -o ' | ' -n), which preserves original spacing for empty fields. Updated 2026-11-27 column's -o (custom output delimiter) and -n (preserve empty fields) are Linux util-linux extension parameters. Native BSD column(1) built into FreeBSD does not support -o and -n; if formatting tables on FreeBSD, use awk instead (see Section 4) or process with sed.

documents.t: To generate Markdown or pure ASCII tables that can be pasted directly into documents, use sed to dynamically insert a separator line below the first row.

documents.t: Using custom data containing headers as an example: cat << 'EOF' | column -t -s ',' -o ' | ' | sed 's/^/| /; s/$/ |/' | sed '2s/ [^|]*/ --- /g' User,UID,GID,Home,Shell root,0,0,/root,/bin/bash docker,1000,1000,/home/docker,/bin/bash nobody,65534,65534,/nonexistent,/usr/sbin/nologin EOF Output Effect: | User | UID | GID | Home | Shell | | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | | root | 0 | 0 | /root | /bin/bash | | docker | 1000 | 1000 | /home/docker | /bin/bash | | nobody | 65534 | 65534 | /nonexistent | /usr/sbin/nologin |

documents.s: Running Certbot via Docker for Automatic SSL Certificate Signing and Renewal (Archived)

documents.t: Refer to https://certbot.eff.org/docs/install.html#running-with-docker (Updated 2026-11-27: Official documentation has migrated to eff-certbot.readthedocs.io) sudo docker run -it --rm --name certbot -v "/etc/letsencrypt:/etc/letsencrypt" -v "/var/lib/letsencrypt:/var/lib/letsencrypt" \ certbot/certbot certonly If you want different domains for a specific IP, you can append the parameter -p your_ip:80:80 -p your_ip:443:443 to map them accordingly.

Add the following to crontab: 0 0 * * * docker run --rm -v /etc/letsencrypt:/etc/letsencrypt -ti certbot/certbot renew That's it. Updated 2026-11-27 crontab runs in a non-interactive environment; the -ti flags (especially -t allocating a pseudo-TTY) in the original scheduled command will cause Docker to throw an error the input device is not a TTY and fail. The scheduled command should remove -ti. If using standalone mode for HTTP-01 validation, you must append -p 80:80 (or --network host) during initial signing so the container can receive Let's Encrypt validation requests. Modern container architectures generally use reverse proxies with built-in ACME automatic signing and renewal mechanisms (such as Traefik, Caddy, or Nginx Proxy Manager).
No longer needed... Nowadays, reverse proxies with automatic SSL issuance like Traefik or Nginx Proxy Manager are used, so such a pure tool is no longer required.

documents.s: Deploying MS SQL Server Database with Docker

documents.t: # Docker-compose.yml version: '3' services: mssql: image: mcr.microsoft.com/mssql/server:2019-latest container_name: sql-server environment: - PUID=1000 - ACCEPT_EULA=Y # - MSSQL_PID=<your_product_id | edition_name> (default: Developer)" - SA_PASSWORD=<your@Passw0rd> ports: - 1433:1433 volumes: - /var/lib/docker/volumes/mssql:/var/lib/mssqlql restart: always Updated 2026-11-27 This archived configuration file contains several syntax errors and outdated parameters, preserved for historical comparison: YAML Syntax Error: The mssql service name is missing a trailing colon (should be mssql:). Mount Path Error: The data directory for Microsoft's official SQL Server container is /var/opt/mssql (incorrectly typed as /var/lib/mssqlql in the original), and using Docker named volumes is recommended over hardcoding /var/lib/docker/volumes/.... Compose V2 Standard: Declaring top-level version: '3' is no longer required when using modern docker compose. Environment Variables and Version: 2019-latest is outdated; starting from SQL Server 2022, MSSQL_SA_PASSWORD replaces SA_PASSWORD.

PUID=1000 is specified because SQL Server cannot run as root and requires a separate user, otherwise issues easily arise. However, I noticed many tutorials omit this, so if it runs fine without it, this line can be skipped. (Updated 2026-11-27: Microsoft's official mcr.microsoft.com/mssql/server image does not support the PUID environment variable (which is a LinuxServer.io convention); if non-root execution is required, use user: in Compose along with directory permission settings.) ACCEPT_EULA=Y: This is actually stating the obvious since it cannot run without agreement, but since this image is made by Microsoft, there's no way around it. MSSQL_PID: This is actually the most important parameter because it determines the edition of SQL Server you are running. For enterprise use, put your purchased license key (or edition name) here. SA_PASSWORD: As the name implies, equivalent to the MySQL root password definition.

Getting this running is actually quite simple... as expected of Microsoft... However, it lacks a default graphical management interface; if needed, you have to connect using an external client, so some people install Adminer alongside it for simple management.
We don't use this stuff at home anyway; we always use free SQL databases.

Storage Model: BookStack's article contents, user permissions, and page metadata are stored in MariaDB / MySQL; images, attachments, and uploaded files are stored in the file system directory (/config/www/storage). LinuxServer Variable Renaming Trap: LinuxServer.io image has gradually unified its database environment variable naming convention to align with Laravel's default variables: Legacy parameters: DB_USER / DB_PASS New mandatory parameters: DB_USERNAME / DB_PASSWORD If legacy examples are followed, the container will pick up null values during initialization, causing the container to repeatedly output Database connection error: SQLSTATE[HY000] [1045] Access denied. APP_URL Strict Limitation: The underlying Laravel framework strongly relies on APP_URL to generate static assets (CSS / JS) and page redirection hyperlinks. When running behind an HTTPS reverse proxy, APP_URL must strictly include https:// and the full domain name (cannot be left blank or set to http://localhost), otherwise it will cause front-end Mixed Content breaking issues, login CSRF Token verification failures, or infinite redirect loops.
documents.s: 1. Core Architecture and Major Breaking Changes

documents.t: Deployment uses Traefik v3 for edge SSL termination. The backend container does not expose any host ports externally, communicating uniformly through a shared external Docker network.
documents.s: 2. Docker Compose Deployment Configuration (Integrating Traefik v3)

documents.t: # Create database and application configuration directories sudo mkdir -p /opt/bookstack/db /opt/bookstack/app # Set PUID/PGID aligned owner (using UID 1000 as an example) sudo chown -R 1000:1000 /opt/bookstack
documents.s: Step 1: Create Dedicated Directory and Permissions

documents.t: Orchestrate services in /opt/bookstack/docker-compose.yml: services: bookstack_db: image: lscr.io/linuxserver/mariadb:latest container_name: bookstack_db restart: unless-stopped environment: - PUID=1000 - PGID=1000 - TZ=Asia/Taipei - MYSQL_ROOT_PASSWORD=your_super_root_pass - MYSQL_DATABASE=bookstackapp - MYSQL_USER=bookstack - MYSQL_PASSWORD=your_db_secret_pass volumes: - /opt/bookstack/db:/config networks: - bookstack_internal bookstack: image: lscr.io/linuxserver/bookstack:latest container_name: bookstack restart: unless-stopped depends_on: - bookstack_db environment: - PUID=1000 - PGID=1000 - TZ=Asia/Taipei # Crucial: Must fully include https:// and match the Traefik routing domain - APP_URL=https://wiki.example.com # Database connection (note the new parameter names) - DB_HOST=bookstack_db - DB_DATABASE=bookstackapp - DB_USERNAME=bookstack - DB_PASSWORD=your_db_secret_pass # SMTP mail notification settings (optional) - MAIL_DRIVER=smtp - MAIL_HOST=smtp.example.com - MAIL_PORT=587 - MAIL_ENCRYPTION=tls - MAIL_USERNAME=notify@example.com - MAIL_PASSWORD=your_smtp_password - MAIL_FROM=notify@example.com - MAIL_FROM_NAME=BookStack Wiki volumes: - /opt/bookstack/app:/config networks: - bookstack_internal - proxy-network labels: - "traefik.enable=true" - "traefik.http.routers.bookstack.rule=Host(`wiki.example.com`)" - "traefik.http.routers.bookstack.entrypoints=websecure" - "traefik.http.routers.bookstack.tls=true" - "traefik.http.routers.bookstack.tls.certresolver=myresolver" # Crucial: LinuxServer internal Nginx listens on Port 80, must explicitly specify the load balancing target port - "traefik.http.services.bookstack.loadbalancer.server.port=80" networks: bookstack_internal: driver: bridge proxy-network: external: true Start services: docker compose up -d

The container automatically executes database migration and default seed data population upon first startup: Open in browser: https://wiki.example.com Default High-Privilege Account: Email: admin@admin.com Password: password After logging in, immediately go to "Settings" -> "Users" -> click Admin to change the Email and replace it with a high-strength password.
documents.s: 3. Initial Administrator Login and Security Changes

documents.t: Cause: APP_URL missing or misformatted, or reverse proxy not correctly forwarding proxy headers. Solution: Ensure APP_URL is correctly configured and starts with https://. If using a custom Nginx / NPM reverse proxy, ensure the following headers are passed upstream: proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Proto https; proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Host $host;
documents.s: 4.1 Redirecting to http://localhost:6875 or CSS/JS Breaking (Mixed Content)

documents.t: LinuxServer.io image internally uses S6-overlay to start Nginx + PHP-FPM. The container image may declare multiple listening ports internally. If traefik.http.services.bookstack.loadbalancer.server.port=80 is omitted, Traefik cannot determine the forwarding target in multi-port scenarios, resulting in forwarding to the wrong port and returning a 502 Bad Gateway.
documents.s: 4.2 Why Must Traefik Explicitly Specify server.port=80?

documents.t: Default upload limits are constrained by both PHP and Nginx. If uploading tens of MBs of PDF or video attachments: Edit /opt/bookstack/app/php/php-local.ini (create if non-existent): upload_max_filesize = 100M post_max_size = 100M memory_limit = 512M Edit /opt/bookstack/app/nginx/site-confs/default.conf, add inside the server { ... } block: client_max_body_size 100M; Restart container: docker compose restart bookstack.
documents.s: 4.3 Image or Large File Upload Failure (HTTP 413 Payload Too Large)

documents.t: BookStack data integrity is maintained jointly by "database SQL" and "uploaded file directory", both of which must be backed up synchronously.

#!/bin/bash BACKUP_DIR="/opt/backups/bookstack" DATE=$(date +%F_%H%M%S) mkdir -p $BACKUP_DIR # 1. Export MariaDB database dump docker compose exec -T bookstack_db mysqldump -u bookstack -pyour_db_secret_pass bookstackapp > $BACKUP_DIR/db_$DATE.sql # 2. Archive uploaded attachments, images, and config files tar -czvf $BACKUP_DIR/app_data_$DATE.tar.gz -C /opt/bookstack/app . echo "Backup completed: $DATE"

Start fresh MariaDB and BookStack containers. Restore file system: extract app_data_*.tar.gz overwriting /opt/bookstack/app/ and fix permissions (chown -R 1000:1000). Restore database: docker compose exec -i bookstack_db mysql -u bookstack -pyour_db_secret_pass bookstackapp < /opt/backups/bookstack/db_*.sql Clear Laravel cache and restart: docker compose exec -it bookstack php /app/www/artisan cache:clear docker compose restart bookstack Updated 2026-11-27 This document has been moved to Archive/ for historical reference. Please note the following updates when applying in practice: Docker Compose v2 recommends naming configuration files compose.yaml (docker-compose.yml remains compatible). lscr.io/linuxserver/mariadb:latest (MariaDB 11+) marks mysqldump and mysql commands as deprecated aliases; it is recommended to use mariadb-dump and mariadb instead. It is recommended to wrap $BACKUP_DIR and $DATE variables in double quotes in the backup script ("$BACKUP_DIR", "$DATE"); when performing restore redirection (<), specify a single explicit .sql file path. Using wildcards like db_*.sql when multiple backups exist in the directory will cause a shell error (ambiguous redirect).

tip A long, long time ago, I used MRTG + SNMP to generate traffic graphs, but over the years in China my home servers gradually dropped to a bare-minimum "as long as it runs" standard, so I stopped bothering with it. Recently, during a major cleanup, I wanted to set up something similar again and picked LibreNMS.

documents.t: Mokmoe's Notes - Docker LibreNMS Installation Log (incl. MariaDB, phpMyAdmin) His post is actually very detailed—you can just follow it directly—though I've still written down my slightly adjusted approach below.

vi mariadb.yml # mariadb.yml -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- services: mariadb: image: mariadb:latest container_name: mariadb environment: - MYSQL_ROOT_PASSWORD=${your_DB_root_Passwd} - TZ=Asia/Taipei ports: - ${your_DB_host}:${your_DB_port}:3306 volumes: - /var/lib/docker/volumes/mariadb/data:/var/lib/mysql - /var/lib/docker/volumes/mariadb/mariadbcustom.cnf:/etc/mysql/conf.d/custom.cnf restart: unless-stopped Updated 2026-11-27 The ---- separator line inside the code block lacks a # comment prefix; pasting it directly into YAML will cause a parse failure. MYSQL_ROOT_PASSWORD has been replaced by MARIADB_ROOT_PASSWORD in MariaDB 11+. vi /var/lib/docker/volumes/mariadb/mariadbcustom.cnf # /var/lib/docker/volumes/mariadb/mariadbcustom.cnf -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- [client] default-character-set = utf8mb4 [mysql]" >> /etc/my.cnf default-character-set = utf8mb4 [mysqld] skip-character-set-client-handshake collation_server = utf8mb4_unicode_ci character_set_server = utf8mb4 tmpdir = /var/lib/mysqltmp This defines the defaults for MariaDB so everything uses UTF-8 Unicode. Updated 2026-11-27 The ---- separator line in the block lacks a # comment prefix, and line 4 [mysql]" >> /etc/my.cnf is a copy-paste error resulting in invalid INI syntax (it should be [mysql]). skip-character-set-client-handshake is deprecated in newer MariaDB versions; use character-set-client-handshake = FALSE instead. Also, if /var/lib/mysqltmp is not mounted, the custom tmpdir may fail to start if the path does not exist. sudo docker-compose -f mariadb.yml up -d (Updated 2026-11-27: Docker Compose v1 docker-compose is end-of-life; on modern environments use sudo docker compose -f mariadb.yml up -d instead) This creates and runs the container. sudo docker exec -it mariadb bash # @mariadb container -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- mysql -u root -p # Enter your SQL root password after running this to enter MariaDB # Create the account and database for LibreNMS and grant full privileges on this database to the account; if you dislike CLI commands, you can also do this in phpMyAdmin mysql> CREATE DATABASE librenms CHARACTER SET utf8 COLLATE utf8_unicode_ci; mysql> CREATE USER 'librenms'@'%' IDENTIFIED BY 'user_librenms_password'; mysql> GRANT ALL PRIVILEGES on librenms.* TO 'librenms'@'%' WITH GRANT OPTION; mysql> FLUSH PRIVILEGES; Updated 2026-11-27 In MariaDB 11+ containers, the mariadb CLI command is recommended instead (the mysql symlink is marked deprecated). Official LibreNMS documentation requires the database to use utf8mb4 and utf8mb4_unicode_ci (utf8 in MySQL/MariaDB is actually the legacy 3-byte utf8mb3).

vi librenms.yml #librenms.yml -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- version: '3' services: librenms: image: librenms/librenms:latest container_name: librenms command: su - librenms -c "/opt/librenms/librenms-service.py -v" environment: - TZ=Asia/Taipei - PUID=1000 - DB_HOST=${your_DB_host} - DB_PORT=${your_DB_port} - DB_NAME=librenms - DB_USER=librenms - DB_PASSWORD=user_librenms_passwd - DB_TIMEOUT=10 - LIBRENMS_SNMP_COMMUNITY=${Community_name_you_want} ports: - ${your_Server_ip}:${port_you_want}:8000 volumes: - /var/lib/docker/volumes/librenms/data:/data restart: always A crucial step here is that you must add: command: su - librenms -c "/opt/librenms/librenms-service.py -v" This means running /opt/librenms/librenms-service.py -v as the librenms user. That way its RRD permissions will be correct, otherwise there will be issues (I previously believed this was optional and couldn't get it working—it is mandatory...). Updated 2026-11-27 The ---- separator line in the block lacks #, and version: '3' is deprecated in Docker Compose v2. Modern official librenms/librenms Docker deployments have moved to a multi-container stack (the main librenms service paired with a dispatcher sidecar running librenms-service.py, plus db and redis), rather than overriding command directly on the main container. sudo docker exec -it mariadb bash # Enter the mariadb container -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- mysql -u librenms -p # Log in to MariaDB with the librenms account mysql> use librenms; # Select the librenms database # Modify database schema defaults mysql> ALTER TABLE `notifications` CHANGE `datetime` `datetime` timestamp NOT NULL DEFAULT '1970-01-02 00:00:00' ; mysql> ALTER TABLE `users` CHANGE `created_at` `created_at` timestamp NOT NULL DEFAULT '1970-01-02 00:00:01' ; This fixes database issues (fixing issues reported in Validate Config). Updated 2026-11-27 The ALTER TABLE statements above were only an early workaround for MySQL's NO_ZERO_DATE strict mode; modern LibreNMS manages database schema migrations automatically via lnms migrate, so manually altering table defaults is unnecessary.

Honestly, you rarely need this, but for people who dislike mysql CLI commands, you can use this graphical interface to manage the MySQL database. Because it is very simple, you can just create it directly with a docker run command: # If your ${your_DB_host} uses port 3306 sudo docker run --name phpmyadmin -d -e PMA_HOST=${your_DB_host} -p 8080:80 phpmyadmin/phpmyadmin # If your ${your_DB_host} is not on the default 3306, it is recommended to connect via docker --link sudo docker run --name phpmyadmin -d --link mariadb:db -p 8080:80 phpmyadmin/phpmyadmin Here port 8080 is exposed externally and can be changed to whatever you want. Updated 2026-11-27 --link is a deprecated legacy Docker flag; in modern environments, create a custom bridge network (docker network create) and connect containers via --network.

Honestly, modifying config.php inside the container to serve it under a subdirectory seemed like too much trouble, so I went and registered a dedicated domain name for it instead. The Nginx configuration is just a standard virtual host setup: simply add a .cnf file under /etc/nginx/site-enables/ (Updated 2026-11-27: On Debian/Ubuntu, the correct path is /etc/nginx/sites-available/, then enable it via a symlink into /etc/nginx/sites-enabled/) to define it. Remember to also request a Certbot certificate for this domain name. # librenms.cnf -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- server { listen 80; server_name librenms.exsample.com; return 301 https://$server_name$request_uri; } server { listen 443 ssl http2; server_name librenms.exsample.com; ssl_certificate /etc/letsencrypt/live/librenms.exsample.com/fullchain.pem; ssl_certificate_key /etc/letsencrypt/live/librenms.exsample.com/privkey.pem; # include /etc/letsencrypt/options-ssl-nginx.conf; # ssl_dhparam /etc/letsencrypt/ssl-dhparams.pem; #charset koi8-r; #access_log /var/log/nginx/host.access.log main; client_max_body_size 20M; location / { proxy_pass http://${your_Server_ip}:${port_you_want}; # Change this to the target IP/port to forward to proxy_set_header Host $host; proxy_set_header X-Real-IP $remote_addr; proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for; proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Proto $scheme; proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Protocol $scheme; proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Host $http_host; proxy_buffering off; } error_page 500 502 503 504 /50x.html; location = /50x.html { root /usr/share/nginx/html; Updated 2026-11-27 The example contains an un-commented ---- separator line, a misspelled domain exsample.com, and is missing the closing curly braces } for the location and server blocks at the end. listen 443 ssl http2; is deprecated in Nginx 1.25.1+; modern syntax splits it into listen 443 ssl; and a separate http2 on; directive.
Please refer to the FreeBSD section of the Wiki.

References​ Sugarcane at Dusk (blog.xuite.net) Stars Appear When It Gets Dark (sc8log) After logging into ESXi via SSH esxcli system snmp get # Check SNMP status and current settings esxcli system snmp set -c YOUR_STRING # Set your community string esxcli system snmp set -p 161 # Set your SNMP port; 161 UDP is standard esxcli system snmp set -L "City, State, Country" # Set your location esxcli system snmp set -C noc@example.com # Set your contact email esxcli system snmp set -e yes # Enable SNMP Run on another machine that can query SNMP snmpwalk -v2c -c ${YOUR_STRING} ${your_server_IP} Just verify that data is returned. Updated 2026-11-27 VMware ESXi 6.5 has reached End of Life (EOL), and the referenced blog.xuite.net service was permanently shut down on 2023-08-31.

If you don't want to modify config.php inside LibreNMS, it's easiest not to use a community string other than public so discovery is simpler. It takes at least a few hours after enabling these before clear graphs appear—don't panic, you won't get data immediately right after configuration. Updated 2026-11-27 For security reasons, keeping the default public SNMP community string is not recommended in real-world or internet-facing environments; use a custom complex string or upgrade to SNMPv3 with authentication and encryption.
Low usage — I barely used it after setting it up. There are alternatives like netdata, and since I also installed it directly on the Gateway and DHCP hosts, LibreNMS became even less useful.

Below is a comparison with modern Docker and Node-RED: Docker Compose v2 has dropped the top-level version: '3.3' field, and recommends using compose.yaml and the docker compose command. It is not recommended to run chmod 777 directly on mounted directories; a safer practice is to run chown -R 1000:1000 /var/lib/docker/volumes/node-red to align with the container's default UID 1000. The correct filename for the Node-RED configuration file is the lowercase plural settings.js (not Setting.js); the built-in command in newer official containers is node-red admin hash-pw, eliminating the need to install global node-red-admin.
documents.s: Workflow Automation Engine: Node-RED (Docker + Traefik Archival Notes)

documents.t: Node-RED Official Website
Actually, the installation part is the easiest part...

version: '3.3' services: node-red: image: nodered/node-red container_name: node-red # ports: # - '1880:1880' environment: - TZ=Asia/Taipei volumes: - /var/lib/docker/volumes/node-red:/data restart: unless-stopped labels: traefik.enable: true traefik.http.routers.node-red.rule: Host(`<Domain>`) traefik.http.routers.node-red.tls: true traefik.http.routers.node-red.tls.certresolver: myresolver traefik.http.services.node-red.loadbalancer.server.port: 1880 networks: default: external: true name: traefik_backend

Volumes Permissions Because the default UID permission is 1000, creating the container as root will cause it to fail to run properly due to write permission issues. The solution is to define it as root or directly change the directory permissions (I changed them to 777). settings.js (written as Setting.js in the original text) Configuration Since I use Traefik to handle SSL, only the login permission part needs attention. Basically, enabling login settings is very easy: adminAuth: { type: "credentials", users: [ { username: "admin", password: "$2a$08$zZWtXTja0fB1pzD4sHCMyOCMYz2Z6dNbM6tl8sJogENOMcxWV9DN.", permissions: "*" }, { username: "george", password: "$2b$08$wuAqPiKJlVN27eF5qJp.RuQYuy6ZYONW7a/UWYxDTtwKFCdB8F19y", permissions: "read" } ] } Just change the username part to your preferred ID, then via docker exec -it <NodeRed_container_name> bash run node-red-admin hash-pw, and it will let you enter your desired password and generate the hash string. Copy and paste it into the configuration above.

Updated 2026-11-27 This is an archived record from the early Hexo + Isso era. Below are modern environment comparison notes: Modern Docker Compose v2 recommends using the compose.yaml filename and running with the docker compose command. isso.conf is in INI format and will not expand $(...) shell variables. During actual deployment, you must directly replace them with the real database filename and Blog URL; it is also recommended to explicitly specify traefik.http.services.isso.loadbalancer.server.port=8080. The official Isso website and documentation have migrated to https://isso-comments.org/, and this site has migrated from Hexo to Docusaurus and deprecated Isso.
Hexo-theme-Next Comment Documentation Isso QuickStart

documents.t: version: '2' services: mariadb: image: docker.io/bitnami/mariadb:10.3 environment: - ALLOW_EMPTY_PASSWORD=yes - MARIADB_USER=bn_phpbb - MARIADB_DATABASE=bitnami_phpbb volumes: - /var/lib/docker/volumes/phpbb/mariadb:/bitnami/mariadb phpbb: image: docker.io/bitnami/phpbb:3 ports: - 192.168.131.2:8082:8080 environment: - PHPBB_DATABASE_HOST=mariadb - PHPBB_DATABASE_PORT_NUMBER=3306 - PHPBB_DATABASE_USER=bn_phpbb - PHPBB_DATABASE_NAME=bitnami_phpbb - ALLOW_EMPTY_PASSWORD=yes volumes: - /var/lib/docker/volumes/phpbb/phpbb:/bitnami/phpbb depends_on: - mariadb Updated 2026-11-27 The historical configuration above contains several outdated or discouraged practices, kept solely for archival reference: The top-level version: '2' attribute is deprecated in modern Docker Compose v2 (docker compose); omit version and start directly with services:. bitnami/mariadb:10.3 has reached EOL and is unmaintained, and older free Bitnami images have since migrated to bitnamilegacy with revised maintenance policies; in practice, use official mariadb:11 or another long-term supported image, and never set ALLOW_EMPTY_PASSWORD=yes. Mounting bind mounts directly to /var/lib/docker/volumes/... (which is the internal managed named volumes directory of Docker Engine) is discouraged; mount to independent host paths such as /opt/phpbb/... instead. To be honest, I was already running another MariaDB at the time, and theoretically they could have been integrated, but for simplicity I just ran an additional separate MariaDB container. If using this approach, make sure container names and ports do not conflict. However, this Compose file does not expose database ports externally by default, so network isolation security for the database is maintained even when run independently.

Personally, I am not very fond of Bitnami image permission conventions: after the container starts, you usually have to adjust the permissions of the /var/lib/docker/volumes/phpbb directory. Since the image runs as UID=1001 by default, rather than using chown 1001, or directly using chmod 777 (Updated 2026-11-27: In practice, never use chmod 777 as it poses severe security risks; use chown -R 1001:1001 to precisely assign container UID permissions instead), otherwise the service will fail to start properly due to lack of write permissions.

This approach places both the DB and the AP inside the same docker-compose.yml. Looking back, it is indeed true that avoiding tightly coupling the DB makes containerization more convenient and makes splitting services like this much easier.

First use docker run to run the script inside the image to generate the initial DB. Use a compose file to create the DB standalone first (and define volumes to persist data). Import the initial DB into the DB container's database inside the DB container (persisting the result via volumes). Remove the standalone DB container (technically you don't have to remove it, though subsequent adjustments are more tedious). Use docker-compose.yml to create all related containers directly (including the DB container).

docker pull guacamole/guacamole docker pull guacamole/guacd docker pull mariadb/server Updated 2026-11-27 mariadb/server is an unmaintained legacy image; modern deployments should use the official mariadb:lts image instead (the MARIADB_* prefix is also recommended for environment variables).
docker run --rm guacamole/guacamole /opt/guacamole/bin/initdb.sh --mysql > guac_db.sql

initial.yml​ version: '3' services: guacdb: container_name: guacdb image: mariadb/server:latest restart: unless-stopped environment: MYSQL_ROOT_PASSWORD: '<PASSWD_YOU_WANT>' MYSQL_DATABASE: 'guacamole_db' MYSQL_USER: 'guacamole_user' MYSQL_PASSWORD: '<PASSWD_YOU_WANT>' volumes: - /var/lib/docker/volumes/<Dir_you_want>:/var/lib/mysql Commands​ # Establish initial DB Container docker-compose up -d # Copy initial sql into db container docker cp guac_db.sql guacdb:/guac_db.sql # Opening a shell and initializing the db: docker exec -it guacdb bash cat /guac_db.sql | mysql -u root -p guacamole_db exit # Remove initial DB OS docker-compose -f /where/is/your/docker-compose down Updated 2026-11-27 docker-compose v1 has reached end of life; in modern environments, use docker compose v2 instead (for example, docker compose -f initial.yml up -d and docker compose -f initial.yml down; the last line of the original commands was also missing the .yml extension). The top-level version: '3' field in Compose YAML is obsolete in Compose v2 and can simply be omitted.

docker-compose.yml​ version: '3' services: guacdb: container_name: guacdb image: mariadb/server:latest restart: unless-stopped networks: - traefik environment: MYSQL_ROOT_PASSWORD: '<PASSWD_YOU_WANT>' MYSQL_DATABASE: 'guacamole_db' MYSQL_USER: 'guacamole_user' MYSQL_PASSWORD: '<PASSWD_YOU_WANT>' volumes: - /var/lib/docker/volumes/guacamole/db:/var/lib/mysql guacd: container_name: guacd image: guacamole/guacd restart: unless-stopped networks: - traefik guacamole: container_name: guacamole image: 'guacamole/guacamole:latest' restart: unless-stopped networks: - traefik # ports: # - '8080:8080' environment: GUACD_HOSTNAME: "guacd" MYSQL_HOSTNAME: "guacdb" MYSQL_DATABASE: "guacamole_db" MYSQL_USER: "guacamole_user" MYSQL_PASSWORD: "<PASSWD_YOU_WANT>" depends_on: - guacdb - guacd labels: traefik.enable: true traefik.http.routers.guacamole.rule: Host(`<hostname.you.want>`) traefik.http.routers.guacamole.tls: true traefik.http.routers.guacamole.tls.certresolver: myresolver traefik.http.services.guacamole.loadbalancer.server.port: 8080 networks: traefik: external: true name: web-service Updated 2026-11-27 As above, Compose v2 does not need version: '3', and mariadb/server:latest should be changed to mariadb:lts (in the new official image, the client tool is the mariadb CLI).
Poor security: this setup essentially punches a hole through the firewall. Replaced with WireGuard + VNC, which is relatively safer and simpler.
Photon OS comes with Docker Engine pre-loaded in its official package repository: # Enable and start on boot systemctl enable --now docker # Check status systemctl status docker

Install the latest version using Docker's official APT repository: # 1. Update package lists and install basic prerequisites sudo apt-get update sudo apt-get install -y ca-certificates curl gnupg # 2. Add Docker's official GPG key sudo install -m 0755 -d /etc/apt/keyrings curl -fsSL https://download.docker.com/linux/$(. /etc/os-release && echo "$ID")/gpg | sudo gpg --dearmor -o /etc/apt/keyrings/docker.gpg sudo chmod a+r /etc/apt/keyrings/docker.gpg # 3. Set up the APT repository echo \ "deb [arch=$(dpkg --print-architecture) signed-by=/etc/apt/keyrings/docker.gpg] https://download.docker.com/linux/$(. /etc/os-release && echo "$ID") \ $(. /etc/os-release && echo "$VERSION_CODENAME") stable" | \ sudo tee /etc/apt/sources.list.d/docker.list > /dev/null # 4. Install Docker Engine and CLI plugins sudo apt-get update sudo apt-get install -y docker-ce docker-ce-cli containerd.io docker-buildx-plugin docker-compose-plugin # 5. Enable and start on boot sudo systemctl enable --now docker

Configure the official repository using DNF / YUM: # 1. Install necessary utilities sudo dnf install -y dnf-utils # 2. Add Docker's official repo sudo dnf config-manager --add-repo https://download.docker.com/linux/centos/docker-ce.repo # 3. Install Docker packages sudo dnf install -y docker-ce docker-ce-cli containerd.io docker-buildx-plugin docker-compose-plugin # 4. Enable and start on boot sudo systemctl enable --now docker (Note: In environments using DNF 5 such as Fedora 41+ or RHEL 10, the step 2 command syntax changes to sudo dnf config-manager addrepo --from-repofile=https://download.docker.com/linux/centos/docker-ce.repo.)

Alpine uses OpenRC as its service manager and provides packages in the Community repository by default: # 1. Enable Community repository (if not enabled, edit /etc/apk/repositories and uncomment the community line) # 2. Install Docker apk update apk add docker # 3. Add to default boot runlevel and start rc-update add docker boot service docker start

Modern standards have completely deprecated the old Python pip installation method (pip install docker-compose) in favor of Docker Compose V2 (the Go-written CLI plugin docker compose), which offers great compatibility without interfering with the system Python environment. Distribution Recommended Installation Method Command Photon OS Official package repo native install (V1/V2 binary) tdnf -y install docker-compose Ubuntu / Debian APT official plugin (Recommended) sudo apt-get install -y docker-compose-plugin RHEL / Rocky Linux DNF official plugin (Recommended) sudo dnf install -y docker-compose-plugin Alpine Linux APK package repo (docker-cli-compose) apk add docker-cli-compose Universal Manual Install Official GitHub Binary Standalone / Plugin See "Universal Manual Deployment" below
documents.s: 2. Docker Compose Installation and Deployment Methods

documents.t: When distribution package repositories are outdated or on minimalist systems, download the binary directly and install it to the CLI plugin path: # 1. Create Docker CLI plugins directory sudo mkdir -p /usr/libexec/docker/cli-plugins # 2. Automatically fetch and download the latest version (using x86_64 as an example; change to aarch64 for ARM) COMPOSE_VERSION=$(curl -s https://api.github.com/repos/docker/compose/releases/latest | grep '"tag_name":' | sed -E 's/.*"([^"]+)".*/\1/') sudo curl -SL "https://github.com/docker/compose/releases/download/${COMPOSE_VERSION}/docker-compose-linux-$(uname -m)" -o /usr/libexec/docker/cli-plugins/docker-compose # 3. Grant execution permissions sudo chmod +x /usr/libexec/docker/cli-plugins/docker-compose # 4. (Optional) Create a global symlink for legacy command compatibility sudo ln -sf /usr/libexec/docker/cli-plugins/docker-compose /usr/local/bin/docker-compose # 5. Verify docker compose version
documents.s: Universal Manual Deployment (Applicable to Any x86_64 / aarch64 Linux)

documents.t: To avoid using root for daily operations: # Add target user to the docker group sudo usermod -aG docker $USER # Apply group permissions (or re-login to SSH) newgrp docker

Create or overwrite /etc/docker/daemon.json to prevent container logs from filling up disk space and to enable live-restore: { "log-driver": "json-file", "log-opts": { "max-size": "50m", "max-file": "3" }, "storage-driver": "overlay2", "live-restore": true, "default-ulimits": { "nofile": { "Name": "nofile", "Hard": 65535, "Soft": 65535 } } } Apply settings: sudo systemctl daemon-reload sudo systemctl restart docker

If container networks cannot communicate externally or port exposure fails, ensure IPv4 forwarding is enabled: # Check status (returns 1 if normal) sysctl net.ipv4.ip_forward # If 0, write to configuration file for persistence echo "net.ipv4.ip_forward = 1" | sudo tee /etc/sysctl.d/99-docker-forward.conf sudo sysctl -p /etc/sysctl.d/99-docker-forward.conf

In addition to declaring restart: always or restart: unless-stopped in compose.yaml, production environments benefit from encapsulating entire Compose projects into Systemd Units for standard OS monitoring, dependency ordering, and auto-restart mechanisms.
documents.s: 4. Managing Docker Compose Services on Boot with Systemd

documents.t: Taking /opt/apps/my-stack as an example: sudo mkdir -p /opt/apps/my-stack cd /opt/apps/my-stack Create docker-compose.yml: services: app: image: nginx:alpine ports: - "8080:80"
documents.s: Step 1: Create Project Directory and Compose File

documents.t: Create the file /etc/systemd/system/docker-compose@.service (using the instantiation template @ to support multiple Compose projects simultaneously): [Unit] Description=Docker Compose Application Service (%i) Requires=docker.service After=docker.service network-online.target Wants=network-online.target [Service] Type=oneshot RemainAfterExit=yes WorkingDirectory=/opt/apps/%i # Pull images and start container stack before starting ExecStartPre=-/usr/bin/docker compose pull ExecStart=/usr/bin/docker compose up -d --remove-orphans # Gracefully stop all containers on shutdown ExecStop=/usr/bin/docker compose down # Reload configuration ExecReload=/usr/bin/docker compose pull ExecReload=/usr/bin/docker compose up -d --remove-orphans # Timeout settings TimeoutStartSec=300 TimeoutStopSec=60 [Install] WantedBy=multi-user.target Note: Verify the path using which docker. If it is /usr/local/bin/docker, adjust the Exec* paths accordingly.

The template unit automatically matches directory names. For instance, if the directory is /opt/apps/my-stack, the service name is docker-compose@my-stack: # 1. Reload systemd configuration sudo systemctl daemon-reload # 2. Start service and enable on boot sudo systemctl enable --now docker-compose@my-stack # 3. Check service running status sudo systemctl status docker-compose@my-stack # 4. View container operational logs journalctl -u docker-compose@my-stack -f

Regularly run maintenance commands to reclaim unreleased space: # 1. View current Docker space usage docker system df # 2. Clean up all stopped containers, unused networks, and dangling images docker system prune -f # 3. Deep cleanup: Delete images not used by any existing container as well docker system prune -a -f # 4. Clean up orphaned volumes (Warning: Destructive, may delete data no longer mounted) docker volume prune -f

# Run container in background with name, port mapping, auto-restart, and environment variables docker run -d \ --name web-app \ -p 8080:80 \ -e ENV=production \ --restart unless-stopped \ nginx:alpine # Enter temporary container in interactive mode (automatically destroyed upon exit) docker run --rm -it alpine:latest sh # Limit CPU and memory quotas docker run -d \ --name limited-app \ --memory="512m" \ --cpus="1.5" \ nginx:alpine

# List running containers docker ps # List all containers (including stopped or Exited), showing only ID and name docker ps -a --format "table {{.ID}}\t{{.Names}}\t{{.Status}}\t{{.Ports}}" # Start / Stop / Restart container docker start <container_id_or_name> docker stop <container_id_or_name> docker restart <container_id_or_name> # Force stop container (send SIGKILL) docker kill <container_id_or_name> # Pause and unpause container processes (freeze cgroup) docker pause <container_id_or_name> docker unpause <container_id_or_name> # Remove stopped container docker rm <container_id_or_name> # Force remove running container (equivalent to kill + rm) docker rm -f <container_id_or_name>

# Enter running container's Shell (most common) docker exec -it <container_name> /bin/sh # If bash is installed docker exec -it <container_name> /bin/bash # Execute a specific single-line command inside the container as root docker exec -u 0 -it <container_name> whoami # Tail logs in real-time, limiting line count and timestamps docker logs -f --tail 100 -t <container_name> # View logs since a specific timestamp docker logs --since "2026-09-01T00:00:00" <container_name>

# Real-time container resource utilization (CPU, Memory, Network I/O, Block I/O) docker stats # Formatted non-streaming resource usage snapshot docker stats --no-stream --format "table {{.Name}}\t{{.CPUPerc}}\t{{.MemUsage}}\t{{.NetIO}}" # View process list inside the container (from Host perspective) docker top <container_name>
documents.s: 2.2 Dynamic Resource Monitoring and Process Inspection

documents.t: # Copy local file into container docker cp /path/to/local/file.conf <container_name>:/etc/app/file.conf # Copy container file to local host docker cp <container_name>:/var/log/app.log ./app.log # View container filesystem modifications compared to the Image (A: Added, C: Changed, D: Deleted) docker diff <container_name> # Inspect full container low-level JSON properties (IP, Mounts, Env, Config, etc.) docker inspect <container_name> # Quickly extract container IP using jq or Go templates docker inspect -f '{{range .NetworkSettings.Networks}}{{.IPAddress}}{{end}}' <container_name>

# Search Docker Hub for images docker search nginx # Pull specific version of an image docker pull ubuntu:24.04 # List existing local images docker images # Display sorted by image size docker images --format "table {{.Repository}}\t{{.Tag}}\t{{.Size}}" | sort -k 3 -h # Build image (specifying Dockerfile and tag) docker build -t my-app:v1.0 . # Force rebuild without cache docker build --no-cache -t my-app:v1.0 . # Tag image for pushing to a Private Registry docker tag my-app:v1.0 registry.example.com/proj/my-app:v1.0 # Push to Registry docker push registry.example.com/proj/my-app:v1.0 # View image layer structure and build history (for troubleshooting bloated images) docker history --no-trunc my-app:v1.0 # Export and import images (offline deployment) docker save -o my-app.tar my-app:v1.0 docker load -i my-app.tar # Remove specific image docker rmi <image_id_or_name> # Force remove image (even if referenced by stopped containers) docker rmi -f <image_id_or_name>

# Create named volume docker volume create my-data-vol # List all volumes docker volume ls # List dangling volumes (not used by any container) docker volume ls -f dangling=true # Inspect actual host mountpoint of a volume docker volume inspect my-data-vol # Remove specific volume (must not be in use by any container) docker volume rm my-data-vol # Prune all unused volumes docker volume prune -f

# List all network drivers and network lists docker network ls # Create custom bridge network (supports direct DNS resolution between containers by service/container name) docker network create --driver bridge my-isolated-net # Create custom network with specific subnet docker network create --subnet 172.28.0.0/16 my-custom-net # Inspect network configuration, connected containers, and IPs docker network inspect my-isolated-net # Dynamically connect running container to network docker network connect my-isolated-net <container_name> # Disconnect container from network docker network disconnect my-isolated-net <container_name> # Remove unused network docker network rm my-isolated-net docker network prune -f

Compose V2 is integrated directly into the Docker CLI using Go, with commands structured around docker compose: # Start and run in background (auto-create networks and volumes) docker compose up -d # Force recreate containers (apply configuration or daemon.json changes) docker compose up -d --force-recreate # Build and start services docker compose up -d --build # Stop and remove Compose project containers and custom networks docker compose down # Stop and remove along with volume data (destructive operation, use with caution) docker compose down -v # Stop and remove all images (--rmi all or local) docker compose down --rmi local # Tail logs for all containers in project in real-time docker compose logs -f # Tail logs for specific service only docker compose logs -f <service_name> # View project container running status and port mapping docker compose ps # Restart specific single service docker compose restart <service_name> # Run a one-off command for a service temporarily (without exposing ports) docker compose run --rm <service_name> sh

# View Docker engine version and detailed architecture (Kernel, Storage Driver, OS, etc.) docker version docker info # Listen in real-time to Docker daemon events (container start, stop, OOM, etc.) docker events # Check resource usage breakdown by type docker system df # View detailed disk usage breakdown docker system df -v # One-click cleanup: stopped containers + unused networks + dangling images (<none>) docker system prune -f # Deep cleanup: includes all unreferenced images and build cache docker system prune -a -f
When system alerts trigger or the disk is full, avoid blind cleaning and locate the spatial distribution first.
documents.s: 1. Space Localization: What Is Eating Up the Hard Drive?

documents.t: Use Docker's built-in analysis tools to quickly pinpoint whether Images, Containers, Local Volumes, or Build Cache are taking up space: # View Docker overall resource usage summary docker system df # View detailed usage breakdown for each item (including container IDs, image sizes, and volume sharing info) docker system df -v

The default Docker storage path is /var/lib/docker (the following operations usually require root or sudo privileges). If docker system df shows anomalies but fails to catch the culprit, it is usually standard output logs (*-json.log) accumulated under /var/lib/docker/containers/. # Find the top 20 largest files or directories under /var/lib/docker (avoiding cross-filesystem scanning) sudo du -ahx /var/lib/docker | sort -rh | head -n 20 # Specifically check the JSON Log sizes of all containers and sort by capacity (descending) sudo find /var/lib/docker/containers/ -name "*-json.log" -exec du -h {} + | sort -rh | head -n 20
documents.s: 1.2 Linux System-Level Investigation (Hunting Hidden Bloated Files)

documents.t: When you discover that a container's log reaches tens of GBs, never delete it directly using rm -f <container_id>-json.log! Why can't you use rm? In the Linux kernel, as long as the Docker daemon (dockerd) still holds the file's File Descriptor (FD), even if the directory pointer is removed, the Inode remains in the (deleted) state and disk space will not be released until the Docker service is restarted.
documents.s: 2. Emergency Response: Log File Bloat First Aid (Live Truncation)

documents.t: Use the truncate command to reduce the file length to 0, which preserves the File Descriptor while immediately returning disk space: # Syntax: # sudo truncate -s 0 /var/lib/docker/containers/<CONTAINER_ID>/<CONTAINER_ID>-json.log # Example: Clear a single container's log sudo truncate -s 0 /var/lib/docker/containers/a1b2c3d4e5f6.../a1b2c3d4e5f6...-json.log # Universal first-aid command: One-click zeroing of all Docker json-logs larger than 100M on the host sudo find /var/lib/docker/containers/ -name "*-json.log" -size +100M -exec truncate -s 0 {} \;

Clearing is only for emergencies; without setting up Log Rotation, logs will eventually fill up the hard drive again. Restriction methods are divided into "global defaults" and "single project/container customization".
documents.s: 3. Permanent Solution: Limiting Log Limits and Auto-Rotation (Log Rotation)

documents.t: Once configured, all subsequently created containers will inherit this limit rule. Edit /etc/docker/daemon.json: { "log-driver": "json-file", "log-opts": { "max-size": "50m", "max-file": "3" } } max-size: Triggers rotation when a single log file reaches this size (e.g., 50m or 100m). max-file: Upper limit of rolling backup files retained. When exceeded, the oldest file is automatically overwritten. In this example, it uses a maximum of 50m * 3 = 150m. Reload settings and restart Docker service: systemctl daemon-reload systemctl restart docker Updated 2026-11-27 There are three things to note regarding the reload commands above: systemctl daemon-reload is only used to reload systemd .service unit files; modifying /etc/docker/daemon.json does not require running this command. systemctl restart docker will interrupt and restart all running containers on the host (unless "live-restore": true is enabled beforehand). If you only need to apply daemon.json options supporting hot-reloading, you can run sudo systemctl reload docker first; however, whether using reload or restart, log-driver and log-opts will still only apply to newly created containers afterwards. If docker compose down was already executed in the example below, containers and networks have been removed, and executing docker compose up -d right after will rebuild them without needing an additional --force-recreate; if you want to rebuild containers in place without tearing down the network, run docker compose up -d --force-recreate directly. Important Trap Reminder: Modifying daemon.json only takes effect for "newly created" containers after restart. Existing containers must be recreated to apply: # Containers managed by traditional run: docker stop <name> && docker rm <name> && docker run ... # Containers managed by Docker Compose: docker compose down && docker compose up -d
documents.s: Option A: Global Configuration (/etc/docker/daemon.json) —— Highly Recommended

documents.t: If certain applications (such as high-traffic Nginx, database synchronization services) require individual log quotas, you can declare them at the service level: services: app-service: image: my-app:latest logging: driver: "json-file" options: max-size: "10m" max-file: "3" Apply changes: docker compose up -d --force-recreate
documents.s: Option B: Compose Project Individual Configuration (compose.yaml)

documents.t: Before cleaning, make sure to clarify the impact scope of each level of cleanup commands to avoid accidentally deleting production data.

# 1. Safe cleanup (Daily use) # Deletes: All stopped containers, unused networks, dangling images (images without a tag like <none>) docker system prune -f # 2. Deep cleanup (Reclaiming large amounts of space) # Deletes: All stopped containers, unused networks, and "all images not currently referenced by any container" # Note: Re-opening applications will require pulling images again docker system prune -a -f # 3. Clean build cache # Caches left behind during Dockerfile build, which often accumulate tens of GBs over years docker builder prune -a -f

By default, docker system prune does not proactively delete Volumes, because Volumes usually store databases or persistent data. # List orphaned volumes (volumes not mounted by any container) docker volume ls -f dangling=true # Clear all orphaned volumes (Warning: If there are database containers out of maintenance but needed later, their data will be permanently lost!) docker volume prune -f # Ultimate cleanup (Sweeps up unmounted volumes as well; do not use lightly unless resetting the environment) docker system prune -a --volumes -f
documents.s: 4.2 Volume Cleanup (Most Dangerous, Extreme Caution Required)

documents.t: If there are legacy containers in the environment that cannot easily be refactored to apply max-size, you can use the host system's logrotate to create scheduled backups. Create /etc/logrotate.d/docker-containers (suggested precise match *-json.log): /var/lib/docker/containers/*/*-json.log { rotate 3 daily copytruncate compress missingok notifempty maxsize 100M } copytruncate: Very crucial. It copies the log file first and then truncates the original file to zero, without interrupting Docker's File Descriptor, equivalent to automating truncate. Test if configuration is correct (no actual changes, requires sudo privileges): sudo logrotate -d /etc/logrotate.d/docker-containers
documents.s: 5. Automated Blast-Proofing Mechanism: Linux Logrotate System Backup

If Logs are Bloated (du -ahx /var/lib/docker | grep -i 'json\.log') │ └─ Immediate First Aid ──> truncate -s 0 <path_to_log> │ └─ Permanent Fix ──> Configure /etc/docker/daemon.json (max-size/max-file) │ └─ Recreate containers to apply (docker compose down && docker compose up -d) │ └─ 3. documents.s: Portainer-CE and Portainer Agent Multi-Node Centralized Management

documents.t: Portainer adopts a typical Server-Agent architecture:

9443 (TCP): The default HTTPS management interface for modern Portainer-CE (older versions used 9000 for unencrypted HTTP; modern versions strongly recommend switching entirely to 9443). 9001 (TCP): Portainer Agent communication port. The agent listens on this port on managed nodes, waiting for the server to initiate connections (featuring bi-directional mTLS encryption). 8000 (TCP): Edge Agent reverse tunnel listening port (Edge Tunnel Server). When managed nodes are behind a NAT intranet or have firewalls strictly blocking external connections, the Edge Agent actively establishes a tunnel to the server's port 8000.
It is recommended to manage deployment with docker-compose.yml for easy volume configuration, automatic restarts, and reverse proxy integration.
mkdir -p /opt/portainer/data cd /opt/portainer
documents.s: Step 1: Create Dedicated Directory and Persistent Volumes

documents.t: services: portainer: image: portainer/portainer-ce:latest container_name: portainer restart: unless-stopped ports: - "9443:9443" # Official standard HTTPS interface - "8000:8000" # Edge Agent edge tunnel (open if connecting intranet nodes is needed) volumes: - /etc/localtime:/etc/localtime:ro - /var/run/docker.sock:/var/run/docker.sock:ro - /opt/portainer/data:/data networks: - portainer-net networks: portainer-net: driver: bridge Start the service: docker compose up -d Security Countdown Notice: After starting Portainer-CE for the first time, you must access https://<Server_IP>:9443 in a browser within 5 minutes to complete the initial administrator username and password setup. If timed out, the system will forcibly shut down to prevent unauthorized hijacking; in this case, restart the container (docker compose restart) to reset the timer.
Deploy portainer/agent on each VPS / node that needs to be managed.

Create /opt/portainer-agent/docker-compose.yml: services: agent: image: portainer/agent:latest container_name: portainer_agent restart: always ports: - "9001:9001" volumes: - /var/run/docker.sock:/var/run/docker.sock - /var/lib/docker/volumes:/var/lib/docker/volumes # Disable unnecessary privileged mode; relying solely on socket and volumes is sufficient Start the Agent: docker compose up -d

/var/run/docker.sock:/var/run/docker.sock: Allows the Agent to call the host's Docker API, reporting container operation status in real time and forwarding management commands. /var/lib/docker/volumes:/var/lib/docker/volumes: Allows the management console to directly browse, download, or upload files within volumes when clicking "Volumes" on the Web UI.

Log in to the Portainer Server Web interface. Click Environments -> Add environment in the left navigation bar. Select Docker Standalone -> Click Start Wizard. Select Portainer Agent: Name: Enter an identification name (e.g., VPS-Tokyo-01). Environment address: Enter the IP and port of the remote managed node in the format <VPS_IP>:9001. Click Connect. Once connected successfully, the remote VPS will appear in the home list. Click into it to manage containers, images, networks, and volumes on that machine just like managing the local host.
documents.s: 4. Adding Remote Nodes (Environments) in Portainer Server UI

documents.t: Exposing Portainer and Agents on a public VPS without proper protection is equivalent to handing over root privileges of the server.

While portainer/agent has built-in connection pairing verification, it is strongly recommended to restrict access in the managed VPS firewall (ufw or cloud security groups) to allow only the Portainer Server's public IP to access port 9001: # Execute on the managed VPS (using UFW as an example): sudo ufw default deny incoming sudo ufw allow ssh # Allow only the central Server IP to access port 9001 sudo ufw allow from <PORTAINER_SERVER_IP> to any port 9001 proto tcp sudo ufw reload
documents.s: 5.1 Strictly Limit Source IPs for Agent (Port 9001)

documents.t: If the managed node is behind a dynamic IP, NAT intranet, or you prefer not to expose port 9001 externally, you should use the Edge Agent instead: Select Edge Agent when adding an Environment on the Server side. The system will automatically generate a docker run command containing a key (Edge ID / Key). Paste and execute it on the managed node. The managed node will actively establish a secure reverse connection to the server's Port 8000, requiring zero inbound ports to be opened on the managed node.
documents.s: 5.2 Alternative Solution for Dynamic Public IPs: Edge Agent (Active Outbound Mode)

documents.t: If hosting the Server behind a reverse proxy to obtain a legitimate SSL certificate, note the following: WebSocket Support: Portainer's web terminal (Exec Console) relies on WebSockets, so the reverse proxy must maintain connection upgrading (in NPM, ensure Websockets Support is checked). Proxy Target Port: If NPM / Traefik and Portainer are on the same Docker network, it is recommended to reverse proxy directly to http://portainer:9000 (if the image still supports internal HTTP) or configure ignoring self-signed certificates when proxying https://portainer:9443.

documents.s: vlmcsd Local KMS Service Setup and Future Trends Analysis

documents.t: KMS Activation Essence: The KMS license period is 180 days. Clients automatically send renewal requests to the KMS server every 7 days; if the server is online, it resets to 180 days after each renewal. Supported Version Limitations: Windows: Only supports Volume License editions, Pro, Enterprise, Education, and Windows Server. Home Edition lacks KMS client components and cannot be activated directly (must be upgraded to Pro first). Office: Only supports Volume License editions (Office LTSC / Volume License). General retail editions (Retail / Click-to-Run Home editions) or Microsoft 365 subscription editions cannot be activated directly via KMS and require installing volume license editions through the Office Deployment Tool (ODT). GVLK (Generic Volume License Key): Generic volume license keys publicly provided by Microsoft. Their sole purpose is to guide the system to "seek authentication from the KMS server within the local network," and they are not pirated serial numbers.
vlmcsd resource consumption is extremely low (memory is typically less than 5MB), and it only needs to listen on the standard KMS protocol port TCP 1688.
mkdir -p /opt/vlmcsd cd /opt/vlmcsd
services: vlmcsd: image: mikolatero/vlmcsd:latest container_name: vlmcsd restart: unless-stopped ports: - "1688:1688" Start the service and check logs: docker compose up -d docker compose logs -f

Open Command Prompt (CMD) as Administrator or PowerShell (Updated 2026-11-27: The following example uses CMD's dedicated :: comment syntax; please run it in CMD. If using PowerShell, replace :: with #): :: 1. (Optional) Clear previously bound product key slmgr.vbs /upk :: 2. Install the official Microsoft GVLK key for your corresponding version slmgr.vbs /ipk <GVLK-KEY> :: 3. Point to your vlmcsd server IP or internal network hostname slmgr.vbs /skms <DOCKER_HOST_IP>:1688 :: 4. Trigger connection activation slmgr.vbs /ato :: 5. View detailed authorization status and expiration countdown slmgr.vbs /dlv
