documents.s: Traefik v3 Reverse Proxy and Automated SSL Deployment

documents.t: Traefik's data flow and configuration logic consist of three core abstractions: [External Request (Client)] │ (Port 80 / 443) ▼ [EntryPoints] ─── (web / websecure: Defines listened protocols and ports) │ ▼ [Routers] ─── (Resolves requests based on Rules such as Host(`app.example.com`)) │ ├─► [Middlewares] ─── (Intermediate processing: HTTP to HTTPS, Basic Auth, Rate Limit, etc.) │ ▼ [Services] ─── (Forwards to corresponding container IP and internal Port) │ ▼ [Backend Container (Backend App)] Static Configuration: Defines global infrastructure (EntryPoints, Providers, ACME certificate resolvers). Loaded at startup, supports CLI arguments (command:) or static configuration files (traefik.yml). Dynamic Configuration: Defines routing rules (Routers, Services, Middlewares), dynamically injected by Providers (Docker Labels in this case). When containers restart or change, Traefik itself does not need to be restarted. SSL Certificate Storage (acme.json): Traefik integrates the ACME client, and all private keys and certificates issued by Let's Encrypt are stored in a single JSON file. The permissions of this file must be strictly restricted to 600, otherwise Traefik will refuse to load it for security reasons.

Compared to the older v2.5, Traefik v3 brings several modern and simplified improvements: EntryPoints Native Support for HTTP to HTTPS: No longer requires declaring tedious hostregexp catch-all and RedirectScheme middlewares in Routers; enabling redirections directly on the EntryPoint applies it globally. ACME Challenge Mutual Exclusivity: You cannot enable httpChallenge and tlsChallenge simultaneously; choose one (generally tlsChallenge is recommended, using port 443 for maximum simplicity). Security Hardening: The Dashboard by default must be protected with explicit middleware validation (such as BasicAuth) and is not allowed to be exposed unprotected.

To prevent interference between project containers and the Traefik network, create a global shared Docker Bridge network: # Create Traefik dedicated shared external network docker network create proxy-network # Create directory for certificates and initialize acme.json permissions (must be 600) mkdir -p /opt/traefik/letsencrypt touch /opt/traefik/letsencrypt/acme.json chmod 600 /opt/traefik/letsencrypt/acme.json # Create BasicAuth username and password (using admin / secret123 as an example, requires apache2-utils or openssl/htpasswd) # Format: username:hashed_password (Note: $ must be written as $$ in YAML to avoid escaping) echo $(htpasswd -nb admin secret123) # Output example: admin:$apr1$xyz123... -> When writing to label, convert to admin:$$apr1$$xyz123...
documents.s: Step 1: Create Dedicated Network and Mount Directories

documents.t: Configure in /opt/traefik/docker-compose.yml: services: traefik: image: traefik:v3.1 container_name: traefik restart: unless-stopped security_opt: - no-new-privileges:true networks: - proxy-network ports: - "80:80" - "443:443" # To directly access debug/dashboard, port 8080 can be opened; in production, accessing via internal Router and closing port 8080 mapping is recommended # - "8080:8080" volumes: - /etc/localtime:/etc/localtime:ro - /var/run/docker.sock:/var/run/docker.sock:ro - /opt/traefik/letsencrypt/acme.json:/letsencrypt/acme.json command: #### 1. API and Dashboard #### - --api.dashboard=true - --api.insecure=false #### 2. Logging and Debug Records #### - --log.level=INFO - --accesslog=true #### 3. Docker Provider Settings #### - --providers.docker=true - --providers.docker.exposedbydefault=false # Do not expose by default, must explicitly add label to proxy - --providers.docker.network=proxy-network # Explicitly specify default communication network #### 4. EntryPoints (Port Definitions) #### # HTTP (Port 80) - v3 natively built-in global redirect to HTTPS - --entrypoints.web.address=:80 - --entrypoints.web.http.redirections.entrypoint.to=websecure - --entrypoints.web.http.redirections.entrypoint.scheme=https - --entrypoints.web.http.redirections.entrypoint.permanent=true # HTTPS (Port 443) - --entrypoints.websecure.address=:443 #### 5. Certificate Resolver (Let's Encrypt ACME) #### # Use TLS-ALPN-01 challenge (verifies directly on port 443, no extra file directory opening required) - --certificatesresolvers.myresolver.acme.tlschallenge=true - --certificatesresolvers.myresolver.acme.email=your-email@example.com - --certificatesresolvers.myresolver.acme.storage=/letsencrypt/acme.json labels: - "traefik.enable=true" # --- Dashboard Routing Configuration (HTTPS) --- - "traefik.http.routers.traefik-dashboard.rule=Host(`traefik.example.com`)" - "traefik.http.routers.traefik-dashboard.entrypoints=websecure" - "traefik.http.routers.traefik-dashboard.service=api@internal" - "traefik.http.routers.traefik-dashboard.tls=true" - "traefik.http.routers.traefik-dashboard.tls.certresolver=myresolver" # --- Dashboard Security Defense (BasicAuth Middleware) --- - "traefik.http.routers.traefik-dashboard.middlewares=auth" # Note: $ symbols in password strings must be escaped as $$ in compose - "traefik.http.middlewares.auth.basicauth.users=admin:$$apr1$$xyz123...YourHash..." networks: proxy-network: external: true

When deploying any web service, there is no need to declare ports to expose to the Host, you only need to meet two conditions: Join the shared external network proxy-network. Annotate labels to tell Traefik the service's domain name and target Port.
The hierarchical rules of Traefik Labels follow: traefik.<protocol>.<component_type>.<custom_identifier>.<specific_parameter>=<value>

services: whoami: image: traefik/whoami container_name: test-whoami restart: unless-stopped networks: - proxy-network # No need to write ports: ["80:80"], container resides entirely in internal network, enhancing host security labels: # 1. Enable Traefik awareness - "traefik.enable=true" # 2. Define HTTPS Router rule - "traefik.http.routers.whoami.rule=Host(`whoami.example.com`)" - "traefik.http.routers.whoami.entrypoints=websecure" # 3. Enable automatic TLS certificate request - "traefik.http.routers.whoami.tls=true" - "traefik.http.routers.whoami.tls.certresolver=myresolver" # 4. Specify internal forwarding Port (mandatory if the image exposes multiple ports or uses a custom port) - "traefik.http.services.whoami.loadbalancer.server.port=80" networks: proxy-network: external: true
documents.s: Example: Deploying Whoami Test Service and Independent Applications (e.g., V2ray / Web App)

documents.t: In Docker Labels, various security and filtering middlewares can be mounted in front of applications:

labels: - "traefik.http.middlewares.sec-headers.headers.sslredirect=true" - "traefik.http.middlewares.sec-headers.headers.stsseconds=31536000" - "traefik.http.middlewares.sec-headers.headers.browserxssfilter=true" - "traefik.http.middlewares.sec-headers.headers.contenttypenosniff=true" - "traefik.http.routers.myapp.middlewares=sec-headers" Updated 2026-11-27 headers.sslredirect was officially removed in Traefik v3; keeping this parameter in v3 configuration files will cause startup failure. For HTTP to HTTPS redirection, please instead use the EntryPoints global redirection configuration demonstrated in Section 2 (--entrypoints.web.http.redirections.entrypoint.*) or use the redirectScheme middleware. Additionally, browserxssfilter (X-XSS-Protection) has also been deprecated by modern browsers.

Prevent brute-force attacks on APIs or login endpoints: labels: # Average 100 requests per second, maximum burst of 50 - "traefik.http.middlewares.my-ratelimit.ratelimit.average=100" - "traefik.http.middlewares.my-ratelimit.ratelimit.burst=50" - "traefik.http.routers.myapp.middlewares=my-ratelimit"

Automatically strip /api when forwarding example.com/api/* to the container: labels: - "traefik.http.routers.myapi.rule=Host(`example.com`) && PathPrefix(`/api`)" - "traefik.http.middlewares.api-strip.stripprefix.prefixes=/api" - "traefik.http.routers.myapi.middlewares=api-strip"

Backend containers (such as Nextcloud, WordPress, V2ray, etc.) should run HTTP internally, and self-signing certificates or running HTTPS inside containers is strictly prohibited. All certificate encryption and decryption are completed at the Traefik boundary (SSL Offloading). Communication between containers and Traefik runs over pure HTTP via internal Docker networks, greatly reducing computing overhead and avoiding certificate conflicts.

Common Error Phenomenon Root Cause Troubleshooting Action permissions of /letsencrypt/acme.json are too open File permissions are not 600 Run chmod 600 /opt/traefik/letsencrypt/acme.json and restart Traefik. Cannot obtain certificates: 403 / 400 urn:ietf:params:acme:error External Port 80/443 closed or DNS not effective Verify external firewall/router maps 80/443 to the host, and Public DNS A record fully points to the local public IP. Bad Gateway (502) Traefik cannot reach backend container 1. Check if backend container joined proxy-network. 2. Check if loadbalancer.server.port matches container internal listening port. Forwarding confusion when container has multiple ports Image defines multiple EXPOSE ports Must explicitly lock down via traefik.http.services.<name>.loadbalancer.server.port=<port>.

NPM stores Proxy Hosts, Redirections, and user account information in its backend. SQLite (Strongly Recommended): Modern NPM versions include built-in SQLite by default. Unless you have multi-node load balancing or clustering requirements, using SQLite eliminates external relational database dependencies entirely, saving memory and greatly reducing maintenance complexity. MariaDB / MySQL: If your environment already features a centralized DB (such as a shared LibreNMS or WordPress pool) or has high availability requirements, you can switch via environment variables.

It is recommended to create an independent, global Docker network (e.g., npm-network) so that other backend containers can easily join this network and communicate directly via Container Names, without requiring any physical port mapping on the host.
# Create shared network (if not already created) docker network create npm-network # Create persistent data directories mkdir -p /opt/npm/data mkdir -p /opt/npm/letsencrypt
documents.s: Step 1: Create Pre-requisite Directories and Custom Network

documents.t: Define the service in /opt/npm/docker-compose.yml: services: npm: image: jc21/nginx-proxy-manager:latest container_name: nginx-proxy-manager restart: unless-stopped ports: - "80:80" # HTTP forwarding and ACME challenges - "81:81" # Web management dashboard - "443:443" # HTTPS forwarding volumes: - /opt/npm/data:/data - /opt/npm/letsencrypt:/etc/letsencrypt networks: - npm-network networks: npm-network: external: true Start the service: docker compose up -d

Access via browser: http://<Host_IP>:81 Default Credentials: Email: admin@example.com / Password: changeme (Updated 2026-11-27: Modern NPM versions prompt you to create an administrator account directly upon first opening the WebUI, bypassing default credentials. Default credentials are only applicable to legacy versions and require a mandatory password change upon first login) Email: admin@example.com Password: changeme Upon initial login, the system mandates changing the administrator name, email, and password. Please store your new credentials securely.

Beyond exposing services externally, NPM's most elegant usage in internal environments (paired with internal DNS like AdGuard Home, Pi-hole, or Unbound) is forwarding directly using the "Container Name" as the destination.
documents.s: 4. Core Architecture Highlight: Internal Container Name Redirection (Zero-Port Mapping)

documents.t: Same Docker Network: Docker features a built-in Embedded DNS Server (127.0.0.11). As long as two containers share a custom bridge network (e.g., npm-network), they can resolve each other's internal IP addresses directly using container names. Backend Containers Need No Port Mapping: Backend containers (such as Emby, Jellyfin, Vaultwarden) do not need to expose ports to the host via ports: at all; they only need to listen on internal ports inside the container. This prevents host port conflicts and significantly reduces the internal attack surface.

services: emby: image: amir20/clash # or any other image; using emby as an example here container_name: emby restart: unless-stopped # Crucial: No ports: - "8096:8096" mapping required at all networks: - npm-network networks: npm-network: external: true Updated 2026-11-27 image: amir20/clash in the example above was a misattribution (amir20 is actually the developer of Dozzle, and Clash is not a media server). For actual Emby deployments, use the official image emby/embyserver:latest or lscr.io/linuxserver/emby:latest.

Navigate to Hosts -> Proxy Hosts -> Add Proxy Host. Fill out the Details tab: Domain Names: emby.internal.local (resolved to the NPM host IP in internal DNS) Scheme: http Forward Hostname / IP: emby (enter the container name directly) Forward Port: 8096 (enter the container's internal listen port) Check Block Common Exploits and Websockets Support (if the application requires real-time communications).
Many mistakenly believe NPM can only renew certificates through the UI via Let's Encrypt, but NPM fully supports importing existing local certificates (Custom Certificates):
documents.s: 5. Certificate Management: Custom SSL and Let's Encrypt

documents.t: If you have already obtained certificates on the host or via acme.sh / DNS API: Go to SSL Certificates -> Add SSL Certificate -> Select Custom. Name the certificate (e.g., My-Wildcard-Cert). Paste or upload files: Certificate Key: Paste private key content (*.key). Certificate: Paste the full certificate chain (fullchain.pem or a file combining the certificate body and intermediate CA). Save, and select the custom certificate from the dropdown in the Proxy Host's SSL tab.

HTTP-01 Challenge: Enter domain names directly; requires port 80 to be accessible from the public internet. DNS-01 Challenge (Wildcard Certificate Recommended): Check Use a DNS Challenge, select your DNS provider (e.g., Cloudflare), and enter your API Token to automatically issue *.example.com wildcard certificates.
documents.s: 5.2 Automatic Let's Encrypt Generation via NPM

documents.t: Applications like Calibre-Web are sensitive to reverse proxy headers and script names. Solution: In the NPM Host settings under Custom Locations -> Add the corresponding path, click the gear icon (advanced settings), and paste the following Nginx header directives: proxy_bind $server_addr; proxy_set_header Host $http_host; proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for; proxy_set_header X-Scheme $scheme; proxy_set_header X-Script-Name /${your_location};
documents.s: 6.1 Calibre-Web Layout Breaking or Redirection Failure Under Subpaths / Reverse Proxy

documents.t: Root Cause: Portainer-CE frontend Angular/Vue resource paths use absolute paths relative to root /. Embedding it under subpaths like /portainer causes numerous JS/CSS 404 errors, and WebSockets (/api/websocket/...) are easily disrupted. Best Practice: It is strongly recommended not to use subpaths; always mount virtual hosts using independent subdomains (e.g., portainer.internal.local). Important Configuration: When reverse proxying Portainer, ensure Websockets Support is checked in NPM, otherwise the web terminal (Console / Exec) will disconnect immediately.

If a domain name points directly to NPM without matching any host, it displays NPM's default "Congratulations" page. Practical Tip: Create a dashboard container (such as Homepage, Dashy, or Heimdall) and set up a default fallback or primary domain Proxy Host in NPM pointing to that dashboard container to serve as your HomeLab entry navigation homepage.

Comparison Metric Nginx Proxy Manager (NPM) Traefik (v3) Primary Focus Graphical management, intuitive operations, traditional Nginx extensions Cloud-Native, declarative configuration, microservice edge routing Configuration Entry Web UI (stored in DB) Docker Labels or static/dynamic YAML/TOML Auto-Discovery Manual Host and Port addition via UI Auto-monitors docker.sock, automatically brings up containers on startup External Non-Docker Services Extremely friendly (supports entering physical host IP:Ports arbitrarily in UI) Requires writing extra dynamic configuration files via File Provider Learning Curve Extremely low, 5 minutes to get started Moderate, requires understanding Router / Middleware / Service concepts Best Scenario Internal DNS redirection, small projects, mixed non-containerized bare-metal environments Pure Docker / K8s environments, high-dynamic container stacks, unattended automated deployments
documents.s: 7. Traefik vs. Nginx Proxy Manager Quick Selection Guide

documents.t: WireGuard adopts a peer-to-peer (P2P) concept. Every machine in the architecture is essentially a "Peer," though the host with a fixed public IP address is typically treated as the "Server / Relay Node": [Client (Phone / Laptop)] (WireGuard IP: 10.13.13.2) │ │ UDP (Encrypted packets, default port 51820) ▼ [WireGuard Server Container] (WireGuard IP: 10.13.13.1 / Host Public IP:Port) │ ├─► [LAN Devices (LAN Access)] (192.168.1.0/24) └─► [Internet (Full Tunnel Forwarding)] (0.0.0.0/0) UDP Protocol: WireGuard runs entirely on UDP. When no data is being transmitted, it sends zero probe packets, behaving essentially like "silence with no response" and offering excellent scan-resistance. Cryptokey Routing: The server strongly binds each client's Public Key to its assigned internal IP. Only packets with a valid signature and a source IP matching the declared IP are accepted.

The standout feature of LinuxServer.io's image is that upon startup, based on the PEERS names declared in environment variables, it automatically generates the corresponding client configuration files (peer_*.conf) and terminal QR codes, saving you from the tedious process of manually generating keys and setting up routes.
sudo mkdir -p /opt/wireguard/config

Define in /opt/wireguard/docker-compose.yml: services: wireguard: image: ghcr.io/linuxserver/wireguard:latest container_name: wireguard restart: unless-stopped cap_add: - NET_ADMIN - SYS_MODULE environment: - PUID=1000 - PGID=1000 - TZ=Asia/Taipei # 1. External access address (Public static IP or DDNS domain name) - SERVERURL=vpn.example.com # 2. External listening UDP port - SERVERPORT=51820 # 3. Client naming list (comma-separated, automatically generates corresponding configuration files) - PEERS=phone,laptop,ipad # 4. DNS servers assigned to clients (can be 1.1.1.1, 8.8.8.8, or internal AdGuard Home IP) - PEERDNS=1.1.1.1 # 5. WireGuard internal virtual subnet (Server automatically acquires .1 in this subnet) - INTERNAL_SUBNET=10.13.13.0/24 # 6. Default AllowedIPs range pushed to clients (0.0.0.0/0 means full traffic forwarding) - ALLOWEDIPS=0.0.0.0/0 volumes: - /opt/wireguard/config:/config - /lib/modules:/lib/modules:ro ports: - "51820:51820/udp" sysctls: - net.ipv4.conf.all.src_valid_mark=1 Core Parameters & Permissions Note: cap_add: [NET_ADMIN, SYS_MODULE]: The container needs to manipulate the host's virtual network interface (TUN) and load the WireGuard kernel module. /lib/modules:/lib/modules:ro: Allows the container to load the host's WireGuard kernel driver for ultimate performance (natively built into Linux 5.6+ kernels). net.ipv4.conf.all.src_valid_mark=1: Prevents packets from being dropped by rp_filter in multi-routing-table environments. Start the service: docker compose up -d

Install the official WireGuard app from Google Play or App Store. View the QR code generated by the container: # View logs to find the QR code for a specific peer docker compose logs -f wireguard # Or use the container's internal tool to display a specific peer (e.g., phone) docker compose exec wireguard /app/show-peer phone Open the mobile WireGuard app, tap the + button -> select "Scan from QR code" to instantly import and enable it.

All generated configuration files are saved in the host's mounted directory: # View generated configuration files ls -l /opt/wireguard/config/peer_laptop/ # Contents include: # - peer_laptop.conf (Standard configuration file) # - peer_laptop.png (QR code image file) # - privatekey-peer_laptop / publickey-peer_laptop
On Linux desktops or servers, there are two main connection methods: the traditional wg-quick CLI tool, and NetworkManager integrated with desktop network management.
documents.s: 4. Linux Client Setup Practice (Taking Arch / Manjaro / Debian / Ubuntu as Examples)

documents.t: Install utility packages: # Arch / Manjaro sudo pacman -S wireguard-tools # Ubuntu / Debian sudo apt-get install -y wireguard-tools Deploy configuration file: Copy the server-generated peer_laptop.conf to the client's /etc/wireguard/ and rename it to your preferred interface name (e.g., wg0.conf): sudo mkdir -p /etc/wireguard sudo cp peer_laptop.conf /etc/wireguard/wg0.conf # Strictly limit key file permissions (otherwise wg-quick will warn) sudo chmod 600 /etc/wireguard/wg0.conf Start and stop connections: # Start connection (interface name corresponds to filename wg0) sudo wg-quick up wg0 # View connection status and transfer volume (Transfer RX/TX) sudo wg show # Disconnect sudo wg-quick down wg0 (Optional) Set up automatic connection on boot: sudo systemctl enable wg-quick@wg0
documents.s: Method A: Using wg-quick CLI (Recommended for Servers or Lightweight Environments)

documents.t: If you use desktop systems like GNOME / KDE, you can import with a single nmcli command and then use the network icon in the top right corner of the system to toggle it: # Import config file to create connection profile with a single command sudo nmcli connection import type wireguard file /etc/wireguard/wg0.conf # Enable connection nmcli connection up wg0 # Disconnect nmcli connection down wg0 (After importing, you can freely toggle switches and modify settings in the system's "Network Settings" graphical interface).
documents.s: Method B: Importing into NetworkManager / GUI (Recommended for Desktop Environments)

documents.t: AllowedIPs in the client configuration file is the most common cause of "original network breaking as soon as VPN turns on" or "other server services becoming unreachable." It has dual functions: Local Route Injection: Determines which destination IP traffic from the local machine should be pushed into the WireGuard tunnel. Inbound Packet Filtering: Determines which source IP packets are allowed to be received by the WireGuard interface.
documents.s: 5. Core Pitfall: AllowedIPs Routing Planning (Full Tunnel vs. Split Tunnel)

documents.t: When connecting to public Wi-Fi away from home, you want all network traffic to proxy out via your home / VPS WireGuard server: [Peer] # Includes all IPv4 and IPv6 subnets AllowedIPs = 0.0.0.0/0, ::/0 Note: When set to 0.0.0.0/0, WireGuard takes over the Default Gateway. If there are other services or local servers on the client's local subnet, you may need to ensure local LAN routes are excluded.

You only want to securely access remote home / datacenter internal devices (such as connecting back to a NAS, HomeLab, or viewing internal web pages), while regular web browsing (YouTube, Google) still goes through your original broadband: [Peer] # Route only remote internal subnets (e.g., 192.168.1.0/24) and WireGuard's own subnet (10.13.13.0/24) through VPN AllowedIPs = 10.13.13.0/24, 192.168.1.0/24
documents.s: Scenario 2: Split Tunnel (Access Internal Network Devices Only)

documents.t: WireGuard is stateless by default. If your client is behind NAT (home router, mobile hotspot 4G/5G), the router's NAT mapping table typically clears expired UDP connection states after tens of seconds to a few minutes. This causes "the client can send requests to the server, but when the server proactively sends data, it cannot reach the client" (e.g., delayed push notifications on the client).

Add the following to the [Peer] section of the client configuration file: [Peer] # Actively send a lightweight keepalive packet to the server every 25 seconds to maintain NAT hole punching PersistentKeepalive = 25 (The peer.conf generated by LinuxServer.io by default usually includes this setting).

Anomaly Symptom Root Cause Troubleshooting Steps Client has no internet access at all after connecting Linux kernel on the host has not enabled IPv4 Forwarding Run on the host: `echo "net.ipv4.ip_forward = 1" Connected, but only TX increases in transfer volume while RX is 0 1. External firewall has not allowed UDP 51820. 2. SERVERURL or SERVERPORT entered incorrectly. 3. Cloud platform (e.g., OCI, AWS, GCP) security group missed opening UDP. 1. Confirm cloud console allows 0.0.0.0/0 -> UDP 51820. 2. Check listening on host: `sudo ss -ulpn Client phone connects normally, but occasionally freezes after IP change MTU is too large, causing packet fragmentation to be dropped by ISP Mobile clients usually work fine with default 1420. If unstable under mobile network, try manually adding MTU = 1280 to client [Interface]. Want to dynamically add more Peers Compose file environment variable changes 1. Edit docker-compose.yml, append new names after PEERS= (e.g., PEERS=phone,laptop,ipad,newpc). 2. Run docker compose up -d, container will automatically generate config files for new peers without affecting existing ones.
documents.s: 7. Server-Side Core Forwarding and Common Troubleshooting

documents.t: Dashboard Portal: Consolidates cluttered intranet ports (e.g., Portainer :9443, LibreNMS :8000, Node-RED :1880, Nextcloud) into visual cards. SSL Offloading Mechanism: Since frontend traffic is typically handled by NPM / Traefik for HTTPS certificates, Heimdall itself does not need port 443 exposed externally. It only needs to listen on port 80 internally, eliminating certificate management overhead. Data Persistence: All user settings, card arrangements, custom icons, and the built-in SQLite database are stored in the container's /config directory.
sudo mkdir -p /opt/heimdall/config sudo chown -R 1000:1000 /opt/heimdall/config
documents.s: Step 1: Create Persistent Directory and Permissions

documents.t: Define in /opt/heimdall/docker-compose.yml: services: heimdall: image: ghcr.io/linuxserver/heimdall:latest container_name: heimdall restart: unless-stopped environment: - PUID=1000 - PGID=1000 - TZ=Asia/Taipei volumes: - /opt/heimdall/config:/config # If using a reverse proxy, expose the internal port or attach directly to a shared network ports: - "8081:80" networks: - proxy-network networks: proxy-network: external: true Start the service: docker compose up -d

Add a Proxy Host in NPM: Domain Names: home.example.com (or your main domain name) Forward Hostname / IP: heimdall (use the container name directly when on the same proxy-network) Forward Port: 80 Check Websockets Support and Block Common Exploits. Request or mount an SSL certificate and enable Force SSL.
documents.s: 3.1 Using Nginx Proxy Manager (NPM) as Default Homepage

documents.t: If using Traefik, you can add labels directly to the heimdall service section in docker-compose.yml and remove the ports: mapping: labels: - "traefik.enable=true" - "traefik.http.routers.heimdall.rule=Host(`home.example.com`)" - "traefik.http.routers.heimdall.entrypoints=websecure" - "traefik.http.routers.heimdall.tls=true" - "traefik.http.routers.heimdall.tls.certresolver=myresolver" - "traefik.http.services.heimdall.loadbalancer.server.port=80"
Heimdall cards are not just static shortcuts; they also support connecting to backend APIs to display real-time data in real time (Enhanced Apps).

Click the "+" button (Add item) in the bottom-right corner of the homepage. Enter the service name in Application Name (e.g., Nextcloud or Portainer). The system will automatically pull from the official supported list and fill in the default icon and background color. Enter the URL (e.g., https://cloud.example.com).

If the service supports API integration (such as Pi-hole, AdGuard Home, qBittorrent, Transmission, Plex, Proxmox): A Config section will appear below the card settings. Enter the application's API Key, Token, or username and password. Effect: The card will directly display Pi-hole's "Blocked Ads / Total Queries", the downloader's "Real-Time Download / Upload Speed", or the media library's "Now Playing Count".
documents.s: 4.2 Enabling Enhanced Apps Real-Time Status Display

documents.t: The default solid color background and large block style are relatively plain, but can be upgraded via built-in features and custom CSS:

Click the gear icon (Settings) in the bottom-right corner. Background Image: Upload a 4K wallpaper (or specify an Unsplash random wallpaper URL). Background Blur / Opacity: If card text is hard to read, adjust the background blur and overlay darkness in settings. Check Dark Mode.
documents.s: 5.1 Custom High-Resolution Wallpaper and Dark Mode

documents.t: Most of Heimdall's built-in icons are PNG raster images, which blur when enlarged. You can download corresponding SVGs / high-resolution PNGs from community-maintained open-source icon libraries (such as walkxcode/dashboard-icons) and upload custom icons directly when editing cards.
documents.s: 5.2 Importing Community High-Quality Vector Icons (Dashboard Icons)

documents.t: Heimdall supports custom stylesheet files on the host. Edit /opt/heimdall/config/www/custom.css (create if it doesn't exist): /* Make cards translucent with frosted glass effect */ .item { background: rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.1) !important; backdrop-filter: blur(12px) !important; -webkit-backdrop-filter: blur(12px) !important; border: 1px solid rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.18) !important; border-radius: 12px !important; box-shadow: 0 8px 32px 0 rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.37) !important; transition: transform 0.2s ease, box-shadow 0.2s ease !important; } /* Slightly float and scale up on mouse hover */ .item:hover { transform: translateY(-4px) scale(1.02) !important; box-shadow: 0 12px 40px 0 rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.5) !important; } /* Hide extra edit button in bottom-right corner when not logged in (cleaner guest mode) */ body:not(.logged-in) #edit-toggle { display: none; } After editing, hard refresh your browser (Ctrl + F5) to apply the changes.
documents.s: 5.3 Injecting Custom CSS for Glassmorphism Cards

documents.t: Heimdall's advantage lies in completing all configurations purely through Web UI clicks, but if you seek more powerful real-time system monitoring, Docker container status linking, or declarative (YAML) maintenance, you can evaluate mainstream community alternatives in recent years: Dashboard Name Configuration Method Resource Usage Core Features Target Audience Heimdall Pure Web GUI Very low (~30MB) Click-based operation, built-in simple API data cards, 1-minute quick start Users who want intuitive operation without writing config files Homepage (gethomepage.dev) Pure YAML File Low (~50MB) Highly modular, auto-aware Docker status, rich system resource Widgets (CPU/RAM/Disk) Players who like code-based management (GitOps / Infrastructure as Code) Homarr Web GUI + Drag-and-Drop Medium (~150MB) Free grid drag-and-drop layout, built-in file manager, torrent search and Docker management Users pursuing highly customizable dashboard layouts Dashy YAML + Web GUI Dual Higher (~200MB) Extremely rich features, custom appearance themes support, Status Check health checks Advanced users requiring high-density information display and precise pixel control

All Heimdall configurations (including users, cards, background images, and uploaded icons) are centralized within the /config directory: # Backup configuration sudo tar -czvf /opt/backups/heimdall-$(date +%F).tar.gz -C /opt/heimdall config # Restore configuration sudo tar -xzvf /opt/backups/heimdall-*.tar.gz -C /opt/heimdall/ sudo chown -R 1000:1000 /opt/heimdall/config docker compose restart heimdall Updated 2026-11-27 If the wildcard heimdall-*.tar.gz in the restore command above matches multiple backup files in the directory, tar will fail; please specify a single exact filename during actual restoration (e.g., heimdall-2026-09-04.tar.gz).

Image Selection: Strongly prefer the official standard image nextcloud:apache (or nextcloud:latest). It bundles an integrated Apache + PHP-FPM environment and has the most mature compatibility with X-Forwarded-* headers. Strictly avoid LinuxServer.io's Nextcloud image: That image ships with a pre-installed Nginx and self-signed SSL workflow, which seriously conflicts with SSL offloading at an external reverse proxy. Permission Trap (UID 33): Inside the official container, the process runs as www-data, whose UID and GID are both 33. Host-mounted directories must be owned by 33:33; otherwise startup will fail because .ocdata or the data directory cannot be read or written. Data Directory Separation (NEXTCLOUD_DATA_DIR): Mount user-uploaded data separately at /var/www/data (outside the web root /var/www/html). This both improves security and makes it easy to snapshot or mount external disk volumes independently.

# Create the application directory and a separate data storage directory sudo mkdir -p /opt/nextcloud/html sudo mkdir -p /opt/nextcloud/data # Grant ownership to www-data (UID 33) inside the container sudo chown -R 33:33 /opt/nextcloud/html /opt/nextcloud/data sudo chmod 750 /opt/nextcloud/data
documents.s: Step 1: Create Dedicated Directories and Fix Permissions

documents.t: Configure /opt/nextcloud/docker-compose.yml: services: nextcloud: image: nextcloud:apache container_name: nextcloud restart: unless-stopped environment: - TZ=Asia/Taipei # 1. Initial database configuration (using SQLite) - SQLITE_DATABASE=nextcloud # 2. Separate data directory path (avoids nested mount issues) - NEXTCLOUD_DATA_DIR=/var/www/data # 3. Trusted domains on initial install (space-separated for multiple) - NEXTCLOUD_TRUSTED_DOMAINS=cloud.example.com # 4. Trusted proxy subnets (Docker default subnets) - TRUSTED_PROXIES=172.16.0.0/12 10.0.0.0/8 192.168.0.0/16 # 5. Force external URLs to be recognized as HTTPS (key to preventing http redirects on login and CSRF failures) - OVERWRITEPROTOCOL=https - OVERWRITECLIURL=https://cloud.example.com - OVERWRITEHOST=cloud.example.com # 6. PHP runtime quota tuning - PHP_MEMORY_LIMIT=1024M - PHP_UPLOAD_LIMIT=16G volumes: - /opt/nextcloud/html:/var/www/html - /opt/nextcloud/data:/var/www/data networks: - proxy-network labels: - "traefik.enable=true" # --- [Basic Router Settings] --- - "traefik.http.routers.nextcloud.rule=Host(`cloud.example.com`)" - "traefik.http.routers.nextcloud.entrypoints=websecure" - "traefik.http.routers.nextcloud.tls=true" - "traefik.http.routers.nextcloud.tls.certresolver=myresolver" # Attach middleware chain - "traefik.http.routers.nextcloud.middlewares=nc-dav,nc-wellknown,nc-headers" # Explicitly forward to port 80 of Apache inside the container - "traefik.http.services.nextcloud.loadbalancer.server.port=80" # --- [Middleware 1: CalDAV / CardDAV Redirect] --- - "traefik.http.middlewares.nc-dav.redirectregex.regex=^https://(.*)/\\.well-known/(card|cal)dav(.*)" - "traefik.http.middlewares.nc-dav.redirectregex.replacement=https://$${1}/remote.php/dav$${3}" - "traefik.http.middlewares.nc-dav.redirectregex.permanent=true" # --- [Middleware 2: Webfinger / Nodeinfo Redirect (clears newer yellow warnings)] --- - "traefik.http.middlewares.nc-wellknown.redirectregex.regex=^https://(.*)/\\.well-known/(webfinger|nodeinfo)(.*)" - "traefik.http.middlewares.nc-wellknown.redirectregex.replacement=https://$${1}/index.php/.well-known/$${2}$${3}" - "traefik.http.middlewares.nc-wellknown.redirectregex.permanent=true" # --- [Middleware 3: Security Headers & HSTS] --- - "traefik.http.middlewares.nc-headers.headers.stsSeconds=31536000" - "traefik.http.middlewares.nc-headers.headers.stsIncludeSubdomains=true" - "traefik.http.middlewares.nc-headers.headers.stsPreload=true" - "traefik.http.middlewares.nc-headers.headers.contentTypeNosniff=true" - "traefik.http.middlewares.nc-headers.headers.browserXssFilter=true" networks: proxy-network: external: true Start the service: docker compose up -d
After creating the admin account in the web UI, go to "Administration settings" → "Overview". If any warnings appear, resolve them directly as follows:
documents.s: 3. Post-Initialization Configuration and Resolving All Warnings

documents.t: The official image already comes with the APCu module compiled in, but it must be enabled manually in the configuration file: Edit /opt/nextcloud/html/config/config.php and add inside the $CONFIG = array ( block: 'memcache.local' => '\OC\Memcache\APCu', Enable APCu for PHP CLI as well (to prevent errors when running background cron jobs): Create or edit /opt/nextcloud/html/.user.ini and add: apc.enable_cli=1 Restart the container to apply: docker compose restart nextcloud
documents.s: 3.1 Clearing the Warning: "No memory cache has been configured (Memcache)"

documents.t: Run the occ command inside the container to fix them automatically: # Add missing database indices docker compose exec --user 33 nextcloud php occ db:add-missing-indices # Convert filecache columns to BigInt docker compose exec --user 33 nextcloud php occ db:convert-filecache-bigint
documents.s: 3.2 Clearing Warnings: "Missing database indices" or "BigInt columns not converted"

documents.t: Once the container is initialized, environment variables no longer overwrite config.php. If you need to add domains or trusted proxy IPs later, use occ directly: # Add a second domain (e.g., cloud2.example.com) docker compose exec --user 33 nextcloud php occ config:system:set trusted_domains 2 --value="cloud2.example.com" # Add or update trusted proxy subnets (Trusted Proxies) docker compose exec --user 33 nextcloud php occ config:system:set trusted_proxies 0 --value="172.16.0.0/12" docker compose exec --user 33 nextcloud php occ config:system:set trusted_proxies 1 --value="10.0.0.0/8"
documents.s: 3.3 Adding Domains or Adjusting Reverse Proxies After Startup (Do Not Edit Compose!)

documents.t: Nextcloud's default AJAX mode relies on users clicking web pages to trigger maintenance tasks, which both slows down browsing and halts scheduled jobs completely overnight when nobody is active. First switch the setting in the web UI: Go to "Administration settings" → "Basic settings" → set Background jobs to "Cron (Recommended)". Then choose either Option A or Option B on the host to deploy the periodic trigger.
documents.s: 4. Background Job Scheduling: Cron vs. Systemd Timer

documents.t: Best for hosts where you want a quick one-liner without creating extra unit files. Open the root crontab on the host: sudo crontab -e Add the following schedule (runs every 5 minutes): */5 * * * * docker compose -f /opt/nextcloud/docker-compose.yml exec -T --user 33 nextcloud php -f /var/www/html/cron.php > /dev/null 2>&1 -T: Disables TTY allocation so non-interactive runs don't fail with the input device is not a TTY. --user 33: Forces execution as www-data (UID 33) inside the container, preventing cache directory permissions from being polluted by root.
documents.s: Option A: Traditional Crontab (Simple, Lightweight, Fast)

documents.t: Suitable for modern distributions such as Photon OS, Debian, Ubuntu, and Rocky Linux. Provides boot delay, crash timeout protection, unified logging via journalctl, and automatic catch-up after downtime via Persistent=true. Step 1: Create the Service Unit That Runs the Job​ Create /etc/systemd/system/nextcloud-cron.service: [Unit] Description=Nextcloud Background Cron Job Requires=docker.service After=docker.service [Service] Type=oneshot User=root WorkingDirectory=/opt/nextcloud # Adjust the path based on `which docker` output (typically /usr/bin/docker) ExecStart=/usr/bin/docker compose exec -T --user 33 nextcloud php -f /var/www/html/cron.php TimeoutSec=600 [Install] WantedBy=multi-user.target Step 2: Create the Timer Unit That Triggers the Service​ Create /etc/systemd/system/nextcloud-cron.timer (the name must match the .service file): [Unit] Description=Run Nextcloud Cron every 5 minutes [Timer] # Delay first run by 5 minutes after boot to avoid startup spikes OnBootSec=5min # Run every 5 minutes thereafter OnUnitActiveSec=5min # Run immediately on next boot if a scheduled run was missed while powered off Persistent=true [Install] WantedBy=timers.target Step 3: Load, Test, and Enable the Timer​ # 1. Reload systemd configuration sudo systemctl daemon-reload # 2. Manually trigger the service once to test execution sudo systemctl start nextcloud-cron.service # 3. Inspect log output for the single run journalctl -u nextcloud-cron.service -n 20 --no-pager # 4. Enable the timer and start it immediately at boot sudo systemctl enable --now nextcloud-cron.timer # 5. Check countdown to the next timer trigger systemctl list-timers nextcloud-cron.timer
documents.s: Option B: Systemd Timer (Recommended for Modern Distros, Production-Grade Standard)

documents.t: For lightweight deployments using SQLite: Enable WAL (Write-Ahead Logging) to Improve Concurrency: SQLite uses file-level locking, which can cause timeouts when multiple devices upload simultaneously. Edit /opt/nextcloud/html/config/config.php and add to the array: 'sqlite.journal_mode' => 'WAL', One-Command Full Backup: The SQLite database file is located at /opt/nextcloud/data/owncloud.db (Updated 2026-11-27: When using SQLITE_DATABASE=nextcloud as configured in this guide, the actual filename is /opt/nextcloud/data/nextcloud.db; it is owncloud.db only when unspecified or left at the default name). To back up, simply archive the data directory and config file: sudo tar -czvf /opt/backup/nextcloud_$(date +%F).tar.gz \ /opt/nextcloud/data \ /opt/nextcloud/html/config/config.php warning If SQLite WAL mode is enabled or the container is still running, running tar directly on active database files may produce an inconsistent snapshot. Enable maintenance mode before backing up (docker compose exec --user 33 nextcloud php occ maintenance:mode --on), then disable it afterward (--off).

Symptom Root Cause Resolution Redirects back to login page after logging in (login loop / CSRF failure) Missing OVERWRITEPROTOCOL=https, causing the session cookie to be treated as insecure protocol Add OVERWRITEPROTOCOL=https to Compose, recreate the container with docker compose up -d, and clear browser cookies. .ocdata missing error Host directory is not owned by UID 33 Run sudo chown -R 33:33 /opt/nextcloud/data. Mobile app cannot sync calendar and contacts Traefik nc-dav redirect is not taking effect Visit https://<domain>/.well-known/caldav and verify it automatically redirects to /remote.php/dav/. Large file uploads abort Restricted by PHP upload limits Check the PHP_UPLOAD_LIMIT=16G environment variable, or set upload_max_filesize = 16G and post_max_size = 16G in .user.ini.

When focusing on HomeLab internal automation (such as Ansible, Docusaurus, and Docker Compose repositories), the architecture has the following key design highlights: Pure Intranet HTTP Strategy: In an isolated intranet, the Git server is only used by internal VMs or physical nodes to pull code (e.g., ansible-pull -U http://git.internal.local/admin/homelab.git). Using internal HTTP completely eliminates the management hassle of intranet self-signed CA certificate expiration or manually installing a trusted root CA on each client node. Database Selection: Why Abandon SQLite for MySQL / MariaDB? SQLite is inherently a single-file database and triggers database-level locks during high-frequency concurrent writes. When multiple nodes run ansible-pull simultaneously, or when multiple Git hooks/CI runners report status concurrently, it easily triggers fatal database is locked (5) errors, causing Git push/pull operations to fail and abort. Adopting standalone MySQL / MariaDB completely eliminates locking timeout issues through row-level locks and connection pooling. SSH Port Conflict Avoidance: If you want to allow Git over the SSH protocol (git@host:repo.git) inside a container, port 22 inside the container must not be directly mapped to port 22 on the host (to avoid conflicts with the host's own SSH management port). It typically needs to be mapped as 2222:22, or pass-through can be achieved via the host OpenSSH AuthorizedKeysCommand. Alternatively, using Macvlan to assign an independent IP and pointing the SSH domain to that IP avoids port mapping altogether, though HTTP and SSH will connect through different domains.
documents.s: 1. Architectural Positioning and Core Design Principles

documents.t: sudo mkdir -p /opt/gitea/data /opt/gitea/config /opt/gitea/mysql # The official Gitea image runs as UID 1000 by default sudo chown -R 1000:1000 /opt/gitea/data /opt/gitea/config
documents.s: Step 1: Create Dedicated Directories and Permissions

documents.t: Configure /opt/gitea/docker-compose.yml as follows: services: server: image: gitea/gitea:latest container_name: gitea restart: unless-stopped depends_on: db: condition: service_healthy environment: - USER_UID=1000 - USER_GID=1000 - TZ=Asia/Taipei # Crucial: External access URL (affects the generation path of Git clone links copied in the frontend UI) - GITEA__server__ROOT_URL=http://git.internal.local/ - GITEA__server__HTTP_PORT=3000 - GITEA__server__DOMAIN=git.internal.local - GITEA__server__SSH_PORT=2222 - GITEA__server__SSH_LISTEN_PORT=22 # Database connection configuration (supports GITEA__*__* format to auto-override app.ini) - GITEA__database__DB_TYPE=mysql - GITEA__database__HOST=db:3306 - GITEA__database__NAME=gitea - GITEA__database__USER=gitea - GITEA__database__PASSWD=gitea_secret_password volumes: - /opt/gitea/data:/data - /opt/gitea/config:/etc/gitea - /etc/timezone:/etc/timezone:ro - /etc/localtime:/etc/localtime:ro ports: # Git SSH service port (external access uses 2222) - "2222:22" # If going directly through NPM reverse proxy on the same Docker network, port 3000 doesn't even need external mapping - "3000:3000" networks: - backend db: image: mariadb:10.11 container_name: gitea_db restart: unless-stopped command: - "mariadbd" - "--character-set-server=utf8mb4" - "--collation-server=utf8mb4_unicode_ci" - "--innodb-file-per-table=1" environment: - TZ=Asia/Taipei - MARIADB_ROOT_PASSWORD=db_root_secret_password - MARIADB_DATABASE=gitea - MARIADB_USER=gitea - MARIADB_PASSWORD=gitea_secret_password volumes: - /opt/gitea/mysql:/var/lib/mysql networks: - backend healthcheck: test: ["CMD", "healthcheck.sh", "--connect", "--innodb_initialized"] interval: 5s timeout: 5s retries: 10 networks: backend: driver: bridge # If using a shared npm-network, you can mount an external network directly: # external: true # name: npm-network Improvement Notes: Previously, mysql:latest occasionally encountered connection interruptions caused by default authentication plugin updates (such as caching_sha2_password). Here, long-term supported mariadb:10.11 is recommended for lower resource overhead and better compatibility. Added healthcheck and depends_on: condition: service_healthy to ensure Gitea starts only after the database has fully completed initialization, eliminating DB Connection Refused errors during startup.
When connecting NPM and Gitea on the same custom network (such as backend or an external shared npm-network), the reverse proxy configuration is extremely clean:

Go to Hosts -> Proxy Hosts -> Add Proxy Host. Details tab settings: Domain Names: git.internal.local Scheme: http Forward Hostname / IP: gitea (enter the container name directly) Forward Port: 3000 (Gitea container default listening port) Check Websockets Support (required for Gitea internal notifications). Large File Upload Interruption Prevention (Important): Go to the Advanced tab and paste the following into the custom Nginx configuration block: # Allow large Git pushes (default is only 1MB; large projects or binary files will be blocked) client_max_body_size 512M;
When using ansible-pull for self-configuration of nodes in a HomeLab, the advantages of Gitea's pure HTTP are particularly prominent:
Create an account dedicated to automated maintenance in Gitea (e.g., ci-bot). Under Settings -> Applications for that account, create a Personal Access Token with read:repository permissions.
documents.s: 4.1 Create a Passwordless Read-Only Account or Access Token

documents.t: Run automated synchronization on the client host (no SSH keys or trusted certificates required): # Perform pure HTTP pull and execution using the token ansible-pull -U http://ci-bot:<YOUR_TOKEN>@git.internal.local/infra/homelab-ansible.git \ -i localhost, \ local.yml
documents.s: 4.2 Execute ansible-pull on the Node Side

documents.t: Anomaly Symptom Root Cause Troubleshooting Steps Git Push error: RPC failed; HTTP 413 curl 22 The requested URL returned error: 413 Triggered Nginx's default client_max_body_size limit when passing through NPM Add client_max_body_size 512M; (or higher) to NPM's advanced settings, and verify [repository.upload] FILE_MAX_SIZE = 512 in Gitea's app.ini. URL copied from Web UI Clone button turns into http://localhost:3000/... ROOT_URL is not resolved correctly Check if the environment variable GITEA__server__ROOT_URL=http://git.internal.local/ is set (make sure it ends with a slash /), and restart the container. SSH Clone fails (Permission denied / Connection refused) External port mapping confusion or mixed up host vs container SSH 1. Ensure port 2222 is specified during connection: git clone ssh://git@git.internal.local:2222/user/repo.git. 2. To avoid typing 2222, define an alias in the client's ~/.ssh/config. Forgot Administrator Password Unable to log in via Web UI to reset Use the container internal CLI to reset the admin password in one click: docker compose exec --user 1000 server gitea admin user change-password --username admin --password "New_Password"

Gitea provides a dedicated backup command that fully packages database SQL, bare repositories, user settings, and plugin data into a single ZIP archive: # 1. Execute one-click backup command inside the container docker compose exec -T --user 1000 server gitea dump -c /data/gitea/conf/app.ini --file /data/gitea-dump.zip # 2. Move the backup file from the host directory to the backup storage area sudo mv /opt/gitea/data/gitea-dump.zip /opt/backups/gitea-$(date +%F).zip # Restoration method (in a brand new clean directory): # unzip gitea-dump.zip # Import the restored SQL into MariaDB, and overwrite the data directory back to /opt/gitea/data/gitea note When executing gitea dump, please confirm whether the app.ini path specified by -c is /etc/gitea/app.ini or /data/gitea/conf/app.ini based on your container mount and environment variable settings.

On a single host, you can mount /var/run/docker.sock directly; however, when containers are spread across multiple physical machines or VPSs, exposing an unencrypted Docker socket to the public internet is equivalent to granting root privilege escalation. Therefore, the standard secure solution for multi-host monitoring is introducing docker-socket-proxy: [Uptime Kuma Central Server] │ ├─► Monitor local containers: mounts local /var/run/docker.sock:ro │ ├─► Monitor remote Host A: queries via TCP 2375 (read-only protected by docker-socket-proxy) │ ▲ │ └─ [Remote Node A] ── docker-socket-proxy ── /var/run/docker.sock │ ├─► On anomaly trigger ───► Telegram Bot API ───► Real-time push to phone / group │ └─► External visitors ───► Dedicated Status Page ───► Glassmorphism dark theme display How docker-socket-proxy protects the host: Under the hood, it intercepts Docker API requests via HAProxy. Setting POST=0 disables all write, create, and delete permissions, exposing only read-only endpoints such as CONTAINERS=1 to prevent attackers from escalating privileges and taking over the host via an exposed Docker port.
documents.s: 1. Architecture Design and Multi-Host Security Topology

documents.t: Create /opt/dockerproxy/docker-compose.yml on the remote VPS or managed node: services: dockerproxy: image: ghcr.io/tecnativa/docker-socket-proxy:latest container_name: dockerproxy restart: unless-stopped environment: # Expose only the read-only permissions required for monitoring - CONTAINERS=1 - SERVICES=1 - TASKS=1 - POST=0 - BUILD=0 - COMMIT=0 - CONFIGS=0 - DISTRIBUTION=0 - EXEC=0 - IMAGES=0 - INFO=0 - NETWORKS=0 - NODES=0 - PLUGINS=0 - SECRETS=0 - SESSION=0 - SWARM=0 - SYSTEM=0 - VOLUMES=0 ports: # Recommended to expose only on LAN or WireGuard VPN subnet; if over public internet, restrict source IP with a firewall - "2375:2375" volumes: - /var/run/docker.sock:/var/run/docker.sock:ro
documents.s: 2.1 Remote Managed Node: Deploy docker-socket-proxy (For Multi-Host Setups)

documents.t: Create /opt/uptime-kuma/docker-compose.yml: services: uptime-kuma: image: louislam/uptime-kuma:1 container_name: uptime-kuma restart: unless-stopped ports: # Direct connection default port; remove host mapping if behind NPM / Traefik - "3001:3001" volumes: - /opt/uptime-kuma/data:/app/data # Mount local socket to monitor local containers - /var/run/docker.sock:/var/run/docker.sock:ro networks: - monitor-net # Join proxy network if using a reverse proxy - proxy-network networks: monitor-net: driver: bridge proxy-network: external: true Start the service: docker compose up -d Updated 2026-11-27 louislam/uptime-kuma:1 in the original configuration belongs to the legacy v1 branch; for fresh deployments, using the stable louislam/uptime-kuma:2 release is recommended (if upgrading from v1, back up your data first and check the official migration notes).

Search for the official bot @BotFather in Telegram. Send the command /newbot. Enter the bot's display Name and Username in order (the username must end with bot, e.g., HomeLab_alert_bot). Save the returned HTTP API Token (format such as 123456789:ABCdefGhIJKlmNoPQRsTUVwxyZ).
documents.s: Step A: Request a Bot Token from BotFather

documents.t: Search for the bot you just created in Telegram, click Start, or send any message to it. Retrieve the Chat ID: Method 1: Visit https://api.telegram.org/bot<YOUR_BOT_TOKEN>/getUpdates in a browser and locate "chat":{"id": 123456789, ...} in the returned JSON. Method 2: Search for @userinfobot in Telegram and click Start; it will directly return your personal numeric Id.
documents.s: Step B: Obtain Your Personal or Group chat_id

documents.t: Open the Uptime Kuma dashboard (http://<IP>:3001) -> click the avatar in the top-right -> Settings -> Notification -> Setup Notification. Select Telegram as the Notification Type: Bot Token: Paste the API Token you just obtained. Chat ID: Enter the numeric ID. Click Test, confirm you receive the test message in Telegram, and then save.
documents.s: Step C: Bind the Notification Channel in Uptime Kuma

documents.t: Click "Add New Monitor" in the top-left: Monitor local containers: Monitor Type: Select Docker Container. Docker Host: Select the default /var/run/docker.sock. Container Name / ID: Enter the target container name (e.g., nextcloud, gitea). Monitor remote node containers (via Socket Proxy): Go to Settings -> Docker Hosts -> Add Docker Host. Choose TCP Socket as the connection type and enter tcp://<REMOTE_VPS_IP>:2375. When adding a monitor, switch the dropdown to that remote host, then enter the container name on that host for cross-machine monitoring.

Regular monitors actively ping a target, but if you want to verify whether backup scripts, NAS jobs, or cron jobs finished on schedule, use Push mode: Select "Push" as the Monitor Type and set the heartbeat interval (e.g., 86400 seconds = 1 day). Kuma generates a dedicated Webhook URL: https://kuma.example.com/api/push/keyXYZ?status=up&msg=OK&ping= Add a check-in command at the end of your backup script: curl -fsS -m 10 --retry 3 "https://kuma.example.com/api/push/keyXYZ?status=up&msg=BackupSuccess" If the script crashes or hangs, Kuma will immediately trigger an alert when it fails to receive a check-in within the configured window.
documents.s: 5.1 "Dead Man's Switch": Passive Push Heartbeat Monitoring

documents.t: When a container goes down unexpectedly, in addition to sending a notification, you can trigger an external service to automatically recover it: Add a Webhook under Notification settings. Connect it to Node-RED or a lightweight webhook server (such as adnanh/webhook). When a DOWN event is received, have the background service automatically execute docker restart <container_name> to achieve self-healing.
documents.s: 5.2 Auto-Restart on Service Crash (Self-Healing) via Webhook

documents.t: Select HTTP(s) as the Monitor Type and enter the domain name; Kuma automatically inspects the TLS certificate chain and sends alerts by default at 21, 14, and 7 days before expiration, preventing outages caused by failed Let's Encrypt renewals.
Uptime Kuma supports creating standalone status pages so visitors can check service availability.
documents.s: 6. Public Status Page and Custom CSS Glassmorphism Styling

documents.t: Click Status Pages in the top menu -> New Status Page. Set the page name, slug (e.g., /status), and monitor groups. Click Edit in the top-right and expand the Custom CSS section at the bottom.

Paste the following CSS verbatim into the Custom CSS field and save: /* ============================================================ Uptime Kuma Status Page - Modern Glassmorphism Theme ============================================================ */ /* 1. Global dark gradient background */ body { background-color: #0d1117 !important; background-image: radial-gradient(at 0% 0%, rgba(56, 189, 248, 0.12) 0px, transparent 50%), radial-gradient(at 100% 100%, rgba(139, 92, 246, 0.12) 0px, transparent 50%), radial-gradient(at 50% 50%, rgba(15, 23, 42, 0.8) 0px, transparent 100%) !important; background-attachment: fixed !important; color: #e2e8f0 !important; font-family: -apple-system, BlinkMacSystemFont, "Segoe UI", Roboto, "Helvetica Neue", Arial, sans-serif !important; } /* 2. Glassmorphism for header and overall status banner */ header, .overall-status { backdrop-filter: blur(16px) !important; -webkit-backdrop-filter: blur(16px) !important; } .overall-status { background: rgba(30, 41, 59, 0.45) !important; border: 1px solid rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.08) !important; border-radius: 16px !important; box-shadow: 0 8px 32px 0 rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.3) !important; padding: 24px !important; } /* 3. All Uptime Kuma monitors, custom alert rules, and historical statistics are stored in /app/data/kuma.db (SQLite): # 1. Back up the data directory sudo tar -czvf /opt/backups/uptime-kuma-$(date +%F).tar.gz -C /opt/uptime-kuma data # 2. Restore backup to a new environment sudo tar -xzvf /opt/backups/uptime-kuma-*.tar.gz -C /opt/uptime-kuma/ docker compose restart uptime-kuma Updated 2026-11-27 Run docker compose stop uptime-kuma before backing up or restoring /opt/uptime-kuma/data to avoid data inconsistency in a running SQLite database (kuma.db WAL mode). If multiple backup files exist in /opt/backups/, the wildcard uptime-kuma-*.tar.gz in the restore command will cause tar to fail; specify an explicit backup filename instead.

tip FreeBSD Gateway can utilize ipfw to achieve traffic limitation functionality, which requires the dummynet kernel module to operate properly. info This article was automatically translated by Google "Gemini". The author does not guarantee its accuracy or wording.
documents.s: FreeBSD IPFW and Dummynet Traffic Control Practical Configuration

documents.t: Since most environments now use a Generic Kernel (saving the effort of recompiling the kernel yourself), you can directly use kldload to dynamically load dummynet.ko. Manual Loading​ kldload dummynet To confirm whether the module has been loaded, run: kldstat This command will list all dynamically loaded .ko modules; please verify that the output includes dummynet.ko. Automatic Loading at Boot​ To make the settings persist after rebooting, modify /boot/loader.conf: # /boot/loader.conf dummynet_load="YES" It will then be automatically loaded upon every subsequent reboot.

Define in /etc/rc.conf how the system enables the firewall and loads rule scripts upon startup (ensure that /etc/ipfw.conf has executable permissions or is a valid Shell script): # /etc/rc.conf firewall_enable="YES" firewall_script="/etc/ipfw.conf" # Path to configuration file firewall_type="unknown" # Tells the system we are running our own script natd_enable="NO" # Do not start natd

/etc/ipfw.conf This is the core part. The recommended approach is to maintain interface, subnet, and bandwidth variables separately from actual rules: #!/bin/sh # Define ipfw command path IPFW="/sbin/ipfw" # --- Define Interfaces --- EXT_IF="ext0" INT_IF="int0" # --- Define Networks and IPs --- DMZ_NET="192.168.0.0/24" GUEST_NET="192.168.2.0/24" VPN_NET="10.8.0.0/24" # Correction: Added previously missing definition P2P1_IP="192.168.0.100" # Correction: Added previously missing definition P2P2_IP="192.168.0.101" # --- Define Bandwidth Types and Speeds --- P2P_UP="100KBytes/s" VPN_UP="500KBytes/s" RDP_P2P="500KBytes/s" SERV_UP="350KBytes/s" GUEST_BAND="30KBytes/s" # --- Rules Begin --- # 1. Flush all existing rules and pipes $IPFW -f flush $IPFW -f pipe flush # 2. Allow local loopback traffic (Important: Without this rule, system services will cut themselves off) $IPFW add 10 allow ip from any to any via lo0 # 3. Use ipfw pipe to define each traffic limit and number $IPFW pipe 1 config bw $VPN_UP $IPFW pipe 2 config bw $P2P_UP $IPFW pipe 3 config bw $RDP_P2P $IPFW pipe 4 config bw $SERV_UP $IPFW pipe 5 config bw $GUEST_BAND # 4. Use pipes to define traffic rules (smaller numbers have higher priority) # VPN traffic limitation $IPFW add 20 pipe 1 ip from any to $VPN_NET # RDP specific traffic (Correction: Added port 3389 to ensure precision) $IPFW add 25 pipe 3 tcp from $P2P1_IP to any 3389 in recv $INT_IF # P2P traffic limitation $IPFW add 30 pipe 2 ip from $P2P1_IP to any in recv $INT_IF $IPFW add 40 pipe 2 ip from $P2P2_IP to any in recv $INT_IF # Guest network throttling (limit both incoming and outgoing) $IPFW add 110 pipe 5 ip from $GUEST_NET to any $IPFW add 120 pipe 5 ip from any to $GUEST_NET # DMZ egress traffic limitation (Correction: Used variable $EXT_IF to replace hardcoded value in source) $IPFW add 210 pipe 4 ip from $DMZ_NET to any via $EXT_IF # 5. Allow all remaining traffic at the end $IPFW add 65534 allow ip from any to any

Nowadays, most firewalls on FreeBSD have switched to PF (Packet Filter), and IPFW is less commonly used purely for security filtering; however, PF's bandwidth throttling configuration is not as intuitive or simple as IPFW + dummynet. Therefore, in practice, a dual-layer firewall division of labor is very suitable: PF handles security filtering and NAT, while IPFW specializes in Traffic Shaping.

documents.s: FreeBSD System and Package Update Guide

documents.t: Unlike Linux which uses a single package manager to update the entire system and packages, FreeBSD uses different commands for updating the system and packages.
# Debian/Ubuntu apt update && apt upgrade # Arch pacman -Syu One command solves everything.

# Update patches for existing version freebsd-update fetch && freebsd-update install # Upgrade to x.y-RELEASE freebsd-update upgrade -r x.y-RELEASE && freebsd-update install Updated 2026-11-27 When performing cross-version upgrades using freebsd-update upgrade -r x.y-RELEASE, the first execution of freebsd-update install only installs the new kernel. You must first reboot (shutdown -r now) and then run freebsd-update install a second time to complete the userland update. If third-party packages were rebuilt after removing old libraries, you must run freebsd-update install one final time at the end.

Actually, if you don't need to compile yourself, using pkg is much more convenient. # Install pkg install <pkg_name> # Remove pkg delete <pkg_name> # Autoremove pkg autoremove # Check pkgs version pkg version # Update repo pkg update # Update pkg pkg upgrade
In the past, most software in FreeBSD was compiled using ports. Nowadays, unless special compilation parameters are required, pkg is basically used for installation.

cd /usr/ports # First time use portsnap fetch && portsnap extract && portsnap update # Subsequent use portsnap fetch && portsnap update Updated 2026-11-27 The portsnap tool has been deprecated since FreeBSD 13 and officially removed starting from FreeBSD 14.0 (the Ports Tree is now fully hosted via Git). Modern FreeBSD environments should install git (e.g., pkg install git), initially acquire the Ports Tree via git clone https://git.FreeBSD.org/ports.git /usr/ports, and subsequently update using git -C /usr/ports pull.
portmaster -a

Nowadays, I use general parameters, so I've lost the necessity of using port and only use pkg. I wonder if it's because I spent the past several years using the penguin (Linux) and didn't continue putting skill points into the FreeBSD series, so my usage habits were influenced by the penguin—directly installing binary packages...

documents.s: FreeBSD System Password and Expiration Management

documents.t: FreeBSD's mechanism differs from Linux; it controls lifecycle through Login Classes and account management commands. Setting Expiration via Login Classes (/etc/login.conf) Edit the /etc/login.conf file, adding expiration parameters within the target group section (usually default:\): default:\ :passwdtime=90d:\ :passwordlength=12:\ :tc=std-default: Updated 2026-11-27 The aforementioned login.conf(5) field names were incorrect: the correct FreeBSD parameters for password expiration and minimum length are passwordtime (not passwdtime) and minpasswordlen (not passwordlength), and the standard /etc/login.conf default: section does not have a built-in tc=std-default:. Corrected example: default:\ :passwordtime=90d:\ :minpasswordlen=12: :passwdtime=90d: (Updated 2026-11-27: The correct parameter name is :passwordtime=90d:) indicates that user passwords under this class expire after 90 days. After modification, you must recompile the database via command for it to take effect: sudo cap_mkdb /etc/login.conf Modifying Single Account Restrictions via the pw Command If you do not want to apply it globally by class, you can operate directly on specific users: Set Password Expiration Date: sudo pw usermod john -p 2026-12-31 Updated 2026-11-27 FreeBSD pw(8)'s -p parameter does not accept the YYYY-MM-DD format, supporting only dd-mmm-yyyy (such as 31-Dec-2026), relative time offsets (such as +90d), or UNIX Epoch seconds. Corrected examples: sudo pw usermod john -p 31-Dec-2026 or sudo pw usermod john -p +90d. Lock or Unlock Account: sudo pw lock john sudo pw unlock john

FreeBSD adopts the Pluggable Authentication Modules (PAM) mechanism, limiting password strength through the pam_passwdqc module. Edit /etc/pam.d/passwd file, adjusting or adding checking rules: password required pam_passwdqc.so min=disabled,disabled,12,8,6 The five numerical values of the parameter respectively represent: minimum length restrictions when the password is a passphrase, long word, short word, general mixed string, and extremely short string (Updated 2026-11-27: According to the pam_passwdqc(8) specification, min=N0,N1,N2,N3,N4 sequentially correspond to minimum length restrictions for "single character class", "two character classes", "passphrase", "three character classes", and "four character classes"; taking disabled,disabled,12,8,6 as an example, it means disabling 1-2 character class passwords, requiring passphrases to be at least 12 characters, 3-character-class passwords at least 8 characters, and 4-character-class passwords at least 6 characters), thereby filtering out overly simple weak passwords.

Workaround When Stuck at SSH Login Due to Expired Password: If you have root privilege on the machine or another account with sudo capability (or via cloud host serial console / Recovery mode), directly execute the following command to lift the restriction, allowing you to log in again and reset your password: sudo chage -M -1 <Username> Updated 2026-11-27 chage is a Linux (shadow-utils) specific command; FreeBSD systems do not have this tool. To clear or remove account password expiration restrictions on FreeBSD, use sudo pw usermod <Username> -p 0 (or chpass -p 0 <Username>) instead.

documents.t: 柯仓无居所 (Updated 2026-11-27: Most original Leanote external links are broken; retained for historical reference only)

FreeBSD has built-in bsnmp. vi /etc/rc.conf # /etc/rc.conf -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- bsnmpd_enable="YES" pkg install bsnmp-ucd vi /etc/snmpd.conf # Append the following contents to /etc/snmpd.conf -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- begemotSnmpdModulePath."ucd" = "/usr/local/lib/snmp_ucd.so" %ucd updateInterval = 500 extCheckInterval = 100 extUpdateInterval = 3000 extTimeout = 60 memMinimumSwap = 1600 memSwapErrorMsg = "No free swap!" laConfig.1 = "6.0" laConfig.2 = "5.0" laConfig.3 = "4.0" laErrMessage.1 = "1min load average is high!" laErrMessage.2 = "5min load average is high!" laErrMessage.3 = "15min load average is high!" # Process table prNames.0 = "httpd" prMin.0 = 3 prMax.0 = 100 prErrFix.0 = 1 prErrFixCmd.0 = "/usr/local/etc/rc.d/apache22 restart" # Extension commands (extTable) extNames.0 = "uname" extCommand.0 = "/usr/bin/uname -a" extNames.1 = "uptime" extCommand.1 = "/usr/bin/uptime" # example of extension with fix command extNames.2 = "apache" extCommand.2 = "/usr/local/etc/rc.d/apache status" extErrFix.2 = 1 extErrFixCmd.2 = "/usr/local/etc/rc.d/apache restart" /etc/rc.d/bsnmpd restart bsnmpwalk -v 2c -c public If data is retrieved successfully, it is okay. Updated 2026-11-27 apache22 in the example has been deprecated in FreeBSD Ports (modern versions use apache24). On modern FreeBSD, it is recommended to use service bsnmpd restart instead of directly executing /etc/rc.d/bsnmpd restart. FreeBSD's built-in bsnmpwalk(1) does not support net-snmp's -c flag; specifying the community and target host should be done via -s: bsnmpwalk -v 2c -s public@localhost (v2c is the default and can also be abbreviated as bsnmpwalk -s public@localhost).
pkg install bash ipmitool libstatgrab git Because check_mk_agent needs to run with bash, it will not work without bash.

Fetch check_mk_agent & grant execution permissions git clone https://github.com/librenms/librenms-agent.git cp librenms-agent/check_mk_agent_freebsd /usr/local/bin/check_mk_agent chmod +x /usr/local/bin/check_mk_agent The method above is outdated... because it is now supported in ports. /usr/ports/net-mgmt/check_mk_agent/ cd /usr/ports/net-mgmt/check_mk_agent/ make install clean Updated 2026-11-27 In addition to compiling via Ports, modern FreeBSD can also install precompiled binary packages directly: pkg install check_mk_agent (which automatically installs dependencies such as bash and libstatgrab). vi /etc/services # /etc/services -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- check_mk 6556/tcp #check_mk agent This is added. vi /etc/inetd.conf # /etc/inetd.conf -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- check_mk stream tcp nowait root /usr/local/bin/check_mk_agent check_mk_agent This is also added. vi /etc/rc.conf # /etc/rc.conf -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- inetd_enable=yes inetd_flags=-wW This is also added. vi /etc/hosts.allow # /etc/hosts.allow -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- # Allow nagios server to access us check_mk_agent : 192.168.56.3 : allow check_mk_agent : ALL : deny This is also added. /etc/rc.d/inetd start Confirm with telnet telnet bsdhost 6556 <<<check_mk>>> Version: 1.1.13i1 AgentOS: freebsd This is all set. Updated 2026-11-27 Standard syntax for /etc/rc.conf should include double quotes (inetd_enable="YES", inetd_flags="-wW"), starting the service should preferably use service inetd start, and verifying port connectivity can use nc bsdhost 6556 instead of telnet.

Although I don't really like enabling inetd to run this, these machines and ports are basically restricted by firewalls, and LibreNMS is deployed internally, so the risk should not be that high. It can still barely be used this way.

Starting the SSH service in the WebGUI fails with Error Code 1. Even if host keys are generated manually in the terminal (ssh-keygen -A), returning to the WebGUI and clicking Save causes the service to crash again immediately.

Run the following command in the console to test the SSH configuration file and force error output display: /usr/sbin/sshd -t -f /var/etc/ssh/sshd_config 2>&1 If the output is sshd: no hostkeys available -- exiting., it indicates that the private keys recorded in the underlying config.xml are corrupted or missing, causing the WebGUI to overwrite the system with incorrect keys every time settings are applied.

You must force the system to regenerate and record new host keys via the WebGUI. Go to the WebGUI and navigate to Services -> SSH. Scroll down to find the Private Keys section. Clear the contents of all four text boxes (RSA, DSA, ECDSA, Ed25519). (Updated 2026-11-27: OpenSSH 10.0+ has completely removed DSA key support; newer XigmaNAS interfaces may only retain RSA, ECDSA, and Ed25519) Scroll to the bottom of the page and click Save and Restart. Detecting the empty values, the system will automatically generate brand new host keys and write them to config.xml, allowing the SSH service to start normally.

When XigmaNAS is used in Embedded mode, the system root directory (/) resides in memory (RAM Disk), which can be confirmed via mount | grep ' / ' (/dev/md0). This means: By default, there is no ~/.ssh directory. Any /root/.ssh/authorized_keys written via ssh-copy-id will disappear immediately upon reboot. To solve this problem, you must store the public key on the physical USB boot drive (/cf partition) and instruct the SSH service to read that physical file directly.

By default, the USB partition (/cf) is in Read-Only protection mode. You must first switch it to read-write mode. Mount as Read-Write: mount -u -w /cf Create the key directory and set permissions: mkdir -p /cf/conf/ssh_config chmod 700 /cf/conf/ssh_config Write the public key: Use an editor to paste the public key of the Ansible control node or client (id_ed25519.pub or zeon.key.pub) into the file. vi /cf/conf/ssh_config/authorized_keys Set file permissions: (Incorrect permissions will cause SSH to refuse reading the key) chmod 600 /cf/conf/ssh_config/authorized_keys Relock as Read-Only: Protect the USB flash drive to prevent damage from frequent writes. mount -u -r /cf
documents.s: Step 1: Unlock and Write Public Key to USB Boot Drive

documents.t: Tell the XigmaNAS SSH service to bypass memory and read settings directly from the USB flash drive. Go to the WebGUI and navigate to Services -> SSH. Ensure Permit root login is checked (if root automation is required). Scroll down to the Extra options text box. Paste the following parameter: AuthorizedKeysFile /cf/conf/ssh_config/authorized_keys Click Save and Restart.
Run a test from the connecting endpoint to confirm that you can log in directly without a password: ssh -i ~/.ssh/ssh.key root@<XigmaNAS_IP>
