documents.s: Arch-Based Pacman / Yay Practical Commands and Maintenance Tips

documents.t: In Arch systems, software outside the official repositories resides in the AUR (Arch User Repository). yay is a powerful tool written in Go that is compatible with pacman syntax and seamlessly helps you download and compile software from the AUR. Depending on the Arch branch you are using, the difficulty of installing yay varies: 1. Vanilla Arch Linux or ArchWSL (Updated 2026-11-27: The third-party ArchWSL project has been archived; you can now install Arch directly via the official WSL image wsl --install -d archlinux) Since official vanilla Arch repositories do not include an AUR helper, you must manually clone the source code and compile it the first time: # 1. Install essential compilation tools and Git sudo pacman -S --needed git base-devel # 2. Clone the yay source code and enter the directory git clone https://aur.archlinux.org/yay.git cd yay # 3. Compile and install (-s automatically resolves dependencies, -i automatically installs after compilation) makepkg -si 2. Manjaro Manjaro officially puts yay into their community repository (Updated 2026-11-27: Manjaro has merged community into the extra repository), so it can be installed directly using pacman: # Although you can install yay directly, it is recommended to install base-devel together so compilation won't throw errors when building AUR software later sudo pacman -S base-devel yay 3. EndeavourOS / Garuda Linux These two out-of-the-box Arch branches come with yay pre-installed by default when you set up the system, so no manual work is needed. If it happens to be removed by accident, because they have their own repositories mounted, you can run the command directly as well: sudo pacman -S yay Once installed, you can basically replace pacman with yay for your daily package management.
documents.s: I. Getting Started: How to Install Yay (According to Different Arch Branches)

documents.t: 1. Comprehensive System Update and Downgrade Synchronization Under normal circumstances, this updates both official packages and AUR packages simultaneously: yay -Syu Advanced Knowledge: What is the difference between yay -Syu and yay -Syyuu? -Syu (Standard Update): -y synchronizes the latest package databases, -u upgrades all outdated packages. This is the most frequently used command for daily updates. -Syyuu (Force Synchronization and Allow Downgrades): -yy: Forces re-downloading and syncing from the server regardless of whether your local database is up to date (usually used when you just changed mirrors or if your database is corrupted). -uu: Allows package downgrades. If the software version on the server is older than the one on your computer (e.g., officials discovered a critical bug in a new version and urgently rolled it back), appending two u's forces the system to revert to the older version to match the official repository state. 2. Searching and Installing Packages # Install a specific package yay -S <package_name> # If you don't know the exact name, just type yay followed by a keyword to list matching choices yay <keyword>
documents.s: II. Basic Maintenance: Installing and Updating the System

documents.t: In Arch, the biggest pitfall is using pacman -R to remove the main program while leaving behind a pile of dependencies that were installed for it. 1. Clean Package Removal (Including Dependencies) Make it a habit to append s when removing software, and append n if you also want to purge global configuration files: sudo pacman -Rns <package_name> # or yay -Rns <package_name> 2. Cleaning Up Orphan Packages Through system rolling updates or repeated software installation and removal, some "orphan packages" with no remaining software dependencies will accumulate. Pacman Native Approach: # One-click removal of all orphan packages sudo pacman -Rns $(pacman -Qtdq) Yay Built-in Master Trick (Recommended): Instead of memorizing the command above, yay has a dedicated built-in cleanup command: yay -Yc

Every installation package downloaded or updated accumulates in /var/cache/pacman/pkg/, which can consume a massive amount of disk space over time. 1. Manual Cache Cleaning # Safe cleanup: Only delete cache files of packages that have already been uninstalled yay -Sc # Deep cleanup: Clear "all" caches (frees up maximum space, but local older files will not be available for future downgrades) yay -Scc 2. Advanced Technique: Using Systemd for Automatic Scheduled Cleaning Utilize the paccache -r command (by default, it keeps the latest 3 versions and deletes older files). Note: Requires installing the pacman-contrib package (yay -S pacman-contrib). Create the service file /etc/systemd/system/paccache.service: [Unit] Description=Clean-up old pacman pkg cache [Service] ExecStart=/usr/bin/paccache -r Create the timer file /etc/systemd/system/paccache.timer: [Unit] Description=Clean-up old pacman pkg cache [Timer] OnCalendar=monthly # Set to run once a month Persistent=true # Ensure scheduled runs aren't missed due to shutdown [Install] WantedBy=multi-user.target Enable and start the timer: sudo systemctl enable paccache.timer sudo systemctl start paccache.timer Updated 2026-11-27 After installing pacman-contrib, the system includes /usr/lib/systemd/system/paccache.service and paccache.timer by default (scheduled weekly). Usually, you can simply run sudo systemctl enable --now paccache.timer without manually creating new unit files. If you need to customize a .timer file, systemd unit files do not support inline # comments on the same line as Key=Value (e.g., OnCalendar=monthly # ... and Persistent=true # ... in the example above will cause syntax parsing errors); comments must be written on their own separate lines.
documents.s: IV. Freeing Up Disk Space: Cache Cleaning

documents.t: Arch is a rolling release distribution, so you will inevitably encounter situations where a software update or kernel breaks things. In such cases, you need the downgrade tool to revert to a stable previous version. 1. Installing the Downgrade Tool This program is hosted in the AUR; install it via yay: yay -S downgrade 2. Downgrading a Specific Package When you find that a package (such as Firefox or the Linux Kernel) broke after an update, run: sudo downgrade <package_name> Post-Execution Workflow and Tips: The program will list all historical versions of the package. It will first check your local cache (/var/cache/pacman/pkg/); if not found locally, it will connect to the Arch Linux Archive (A.L.A.) cloud history repository to fetch it. Type the "number" corresponding to the desired version and press Enter. ⚠️ Critical Step: After the downgrade completes, the terminal will ask: add <package_name> to IgnorePkg? [y/N] It is strongly recommended to select y. This adds the package to pacman's blacklist, so the next time you run a global update with yay -Syu, pacman will automatically skip it, preventing it from being stealthily upgraded back to the broken version. 3. How to Lift the Downgrade Lock (Remove IgnorePkg) When the official team releases a fix update and you want to allow the software to upgrade again, edit /etc/pacman.conf: sudo vim /etc/pacman.conf Find the line IgnorePkg = <package_name>, delete it or comment it out by prepending #, save and exit, and normal updates will resume next time.

documents.t: Under modern UEFI architectures, an increasing number of native Arch users and archinstall scripts choose systemd-boot (formerly Gummiboot). Compared to GRUB, which has bulky configuration files and relies on grub-mkconfig for regeneration, systemd-boot offers the following advantages: Native Integration: Built directly into systemd, eliminating the need to install bulky standalone bootloader packages. Modular Configuration: Each kernel boot entry is an independent .conf file without mutual interference. Blazing Fast Boot: Directly calls UEFI firmware interfaces to load EFI executables, resulting in extremely low boot latency.
documents.s: 1. Introduction to systemd-boot: A Lighter Modern UEFI Bootloader than GRUB

documents.t: All configurations and kernel image files for systemd-boot are stored in the EFI system partition (typically mounted at /boot or /efi, referred to as /boot below).
documents.s: 2. systemd-boot Core Structure and Daily Management

documents.t: /boot/ ├── EFI/ │ ├── systemd/systemd-bootx64.efi │ └── BOOT/BOOTX64.EFI └── loader/ ├── loader.conf # Global boot configuration file └── entries/ # Boot menu entries storage ├── arch.conf # Default Linux kernel └── arch-linux-zen.conf # Zen performance kernel

title Arch Linux (Linux-Zen) linux /vmlinuz-linux-zen initrd /intel-ucode.img # Use amd-ucode.img if using AMD initrd /initramfs-linux-zen.img options root=UUID=xxxx-xxxx-xxxx rw quiet Updated 2026-11-27 Boot Loader Specification .conf configuration files treat only lines starting with # at the beginning of the line as comments and do not support inline trailing # comments. When writing to /boot/loader/entries/*.conf, please move explanatory notes like # 若為 AMD... to an independent line or remove them to prevent path parsing errors that lead to boot failures.

Daily maintenance requires no manual searching through configuration files; common operations can be completed via bootctl: # View current boot status, default kernel, and all detected boot entries bootctl status # List all available boot entries bootctl list # Change the default boot entry with one click (the name corresponds to the filename in entries without the extension) sudo bootctl set-default arch-linux-zen # Set boot menu timeout (e.g., 3 seconds) sudo bootctl set-timeout 3 Updated 2026-11-27 The ID parameter for bootctl set-default must be the full item identification name displayed by bootctl list (including the .conf extension), such as sudo bootctl set-default arch-linux-zen.conf (or use wildcards like arch-linux-zen*).

When using systemd-boot, there are two common breakdown scenarios: Bootloader binary not synchronized after systemd package updates: The system upgraded systemd, but /boot/EFI/systemd/systemd-bootx64.efi remains at the old version. Missing initramfs during multi-kernel switching: When installing or removing new kernels (e.g., switching between linux and linux-zen), failure to promptly run mkinitcpio -P to regenerate images will cause reboots to hang directly on UEFI boot errors.
documents.s: 3. Core Pain Points: Why Are Kernel Updates Prone to Breaking Things?

documents.t: In the Arch Linux philosophy, the most elegant solution is utilizing Pacman Hooks to automatically trigger maintenance scripts in the background after package installations or updates, completely eliminating human omissions.
documents.s: 4. Ultimate Automation: Deploying Pacman Hooks Once and for All

documents.t: Create /etc/pacman.d/hooks/95-systemd-boot.hook: [Trigger] Type = Package Operation = Upgrade Target = systemd [Action] Description = Updating systemd-boot in EFI system partition... When = PostTransaction Exec = /usr/bin/bootctl update Effect: Whenever the systemd package is upgraded, the system automatically executes bootctl update to ensure the bootloader binary within the EFI partition remains synchronized with the system, preventing version drift.
documents.s: 1. Hook One: Automatically Upgrade Bootloader When systemd Updates

documents.t: Although Arch's default 90-mkinitcpio-install.hook automatically compiles images, if you frequently switch custom kernels or DKMS modules, you can create a custom check hook /etc/pacman.d/hooks/99-boot-integrity.hook: [Trigger] Type = Package Operation = Install Operation = Upgrade Operation = Remove Target = linux Target = linux-zen Target = linux-lts [Action] Description = Verifying bootloader entries integrity... When = PostTransaction Exec = /usr/bin/bootctl --dry-run list Effect: After any kernel installation, upgrade, or removal, it dry-runs and verifies the integrity of the boot menu configuration files in the terminal background. If paths are corrupted, warnings will be output directly within the pacman update flow, allowing you to fix them before shutting down. Updated 2026-11-27 The --dry-run (-n) parameter for bootctl is only applicable to unlink and cleanup subcommands and has no actual effect on list. It is recommended to use Exec = /usr/bin/bootctl --no-pager list instead (list itself is already a read-only command). Additionally, bootctl list only checks entry file syntax and whether corresponding kernel/initrd file paths exist; it does not verify the internal integrity of the initramfs image itself.
documents.s: 2. Hook Two: Automatic Protection and Status Check After Kernel Updates

If you are still manually typing pacstrap and writing fstab by hand, you've earned my respect. Installing Arch Linux now requires only one core prerequisite: confirming that network connectivity works. As long as the network is connected, a single command archinstall lets you experience the thrill of "automated installation". It is not just a script; it is a menu-driven interactive installer (TUI). Compared to bloated Calamares GUI interfaces like Ubuntu or Manjaro, archinstall is faster, more stable, and most importantly: it gives you complete control over your system without wasting time on repetitive grunt work.
documents.s: Archinstall: The Modern Standard for Arch Linux Installation

documents.t: After entering the Arch Live environment, don't rush to partition; follow these three steps: Check Network: Run ping google.com to check. If using Wi-Fi, connect using iwctl; if this step fails, there's no need to discuss the rest. Launch the Magic Tool: Simply enter the following in the Shell: archinstall Multiple-Choice Quiz Time: A series of menus will appear. This isn't an exam, just fill them out according to your intuition (see advanced configuration below for details).

Although it's automated, choosing the right options will make your Arch truly "take off": 1. Disk Layout —— Recommended to select Btrfs​ Stop using traditional ext4. Select "Wipe all selected drives" and specify Btrfs as the filesystem. It supports compression and subvolumes, making future snapshot backups (like Timeshift) super convenient. 2. Kernels —— A Must-Choose for Performance Enthusiasts​ For stability: select linux. For rocket speed: select linux-zen. For desktop users, the responsiveness and scheduling optimization of the Zen kernel are genuinely noticeable. 3. Profiles —— A Lazy Person's Blessing​ This step is the best. After selecting Desktop, you can directly pick KDE, GNOME, Sway, or Hyprland. It will automatically bundle the relevant Display Manager (such as SDDM or GDM) and base drivers for you. 4. Graphics Drivers​ It automatically detects hardware. If you are an NVIDIA user, select proprietary drivers; if AMD or Intel, selecting open-source drivers is sufficient. It installs more accurately than you could manually fetch them.
documents.s: ⚡ Advanced Configuration Key Points (Don't Fill Randomly, Look Here)

documents.t: This is why I think archinstall completely defeats Calamares. Before finishing the installation, it will ask if you want to save the User Configuration. This generates a JSON file. Be sure to save it! Its Benefits: Next time you get a new computer or need to deploy an identical environment in another virtual machine, you won't even need to click through menus. How to use it: Put that JSON onto a flash drive, and run after booting: archinstall --config my_favorite_setup.json Updated 2026-11-27 Newer versions of archinstall have separated account and password settings into user_credentials.json. For fully unattended deployments, both the configuration file and credentials file need to be passed simultaneously: archinstall --config user_configuration.json --creds user_credentials.json. Then you can go grab a cup of coffee. This is true "Infrastructure as Code", turning your installation habits into code.
documents.s: 💾 Magic Trick: The "Heirloom" Mode for Configuration Files

documents.t: Speed: Calamares frequently hangs on loading graphical interfaces or strange decompression processes. archinstall runs underlying Python logic, and its plain text interface responds extremely fast. Cleanliness: Many GUI installers force a bunch of default software on you. archinstall gives you official, authentic Arch, installing only what you select. Automation Flexibility: You can modify its config.json at any time; this level of customizability is something GUI interfaces can never provide.

Installing Arch used to be about proving technical prowess; installing Arch now is about efficiency. If you pursue "speed, precision, and stability", archinstall is currently the most perfect solution, hands down.

documents.s: Arch Linux KDE Plasma Wayland Setting Up KRDP Remote Desktop Guide

documents.t: For the resident archdesk, after upgrading to KDE Plasma 6.8, the native Wayland display server has deeply integrated the RDP protocol. To achieve more stable connections and better Wayland display support, this guide will walk through phasing out traditional X11-based TigerVNC and migrating to a modern remote desktop solution using krdp + Remmina (FreeRDP).
Run a full system update to ensure you get the latest Plasma 6.8 and related dependencies: sudo pacman -Syu

Clean up the old TigerVNC server and its orphaned dependencies to avoid port or background process conflicts with subsequent RDP services: sudo pacman -Rns tigervnc Remove leftover VNC passwords and configuration files in the user's home directory: rm -rf ~/.vnc

⚠️ Important Concept: krdp is a "user-level" service deeply integrated into KWin Wayland. If the VM reboots and stays at the SDDM login screen, the Wayland session has not started yet, meaning the krdp server will not be in a listening state, resulting in external connections being completely blocked.
documents.s: ⚙️ Phase 2: Core Key — Configuring SDDM Auto-Login

documents.t: Create or edit /etc/sddm.conf.d/autologin.conf on archdesk to have the system automatically load the default Wayland session upon booting: [Autologin] User=kiwi Session=plasma

After configuring auto-login, the system will not receive plaintext passwords at login, so the default KDE KWallet will fail to unlock automatically. Solution: Once you log into the desktop via RDP, open KWalletManager, change the default wallet's password to "blank", and it will eliminate popup interruptions when subsequently opening browsers or other applications. (Note: This setting does not affect SSH agent authorization running in the background as a Systemd User Service)
Install the KDE native RDP server component (krdp), along with the local client tool remmina and its dependent freerdp protocol core: sudo pacman -S krdp remmina freerdp

In KDE Plasma 6 and later Wayland environments, the RDP server is fully integrated into the graphical interface, eliminating the need to manually maintain configuration files: Open System Settings. Navigate to System -> Remote Desktop. Enable the Enable RDP server option. Set the username and password dedicated to remote connections in the interface. (Firewall check): Ensure the local firewall allows standard RDP ports (TCP 3389).

Open Remmina on the client machine initiating the connection (such as the physical Dell laptop at home, IP 192.168.31.21 / .54, etc.) to create a new connection profile: Protocol: Select RDP - FreeRDP plugin. Server: Enter the IP of the target archdesk, 192.168.31.11. Credentials: Enter the RDP username and password created in KDE system settings. Color & Quality: In an intranet environment, it is recommended to set color depth to True color (32 bpp) or enable RemoteFX for optimal graphical rendering performance.

Run sudo reboot to restart archdesk. After waiting about 30 seconds, without opening any ESXi terminal consoles at all, initiate an RDP connection directly from the client. If you can log in directly and see the full KDE desktop, it indicates that both auto-login and the KRDP background service are working successfully.

tip Manjaro was not only the initiation for my Arch-based desktops, but even the initiation for my entire Linux desktop experience; it brought me many wonderful moments until I realized that using Arch directly was enough.

documents.t: The current status is that I don't have any systems running Manjaro, but every one of my Arch Linux desktops has manjaro-zsh-config—a package that has been removed from the AUR but whose Git repo is still retained... Manjaro's impact on me is profound, especially in shaping what I think a Linux desktop should look like, much like how many people encountered Windows 98 the first time they used a computer when young, leaving a lifelong impression that computer operating systems should look that way.

Manjaro was one of the earliest Arch-based distributions specialized for the desktop, featuring many useful small tools and interface embellishments. Personally, I feel that compared to other subsequent Arch-based distros, it is still very excellent, so when useful tools from the AUR catch my eye, I still want to bring them into Arch.

It is actually not much of a problem. Previously, rumors online talked about infighting and arguments causing supporters to churn. I can only say that when love fades, it fades—no need for so many excuses, and even when love fades, one should fairly evaluate its pros and cons. From my perspective, I can only say that switching to Arch Linux was for a cleaner system. This is actually quite contradictory: as a newcomer, I loved how Manjaro took care of everything for me, but once familiar, I complained that it meddled too much and pre-installed too many unnecessary things... It really feels like a scumbag behavior. Therefore, to commemorate the good times using Manjaro, I have kept all my past related notes intact—sort of as a nostalgic keepsake.

documents.t: In the world of Linux, my favorite systems are Arch-based, but installing Arch Linux is not very user-friendly, so I decided to write my own installation script.

This is a general-purpose Arch Linux installation script designed for VMware ESXi, with the following basic default conditions: Intel CPU (The script includes AMD-ucode) 1~2GB RAM 20GB+ HDD space This version performs the following optional items: Update 2021/06/15: Since I moved back to Taiwan and no longer use it, Ver.K has been deleted and this entry is no longer maintained. Simple Arch Linux Basic Arch Linux, installing only essential system tools Single NIC with static MAC Address & Static IP Copy zsh configuration from Live CD V2Ray Server Arch Linux with V2Ray without V2Ray configuration Single NIC with static MAC Address & Static IP Copy zsh configuration from Live CD V2Ray Client Gateway Arch Linux with V2Ray without V2Ray configuration No iptables configuration Dual NIC with static MAC Address External network optional PPPoE or Static IP Internal network with static IP Copy zsh configuration from Live CD V2Ray Client Gateway Kiwi private version Arch Linux with V2Ray with Kiwi's existing settings (encrypted, private use) Directly apply Kiwi's existing iptables (encrypted, private use) Dual NIC with static MAC Address External network optional PPPoE or Static IP Internal network with static IP Copy zsh configuration from Live CD Nextcloud Server (Later found that Docker is actually faster) Arch Linux With Nextcloud from package Single NIC with static MAC Address & Static IP Copy zsh configuration from Live CD

Boot with the Live CD, ensure the network is connected, and run: zsh <(curl -L -s https://Kiwi0093.gitub.io/script/Arch/arch.sh) Updated 2026-11-27 The URL in the historical command above contains a typo (gitub.io should be github.io), and this custom installation script is now deprecated and unmaintained. The official Arch Linux Live ISO now includes the guided installation tool archinstall; it is recommended to use archinstall for installation directly. The Great Firewall blocks https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ via DNS pollution, so if used behind the firewall, you can configure /etc/hosts first to see if it can be overcome. Later I switched to https://Kiwi0093.github.io to host my scripts directly.

documents.s: Integrated Arch Linux Installation Script Architecture Explanation

documents.t: Actually, it didn't need to be this complicated, but when writing it, I wanted to make it detailed while practicing Shell scripting.

Since the installation logic of Arch Linux is as follows: First, perform operations on the HDD within the Live CD OS, then install the new Arch Linux system onto the HDD over the network. Next, chroot into the new system to perform initial configuration and bootloader setup using the new system's environment, and finally exit completely and reboot into the HDD, completing the installation of a new system. Therefore, in the script design, all options executed after arch-chroot were structured as independent scripts, as illustrated in the architecture diagram below:

info This article was automatically translated by Google "Gemini". The author does not guarantee its accuracy or wording. tip This entire series has been retired due to the arrival of the archinstall tool. This document is kept mainly as a historical record and keepsake. Updated 2026-11-27 This script is a historical archive from around 2021 designed for VMware ESXi and MBR environments. It contains multiple commands that are incompatible with or deprecated in modern Arch Linux (such as running pacman -Syyu in the Live ISO, dnsutils being renamed to bind, net-tools/netctl, genfstab -p, and some syntax typos). The original code is preserved below with notes added to the corresponding sections.
documents.s: All-in-One Arch Linux Automated Install Script Guide (arch.sh)

documents.t: First, verify that the system booted from the LiveCD has network connectivity. Check whether the script can be reached with host raw.githubusercontent.com; if not, configure /etc/hosts or your DNS settings. The direct URL to the script is as follows: https://Kiwi0093.github.io/script/Arch/arch.sh You can configure the network manually (if DHCP is not available on your network): #利用ip指令設定網路連線 ip address add $YOUR_IP/24 dev $your_dev ip route add default $Gateway_IP dev $your_dev Updated 2026-11-27 The original example ip route add default $Gateway_IP dev $your_dev is missing the via keyword; the correct syntax is ip route add default via $Gateway_IP dev $your_dev.

Basic Definitions​ #!/bin/sh #Parmeter Pre-Define #Color for warning COLOR_W='\e[35m' #Color for description COLOR1='\e[94m' COLOR2='\e[32m' # Color for Highlight package COLOR_H1='\e[96m' COLOR_H2='\e[34m' NC='\e[0m' In this script, only the display colors are hardcoded by default. You can refer to the Script Syntax Guide to modify the colors, or add variable definitions when customizing it yourself. Update 2021/06/15: Changed to four colors, same as the Manjaro script Warning Banner​ #Notice before use echo -e "${COLOR_W}=====================Warning=======================
${NC}" echo -e "${COLOR_W}= Kiwi's Arch linux Auto install script Ver.1.1 =
${NC}" echo -e "${COLOR_W}= This Script for Kiwi private use. =
${NC}" echo -e "${COLOR_W}= If you have any issue on usage, =
${NC}" echo -e "${COLOR_W}= Please DON'T Feedback to Kiwi =
${NC}" echo -e "${COLOR_W}= And you should take your own responsibility =
${NC}" echo -e "${COLOR_W}===================================================
${NC}" Added a warning banner just like the Manjaro script, along with version numbering. Timezone Configuration​ #start ntp echo -e "${COLOR1}Starting NTP Service${NC}" timedatectl set-ntp true echo -e "${COLOR2}NTP Setup Completed${NC}" Mirrorlist Configuration​ #Modify Mirrorlist to setting country echo -n "${COLOR1}Please Select the country you want to set for mirror list
${NC}${COLOR_H1}C)China
T)Taiwan
*)whatever..I don't care
${NC}" while : do read COUNTRY case $COUNTRY in C) echo -e "${COLOR2}Set China${NC}" sed -i '/Score/{/China/!{n;s/^/#/}}' /etc/pacman.d/mirrorlist break ;; T) echo -e "${COLOR2}SetTaiwan${NC}" sed -i '/Score/{/Taiwan/!{n;s/^/#/}}' /etc/pacman.d/mirrorlist break ;; *) echo -e "${COLOR2}Keep original Setting${NC}" break ;; esac done echo -e "${COLOR2}Completed${NC}" Since Arch Linux does not have a built-in pacman-mirrors command, the official approach of using sed on /etc/pacman.d/mirrorlist is used to configure the mirror list. The pacman -Syyu added later is mainly used to refresh the mirror list. Update 2021/06/15: Added color tags to all options for better visual readability Updated 2026-11-27 Modern Arch Linux Live ISOs use reflector by default to generate /etc/pacman.d/mirrorlist and no longer include # Score markers, so this sed filter rule no longer works. Fdisk & Mount​ #Fdisk echo -e "${COLOR1}Partition your HDD please create sda1 for Data and sda2 for Swap.${NC}" fdisk /dev/sda echo -e "${COLOR2}Partition Setup Completed${NC}" #Format echo -e "${COLOR1}Format /dev/sda1 as EXT4 format${NC}" mkfs.ext4 /dev/sda1 echo -e "${COLOR2}EXT4 formatting Completed${NC}" echo -e "${COLOR1}Format /dev/sda2 as Linux Swap${NC}" mkswap /dev/sda2 echo -e "${COLOR2}Swap Formatting Completed${NC}" echo -e "${COLOR1}Mount /dev/sda1 to /mnt${NC}" mount /dev/sda1 /mnt echo -e "${COLOR2}Completed${NC}" echo -e "${COLOR1}Mount Swap${NC}" swapon /dev/sda2 echo -e "${COLOR2}Completed${NC}" This is one of the main reasons this script cannot be universal: the format section hardcodes the HDD partition layout and mount points, removing flexibility. In addition, because every use case for this script was installing an Arch Linux guest under VMware ESXi, simple fdisk was chosen over other partitioning tools, which also locked the subsequent grub installation to MBR rather than today's standard UEFI. The script uses ext4—the most common format, though not the highest-performing—for this Arch Linux system; if you prefer another filesystem, you can change it to suit your needs. Installation​ #Install echo -e "${COLOR1}Starting Install Archlinux into /mnt${NC}" echo -e "${COLOR1}Please select your CPU vendor and Linux Kernel you want:
${NC}${COLOR_H1}1)Intel+Linux
2)Intel+Linux-LTS
3)Amd+Linux
4)Amd+Linux-LTS
5)Linux-LTS Kernel
*)Whatever, Normal Linux Kernel is good enough to me
${NC}" while : do read CPU case $CPU in 1) echo -e "${COLOR2}Linux Kernel＋Intel${NC}" pacman -Syyu pacstrap /mnt base linux linux-firmware vim zsh curl netctl intel-ucode grub dnsutils open-vm-tools vim net-tools openssh break ;; 2) echo -e "${COLOR2}Linux-LTS Kernel＋Intel${NC}" pacman -Syyu pacstrap /mnt base linux-lts linux-firmware vim zsh curl netctl intel-ucode grub dnsutils open-vm-tools vim net-tools openssh break ;; 3) echo -e "${COLOR2}Linux Kernel＋Amd${NC}" pacman -Syyu pacstrap /mnt base linux linux-firmware vim zsh curl netctl amd-ucode grub dnsutils open-vm-tools vim net-tools openssh break ;; 4) echo -e "${COLOR2}Linux-LTS Kernel＋Amd${NC}" pacman -Syyu pacstrap /mnt base linux-lts linux-firmware vim zsh curl netctl amd-ucode grub dnsutils open-vm-tools vim net-tools openssh break ;; 5) echo -e "${COLOR2}Linux-LTS Kernel${NC}" pacman -Syyu pacstrap /mnt base linux-lts linux-firmware vim zsh curl netctl grub dnsutils open-vm-tools vim net-tools openssh break ;; *) echo -e "${COLOR2}Linux Kernel${NC}" pacman -Syyu pacstrap /mnt base linux linux-firmware vim zsh curl netctl grub dnsutils open-vm-tools vim net-tools openssh break ;; esac done echo -e "${COLOR2}Completed${NC}" Because this installation runs inside the Live CD environment to install packages onto the HDD, you cannot use pacman directly; instead, you must use pacstrap to install packages to the target location. pacstrap /<location> package1 package2 .... We can use this command to directly install the common packages that would otherwise be installed inside arch-chroot. I haven't tested running all packages here yet, though it should not affect systemd operation. Updated 2026-11-27 The official Arch Wiki advises against running pacman -Syyu in the Live ISO environment (it can easily exhaust the in-memory cowspace or cause package conflicts in the Live environment; if you only need to update signing keys, use pacman -Sy archlinux-keyring instead). The dnsutils package has been renamed to bind in Arch Linux; net-tools and netctl are also legacy tools, and modern environments should use iproute2 with NetworkManager or systemd-networkd instead. In the original command, vim is listed twice. Generating fstab for the New System​ #fstab echo -e "${COLOR1}Starting Gernerate fstab${NC}" genfstab -U -p /mnt >> /mnt/etc/fstab echo -e "${COLOR2}Completed${NC}" Because Arch Linux does not have an installer that automatically writes fstab to the new system after partitioning the HDD, genfstab is used to generate it and redirect the output directly into /etc/ on the HDD. Updated 2026-11-27 Newer versions of genfstab from arch-install-scripts already exclude virtual filesystems by default and have deprecated the -p flag. The modern standard usage is genfstab -U /mnt >> /mnt/etc/fstab. Copying zsh Configuration to the New System​ #Copy Zsh echo -e "${COLOR1}Starting Copy ZSH setting file to new Archlinux${NC}" cp -Rv /etc/zsh /mnt/etc/ echo -e "${COLOR2}Completed${NC}" Since I personally quite like the default zshrc configuration style in the Arch Linux Live CD, I simply copy the config files automatically during installation so that every Arch Linux instance installed via this script has a consistent shell style. Choosing Which Install Script to Fetch and Entering arch-chroot​ echo -n "${COLOR1}Please select which type you want${NC}${COLOR_H1}
a)Simple Server
b)Nextcloud Server
c)V2Ray Server
d)V2Ray Gateway
*)I'm the best! let me do by my own!!
${NC}" while : do read SCRIPT case $SCRIPT in a) echo -e "${COLOR2}Simple Arch Linux${NC}" arch-chroot /mnt /bin/zsh <(curl -L -s https://Kiwi0093.github.io/script/simple_arch.sh) break ;; b) echo -e "${COLOR2}Nextcloud Server${NC}" arch-chroot /mnt /bin/zsh <(curl -L -s https://Kiwi0093.github.io/script/nextc_arch.sh) break ;; c) echo -e "${COLOR2}V2Ray Server${NC}" arch-chroot /mnt /bin/zsh <(curl -L -s https://Kiwi0093.github.io/script/arch_v2ray.sh) break ;; d) echo -e "${COLOR2}V2Ray Gateway${NC}" arch-chroot /mnt /bin/zsh <(curl -L -s https://Kiwi0093.github.io/script/arch_v2ray_gate.sh) break ;; *) echo -e "${COLOR2}Yes! you're the chosen one!${NC}" arch-root /mnt /bin/zsh break ;; esac done Because the Arch Linux installation flow is: Prepare the HDD inside the Live CD OS, install the new Arch Linux system onto the HDD over the network, then chroot into the new system to perform initial setup and bootloader configuration, and finally exit and reboot from the HDD to complete the new system installation. So it was built as an option menu to automatically run the corresponding script after entering arch-chroot, or drop directly into arch-chroot for manual setup. Update 2021/06/15: Removed the Kiwi's Private Router option since it is no longer needed Updated 2026-11-27 The *) fallback branch has a typo (arch-root instead of the correct arch-chroot /mnt /bin/zsh), and all auxiliary sub-scripts under Kiwi0093.github.io/script/ have been retired and are no longer available. Entering arch-chroot and Auto-Rebooting After Exit​ echo -e "${COLOR2}Finished Installation, will reboot, Good luck${NC}" # Reboot echo -e "${COLOR2}Rebooting...${NC}" reboot

Updated 2026-11-27 netctl is considered legacy on modern Arch Linux, where systemd-networkd (with .link / .network files) or NetworkManager is typically used instead. Furthermore, netctl profile files should not have a .service extension (it should be /etc/netctl/EXT0 followed by netctl enable EXT0); the original syntax creates a redundant netctl@EXT0.service.service. Changing the root Password and Creating Additional Accounts​ #Root Password echo -e "${COLOR1}Set your root password${NC}" passwd chsh -s /bin/zsh echo -e "${COLOR2}Completed${NC}" #add User echo -e "${COLOR1}Add user account:${NC}" echo -n "${COLOR1}What ID you want:${NC}" read YOURID useradd -m -g root -s /bin/zsh ${YOURID} passwd ${YOURID} echo -e "${COLOR2}Completed${NC}" echo -e "${COLOR1}Add $YOURID into sudo list${NC}" pacman -Syu sudo echo "${YOURID} ALL=(ALL) ALL" >> /etc/sudoers echo -e "${COLOR2}Completed${NC}" Updated 2026-11-27 There are three issues with this section of the script: The zsh package is not installed before running chsh -s /bin/zsh and useradd -s /bin/zsh, which will prevent login. useradd -g root sets the regular user's primary group to root (GID 0), which violates security best practices; the standard approach is useradd -m -G wheel and enabling %wheel in sudoers. pacman -Syu sudo is missing --noconfirm, and appending directly with >> /etc/sudoers risks syntax errors; it is recommended to create a separate drop-in file under /etc/sudoers.d/ and validate it with visudo -c. Installing Packages​ #install Tools echo -e "${COLOR1}Install Packages${NC}" echo -e "${COLOR1}tmux${NC}" pacman -Syu --noconfirm git go base-devel tmux mariadb php php-apcu php-fpm php-gd php-imap php-intl php-imagick nginx certbot certbot-nginx nextcloud echo -e "${COLOR2}Completed${NC}" echo -e "${COLOR1}Install yay${NC}" cd /root git clone https://aur.archlinux.org/yay.git chomd 777 yay cd yay sudo -u kiwi makepkg -si rm -rf yay sudo -u kiwi yay -S php-smbclient Update 2021/06/16: Nextcloud Server essentially requires a Database (MariaDB), PHP, and a Web Server (Nginx), so everything is installed all at once. Updated 2026-11-27 This section of the script contains the following errors and package changes: chomd 777 yay is a typo (it should be chmod). Running sudo -u kiwi makepkg -si inside /root will fail due to insufficient permissions on /root, and the username kiwi is hardcoded instead of using ${YOURID} from earlier (building in /tmp/yay is recommended). Modern Arch Linux official repositories have removed php-imap (moved to PECL/AUR since PHP 8.4), and Arch's nextcloud package often depends on php-legacy / php-legacy-fpm depending on version compatibility. ${NC}" read NCUSER echo -n "${COLOR1}Please input your Password for Nextcloud Database User:
${NC}" read NCPASSWD mysql -u root -p -e"CREATE DATABASE nextcloud DEFAULT CHARACTER SET 'utf8mb4' COLLATE 'utf8mb4_general_ci';GRANT ALL PRIVILEGES ON nextcloud.* TO '${NCUSER}'@'localhost' IDENTIFIED BY '${NCPASSWD}';FLUSH PRIVILEGES;" echo -e "${COLOR2}MariaDB setup compleated${NC}" Updated 2026-11-27 Newer versions of MariaDB have deprecated mysql_secure_installation and mysql as aliases; use mariadb-secure-installation and mariadb instead. Configuration should also be placed in files under /etc/my.cnf.d/ rather than overwriting or appending directly to /etc/my.cnf. In addition, launching mariadbd & in the background inside arch-chroot was only a workaround at the time—it is better to initialize services after booting the system with systemd. PHP​ #Setup PHP echo -e "${COLOR1}change PHP setting$${NC}" curl -o /etc/php/php.ini https://kiwi0093.github.io/script/Arch/php.ini echo -e "${COLOR2}PHP setting completed${NC}" Updated 2026-11-27 change PHP setting$ has an extra $ character. More importantly, the external URL https://kiwi0093.github.io/script/Arch/php.ini is dead, and overwriting system defaults directly with an old php.ini can easily cause incompatible extensions or security settings after major PHP upgrades. The modern approach is to place custom overrides in a separate .ini file under /etc/php/conf.d/ (or /etc/php-legacy/conf.d/). documents.s: Arch Linux Integrated Installation Script: V2Ray Environment Initialization (arch_v2ray.sh)

documents.t: This script defaults to automated execution, but can also be run manually on its own. Original script location: https://Kiwi0093.github.io/script/Arch/arch_v2ray.sh (Updated 2026-11-27: The old personal script link has been deprecated along with the series archive; please refer directly to the historical code below or switch to the official archinstall) Updated 2026-11-27 Below is the original script content retaining historical context, which contains several outdated practices and syntax issues. Do not run it directly in modern environments: Shebang Position and Shell: The full script placed # comments before #!/bin/zsh, which causes the Linux kernel to ignore the shebang (#! must be on the very first line). Furthermore, the Arch ISO / chroot default environment does not pre-install zsh; #!/bin/bash should normally be used. Timezone Abbreviation Typo: The comment CTS(Taipei) is a typo; Taiwan Standard Time should be CST (UTC+8). Network Management Tool: netctl combined with udev custom network interface naming EXT0 is an early approach. Modern Arch Linux recommends using systemd-networkd or NetworkManager. Accounts and Sudo Privileges: useradd -m -g root sets the regular user's primary group to root, and directly appending writes to /etc/sudoers risks configuration corruption. The standard practice is useradd -m -G wheel and enabling the %wheel group via visudo. Dangerous Partial Upgrade: pacman -Sy <package> only synchronizes databases without updating existing packages, which easily causes system library conflicts and corruption on Arch Linux. Installing packages should use pacman -Syu <package>. In addition, practice has largely shifted to replacing old v2ray and screen with xray / sing-box and tmux. Bootloader Mode: grub-install --target=i386-pc /dev/sda is only applicable to legacy BIOS / MBR; modern UEFI machines require --target=x86_64-efi with an ESP partition mounted.

Basic Definitions​ #!/bin/zsh #Parmeter Pre-Define COLOR1='\e[94m' COLOR2='\e[32m' NC='\e[0m' Defines terminal colors for output strings in the script. Setting Timezone and Hardware Clock​ #change Timezone to CTS(Taipei) echo -e "${COLOR1}Please select your time zone
1)Taipei
2)Shanghai
*)Whatever..I don't care
${NC}" while : do read ZONE case $ZONE in 1) echo -e "${COLOR1}Set Time Zone to Asia/Taipei${NC}" ln -sf /usr/share/zoneinfo/Asia/Taipei /etc/localtime hwclock --systohc --utc break ;; 2) echo -e "${COLOR1}Set Time Zone to Asia/Shanghai${NC}" ln -sf /usr/share/zoneinfo/Asia/Shanghai /etc/localtime hwclock --systohc --utc break ;; *) echo -e "${COLOR1}Nobody cares the local time!!${NC}" hwclock --systohc --utc break ;; esac done echo -e "${COLOR2}Completed${NC}" Network Configuration​ #Hostname echo -e "${COLOR1}Please input your hostname
${NC}" read HOSTNAME echo ${HOSTNAME} > /etc/hostname echo "127.0.0.1 localhost ${HOSTNAME}" >> /etc/hosts echo -e "${COLOR2}Completed${NC}" echo -e "${COLOR1}Define your NIC by Mac address${NC}" echo -e "${COLOR1}Please input your MAC Address:
${NC}" read OUTSIDE echo 'SUBSYSTEM=="net", ACTION=="add", ATTR{address}=="'${OUTSIDE}'", NAME="EXT0"' > /etc/udev/rules.d/10-network.rules echo -e "${COLOR2}Completed${NC}" echo -e "${COLOR1}Define your IP for EXT0:${NC}" echo "Description='EXT0 IP SETTING'" > /etc/netctl/EXT0.service echo "Interface=EXT0" >> /etc/netctl/EXT0.service echo "Connection=ethernet" >> /etc/netctl/EXT0.service echo "IP=static" >> /etc/netctl/EXT0.service echo -n "${COLOR1}Please input your IP address:
${NC}" read EXT_IP echo "Address=('${EXT_IP}/24')" >> /etc/netctl/EXT0.service echo -n "${COLOR1}Please input your Gateway IP address:
${NC}" read GATE_IP echo "Gateway='${GATE_IP}'" >> /etc/netctl/EXT0.service echo -n "${COLOR1}Please input your DNS IP address:
${NC}" read DNS_IP echo "DNS=('${DNS_IP}')" >> /etc/netctl/EXT0.service echo -e "${COLOR2}Enable EXT0${NC}" netctl enable EXT0.service echo -e "${COLOR2}Finished.${NC}" This configuration names the network interface as EXT0 using a fixed MAC Address. This configuration uses netctl for static IP management. Changing Root Password and Creating Other Accounts​ #Root Password echo -e "${COLOR1}Set your root password${NC}" passwd chsh -s /bin/zsh echo -e "${COLOR2}Completed${NC}" #add User echo -e "${COLOR1}Add user account:${NC}" echo -n "${COLOR1}What ID you want:${NC}" read YOURID useradd -m -g root -s /bin/zsh ${YOURID} passwd ${YOURID} echo -e "${COLOR2}Completed${NC}" echo -e "${COLOR1}Add $YOURID into sudo list${NC}" pacman -Syu sudo echo "${YOURID} ALL=(ALL) ALL" >> /etc/sudoers echo -e "${COLOR2}Completed${NC}" Installing Programs​ #install Tools echo -e "${COLOR1}Install Packages${NC}" echo -e "${COLOR1}screen${NC}" pacman -Sy screen v2ray certbot certbot-nginx nginx echo -e "${COLOR2}Completed${NC}" Installs screen, v2ray, certbot, certbot-nginx, and nginx. Because back then I didn't want to directly put a config.json or copy someone else's one-click install script, I only installed the basic packages and manually completed the rest of the configuration referencing other materials. Installing Bootloader​ #install Bootloader echo -e "${COLOR1}Install grub Boot Loader into /dev/sda${NC}" grub-install --target=i386-pc /dev/sda grub-mkconfig -o /boot/grub/grub.cfg echo -e "${COLOR2}Completed${NC}" Sync and Exit Arch-chroot​ #Finished install sync sync sync exit

documents.t: Manjaro KDE 21.0.7 Changing the Mirror-list​ Where Manjaro is more user-friendly than Arch is that it provides a tool to directly update the Mirror-list without having to edit configuration files manually (though some people might find editing the file cleaner, simpler, and faster). # 依照國別選擇 sudo pacman-mirrors --country <Country Name> # 依照速度選擇 sudo pacman-mirrors --fasttrack <數量> Previously when I was living in China, I used to set the Mirror-list to China to save a lot of hassle caused by the Great Firewall. Now that I'm back in Taiwan, I'll likely switch to selecting mirrors by speed—or even skip selecting one altogether. Installing the VGA Driver​ sudo mhwd -a [pci or usb connection] [free or nonfree drivers] 0300 This will automatically detect, download, and install the driver. VM Guest OS​ Installer ISO Fails to Boot​ This happened in version 21.0.6, likely because Manjaro adjusted the VM Guest drivers, causing the default driver=free boot option to fail to initialize display output and get stuck at mhwd detection. The workaround was to manually edit the GRUB boot parameter in the boot menu: # 將原先預設參數中的 driver=free # 改成 driver=mesa Switching to mesa for display output allowed it to boot, though this issue was fixed again by version 21.0.7. Unable to Resize Resolution or Auto-Fit Screen After Entering the VM​ This is a quirk in version 21 right now (earlier versions like 20 or 19 didn't have this issue; not sure if future releases will fix it), caused by missing VM display drivers. # 安裝需要的 Package sudo pacman -S open-vm-tools virtualbox-guest-utils While this isn't an official fix—since the video-virtualmachine driver still couldn't be installed (every attempt failed; maybe a later release will fix it)— at least the display started resizing properly, so I just left it at that. Console​ Previously, I would install powerline or power10k myself to prettify my console, but amazingly, starting from 21.0.7, Manjaro's zsh already comes with a nicely configured powerline display out of the box, so I don't need to set it up myself—though it still needs a few adjustments Please refer to Wiki for manjaro-zsh-config (Updated 2026-11-27: The legacy Hexo Wiki site is offline and the original link is dead) tmux​ Refer to another Wiki page (Updated 2026-11-27: The legacy Hexo Wiki site is offline and the original link is dead) yakuake​ This is a drop-down console. I used to remove it, but recently I found it actually very handy, so I kept it. There's nothing special about the settings—basically just: Adjust the drop-down width; I prefer 90% Adjust the drop-down height; I prefer 80% Set the shell to /bin/zsh (you can also just use chsh to change your default shell) When you want to use it, just press F12 (it can probably be rebound to another key, though I personally find F12 pretty good). When you focus another GUI app, it automatically retracts out of the way. As long as you haven't exited, pressing F12 again brings you right back to your running console, which is super convenient. yay​ sudo pacman -S base-devel yay This essential tool is a must-install. Chinese Input Method​ Please refer to Wiki - Fcitx (Updated 2026-11-27: The legacy Hexo Wiki site is offline and the original link is dead)
Since I only use Manjaro as a desktop, I don't use anything overly fancy.

Browser​ Right now I use Brave as my primary browser, and since Brave is in the AUR, it needs to be installed with yay: yay -S brave-bin Make sure to use brave-bin, otherwise waiting for it to compile will take forever. That's it; I also usually remove Firefox since I don't use it. FTP Client​ yay -S filezilla FileZilla also supports SFTP and .ppk files, making it quite convenient. However, nowadays everyone transfers files via web cloud services, so traditional FTP/SFTP is used less and less—you can skip installing it if you don't need it. RDP​ yay -S remmina freerdp This lets you remotely control other Windows machines over RDP. GitHub Desktop (Optional)​ yay -S github-desktop Although you can use git in the console, sometimes a GUI is nicer to use the CLI is still better to use. Hexo (Optional)​ yay -S nodejs npm Since I basically only install Hexo for my own Blog/Wiki, if you just want to try it, pick any directory: sudo npm install -g hexo-cli And you're ready to get started. Updated 2026-11-27 In practice, globally installing packages with sudo npm install -g is not recommended (as it easily causes permission issues); consider using a version manager such as NVM or fnm instead. Furthermore, this site has since migrated from Hexo to Docusaurus. PuTTY (Optional)​ yay -S putty Honestly, on Linux, PuTTY isn't really necessary is just useless bloat taking up space, though since I have a need to use ppk files, it's still better to install it (or you can put the ssh-key into the console the traditional way) Please refer to this Wiki page to convert ppk to pem (Updated 2026-11-27: The legacy Hexo Wiki site is offline and the original link is dead) and then connect directly using ssh—PuTTY on Linux is awful to use.

Typora started charging, so switched to MarkText​ yay -S marktext-bin Please refer to this guide to install and configure PicGo (Updated 2026-11-27: The legacy Hexo Wiki site is offline and the original link is dead) Updated 2026-11-27 Upstream development of MarkText has largely stalled in recent years; for purely local Markdown editing needs today, consider actively maintained tools such as Obsidian. OnlyOffice (Optional)​ yay -S onlyoffice-desktopeditors This is a free Office suite with very high compatibility with M$ Office. After installation, only the Word, Excel, and PowerPoint-compatible apps are available. I originally wanted to set up the server edition, but kept failing and got lazy. Update: After all that effort, turns out just using the web version of Office 365 works fine……

VMware Workstation​ yay -S vmware-workstation Nothing special here, just remember to find a serial number otherwise it won't work (Updated 2026-11-27: Since 2024, Broadcom has made VMware Workstation Pro free for both personal and commercial use, so a serial key is no longer required).

If you are on an Arch Linux environment, please use reflector instead (e.g., sudo reflector --country Taiwan,Japan --latest 10 --sort rate --save /etc/pacman.d/mirrorlist). documents.t: Although the issue has been resolved, here is a record of the workaround used at the time: # Enter the grub editor during boot and change: driver=free to driver=mesa That resolves it.

Essentially, it lacks the installation of video-virtualmachine, a driver compatible with both VMware and VirtualBox: # First install the required packages sudo pacman -S virtualbox-guest-utils open-vm-tools sudo mhwd -i pci video-virtualmachine sudo systemctl enable vmtoolsd.service sudo systemctl start vmtoolsd.service In theory, this should suffice. Updated 2026-11-27 Manjaro 21 is an outdated version (the driver=mesa boot issue was fixed after 21.0.7). Additionally, in VMware VMs, you only need to install open-vm-tools (omitting virtualbox-guest-utils, which is strictly for VirtualBox) and enable vmtoolsd.service (along with vmware-vmblock-fuse.service if needed). Modern Linux/Manjaro kernels and Mesa already include built-in vmwgfx support, eliminating the need for the aforementioned legacy GRUB parameters or mhwd workarounds.
How to make Manjaro (KDE 5) work as a xrdp server? · Issue #1456 · neutrinolabs/xrdp · GitHub

yay -S xrdp xorgxrdp Then start the services: sudo systemctl enable --now xrdp.service sudo systemctl enable --now xrdp-sesman.service After that, it is ready to use, and basically no other settings need to be changed.

Remember to modify the contents of ~/.xinitrc: get_session(){ # local dbus_args=(--sh-syntax --exit-with-session) local dbus_args=(--sh-syntax) case $1 in # Remember to remove --exit-with-session, otherwise it will freeze Updated 2026-11-27 This article was written for early X11-era KDE Plasma 5 and the ~/.xinitrc architecture. Today, KDE Plasma 6 defaults to Wayland, and traditional X11 xrdp + xorgxrdp alongside ~/.xinitrc practices are no longer directly applicable (in Wayland environments, KDE Plasma 6 can use the official krdp / KRdp for RDP remote desktop services).

documents.t: bash <(curl -L https://Kiwi0093.github.io/script/Manajro/manjaro.sh) Updated 2026-11-27 This historical script and link (including original typo Manajro in the path) are no longer maintained. Some tools mentioned in the list have also been archived or deprecated, such as Qv2ray which was archived in 2021, and neofetch which was archived in 2024 (modern environments should use fastfetch instead). Here we still use the universal bash <(curl -L URL/script) syntax to run it. Trying curl -L URL/script | bash resulted in issues with user prompts inside the script. I don't fully understand the technical details, but basically, try to avoid running shell scripts via pipes to prevent issues.

The purpose of this script is to quickly port my active Manjaro environment to a newly installed machine or VM, reducing the repeated work of setting up and adjusting the development environment. This document will first outline what gets installed and generated, and the detailed script will be explained section by section below. Terminator : A console application supporting tabbed usage. I saw the terminal used in Garuda previously and it looked pretty nice; if I find other more intuitive ones, I will replace it. PowerLevel10k : This is basically a terminal customization tool. Since we use the terminal so often under Linux, why not make it look gorgeous and pleasing to the eye? Basically it's powerlevel10k combined with some Nerd Fonts, and sometimes neofetch. V2ray Series : Living behind the Great Firewall makes this a must-install program (though machines used only in the dorm might not need it since it's already handled at the gateway). It mainly installs Qv2ray and V2ray for GUI control. Actually, if you want to be more nerdy, you could ditch the GUI and just run pure v2ray + config.json with systemd... but for a desktop environment, having a GUI feels more appropriate. However, several test runs showed that installing Qv2ray is a huge waste of time... and frequently errors out... If I lose patience after a few more tries, I might remove it (or make it optional!?). Rambox : As a person with friends (undoubtedly...), I still need some IM and Mail clients. Rambox currently works as a smooth unified interface (YES, it just integrates various web interfaces). Brave : Since I am not that fond of Firefox, I use Brave instead. Blog/Wiki Writing Suite : This includes Typora (my current favorite Markdown editor), Git & GitHub Desktop (I know CLI git should be enough, but GUI GitHub Desktop is actually very handy, especially for someone like me who isn't super fluent in git CLI commands...), plus PicGo which is needed for uploading images in Typora. PuTTY : To some degree, running the SSH client directly from the terminal is better than the Linux version of PuTTY, but .ppk keys cannot be used directly that way, and opening SSH Tunnels is more convenient with pre-configured PuTTY, so I always install it, though I probably only use it when connecting back home. Remmina : This actually requires freerdp to run RDP directly. I basically use this + SSH Tunnel to connect back to my home P2P Windows. FileZilla : This tool is mostly useless now because the need to perform FTP/SFTP transfers has decreased... but I still install it out of habit just in case. gnome-pie : This is a launcher, but it looks flashy so I like it now, and it's kept in the mandatory installation list. fcitx Series : As a non-native English speaker, I definitely need non-English input methods... so I generally use this to install Chewing and Mozc to handle my Chinese and Japanese typing needs... TeamViewer : Actually I don't use TeamViewer very often, I just habitually install it just in case. VMware Workstation Pro (optional) : I made this an option because some of my machines are already running inside VMs, so I don't play the "VM inside a VM" game... KDE Fun Widgets (optional) : This basically installs some widgets or boot animations... and might include multiple-boot themes later on...
Although it started as a private script for myself, I still try to write it to be general (though somewhat pointless), and make things with strong personal taste optional.

#!/bin/sh #Parmeter Pre-Define #Color for warning COLOR_W='\e[35m' #Color for description COLOR1='\e[94m' COLOR2='\e[32m' # Color for Highlight package COLOR_H1='\e[96m' COLOR_H2='\e[34m' NC='\e[0m' clear #Notice before use echo -e "${COLOR_W}=====================Warning=====================
${NC}" echo -e "${COLOR_W}= This Script for Kiwi private use. =
${NC}" echo -e "${COLOR_W}= If you have any issue on usage, =
${NC}" echo -e "${COLOR_W}= Please DON'T Feedback to Kiwi =
${NC}" echo -e "${COLOR_W}= And you should take your own responsibility =
${NC}" echo -e "${COLOR_W}=================================================
${NC}" This time I split the colors into five different definitions (pretty elaborate, right?) and added a warning banner right at the top. Going forward, I'll probably rewrite all of my scripts to start with this header so they look a bit more legit.

# Choose Country for pacman-mirrors echo -e "${COLOR1}Please choose the loaction you want to set for Mirror
 ${COLOR_H}C) China
 T) Taiwan
 L) Let me type what I want
 F) Fastest Mirror from all country
 Any other) Use Manjaro Default
 >${NC}" while : do read COUNTRY case $COUNTRY in C) echo -e "${COLOR2}Using China Mirrors${NC}" sudo pacman-mirrors -c China break ;; T) echo -e "${COLOR2}Using Taiwan Mirrors${NC}" sudo pacman-mirrors -c Taiwan break ;; L) echo -e "${COLOR2}Please input coutry you want (ie:United_States)
${NC}" read COUNTRY_INPUT sudo pacman-mirrors -c $COUNTRY_INPUT break ;; F) echo -e "${COLOR2}Use All Country for Fastest Mirror${NC}" sudo pacman-mirrors --fasttrack 3 break ;; *) echo -e "${COLOR2}Use Default setting${NC}" break ;; esac done # Apply Mirrorlist and update system echo -e "${COLOR1}Update your system${NC}" sudo pacman -Syyu Updated 2026-11-27 On line 2 of the script, ${COLOR_H} in the prompt string is undefined (the earlier definitions are COLOR_H1 and COLOR_H2), which causes color formatting to fail; additionally, $COUNTRY_INPUT in sudo pacman-mirrors -c $COUNTRY_INPUT is not quoted. Since Manjaro provides pacman-mirrors, it works differently from the Arch Linux script and can be configured directly via commands. Here I also added four options (plus keeping the default): The Walled Country The Celestial Empire (physically staying here right now, so this option is a must) Taiwan (home sweet home, had to include it) Custom input (for anyone else who might use this, or when I feel like typing it manually...) Sort the top 3 fastest mirrors worldwide by speed (theoretically the best option without needing to pick a country, though... running through the full benchmark takes quite a while...) Keep the original settings without changing anything Next is a simple sudo pacman -Syyu, using -Syy to update the Mirrorlist—even if you don't want to upgrade the system, you still have to run sudo pacman -Syy, otherwise configuring the mirrorlist beforehand was a waste of time (Updated 2026-11-27: pacman -Syy forces a re-download of the package repository sync databases rather than updating the Mirrorlist; the Mirrorlist was already updated by pacman-mirrors in the previous step. Furthermore, on Arch/Manjaro you should avoid running pacman -Syy and then installing packages without upgrading the system (partial upgrade); instead, run sudo pacman -Syu for a full sync and system upgrade).

documents.t: # Install Basic tools echo -e "${COLOR1}Install Packages${NC}" sudo pacman -S --noconfirm yay gcc make patch fakeroot binutils neofetch vim terminator pkgconf fcitx fcitx-qt5 fcitx-configtool fcitx-chewing fcitx-mozc zsh zsh-syntax-highlighting zsh-autosuggestions zsh-theme-powerlevel10k awesome-terminal-fonts v2ray putty filezilla remmina freerdp git Updated 2026-11-27 neofetch was discontinued and archived in 2024; fastfetch is recommended for modern environments. The fcitx (Fcitx 4) package group (fcitx, fcitx-qt5, fcitx-configtool, fcitx-chewing, fcitx-mozc) is now legacy; switching to the fcitx5 family (such as fcitx5-im, fcitx5-chewing, fcitx5-mozc) is recommended. If yay is not included in the current distribution's official repositories, you must install base-devel and git first and build it from the AUR via makepkg -si, rather than installing it directly with pacman -S. As mentioned in the introduction, I install all the tools I commonly use here. They're placed in this section mainly because they can all be installed quickly and directly with sudo pacman.

echo -e "${COLOR1}Do you need pre-download ttf files for ${COLOR_H2}ttf-meslo-nerd-font-powerlevel10k${NC}
 ${COLOR_H1}Y) Yes
 N) No need.
 >${NC}" while : do read TTF case $TTF in Y) echo -e "${COLOR2}Download TTF files for install Issue${NC}" mkdir ~/.cache/yay/ttf-meslo-nerd-font-powerlevel10k curl -o ~/.cache/yay/ttf-meslo-nerd-font-powerlevel10k/MesloLGS-NF-Bold-1.000.ttf https://Kiwi0093.github.io/script/Manjaro/MesloLGS-NF-Bold-1.000.ttf curl -o ~/.cache/yay/ttf-meslo-nerd-font-powerlevel10k/MesloLGS-NF-Bold-Italic-1.000.ttf https://Kiwi0093.github.io/script/Manjaro/MesloLGS-NF-Bold-Italic-1.000.ttf curl -o ~/.cache/yay/ttf-meslo-nerd-font-powerlevel10k/MesloLGS-NF-Italic-1.000.ttf https://Kiwi0093.github.io/script/Manjaro/MesloLGS-NF-Italic-1.000.ttf curl -o ~/.cache/yay/ttf-meslo-nerd-font-powerlevel10k/MesloLGS-NF-Regular-1.000.ttf https://Kiwi0093.github.io/script/Manjaro/MesloLGS-NF-Regular-1.000.ttf yay -S --noconfirm ttf-meslo-nerd-font-powerlevel10k # Download Zeon.ttf & Install echo -e "${COLOR2}Download & Install Zeon font for Zeon Icon${NC}" sudo mkdir /usr/local/share/fonts/z sudo curl -o /usr/local/share/fonts/z/zeon.ttf https://Kiwi0093.github.io/script/Manjaro/zeon.ttf break ;; N) echo -e "${COLOR2}Normal Installation${NC}" yay -S --noconfirm ttf-meslo-nerd-font-powerlevel10k # Download Zeon.ttf & Install echo -e "${COLOR2}Download & Install Zeon font for Zeon Icon${NC}" sudo mkdir /usr/local/share/fonts/z sudo curl -o /usr/local/share/fonts/z/zeon.ttf https://Kiwi0093.github.io/script/Manjaro/zeon.ttf break ;; *) echo -e "${COLOR_H1}Please enter your choice Y or A or N${NC}" ;; esac done Updated 2026-11-27 mkdir ~/.cache/yay/ttf-meslo-nerd-font-powerlevel10k lacks -p, so it will fail if ~/.cache/yay does not yet exist; moreover, the external font download URLs point to an archived legacy path. On modern systems, you can directly install Nerd Fonts packages from the official repositories such as ttf-meslo-nerd. Normally, a simple yay -S ttf-meslo-nerd-font-powerlevel10k should handle this, but due to the special network conditions in the Walled Country the Celestial Empire, downloading the required ttf files during installation often fails. That's why I used a pre-download approach, fetching them from the script hosting location first (and if that location isn't reachable, you wouldn't be able to fetch this script to run in the first place). As for what this Nerd Font is used for: Powerlevel10k uses various glyph icons to prettify the prompt, so these font files are needed for them to render properly. I also mischievously made a custom zeon.ttf containing only two glyphs—the emblems of the glorious Principality of Zeon and Neo Zeon. Since it's just for personal use, I didn't worry too much about image licensing.

# Install yay package echo -e "${COLOR1}Prepare to install package via yay${NC}" Because installing programs via yay usually takes longer to download and compile, I turned every package installed this way into an interactive prompt.

# Install Brave echo -e "${COLOR1}Do you want to install ${COLOR_H2}Brave-bin${NC} for your browser?
It should spend much time
 ${COLOR_H1}Y) Yes
 N) No please skip this 
 >${NC}" while : do read BRAVE case $BRAVE in Y) echo -e "${COLOR2}Install Brave-bin via yay${NC}" yay -S --noconfirm brave-bin break ;; N) echo -e "${COLOR2}Skip Brave installation${NC}" break ;; *) echo -e "${COLOR_H1}Please enter your choice Y or A or N${NC}" ;; esac done

# Install Qv2ray echo -e "${COLOR1}Do you want to install ${COLOR_H2}Qv2ray${NC}?
It should spend much time
 ${COLOR_H1}Y) Yes install via yay
 A) Using AppImage version
 N)No Need
 >${NC}" while : do read QV2RAY case $QV2RAY in Y) echo -e "${COLOR2}Install QV2Ray via yay${NC}" yay -S --noconfirm qv2ray break ;; A) echo -e "${COLOR_H1}Please enter Qv2ray Version(ie:2.6.3)${NC}" read Q_VERSION echo -e "${COLOR2}Download QV2Ray AppImage from Github${NC}" mkdir ~/Applications wget https://github.com/Qv2ray/Qv2ray/releases/download/v${Q_VERSION}/Qv2ray.v${Q_VERSION}.linux-x64.AppImage mv ./Qv2ray.v* ~/Applications/Qv2ray.v${Q_VERSION}.linux-x64.AppImage break ;; N) echo -e "${COLOR2}Skip Qv2ray Installation${NC}" break ;; *) echo -e "${COLOR_H1}Please enter your choice Y or A or N${NC}" ;; esac done Updated 2026-11-27 The upstream Qv2ray project ceased development and was archived in 2021; it is no longer recommended for installation or use in new environments. From experience, Qv2ray builds very easily get stuck and are painful to install, so I added an extra option to download the AppImage version instead.

# Install Teamviewer echo -e "${COLOR1}Do you want to install ${COLOR_H2}Teamviewer${NC}?
It should spend much time
 ${COLOR_H1}Y) Yes
 N) No please skip this
 >${NC}" while : do read TEAM case $TEAM in Y) echo -e "${COLOR2}Install Teamviewer via yay${NC}" yay -S --noconfirm teamviewer break ;; N) echo -e "${COLOR2}Skip teamviewer Installation${NC}" break ;; *) echo -e "${COLOR_H1}Please enter your choice Y or A or N${NC}" ;; esac done

# Install Typora echo -e "${COLOR1}Do you want to install ${COLOR_H2}Typora${NC}?
It should spend much time
 ${COLOR_H1}Y) Yes
 N) No please skip this
 >${NC}" while : do read TYPORA case $TYPORA in Y) echo -e "${COLOR2}Install Typora via yay${NC}" yay -S --noconfirm typora echo -e "${COLOR1}Do you need to Install/Set up ${COLOR_H2}Pigco${NC} for picture upload
 ${COLOR_H1}Y) Yes
 N) Please Skip
 >${NC}" while : do read PICGO case $PICGO in Y) echo -e "${COLOR2}Please install by Typora${NC}" typora break ;; N) echo -e "${COLOR2}Skip Picgo${NC}" break ;; *) echo -e "${COLOR2}Please enter your choice Y or A or N${NC}" ;; esac done break ;; N) echo -e "${COLOR2}Skip Typora Installation${NC}" break ;; *) echo -e "${COLOR_H1}Please enter your choice Y or A or N${NC}" ;; esac done Updated 2026-11-27 The script prompt misspells PicGo as Pigco; additionally, Typora became commercial paid software starting from version 1.0, so the old free beta workflow no longer applies. Since Typora and PicGo basically go hand in hand—and the easiest installation method I've tried is simply opening Typora and installing it through its GUI—this section launches Typora for manual installation if you choose to install PicGo.

# Install VMware Workstation echo -e "${COLOR1}Do you want to install ${COLOR_H2}VMware Workstation${NC}?
It should spend much time
 ${COLOR_H1}Y) Yes
 N) No please skip this
 >${NC}" while : do read VMW case $TEAM in Y) echo -e "${COLOR2}Install VMware Workstation via yay${NC}" yay -S --noconfirm vmware-workstation sudo systemctl enable vmware-networks sudo systemctl start vmware-networks sudo systemctl enable vmware-usbarbitrator.service sudo systemctl start vmware-usbarbitrator.service break ;; N) echo -e "${COLOR2}Skip VMware Workstation Installation${NC}" break ;; *) echo -e "${COLOR_H1}Please enter your choice Y or A or N${NC}" ;; esac done Updated 2026-11-27 case $TEAM in in the script mistakenly reuses the $TEAM variable from the preceding TeamViewer section (it should be case $VMW in), preventing this block from properly reading the user's choice for VMware Workstation and potentially causing an infinite loop on invalid input.

# Install Github-Desktop echo -e "${COLOR1}Do you want to install ${COLOR_H2}Github-desktop-bin${NC}?
It should spend much time
 ${COLOR_H1}Y) Yes
 N) No please skip this
 >${NC}" while : do read GITH case $GITH in Y) echo -e "${COLOR2}Install Github-Desktop via yay${NC}" yay -S --noconfirm github-desktop-bin break ;; N) echo -e "${COLOR2}Skip Github-Desktop Installation${NC}" break ;; *) echo -e "${COLOR_H1}Please enter your choice Y or A or N${NC}" ;; esac done

# Install Hexo Set echo -e "${COLOR1}Do you want to install Do you need to Install ${COLOR_H2}Hexo${NC} for Blog or Wiki?
It should spend much time
 ${COLOR_H1}Y) Yes
 N) No please skip this
 >${NC}" while : do read HEXO case $HEXO in Y) echo -e "${COLOR2}Install basic packages for Hexo${NC}" yay -S --noconfirm nodejs npm echo -e "${COLOR1}Do you have set your own Hexo?
 ${COLOR_H1}Y) Yes
 K)I'm Kiwi please apply my setting
 >${NC}" while : do read H_SET case $H_SET in Y) echo -e "${COLOR_H1}Please input your Hexo Blog folder with full path(ie:~/hexo)
 >${NC}" read PATH mkdir $PATH cd $PATH sudo npm install -g hexo-cli break ;; K) echo -e "${COLOR2}Please start restore Kiwi's Blog setting${NC}" mkdir ~/GitHub cd ~/GitHub git clone https://github.com/Kiwi0093/Blog.git git clone https://github.com/Kiwi0093/Wiki-site.git cd ~/GitHub/Blog/ sudo npm install -g hexo-cli npm install hexo-theme-next cd ~/GitHub/Wiki-site sudo npm install -g hexo-cli git clone https://github.com/zthxxx/hexo-theme-Wikitten.git themes/Wikitten npm i -S hexo-autonofollow hexo-directory-category hexo-generator-feed hexo-generator-json-content hexo-generator-sitemap break ;; *) echo -e "${COLOR_H1}Please enter your choice Y or A or N${NC}" ;; esac done break ;; N) echo -e "${COLOR2}Skip Hexo Installation${NC}" break ;; *) echo -e "${COLOR_H1}Please enter your choice Y or A or N${NC}" ;; esac done Updated 2026-11-27 Line 17 read PATH directly overwrites the system environment variable $PATH, causing subsequent commands (such as sudo, npm, etc.) to fail to locate executables; avoid using environment variable names for custom input variables. The author's Blog and Wiki have migrated from Hexo (Kiwi0093/Blog, Kiwi0093/Wiki-site, and hexo-theme-Wikitten) to Docusaurus, so this Hexo deployment workflow is completely retired. This section is mainly for restoring my Blog & Wiki, though I wanted the script to remain somewhat flexible, so I added an Are you Kiwi?-style option. Since cloning my Git repositories wouldn't let anyone else push updates anyway, cloning them wouldn't do much good either.

# Personal setting # change shell to zsh & import powerlevel10k setting echo -e "${COLOR2}Change default shell to zsh${NC}" sudo chsh -s /bin/zsh chsh -s /bin/zsh # download setting and apply echo -e "${COLOR2}Download and apply powerlevel10k setting${NC}" sudo curl -o /etc/zsh/zshrc https://kiwi0093.github.io/script/Manjaro/zsh/zshrc sudo curl -o /etc/zsh/aliasrc https://kiwi0093.github.io/script/Manjaro/zsh/aliasrc sudo curl -o /etc/zsh/p10k.zsh https://Kiwi0093.github.io/script/Manjaro/zsh/p10k.zsh sudo cp /etc/zsh/zshrc /root/.zshrc cp /etc/zsh/zshrc ~/.zshrc Updated 2026-11-27 The external configuration URLs https://kiwi0093.github.io/script/Manjaro/zsh/... are archived legacy paths and are no longer maintained; additionally, you must log out and start a new session after running chsh for the new shell to take effect.

# Chinese Input ENV Setting echo -e "${COLOR2}Setting Fcitx Chinese Input ENV ${NC}" curl -o profile https://Kiwi0093.github.io/script/Manjaro/profile sudo mv ./profile /etc/profile Updated 2026-11-27 This configuration targets the legacy fcitx 4 and directly overwrites the system /etc/profile, which can easily clobber the distribution's global defaults. In modern environments, fcitx5 is recommended, with environment variables set via /etc/environment or the user's home directory.

# Restore Qv2ray Setting echo -e "${COLOR1}Are you Kiwi?
If you are, do you need to restore your private ${COLOR_H2}Qv2ray${NC} setting
 ${COLOR_H1}Y) Yes
 N) No I don't need
 >${NC}" while : do read Q_SET case $Q_SET in Y) echo -e "${COLOR1}Check QV2ray installed${NC}" if [ -f "~/Applications/Qv2ray*AppImage" ]; then echo -e "${COLOR2}AppImage Version Installed${NC}" curl -o qv2ray.e.tar.gz https://Kiwi0093.github.io/script/Manjaro/qv2ray.e.tar.gz openssl enc -d -aes256 -in qv2ray.e.tar.gz -out qv2ray.tar.gz tar zxvf qv2ray.tar.gz rm -rf ~/.config/qv2ray mv ./qv2ray ~/.config/ rm -rf ./qv2ray.* else echo -e "${COLOR2}No Qv2ray AppImage found${NC}" fi if [ -f "/usr/bin/qv2ray" ]; then echo -e "${COLOR2}Qv2ray Installed${NC}" curl -o qv2ray.e.tar.gz https://Kiwi0093.github.io/script/Manjaro/qv2ray.e.tar.gz openssl enc -d -aes256 -in qv2ray.e.tar.gz -out qv2ray.tar.gz tar zxvf qv2ray.tar.gz rm -rf ~/.config/qv2ray mv ./qv2ray ~/.config/ rm -rf ./qv2ray.* else echo -e "${COLOR2}No Qv2ray found${NC}" fi break ;; N) echo -e "${COLOR2}Skip QV2Ray Setting${NC}" break ;; *) echo -e "${COLOR_H1}Please enter your choice Y or A or N${NC}" ;; esac done Updated 2026-11-27 [ -f "~/Applications/Qv2ray*AppImage" ] places ~ and the wildcard * inside double quotes, preventing shell expansion and causing the condition to always fail. openssl enc -d -aes256 omits -pbkdf2, which is a deprecated key derivation method in modern OpenSSL versions and may fail to decrypt older files due to changes in the default digest algorithm. Qv2ray itself ceased maintenance in 2021. Here I added a check to see if Qv2ray is installed—if not, it won't restore anything. Also, because these are private settings, my config archives are encrypted with OpenSSL, so they're useless without the password.

# Open Brave to set SYNC echo -e "${COLOR1}Are you Kiwi?
If you are, do you need to SYNC your private ${COLOR_H2}Brave${NC} setting
 ${COLOR_H1}Y) Yes
 N) No I don't need
 >${NC}" while : do read B_SET case $B_SET in Y) echo -e "${COLOR1}Check Brave installed${NC}" if [ -f "/usr/bin/brave" ]; then echo -e "${COLOR2}Brave Installed${NC}" curl -o brave.e https://Kiwi0093.github.io/script/Manjaro/brave.e openssl enc -d -aes256 -in brave.e -out brave clear echo "" echo "" echo "" cat ./brave echo "" echo "" echo "" echo -e "${COLOR2}please set SYNC for your brave${NC}" brave rm ./brave* else echo -e "${COLOR2}No Brave found${NC}" echo -e "${COLOR2}Skip Brave Setting${NC}" fi break ;; N) echo -e "${COLOR2}Skip Brave Setting${NC}" break ;; *) echo -e "${COLOR_H1}Please enter your choice Y or A or N${NC}" ;; esac done Since Brave sync requires opening the browser and pasting in the SYNC CODE (unless you back up the entire profile directory), I created an encrypted file that, once decrypted, launches Brave and prints the code in the terminal.

# Open restart picgo setting echo -e "${COLOR1}Are you Kiwi?
If you are, do you need to SYNC your private ${COLOR_H2}Picgo${NC} setting
 ${COLOR_H1}Y) Yes
 N) No I don't need
 >${NC}" while : do read P_SET case $P_SET in Y) echo -e "${COLOR1}Check Picgo installed${NC}" if [ -f "~/.config/Typora/picgo/linux/picgo" ]; then echo -e "${COLOR2}Picgo Installed${NC}" curl -o config.json.e https://Kiwi0093.github.io/script/Manjaro/picgo/config.json.e openssl enc -d -aes256 -in config.json.e -out config.json mv ./config.json ~/.picgo/ rm config.json.e else echo -e "${COLOR2}No Picgo found${NC}" echo -e "${COLOR2}Skip picgo Setting${NC}" fi break ;; N) echo -e "${COLOR2}Skip Picgo Setting${NC}" break ;; *) echo -e "${COLOR_H1}Please enter your choice Y or A or N${NC}" ;; esac done Updated 2026-11-27 In [ -f "~/.config/Typora/picgo/linux/picgo" ], ~ inside double quotes is not expanded ($HOME should be used instead), causing the check to always fail; openssl enc -d -aes256 similarly omits -pbkdf2. Because this file contains my GitHub token, encrypting it was the only option...

# Restore Gnome-pie Setting echo -e "${COLOR1}Are you Kiwi?
If you are, do you need to restore your ${COLOR_H2}gnome-pie${NC} setting
 ${COLOR_H1}Y) Yes
 N) No I don't need
 >${NC}" while : do read P_SET case $P_SET in Y) echo -e "${COLOR1}Check Gnome-Pie installed${NC}" if [ -f "/usr/bin/gnome-pie" ]; then echo -e "${COLOR2}Gnome-pie Installed${NC}" curl -o gnome-pie.tar.gz https://Kiwi0093.github.io/script/Manjaro/gnome-pie.tar.gz tar zxvf gnome-pie.tar.gz rm -rf ~/.config/gnome-pie mv ./gnome-pie ~/.config else echo -e "${COLOR2}No Gnome-pie found${NC}" echo -e "${COLOR2}Skip Gnome-pie Setting${NC}" fi break ;; N) echo -e "${COLOR2}Skip Gnome-pie Setting${NC}" break ;; *) echo -e "${COLOR_H1}Please enter your choice Y or A or N${NC}" ;; esac done Gnome-Pie doesn't hold anything sensitive, so it just copies over the plaintext config files directly to restore it.

# Install Kde Plasmaoid echo -e "${COLOR1}Install KDE plasma Widget & Splash\n${NC}" if [ -d "/usr/include/plasma" ];then echo -e "${COLOR2}KDE Plasma Found${NC}" curl -o plasma-simpleMonitor-v0.6.plasmoid https://Kiwi0093.github.io/script/Manjaro/plasma-simpleMonitor-v0.6.plasmoid plasmapkg2 -i plasma-simpleMonitor-v0.6.plasmoid ~/.local/share/plasma/plasmoids/ rm -f plasma-simpleMonitor-v0.6.plasmoid curl -o VioletEvergarden-Splash.tar.gz https://Kiwi0093.github.io/script/Manjaro/VioletEvergarden-Splash.tar.gz plasmapkg2 -i VioletEvergarden-Splash.tar.gz ~/.local/share/plasma/look-and-feel/ rm -f VioletEvergarden-Splash.tar.gz curl -o plasma-org.kde.plasma.desktop-appletsrc https://Kiwi0093.github.io/script/Manjaro/plasma-org.kde.plasma.desktop-appletsrc mv ./plasma-org.kde.plasma.desktop-appletsrc ~/.config/ else echo -e "${COLOR2}KDE Plasma NOT found${NC}" fi Updated 2026-11-27 plasmapkg2 was the package management tool for KDE Plasma 5, and its -i flag only takes the package file path (it should not be followed by a target installation directory). In modern KDE Plasma 6 environments, it has been replaced by kpackagetool6, and legacy Plasma 5 .plasmoid widgets are incompatible with Plasma 6. This just automatically installs my favorite simple monitor widget and a flashy boot splash, though I still have to tweak things manually afterward.
Writing this script was actually pretty fun—I might take the chance later to rewrite the Arch Linux installation script to follow this same standard.
