documents.t: Users who do not plan to use a GUI basically only need this section:

# Initialize keyring sudo pacman-key --init # Populate keyring sudo pacman-key --populate # Apply and update (if mirrorlist adjustment is needed, modify /etc/pacman.d/mirrorlist first) sudo pacman -Syu This step is essential for ArchWSL; otherwise, nothing can be installed without a proper keyring.

# Use systemd [boot] systemd=true # Set default user [users] default=<username> Updated 2026-11-27 The [users] section name in the configuration above is incorrect and will be ignored by WSL; the correct syntax requires the singular [user]: [user] default=<username>

# Requires go, git, and base-devel to be installed first cd <what ever you like> git clone https://aur.archlinux.org/yay.git cd yay makepkg -si yay is currently the most convenient tool for installing from the AUR, so it is strongly recommended.

References: Bug of WSL Preview - Empty /mnt/wslg/.X11-unix & /tmp/.X11-unix Directory # Check Display is :0 echo $DISPLAY :0 # Check if /mnt/wslg/.X11-unix exists, and whether /tmp/.X11-unix -> /mnt/wslg/.X11-unix ls -la /mnt/wslg ls -la /tmp # If /mnt/wslg/.X11-unix exists but is not linked to /tmp/.X11-unix sudo rm -r /tmp/.X11-unix ln -s /mnt/wslg/.X11-unix /tmp/.X11-unix Then test whether your GUI software runs correctly. If it runs, proceed to the next step; if not... check the documentation... /etc/tmpfiles.d/wslg.conf --- # TYPE PATH Mode UID GID Age Argument L+ /tmp/.X11-unix - - - - /mnt/wslg/.X11unix Updated 2026-11-27 sudo should be added when creating the symbolic link manually (sudo ln -s /mnt/wslg/.X11-unix /tmp/.X11-unix). The target path in the last column of the wslg.conf snippet above is missing a hyphen; it should be /mnt/wslg/.X11-unix (instead of .X11unix). Also, the file content should not include the leading filename and ---. Newer WSL/WSLg versions have fixed this issue where systemd startup cleans up /tmp/.X11-unix, so manually creating this configuration file is generally no longer necessary. Run wsl --shutdown in PowerShell and re-enter WSL.

Dolphin is the KDE file manager (similar to Windows Explorer). Installing Dolphin alone results in missing icons, so installing the KDE theme breeze is required for proper appearance: yay -S breeze dolphin
This is a very useful RDP client, but Remmina is only a frontend interface; freerdp must be installed to RDP into other RDP servers: yay -S remmina freerdp
A browser is necessary... otherwise what is the GUI for: yay -S brave-bin

info This article was automatically translated by Google "Gemini". The author does not guarantee its accuracy or wording. tip The latest recommended approach is to install WSL2 directly via the Microsoft Store paired with ArchWSL, which significantly simplifies the steps. info Since I had a Windows machine available with installation permissions to use WSL, I recorded the process of setting up ManjaroWSL at the time.

First, prepare the WSL / WSL2 environment: Open PowerShell with administrator privileges and run the following command to enable the Windows Subsystem for Linux: dism.exe /online /enable-feature /featurename:Microsoft-Windows-Subsystem-Linux /all /norestart Open PowerShell with administrator privileges and run the following command to enable Virtual Machine Platform: dism.exe /online /enable-feature /featurename:VirtualMachinePlatform /all /norestart Download and install the WSL-Kernel Set the default version to WSL2: wsl --set-default-version 2 Updated 2026-11-27 Modern Windows 10 (2004+) and Windows 11 support one-click installation and enabling of required components directly via wsl --install (and wsl --update), eliminating the need to manually run dism.exe or download the WSL2 Kernel update package separately.

ManjaroWSL was pre-packaged; at the time, you could directly download the latest zip file from the Releases page. Updated 2026-11-27 The sileshn/ManjaroWSL project is currently unmaintained/archived. For modern WSL2 environments requiring an Arch-based distribution, it is recommended to use the officially supported wsl --install -d archlinux or the new .wsl image import mechanism.

Place the downloaded zip file into the directory where you intend to store the entire ManjaroWSL system, extract it, and open PowerShell to run: ./Manjaro.exe After it automatically completes extraction and initialization, run it once more: ./Manjaro.exe

Follow the on-screen prompts to decide whether to Resize and create a New User. At the time, it was recommended to select No for both reasons: You won't exceed 250GB of space (and WSL automatically mounts Windows drives to /mnt/). User accounts are uniformly created by subsequent scripts, which conveniently applies a complete Zsh terminal and Xfce environment setup.
Run the initialization script as root: bash <(curl -L -s https://kiwi0093.github.io/script/WSL/manjaro.sh)

Manually specifying the country code at the beginning is usually faster than auto-speed-testing to pick a mirror. When the vi editor interface pops up mid-way for /etc/wsl.conf, add the following settings: [Users] # Add the following information default = <User Name you created and wish to be default> After editing, type :wq to save and exit.

The following excerpts the main configuration sections executed in the script: Mirrorlist & System Upgrade​ # Basic system configuration echo -e "${color1}Basic system configuration started${NC}" echo -e "${color1}Setting your Repo${NC}" echo -e "${color2}Do you want to set location for the mirror-list?(Y for Location, others for fastest 3 location)${NC}" while : do read LT case $LT in Y) echo -e "${color2}Please input location you want(EX, tw for Taiwan, us for USA)\n${NC}" read LT2 pacman-mirrors -c $LT2 break ;; *) pacman-mirrors --fasttrack 3 break ;; esac done echo -e "${color1}Update system${NC}" pacman -Syyu This primarily provides interactive options to execute pacman-mirrors and pacman -Syyu. Basic Tools Install​ echo -e "${color1}Install Basic tools${NC}" pacman -S git yay wget curl rsync sshpass zsh manjaro-zsh-config \ ttf-nerd-fonts-symbols ttf-meslo-nerd-font-powerlevel10k \ ttf-meslo-nerd-font-powerlevel10k powerline-fonts \ nerd-fonts-noto-sans-mono vim wireguard-tools systemd-resolvconf htop --noconfirm This section installs zsh, aesthetic-related fonts/settings, and common tools such as git, yay, rsync, and wireguard. Xfce4 & Manjaro Theme​ echo -e "${color1}Install Xfce4 for GUI${NC}" pacman -S xfce4-gtk3 xfce4-goodies xfce4-terminal network-manager-applet \ xfce4-notifyd-gtk3 xfce4-whiskermenu-plugin-gtk3 tumbler engrampa lightdm \ lightdm-gtk-greeter lightdm-gtk-greeter-settings manjaro-xfce-gtk3-settings \ manjaro-settings-manager --noconfirm This part mainly follows Manjaro's official documentation to install Xfce4 and theme packages. GUI Tools & Chinese Environment​ echo -e "${color1}Install GUI$ tools${NC}" pacman -S terminator brave-browser tigervnc gnome-pie --noconfirm echo -e "${color1}Install Chinese Environment${NC}" pacman -S adobe-source-han-serif-tw-fonts adobe-source-han-serif-hk-fonts \ adobe-source-han-serif-cn-fonts adobe-source-han-sans-tw-fonts \ adobe-source-han-sans-hk-fonts adobe-source-han-sans-cn-fonts \ adobe-source-han-serif-jp-fonts adobe-source-han-sans-jp-fonts \ fcitx fcitx-chewing fcitx-configtool fcitx-mozc fcitx-configtool --noconfirm This section installs basic browsers, terminals, Chinese fonts, and input method packages, alongside some personal configuration imports and account creation. Updated 2026-11-27 In the historical script above, ttf-meslo-nerd-font-powerlevel10k and fcitx-configtool were listed redundantly; additionally, traditional fcitx (v4) has been completely superseded by fcitx5 (fcitx5-im, fcitx5-chewing, fcitx5-mozc) in the Arch / Manjaro ecosystem. Systemd on WSL​ echo -e "${color1}Change your root password & shell to zsh${NC}" sudo -u $USERN yay -S genie-systemd-git echo 'genie -i' > /etc/init.wsl chmod +x /etc/init.wsl genie -i genie -c systemctl disable auditd.service genie -c systemctl disable multipathd.service genie -c systemctl disable systemd-modules-load.service genie -c systemctl enable systemd-resolved.service genie -c systemctl start systemd-resolved.service At the time, practical testing showed that the only relatively simple and functional solution was genie-systemd-git: after installation, initialize the bottle environment with genie -i, and then execute commands or enter a new shell via genie -c. Updated 2026-11-27 Since WSL 0.67.6, WSL2 has natively supported systemd. Modern environments simply require adding [boot] and systemd=true to /etc/wsl.conf and restarting WSL (wsl --shutdown), eliminating the need to install genie-systemd-git or apply the service-disabling workarounds above. Creating Desktop Shortcuts​ Configure using GWSL: Open GWSL Distro Tools → Display/Audio auto exporting Open GWSL Distro Tools → LibGL Indirect Then open Shortcut Creator: Shortcut Label: The shortcut name displayed in the Windows Start menu, customizable. Shortcut Command: When using Xfce4, always enter startxfce4. Display Mode: To display the full desktop environment, select Single Window or Fullscreen. Keep Xserver Instance: If Display Mode is set to Fullscreen, this option must be set to true, otherwise it is prone to crashing. After configuration, you can click Test Configuration to test, and once confirmed working, click Add to Start Menu. Updated 2026-11-27 Windows 11 built-in WSLg natively provides Linux GUI (X11 / Wayland) integration with audio and Chinese input methods, making third-party X servers like GWSL largely unnecessary for general graphical applications.

To be honest, when I first saw WSL I was thrilled, and discovering a Manjaro community distribution made it even more anticipated, but actual installation and usage revealed some gaps for the following reasons: Execution speed was not as smooth as expected, especially when running a full desktop environment. Programs running in multi-monitor environments often failed to switch input methods correctly (perhaps only manageable by defaulting to Chewing and toggling with Shift). Desktop mode tended to freeze directly after being idle for a period of time, bringing down any running applications inside it as well. Although systemd managed to run via third-party tools, its overall stability still had a noticeable gap compared to a native environment. Therefore, if you only need a Linux shell to run tools, or must work simultaneously across Windows and Linux due to special requirements, WSL is a great choice. However, comparing it to a true Linux Desktop falls short, and even remote VNC connection performance to another Linux desktop beats it. But after all, this was an expedient solution adopted for specific scenarios.

GitHub - sileshn/ManjaroWSL2: Manjaro for WSL2 using wsldl This project basically uses the same approach as the previous version, leveraging wsldl: Advanced WSL launcher. Anyone interested in building their own can also do it using wsldl.
documents.s: ManjaroWSL2 (based on wsldl) Installation and Usage Notes

documents.t: Simply extract the downloaded files to your preferred location, then run the extracted Manjaro.exe and click through the prompts.

# make sure you're root # Set your mirrorlist to what you like pacman-mirrors -c tw # system full update pacman -Syyuu # Install basic tools pacman -S yay neovim zsh noto-fonts-cjk .......etc # completed Does reading the above make you feel dumbfounded? After all, it looks exactly the same as a normal Manjaro setup... That's right, basically it is the same (which is why it's great). However, compared to previous version instructions, there are some differences: You can run GUI apps normally without installing a DE. For example, pacman -S brave-browser will install Brave directly, and magically, shortcuts will automatically be generated in Windows without needing to do anything else: You can see that whatever I install will automatically generate shortcuts like this. This allows launching them directly inside Windows without opening wslg.

Since WSL is still a VM after all (especially WSL2), although you can directly run Linux GUI apps, non-English input from Windows cannot be directly typed into Linux GUI apps. This is why you need to install fcitx and its related input methods, such as chewing, etc.

# Add the following to /etc/profile # Add Chinese Input Support export GTK_IM_MODULE=fcitx export XMODIFIERS=@im=fcitx export QT_IM_MODULE=fcitx export DefaultIMModule=fcitx fcitx-autostart &>/dev/null Then shut down WSL in PowerShell using wsl --shutdown, and reopen it using wsl. Remember to set a global hotkey to activate it (since we didn't install a DE, we can't use the mouse to click and switch input methods).

I originally thought the I/O part would be greatly improved, but in actual testing, running common commands like git clone, git push, and hexo g -d inside a Windows folder clearly shows that this I/O performance is not cutting it...

Although it's very appealing that WSL1.0 supports systemd and allows normal use of GUI apps without wslg, as we can see, there are still areas that need polishing—for instance, Chinese input methods sometimes still have issues, and I/O is still slow... etc. However, for light usage (or even moderate usage), it is still quite handy.

"${color4}.........................................................................................completed${NC}" Updated 2026-11-27 This archived script contains several outdated practices and syntax errors and is preserved solely for historical reference: Docker Compose v1 retirement: The script downloads the end-of-life docker-compose 1.29.2 binary from GitHub Releases and runs docker-compose; modern setups should install docker-compose-plugin and use the docker compose (v2) command instead. Additionally, version: '3' / version: '3.3' and links: inside Compose YAML are deprecated in v2 (services on the same network can communicate directly by service name). Script syntax and configuration errors: Lines 46–47 and elsewhere mistakenly use an undefined lowercase ${nc} (whereas uppercase NC='\e[0m' is declared above), causing terminal color resets to fail. In v2ray.yml, the restart: unless-stopped line for the traefik service is misindented under the labels: block instead of at the service level, which causes Compose parsing errors. After generating v2ray.yml, Please input the Domain for Trafik Dashboard is printed twice. Uses end-of-life (EOL) traefik:v2.5, and enables both httpchallenge and tlschallenge simultaneously (only one is needed). System and security recommendations: useradd -m -g root directly assigns root as the rescue account's primary group and manually copies a private key inside the script, posing significant privilege and security risks; modern practice recommends using a separate group with usermod -aG wheel to grant sudo access and authenticating via SSH public keys. Furthermore, yum on Oracle Linux 8+ is actually an alias for dnf, and the external file downloaded by the script (https://kiwi0093.github.io/script/OL8/default) is also an early archived dependency. Basically, it updates the system, installs common tools, and deploys the Portainer Agent and Watchtower containers by default. Since I host the Portainer Master in my home lab environment, every node other than that host only needs to run the Agent.

When I use these Oracle Linux 8 hosts myself, I normally just run git clone on my private repo to spin up services. However, considering others might also use this script—and most of them need to run V2Ray (sigh... the GFW...)—I added logic to deploy V2Ray-related services directly: WebSocket + TLS requires an SSL certificate, so Traefik is bundled as a foundational component. Because Traefik sits at the front end, instead of using V2Ray's built-in HTTP handling directly to accept packets, an Nginx layer is wrapped around it as a reverse proxy. Due to how Traefik works, be sure to configure DNS before starting the service; otherwise, if the service starts before DNS resolves properly, you will hit a Let's Encrypt error that locks out that domain name for at least 30 days (Updated 2026-11-27: Should be "Let's Encrypt"; furthermore, the failed-validation rate limit is 5 failures per hostname per hour, locking out for roughly 1 hour rather than 30 days)... Because I was too lazy to write complex input validation, entering anything other than an exact Yes or No puts you into an infinite loop (and it's case-sensitive too~~~~).

At the end of the day, it all comes down to a single command: sudo su bash <(curl -L -s https://kiwi0093.github.io/script/OL8/setup.sh) Updated 2026-11-27 This remote installation script has been archived and retired following architectural changes. In addition, sudo su starts a new interactive root subshell, so if you copy and paste both lines at once, the second line bash <(...) will not run inside that su session. On modern systems, use sudo when you need root privileges for a single command, and avoid executing remote scripts directly without inspecting them or verifying their checksums.

In the Debian family, the underlying package management tool is dpkg, while the high-level command we use daily is apt (which replaced the older apt-get). Recommended Tool: Nala If you are accustomed to the clean and intuitive interface of Arch's yay, it is strongly recommended to install nala on Debian / Ubuntu. It is a frontend wrapper for apt featuring clearer formatting, parallel download acceleration, and history rollback capabilities. # Install Nala sudo apt update sudo apt install nala Once installed, you can seamlessly replace almost all your daily apt commands with nala (e.g., sudo nala update). The basic commands below will still focus on native apt, but the underlying logic applies to both.
documents.s: I. Introduction: Modern Package Management with Nala (Recommended)

documents.t: 1. Comprehensive System Update Updates in the Debian family involve two steps: refreshing the local package list and then performing the actual upgrade: sudo apt update && sudo apt upgrade -y Advanced Knowledge: Difference between apt upgrade and apt full-upgrade? upgrade (Safe Upgrade): Upgrades existing packages only. If a new version of a package requires "removing" other existing packages to be installed, upgrade chooses to skip that package, keeping the current state for stability. full-upgrade (Full Upgrade): Allows the system to actively remove blocking obsolete dependencies during upgrades. Typically used when performing major distribution upgrades (e.g., Ubuntu 22.04 to 24.04) or when package dependencies are deadlocked. (Note: In legacy commands, the equivalent is apt-get dist-upgrade) 2. Searching and Installing Packages # Install a specific package sudo apt install <package_name> # Search for packages (supports regular expressions) apt search <keyword>
documents.s: II. Basic Maintenance: Installation and System Updates

documents.t: The most common mistake when uninstalling packages in Debian systems is using remove alone, leaving configuration files and dependencies behind. 1. Clean Removal of Main Applications Standard Removal: Deletes the program binary only while retaining configuration files you modified under /etc. sudo apt remove <package_name> Complete Removal (Purge): Removes the program along with all global configuration files (excluding settings inside your personal home directory ~/.config/). sudo apt purge <package_name> 2. Cleaning Up Orphaned Packages Dependencies installed automatically to satisfy a software package often remain even after the main application is uninstalled. Debian provides built-in commands to clean these up: # Remove all orphaned packages that are no longer needed sudo apt autoremove # Advanced: Clean up orphaned packages along with their configuration files (Recommended) sudo apt --purge autoremove

Every .deb installer downloaded via apt install is cached in /var/cache/apt/archives/. On long-running VMs or machines with limited disk space, this consumes significant storage. 1. Manual Cache Cleanup # Safe cleanup: Delete only outdated installer versions that can no longer be downloaded from repositories sudo apt autoclean # Deep cleanup: Completely empty the cache folder to free up maximum space sudo apt clean Automation Tip: Debian / Ubuntu actually has built-in scheduled tasks. As long as unattended-upgrades is installed, the system silently cleans up outdated caches in the background by default, eliminating the need to manually write Systemd Timers like on Arch.
documents.s: IV. Freeing Up Disk Space: Cache Cleanup

documents.t: Although the Debian family is relatively stable, adding third-party PPAs or external repositories can still occasionally introduce broken updates. 1. Finding Historical Versions First, check which older versions are available on the repository servers. apt-cache madison <package_name> # or apt list -a <package_name> This prints all available version numbers for the package (e.g., 1.2.3-1ubuntu2). 2. Performing a Downgrade Installation Once you find the desired version number, force installation by appending = directly (this overwrites the buggy newer version): sudo apt install <package_name>=<version_number> 3. ⚠️ Critical Step: Version Hold to Prevent Upgrades After downgrading, you must "hold" the package to prevent accidentally upgrading it the next time you run apt upgrade: sudo apt-mark hold <package_name> Packages on hold are automatically ignored by apt even when newer versions are released. 4. How to Release a Downgrade Hold (Unhold) When an official bug fix is released and you decide to give it another try, simply release the hold: sudo apt-mark unhold <package_name> Once unheld, the next apt upgrade will upgrade the package normally.
documents.s: V. Lifesaving Tools: Package Downgrade and Hold

documents.t: Previously, when adding third-party software repositories (such as Docker, Node.js, Grafana), we commonly used sudo apt-key add to add GPG keys. Doing so today triggers a prominent apt-key is deprecated warning. Why was it deprecated? Because apt-key places keys into the system's global trusted keyring (/etc/apt/trusted.gpg). This means if you add a key for a minor utility, that key gains permission to forge and verify system-core level packages—a massive security vulnerability. Modern Standard Practice (Signed-by Binding): The modern specification dictates storing keys independently in dedicated directories and strictly specifying in repository configuration files that "this repository may only be verified using this specific key." Below is the standard workflow compliant with Ubuntu 22.04+ and Debian 12+ (taking a fictional example repository as an example): 1. Create a Dedicated Directory for Keys The system now recommends storing third-party keys centrally under /etc/apt/keyrings/ (create the folder if older systems lack it): sudo mkdir -p /etc/apt/keyrings 2. Download and Convert the Key (Dearmor) Most third-party keys are provided as ASCII text files (.asc or .pub), but apt now prefers binary .gpg files. Download via curl and convert using gpg --dearmor into the newly created directory: curl -fsSL https://example.com/key.pub | sudo gpg --dearmor -o /etc/apt/keyrings/example.gpg 3. Add Repository Source and Bind the Key Create a list file for the software under /etc/apt/sources.list.d/, making sure to append [signed-by=...] right after deb: echo "deb [arch=amd64 signed-by=/etc/apt/keyrings/example.gpg] https://example.com/apt stable main" | sudo tee /etc/apt/sources.list.d/example.list Explanation: With signed-by=/etc/apt/keyrings/example.gpg specified, the system verifies software downloaded from example.com using strictly this dedicated key, preventing unauthorized interference with other system packages. 4. Update Cache Files Finally, update the package list to eliminate deprecation warnings: sudo apt update Updated 2026-11-27 In newer Ubuntu 24.04+ and Debian 12 / 13+ environments, consider the following modern details: Directory & Key Permissions: When creating the directory, use sudo mkdir -p -m 0755 /etc/apt/keyrings, and ensure the converted .gpg file is readable (sudo chmod a+r /etc/apt/keyrings/example.gpg) to prevent the low-privilege _apt user from failing to read the key during apt update. Dynamic Architecture Detection: Hardcoding arch=amd64 on ARM64 hosts (such as Raspberry Pi) causes fetch failures; substitute it with arch=$(dpkg --print-architecture). DEB822 .sources Format: Modern systems are phasing out traditional single-line .list files in favor of structured /etc/apt/sources.list.d/example.sources (using the Signed-By: field); APT 3.0+ (Debian 13 / Ubuntu 24.10+) also provides sudo apt modernize-sources to automatically convert legacy .list files to .sources format.
documents.s: VI. Advanced: Adding Third-Party Repositories and GPG Keys Correctly (Saying Goodbye to apt-key)

documents.t: Some graphical user interface (GUI) applications (such as SonicWall NetExtender) provide an operation interface, but require root privileges when invoking underlying system core tools in the background (such as pppd, network routing configuration, etc.). Running them directly as a regular user often results in connection failure due to insufficient permissions. Updated 2026-11-27 When using the following methods in modern Linux desktop environments, please note these compatibility limitations: Wayland Environment Limitations: In modern Wayland desktops like KDE Plasma 6 and GNOME, launching GUI programs directly with su, sudo, or pkexec usually fails due to inability to access the user's Wayland socket; if the program runs via XWayland, running xhost +SI:localuser:root beforehand is often required (it is recommended to revert with xhost -SI:localuser:root afterwards). pkexec GUI Launching: pkexec clears environment variables like DISPLAY and XAUTHORITY by default; you must create a corresponding .policy configuration file under /usr/share/polkit-1/actions/ with <annotate key="org.freedesktop.policykit.exec.allow_gui">true</annotate> to open windows normally. kdesu Path Differences: Most modern KDE distributions no longer place kdesu in $PATH (often located at /usr/lib/kf6/kdesu or /usr/lib/kf5/kdesu). Polkit Group Names: subject.isInGroup("wheel") in the example below applies to Arch / Fedora / RHEL families; if using Debian / Ubuntu families, change it to the "sudo" group.
documents.s: Running GUI Applications as root in Linux Desktop Environments

documents.t: Switch identity via su: Directly switch to the root account and then launch the application. su - netExtenderGui Temporary privilege escalation via sudo: Requires ensuring that the current user is added to the sudoers list. sudo netExtenderGui

If you want the system to automatically pop up a password prompt and run as root when clicking the application menu or desktop shortcut, you must modify the corresponding .desktop file (usually located in /usr/share/applications/ or ~/.local/share/applications/). KDE Desktop Environment (kdesu) Open the .desktop file with a text editor and modify the Exec= field to use kdesu: # Before modification Exec=/usr/bin/netExtenderGui # After modification Exec=kdesu /usr/bin/netExtenderGui GNOME / XFCE / Generic Desktop Environments (pkexec) For non-KDE environments, it is recommended to use the modern Linux standard PolicyKit privilege escalation tool pkexec: # After modification Exec=pkexec /usr/bin/netExtenderGui (After modification, if it does not take effect immediately, run the following command to refresh the desktop database:) update-desktop-database ~/.local/share/applications/
documents.s: Desktop Shortcut and Menu Modification Method (.desktop)

documents.t: If you do not want to manually input the root password every time you launch the GUI software, you can establish an authorization whitelist through PolicyKit rules. Create a configuration file under the /etc/polkit-1/rules.d/ directory (e.g., 49-netextender.rules): sudo nano /etc/polkit-1/rules.d/49-netextender.rules Write the following rule content (allowing users belonging to the wheel or sudo group to run passwordlessly): polkit.addRule(function(action, subject) { if (action.id == "org.freedesktop.policykit.exec" && action.lookup("program") == "/usr/bin/netExtenderGui" && subject.isInGroup("wheel")) { return polkit.Result.YES; } });
documents.s: Advanced Application: Passwordless Execution via Polkit

documents.t: When installing software in Gentoo, the system defaults to fetching source code and compiling it "live" on your machine. This introduces Gentoo's most powerful core feature: USE Flags. By defining USE Flags, you can decide at compile time whether to exclude or include specific features (e.g., compiling the entire system without Bluetooth support, or without GUI interfaces), achieving ultimate lightweight optimization. Global configuration files are typically located at /etc/portage/make.conf, while fine-grained settings for individual packages are placed in /etc/portage/package.use/.
documents.s: I. Introduction: The Philosophy of Portage and USE Flags

documents.t: Gentoo's update command is playfully referred to by players as "chanting a spell" because the parameters are very long, but every single one of them is crucial. 1. Sync the Portage Tree (Sync) First, fetch the latest compilation script (ebuilds) directory from the remote repository: # Traditional usage sudo emerge --sync # Modern recommended usage (faster, supports multiple repositories) sudo emaint sync -a 2. Comprehensive System Update (World Update) This line is the ultimate command most familiar to Gentoo users: sudo emerge --ask --verbose --update --deep --newuse @world # Usually abbreviated as: sudo emerge -avuDN @world Parameter Breakdown: -a (ask): List packages and ask for confirmation before compiling (essential to prevent typos). -v (verbose): Display detailed information (including USE Flag changes). -u (update): Update packages. -D (deep): Check updates along the entire dependency chain of dependencies. -N (newuse): If you modify USE Flags, this automatically catches affected packages and "recompiles" them to apply the new settings. 3. Updating Configuration Files (Dispatch-conf) After updating software, if global configuration files conflict, Gentoo will not overwrite them directly. You need to run: sudo dispatch-conf # Or sudo etc-update Press u to apply new settings, or z to discard them.
documents.s: II. Basic Maintenance: Syncing and Updating the System

documents.t: 1. Searching and Installing Packages # Search for packages (though native search is very slow; an alternative eix will be introduced later) emerge --search <keyword> # Install a package (and record it in the world file) sudo emerge -av <package_name> # ⚠️ Key Tip: Install without recording (Oneshot) # Use this when you want to install a build tool or dependency without recording it as primary software: sudo emerge -av --oneshot <package_name> 2. Uninstallation and Depclean (Orphan Cleanup) Gentoo's removal logic is extremely rigorous. If you forcibly remove a package using emerge -C <package> (unmerge), you can easily break other packages' dependencies and cause system failure. Standard and Safe Removal Workflow: # 1. Unselect the specified package, removing it from the @world list (it checks dependencies and will block you if anyone else needs it) sudo emerge --deselect <package_name> # 2. Run dependency cleanup (Depclean)! This will clean up all orphan packages that are neither in @world nor needed by anyone else sudo emerge --ask --depclean # Abbreviated as: sudo emerge -a --depclean Updated 2026-11-27 Additional note: emerge --deselect <package_name> only removes the package from the @world list and does not immediately check reverse dependencies or uninstall the package; actual dependency checks and safe removal are handled by step 2 (emerge -a --depclean). (If you only want to check and remove a specific package individually, you can use emerge -a --depclean <package_name>.) 3. Rebuilding Broken Dynamic Libraries (Preserved-rebuild) After cleaning up or upgrading core libraries (such as glibc, openssl), some older software might fail to find .so files. Running this line automatically identifies affected software and recompiles them: sudo emerge @preserved-rebuild

Gentoo downloads all source code archive files (tarballs) before compilation, storing them all in /var/cache/distfiles/. Over time, this consumes a terrifying amount of space. 1. Install Gentoolkit This is an official toolkit containing powerful management utilities, a must-install: sudo emerge -av app-portage/gentoolkit 2. Clean Cache Using eclean # Safe cleanup: Keep source archives for currently installed packages, delete outdated versions sudo eclean-dist # Deep cleanup: Aggressive! Delete everything that is not the latest version in the Portage tree (-d = deep) sudo eclean-dist -d # If you build binary packages (buildpkg), clean old binary packages sudo eclean-pkg -d
documents.s: IV. Freeing Disk Space: Source Code Cache Cleanup

documents.t: In Gentoo, version control is implemented via /etc/portage/package.mask (blacklist/disable) and /etc/portage/package.accept_keywords (unlock testing versions). 1. Installing a Specific Older Version (Downgrade) If you find a bug in a newer version, you can use = to specify the version number and force-install an older version: # Note that the leading = sign is mandatory, and the full category path must be provided sudo emerge -av =sys-kernel/gentoo-sources-6.1.60 2. Locking Versions to Prevent Upgrades (Masking) To prevent the system from automatically upgrading it back when running emerge -avuDN @world next time, you must "Mask" the newer version. Edit or create the /etc/portage/package.mask file (or create a directory with the same name and place text files inside): # Tell Portage: I do not want any version greater than or equal to 6.2 of this software >=sys-kernel/gentoo-sources-6.2.0 Once configured, Portage will act as if versions 6.2 and above do not exist in the world.
documents.s: V. Lifesaving Tools: Package Downgrading, Version Locking, and Masking

documents.t: 1. Eix: Ultra-Fast Search Tool Native emerge --search scans the entire text database every time, which is excruciatingly slow. Be sure to install eix. sudo emerge -av app-portage/eix # Initialize and build the index database sudo eix-update # Ultra-fast package search eix <keyword> 2. Compilation Acceleration: MAKEOPTS Because everything is compiled from source, compilation speed depends on your CPU core count. Be sure to configure parallel compilation in /etc/portage/make.conf: # Assuming your CPU has 16 threads, typically set to core count or core count + 1 MAKEOPTS="-j16 -l16" 3. Ccache: Compilation Cache If you frequently recompile the same packages (e.g., when tweaking your kernel config or testing different USE Flags), installing and enabling ccache can make secondary compilation times several times faster. This is also a staple setup for Gentoo users.
documents.s: VI. Advanced Power Tools (Acceleration and Search)

documents.t: In the world of Nix, there are no traditional /usr/bin or /lib directories. All software installations, dependencies, and configuration files are assigned a content-derived Hash value and uniformly dumped into /nix/store/ (e.g., /nix/store/1a2b3c...-python-3.10). This brings two massive benefits: No Dependency Hell: Software A needs Python 3.9, and Software B needs Python 3.10; both can coexist perfectly in the system without interfering with each other. Painless Rollback: Every system modification generates a new "Generation". Did an upgrade break something? Instantly switch back to the previous generation in a second. (Note: The commands below are categorized into two scenarios: "Standalone Nix Package Manager" and "NixOS Operating System".)
documents.s: I. Getting Started: The Immutable /nix/store and Generations

documents.t: In Nix, we are currently in a transition period between the legacy nix-env command and the new nix command; this guide focuses on the most stable and commonly used syntax. 1. System-wide Updates and Application for NixOS If you use NixOS, you rarely install software manually via commands; instead, you modify the declarative configuration file /etc/nixos/configuration.nix and let the system "realize" it: # Edit your system configuration file and add required packages sudo vim /etc/nixos/configuration.nix # Let the system compile/download and switch to the new state based on the configuration file sudo nixos-rebuild switch # If you only want to test the state temporarily, rebooting will revert to the previous state (great for testing high-risk settings): sudo nixos-rebuild test 2. Daily Package Management for Standalone Nix If you are simply using Nix as a package manager on Ubuntu or macOS: # Search for packages (recommended to use the web version search.nixos.org for speed) nix-env -qaP <keyword> # Install a package (strongly recommended to use the -A flag to install from attribute paths for speed and precision) nix-env -iA nixpkgs.<package_name> # Upgrade all installed user packages nix-env -u
documents.s: II. Basic Maintenance: Installing and Updating Systems

documents.t: This is the most important maintenance action in Nix! Due to Nix's immutable nature, by default it never deletes any old software (to allow you to roll back at any time). If left unmanaged, /nix/store will quickly fill up your hard drive. 1. Manually Trigger Garbage Collection (GC) # Find and delete orphan files in the current system that are "not referenced by any generation" nix-collect-garbage # ⚠️ Ultimate Cleanup (Deep Clean): Delete all old generations, keeping only the version "currently in use" # Note: After running this, you will no longer be able to roll back to previous states! nix-collect-garbage -d # Requires root privileges to clean system-level waste (Mandatory for NixOS) sudo nix-collect-garbage -d 2. Configure Automatic Garbage Collection (NixOS Only) Add this block to your configuration.nix to let the system automatically collect garbage weekly and prune old generations older than 7 days: nix.gc = { automatic = true; dates = "weekly"; options = "--delete-older-than 7d"; };
documents.s: III. Environment Cleanup and Garbage Collection

documents.t: This is Nix's super killer feature. When you update the system or install new software and services fail to start or the system crashes, the recovery method is extremely simple and brutal. 1. System-wide Rollback for NixOS # List all system generations and timestamps sudo nix-env --list-generations --profile /nix/var/nix/profiles/system # If the newly applied configuration is broken, mindlessly revert to the previous generation sudo nixos-rebuild switch --rollback (Even if your system fails to boot, the NixOS bootloader menu (GRUB/systemd-boot) lists all historical generations by default; simply select the previous generation to boot up fully restored!) 2. User Package Rollbacks (Standalone Nix) # List the package modification history of the current account nix-env --list-generations # Revert to the state before the last operation nix-env --rollback
documents.s: IV. Lifesaving Tools: Time Machine and Generation Rollbacks

documents.t: For those who frequently develop and test different environments or manage IaC automation pipelines, nix-shell is an absolute divine tool. It helps you create a "clean, disposable environment". Scenario: I just want to temporarily run a Python script requiring Ansible without installing them globally and messing up my environment! # Temporarily spin up a virtual terminal environment containing python3 and ansible nix-shell -p python3 ansible Once inside this shell, you can use python3 and ansible normally. As soon as you type exit to leave this terminal, these packages act as if they never existed and are not left in your global environment (though downloaded files remain cached in /nix/store until cleared by the next garbage collection). This perfectly solves the problem of messy temporary dependencies scattered all over development machines!
documents.s: V. Advanced Magic Weapon: Nix Shell (A Feature You Won't Want to Live Without)

documents.t: In the Red Hat family, veteran users are likely very accustomed to using yum. However, starting from RHEL 8 / CentOS 8, the underlying package management tool has been completely replaced by dnf (Dandified YUM). dnf solved the issues of excessive memory usage and slow dependency resolution that plagued yum in the past. Although typing yum in the terminal still works (due to a system alias pointing to dnf), it is strongly recommended to build the muscle memory of typing dnf directly. (Note: If you are using a minimalist container image or VMware Photon OS, you might see microdnf or tdnf, which are lightweight C-language implementations of dnf with over 95% commonality in command usage.)
documents.s: I. Introduction: The Modern Transition from YUM to DNF

documents.t: 1. Comprehensive System Upgrade This automatically compares repositories and updates all installed software: sudo dnf upgrade -y # (Note: In dnf, update and upgrade are basically synonyms; official recommendation is to use upgrade) 2. Searching and Installing Packages # Install a specific package sudo dnf install <package_name> # Fuzzy search for packages dnf search <keyword> # Magic command: Use a "file path" to reverse-lookup which package provides it (Provides) # For example, if you miss a command and don't know what package to install, you can directly query: dnf provides */ifconfig
documents.s: II. Basic Maintenance: Installing and Updating Systems

documents.t: The Red Hat family's mechanism for cleaning up orphaned packages is much smarter than Debian's default. Modern DNF defaults (clean_requirements_on_remove=True) automatically sweep away unneeded dependency packages when removing software. 1. Remove a Package sudo dnf remove <package_name> 2. Clear Orphaned Packages (Orphans) Although DNF removes things cleanly, repository changes can sometimes leave behind unwanted dependencies. Regularly clearing them keeps things tidy: sudo dnf autoremove

Every time DNF downloads metadata and installation files (.rpm), it stores them in /var/cache/dnf/. This is often the primary culprit behind consumed VM disk space. 1. Manual Cache Cleanup # Safe cleanup: Only clear downloaded rpm installation files, keeping metadata sudo dnf clean packages # Deep cleanup: Clear both installation files and metadata entirely (frees maximum space) sudo dnf clean all Note: After running clean all, the next time you run dnf install or dnf search, the system will take longer to re-download several tens of megabytes of lists (Metadata).
documents.s: IV. Freeing Disk Space: Cache Cleaning

documents.t: This is DNF's most powerful killer feature! Compared to Arch or Debian, which require manually hunting down old files for downgrading, DNF has a built-in "time machine." 1. Super Skill: Using History to Roll Back to Pre-Update State If your system breaks after an update, don't panic—use history to "undo" the entire update action: # 1. Query DNF execution history (lists a log with an ID number on the far left) dnf history # 2. Inspect what a specific ID installed/updated (assuming ID is 15) dnf history info 15 # 3. Time travel! "Undo" all changes made by ID 15 sudo dnf history undo 15 2. Direct Downgrade of a Single Package If you don't want to use history and simply want to revert a specific package to the previous version: sudo dnf downgrade <package_name> 3. Package Anti-Upgrade Locking (Versionlock) When you have downgraded a piece of software (e.g., a specific version of Docker) and do not want it to be upgraded during the next update, you need to install the versionlock plugin: # Install DNF core plugin package sudo dnf install dnf-plugins-core # Lock a package sudo dnf versionlock add <package_name> # Query currently locked packages dnf versionlock list # Unlock sudo dnf versionlock delete <package_name> # Or unlock all sudo dnf versionlock clear Updated 2026-11-27 In Fedora 41+ (which has switched to DNF5), the plugin package name has changed to dnf5-plugins (install using sudo dnf install dnf5-plugins instead); RHEL 8 / 9 / 10 and Rocky / AlmaLinux retain dnf-plugins-core.
documents.s: V. Lifesaving Tools: History Rollback (History) and Package Locking (Versionlock)

documents.t: In Red Hat / Rocky / AlmaLinux, default official repositories are very conservative for the sake of stability, meaning many useful open-source software packages (such as htop, newer versions of nginx, certbot) are not available by default. 1. Essential Repository: EPEL (Extra Packages for Enterprise Linux) Maintained by the Fedora community, this is a high-quality extra repository specifically for Enterprise Linux. Installing it is the first thing to do on a new machine: sudo dnf install epel-release sudo dnf upgrade 2. Adding Third-Party Repositories Red Hat family repository configuration files are located under /etc/yum.repos.d/ with the extension .repo. To add a third-party source (such as Docker's official source), you don't need to create files manually; using the built-in config-manager is fastest: # Add a .repo file sudo dnf config-manager --add-repo https://download.docker.com/linux/centos/docker-ce.repo Updated 2026-11-27 The --add-repo syntax above applies to DNF4 (RHEL 8 / 9 / 10, Rocky / AlmaLinux). In Fedora 41+ (DNF5), it has changed to the addrepo subcommand and --from-repofile= parameter: sudo dnf config-manager addrepo --from-repofile=https://download.docker.com/linux/fedora/docker-ce.repo 3. GPG Key Management DNF handles keys automatically by default. When you first download software from a new repo, the terminal prompts you whether to accept the key—pressing y suffices. For automated deployment scripts, keys can be imported manually ahead of time: sudo rpm --import https://download.docker.com/linux/centos/gpg
documents.s: VI. Advanced: Third-Party Repositories and EPEL (Essential for Enterprise)

documents.t: If you are running VMware Photon OS, which is optimized specifically for containers in a virtualization environment (such as ESXi), the built-in package manager will be tdnf (Tiny DNF). Why TDNF? Full DNF heavily depends on a bulky Python environment and libraries. To keep the operating system image extremely lean, reduce the attack surface, and minimize resource consumption, the development team rewrote DNF in C, completely stripping out Python dependencies—hence the origin of tdnf. 1. Seamlessly Transferable Basic Operations Because it is a compatible implementation, the muscle memory built from DNF can be applied almost 100% to tdnf: # Comprehensive system update sudo tdnf upgrade -y # Install and remove packages sudo tdnf install <package_name> sudo tdnf remove <package_name> # Search packages tdnf search <keyword> # Clean cache (essential for saving space) sudo tdnf clean all 2. Limitations and Differences of TDNF (Pitfall Guide) Although command syntax is nearly identical, because it is a "minimalist version" lacking the massive plugin ecosystem, there are several key differences to note in practice: No History Time Machine: tdnf lacks a built-in local database as robust as original DNF to track every installation history, so advanced rollback functions like tdnf history undo are unavailable. Before performing core upgrades or major updates, be sure to take a VM snapshot at the Hypervisor level just in case. Completely Independent Repository Ecosystem: Photon OS has its own dedicated official software repository. Never attempt to force CentOS / RHEL / Fedora EPEL (Extra Packages for Enterprise Linux) configuration files onto Photon OS; differences in underlying glibc and kernel versions are highly likely to crash the system directly. No Python Extension Support: High-level Python-dependent plugins such as dnf-plugins-core or version-locking versionlock cannot be used on TDNF. 3. Repository Configuration and Cache Reconstruction TDNF repository configuration files are identical to standard Red Hat families, stored under /etc/yum.repos.d/. If you manually added or modified a .repo file, or if network connectivity issues prevent fetching the latest software, you can forcibly clear and rebuild the cache: # Clear old cache and force re-download metadata from the server sudo tdnf clean all sudo tdnf makecache
documents.s: VII. Ultimate Bonus: Minimalist Variant TDNF (Tiny DNF) Built for Container Hosts

tip As I plan to gradually migrate all network services to Docker containerized deployments, I decided to switch the underlying system to VMware's container-specialized lightweight Linux distribution: Photon OS.
documents.s: VMware Photon OS Installation and System Configuration

documents.t: After downloading the ISO image, create a new virtual machine on VMware Workstation or VMware ESXi (select VMware Photon OS 64-bit or the latest Linux Kernel 64-bit for guest OS type), boot from the ISO, and complete the installation using the setup wizard. Photon OS itself requires minimal memory and disk space, but primary resource consumption will stem from subsequently running Docker containers. Plan RAM and disk capacity reasonably based on your anticipated services when creating the VM.

Verify Basic Services Verify that core system services (such as open-vm-tools) are running properly: systemctl status vmtoolsd.service Account Setup The root password is configured during installation. For daily operational security, you can create a standard user account using useradd: # Add user (-m creates home directory, -g specifies root group) useradd -m -g root $(your_id) # Set password for your account passwd $(your_id) Updated 2026-11-27 $(your_id) in the example above will be evaluated as command substitution in Bash; replace it directly with the target username when executing (e.g., useradd -m -G wheel <your_id>). Additionally, it is practically recommended to grant privilege escalation via -G wheel or sudo rather than setting the regular user's primary group directly to root. Since system administration frequently requires root privileges, you can choose according to personal preference whether to create a standard account combined with su / sudo, or modify /etc/ssh/sshd_config to permit root logins via SSH.

The default post-installation system enables DHCP. If you require only a single IP and the local network already utilizes a DHCP Server with MAC address reservation controls, you can keep the defaults; if you have advanced requirements like static IPs, modify the following configuration files. Disable DHCP Edit /etc/systemd/network/99-dhcp-en.network: [Match] Name=e* [Network] DHCP=no # Change to no to disable DHCP IPv6AcceptRA=no Static IP Configuration Method Edit /etc/systemd/network/10-static-en.network: [Match] Name=ens160 # Network interface name [Network] Address=10.1.10.9/24 # IP address, can be repeated in multiple lines Gateway=10.1.10.1 # Gateway IP DNS=10.1.10.1 # DNS IP # NTP settings, separated by spaces for multiple servers NTP=tock.stdtime.gov.tw watch.stdtime.gov.tw time.stdtime.gov.tw # Disable IPv6 LinkLocalAddressing=no IPv6AcceptRA=no Customizing Network Interface Names Edit /etc/systemd/network/10-ethusb0.link: [Match] MACAddress=00:00:00:00:00:00 # Network card MAC address [Link] Description=USB to Ethernet Adapter # Description Name=ethusb0 # Interface name If you have multiple network cards, simply create corresponding .link and .network files specifying their respective MAC addresses and interface names.

Correction Note: The underlying package management tool in Photon OS is actually tdnf. While the system provides an alias so that running yum works interchangeably, it is recommended to build the habit of using tdnf directly. tdnf update -y # Upgrade system packages tdnf install -y vim # Install vim tdnf search python # Search packages containing python in their name

In practice, Docker volume directories are commonly mounted to backup/shared directories on a NAS, offering several benefits: Simplifies centralized data backups. Reduces disk space consumption on the Photon OS virtual machine itself. Enables direct access for Docker services that need to read NAS files (e.g., personal music libraries stored on a NAS are very convenient to access via SMB/CIFS). First, install cifs-utils on Photon OS using tdnf: tdnf install -y cifs-utils Next, create the credentials file /root/secret: username=sushi # SMB account password=yummy # SMB password It is recommended to restrict /root/secret permissions to 0400 for security (chmod 0400 /root/secret). Add the mount configuration to /etc/fstab: \\winbox\getme /mnt/win cifs user,uid=500,rw,noauto,suid,credentials=/root/secret 0 0 Updated 2026-11-27 When writing CIFS shared paths in Linux /etc/fstab, use forward slashes //winbox/getme (backslashes \\ are treated as escape characters in fstab, causing parsing errors), and modern NAS environments typically require SMB version parameters like vers=3.0. Furthermore, in addition to the independent systemd service approach below, modern systems can also append _netdev,x-systemd.automount directly to /etc/fstab mount options to ensure automatic mounting once the network is ready. Using systemd for Automatic Boot Mounting I previously experimented with autofs (which proved ineffective on Photon OS) and direct auto mounting in /etc/fstab, which frequently failed because mounting occurred before network connectivity was established. Therefore, the most stable approach is creating a systemd service that explicitly triggers mounting after the network is online. Edit /etc/systemd/system/mount-nas.service: [Unit] Description=mount CIFS # Ensure execution occurs after network connectivity is truly established After=network-online.target Wants=network-online.target [Service] Type=oneshot ExecStart=/bin/mount -a RemainAfterExit=yes [Install] WantedBy=multi-user.target The key is setting After=network-online.target to ensure mounts run only after network connectivity is confirmed. Once configured, reload and enable the service: systemctl daemon-reload systemctl enable --now mount-nas.service

After running for a while, even with space conservation, the initial disk capacity allocated to the virtual machine may become insufficient (I've encountered this two or three times). When using Windows VMs in the past, one would typically add a virtual disk and mount it as a new drive letter; under Photon OS, however, you usually want to expand the original /dev/sda directly. 1. Adjusting Virtual Disk Capacity in ESXi Go to the ESXi backend, edit the virtual machine settings, and increase the hard disk capacity. 2. Rescanning and Expanding Partitions in the System If parted is not installed, install it first: tdnf -y install parted Next, rescan disk changes and launch parted: # Rescan block devices so the system detects space added by ESXi echo 1 > /sys/class/block/sda/device/rescan # Enter parted interactive shell parted /dev/sda Inside parted, run the following sequentially: # List partitions; if the system prompts that all disk space is not yet applied and asks whether to fix, enter f (or fix) (parted) print # Confirm the primary partition number in use (usually 1 or 3), then use resizepart to allocate all space (100%) (parted) resizepart 1 100% # Quit parted when finished (parted) quit 3. Expanding the File System Correction Note: resize2fs should take the partition device name (e.g., /dev/sda1) rather than the entire disk (/dev/sda). Use resize2fs to expand the file system on that partition (assuming the first partition was expanded): resize2fs /dev/sda1 Once completed, verify whether capacity has expanded successfully using df -H!

documents.s: openSUSE / SUSE / Zypper Practical Commands and Maintenance Tips Notes

documents.t: Zypper is the command-line package management tool for the SUSE family (including stable openSUSE Leap, rolling-release Tumbleweed, and enterprise-grade SLES). Its two signature features: The World's Strongest Dependency Resolver (SAT Solver): When encountering package conflicts, Zypper does not simply throw an error and quit; instead, it provides multiple solutions (e.g., downgrade A, remove B, or keep status quo), letting you solve conflicts like answering multiple-choice questions. Extremely Comprehensive Abbreviation Support: Almost all commands can be abbreviated (e.g., install = in, search = se), making typing extremely fast.
documents.s: 1. Getting Started: Understanding Zypper and the Super-Powered Dependency Resolver

documents.t: There is an extremely important concept here! openSUSE is divided into two editions, and their update commands are completely different. Entering the wrong command may throw your system into chaos. 1. openSUSE Leap (Fixed-version release, similar to Ubuntu/Debian) Only receives security updates and bug fixes. Please use: sudo zypper update # Abbreviation: sudo zypper up 2. openSUSE Tumbleweed (Rolling release, similar to Arch) Because all packages including the kernel are constantly advancing, you must use the distribution upgrade command. It automatically handles package downgrades, removals, and dependency reorganization: sudo zypper dist-upgrade # Abbreviation: sudo zypper dup
documents.s: 2. Basic Maintenance: Daily Updates (Leap vs. Tumbleweed Differences)

documents.t: Zypper's command abbreviations are very intuitive; daily operations take almost two or three letters. 1. Search and Install # Search for packages (Search) zypper se <keyword> # Display detailed package information (Info) zypper info <package_name> # Install packages (Install) sudo zypper in <package_name> 2. Clean Removal and Orphaned Package Cleanup Similar to apt, if you only run zypper rm, dependent packages will be left behind. # Cleanly remove a package, along with "dependencies originally installed for it that are now unused" (-u = clean-deps) sudo zypper rm -u <package_name> # Find all orphaned packages in the system (packages with no dependents) zypper packages --unneeded # Practical trick: One-click purge of all orphaned packages sudo zypper rm -u $(zypper packages --unneeded | awk -F'|' 'NR>4 {print $3}')

This is a feature where the SUSE family stands proud above others. As long as you choose the default Btrfs filesystem during system installation, you don't even need to manually take snapshots. When you run zypper in (install) or zypper dup (major upgrade), Zypper automatically triggers Snapper in the background to take a "pre-update" and "post-update" snapshot for you. What if a system update breaks and it fails to boot? Reboot and select Start bootloader from a read-only snapshot in the GRUB boot menu. The menu will list your recent Zypper operation logs and timestamps. Select a snapshot that worked normally before the update and press Enter to enter the system. Once inside this read-only "time-machine system", open a terminal to verify everything is normal, then run: sudo snapper rollback The system will immediately set your current state as default. After rebooting, you are fully resurrected! There is no need to log into a hypervisor to fiddle with virtual machine snapshots.
documents.s: 4. Killer Feature: Btrfs + Snapper System Snapshot Painless Rollback

documents.t: 1. Patterns (Software Groups) Zypper isn't limited to single packages; it bundles many related software pieces into Patterns (e.g., the entire KDE desktop, a LAMP server environment, C/C++ development environment). # List all patterns in the system zypper patterns # Abbreviation: zypper pt # Install a specific pattern (e.g., KVM virtualization host environment) sudo zypper in -t pattern kvm_server 2. Package Locking (Locks) If you do not want a specific software to be upgraded (such as a specific version of Docker), you can lock it. # Add a lock (Add Lock) sudo zypper al <package_name> # List all currently locked packages (List Locks) zypper ll # Remove a lock (Remove Lock) sudo zypper rl <package_name> 3. Clear Cache Used for freeing up disk space: # Clean all downloaded installation packages and metadata cache sudo zypper clean -a # Abbreviation: sudo zypper cc -a
documents.s: 5. Advanced Techniques: Patterns and Package Locking

documents.t: Alpine Linux became the king of Docker base images because it discards bulky GNU toolchains (such as glibc) in favor of the ultra-lightweight musl libc and BusyBox. A pristine Alpine image is under 5MB! Its accompanying tool, apk, features very intuitive operation logic and extremely fast execution speed. Configuration files are primarily located at /etc/apk/repositories.
documents.s: I. First Step: Understanding apk and Alpine's Minimalist Philosophy

documents.t: If you are maintaining Alpine as a standalone VM or LXC container, the basic commands are as follows: 1. System Update Similar to apt, updating the local index directory is required before running upgrades: # Update package index apk update # Upgrade all installed packages apk upgrade # Or do it in one line apk update && apk upgrade 2. Search and Query # Search for packages apk search <keyword> # Query detailed information of an installed package apk info <package_name> # List all installed packages apk info
documents.s: II. Basic Maintenance: Routine System Installation and Updates

documents.t: If you are writing a Dockerfile, forget the apk update trick mentioned above. In container packaging best practices, we have smarter parameters to compress image sizes to the minimum. 1. God-tier parameter: --no-cache (Replacing update and cache cleanup) When writing Dockerfiles in Debian/Ubuntu, we are often forced to write long, ugly commands to avoid residual caches: apt-get update && apt-get install -y xxx && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/* In Alpine, you only need to append --no-cache. It automatically fetches the latest index from the server, installs the software, and leaves zero cache or index files on the local disk, all in one line: # Perfect, clean, and trace-free installation method RUN apk add --no-cache curl nginx
documents.s: III. Essential Dockerfile Skill: Ultimate Image Slimming

documents.t: apk automatically checks and removes "orphan packages no longer depended on by any software" by default during uninstallation, so frequent autoremove commands like in other systems are rarely needed. 1. Remove Package apk del <package_name> 2. Force Orphan Cleanup (For Insurance) If you manually deleted files or want to ensure extreme system cleanliness, although there is no native autoremove command, you can root out unrecorded orphans with this trick: # Fix and clean all system dependencies (packages not belonging to the world list will be purged) apk fix

Alpine repositories are primarily divided into main (core support) and community (community maintained). Many great open-source software packages are in community by default, but the repository might not be enabled. 1. Enable Community Repository Edit /etc/apk/repositories: vi /etc/apk/repositories You will see content similar to this; remove the # comment in front of the line starting with community: http://dl-cdn.alpinelinux.org/alpine/v3.18/main http://dl-cdn.alpinelinux.org/alpine/v3.18/community Updated 2026-11-27 Alpine Linux v3.18 reached End-of-Life (EOL) on May 9, 2025. When configuring /etc/apk/repositories, please match the active version branch currently used by the host (such as v3.21 or latest-stable), and it is recommended to switch entirely to the https:// protocol. Remember to run apk update once after modifying. 2. Temporarily Targeting Edge Repository for a Single Package If you urgently need the latest version of a software but do not want to upgrade the entire system to an unstable testing branch, you can cross-repository install temporarily with this command: # Temporarily use the edge repository to install the latest version of a specific software apk add --no-cache <package_name> --repository=http://dl-cdn.alpinelinux.org/alpine/edge/community Updated 2026-11-27 In modern Alpine environments, it is recommended to update the URL above to https://dl-cdn.alpinelinux.org/alpine/edge/community to ensure transmission security.

Linux system account password expiration policies are controlled by the shadow file and most commonly adjusted using the chage command. Below are core parameters and practical examples: View Full Account Status (-l) sudo chage -l john The output will include: last password change date, password expiration date, number of warning days before password invalidation, account deactivation date, and minimum/maximum password change intervals. Set Maximum Password Validity Days (-M) sudo chage -M 90 john Forces the user to change their password every 90 days. Setting it to -1 means the user's password never expires. Set Minimum Password Change Days (-m) sudo chage -m 7 john Requires users to wait at least 7 days after changing their password before modifying it again, preventing users from bypassing password history restrictions through consecutive changes. Set Password Expiry Warning Days (-W) sudo chage -W 14 john When there are 14 days remaining before the password expires, the user will receive a warning message every time they log into the terminal. Set Absolute Account Expiration Date (-E) sudo chage -E 2026-12-31 john Specifies the final deadline the account can be used (formatted as YYYY-MM-DD). After this day, the account will be locked directly, regardless of password validity.
documents.s: chage Command Set and Parameter Details

documents.t: Modern Linux distributions typically use libpwquality to verify password strength. Modify the /etc/security/pwquality.conf file to define password strength policies: Parameter Setting Default or Recommended Value Description minlen 12 Minimum allowed total password length. minclass 3 Required number of different character classes (uppercase, lowercase, numbers, special symbols). dcredit -1 Negative numbers indicate the minimum required count of digits (e.g., -1 means at least 1). ucredit -1 Minimum required count of uppercase letters. lcredit -1 Minimum required count of lowercase letters. ocredit -1 Minimum required count of special symbols. maxrepeat 3 Maximum allowed consecutive repetitions of the same character.
