Recently, as I was sorting through some useful advanced mixing techniques, I decided to write them down independently into this note. When writing technical blogs (such as Docusaurus, Obsidian, or Typora), Markdown serves as the core syntax for recording notes and knowledge bases. Beyond standard formatting rules, mixing HTML tags allows for many advanced visual effects. This article provides a comprehensive overview ranging from basic syntax to advanced HTML techniques.
documents.s: Complete Guide to Markdown Basics and HTML Mixing Tips

documents.t: Most modern Markdown editors (such as Typora) support real-time preview and shortcuts, but mastering native markup ensures stable rendering across any Wiki platform.
Corresponding to HTML <h1> through <h6>, there are six size hierarchies:
#### H4 Heading​ ##### H5 Heading​ ###### H6 Heading​

You can use three or more asterisks, hyphens, or plus signs (Updated 2026-11-27: The CommonMark standard specifies underscores _; plus signs +++ are not standard divider syntax) to create horizontal rules: --- *** +++ Updated 2026-11-27 Standard CommonMark / GFM only supports three or more hyphens (---), asterisks (***), or underscores (___); +++ in static site generators is typically reserved for TOML Frontmatter and cannot be rendered as a horizontal divider.
Standard anchor text and URL link syntax: [Title](httpURL) Result: Kiwi's Wiki

Supports italics, bold, strikethrough, and combinations thereof: Syntax 1 Syntax 2 Result *Italic* _Italic_ Italic **Bold** __Bold__ Bold ***Bold Italic*** ___Bold Italic___ Bold Italic ~Strikethrough~ Strikethrough

Unordered Lists (using *, -, or + yields identical results): * First item * Second item * Third item Ordered Lists: 1. First item 2. Second item 3. Third item (Note: Even if numbering is out of order, most editors will automatically sequence them)

Standard Image: ![Alt text](/path/to/img.jpg) Nested Media Link (e.g., wrapping a YouTube thumbnail into a clickable hyperlink): [![Video Title](http://img.youtube.com/vi/SlzBMJvtGHo/0.jpg)](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SlzBMJvtGHo "Video Tooltip") Result (YouTube Example): Updated 2026-11-27 The thumbnail URLs above should preferably use HTTPS (https://img.youtube.com/vi/SlzBMJvtGHo/0.jpg) to avoid triggering browser mixed content blocks or warnings on modern HTTPS sites.

Markdown's core design allows embedding HTML syntax directly. When finer layout control, color customization, or special markers are needed, HTML tags can be used alongside Markdown. ⚠️ Note: When writing content inside HTML <> tags, it is recommended to adopt HTML formatting internally (e.g., using <font> or <del> instead of **) to avoid parser conflicts.
documents.s: II. Advanced Usage: Mixing Markdown with HTML

documents.t: Native Markdown does not directly support underlines (to avoid confusion with links), which require HTML's <u> tag: Syntax Result <u>Underline</u> Underline <del>Strikethrough</del> Strikethrough

Using allows free adjustment of font colors, ideal for highlighting key points in technical notes: Syntax Result Syntax Result Maroon Maroon Red Red Orange Orange Gold Gold Yellow Yellow Green Green Dark Green Dark Green Cyan Cyan Navy Blue Navy Blue Pink Pink Purple Purple Gray Gray Updated 2026-11-27 The tag is deprecated in HTML5 specifications; modern standards recommend using CSS inline styles Text (or style={{color: '#FF0000'}} in Docusaurus MDX v2/v3).
Suitable for mathematical formulas, chemical equations, or version labeling: Syntax Result 3<sup>2</sup>=9 32=9 H<sub>2</sub>O H2O
Directly insert special symbols via HTML Entity References: Target Syntax Result Trademark ® Trademark® Function ƒ(x) ƒ(X)=X+1 ƒ(X)=X+1 Square Root √2 √2 Degree 45° 45°

documents.t: Leverage HTML5 <ruby>, <rt> (ruby/pinyin annotation), and <rp> (parentheses for unsupported browsers) tags to create ruby text: <ruby> Kanji<rp>(</rp><rt>かんじ</rt><rp>)</rp> </ruby> Result: Kanji(かんじ) Practical Example (Dual-Layer Technical Semantics): Combine colors and strikethroughs within annotations for dual-layer semantic effects: I really like <ruby><font color="blue"><del>my fleet</del></font><rp>(</rp><rt><font color="red">VMware ESXi</font></rt><rp>)</rp></ruby> Result: I really like my fleet(VMware ESXi)

The author does not guarantee its accuracy or wording. tip Ever since Typora transitioned to paid software, the open-source MarkText has become an excellent alternative. To break free from the pain of manual image uploads, combining it with the command-line PicGo-Core enables a smooth automated image hosting workflow. This logic can also be seamlessly extended to the Obsidian note-taking environment. Updated 2026-11-27 The MarkText upstream project has been in a stagnant maintenance state since v0.17.1 (2022); for newly established note-taking environments, it is recommended to evaluate Obsidian or other actively maintained Markdown editors. MarkText Common Shortcuts and Formatting Mapping Function Name Shortcut Output Syntax and Effect Insert Image Ctrl + Shift + I ![Alt Text](Image Link) (Pops up a dialog to enter info; if an Image Uploader is configured, it automatically uploads) Code Block Ctrl + Shift + K ``` (Quickly generates a Code Fence code block) Math Formula Ctrl + Shift + $ Inserts a math expression block PicGo-Core Installation Practice on Linux (Manjaro) In a Linux environment (such as Manjaro / Arch), remember not to install the GUI version picgo-appimage commonly found online, because MarkText's image upload plugin cannot directly bind and capture that GUI's background process. You must instead use Node.js's command-line core PicGo-Core: Global Installation Command: sudo npm install picgo -g (Note: sudo is required to ensure full global environment permissions and prevent write path failures.) (Updated 2026-11-27: If using version managers like nvm/fnm, or to avoid root permissions polluting global directories, it is recommended to use user-directory installation or configure npm prefix without sudo) Initialization and Image Bed Configuration: Run the interactive configuration wizard, taking the GitHub image bed as an example: picgo set uploader Sequentially fill in the relevant parameters (such as repo repository name, token permission credentials, path storage path, etc.). Enable Specified Image Bed: After configuration is complete, be sure to run the following command to officially apply it: picgo use uploader Plugin Mapping in MarkText: Open MarkText's preferences, and check picgo under the image upload options. As long as configured correctly, pasting or importing images will automatically upload them via the command-line background. Obsidian PicGo Integration Application Unlike MarkText which focuses on real-time editing with "paste-to-upload", Obsidian defaults to being centered around local Markdown files and folders Vaults. If you wish to enjoy the same automatic cloud image bed upload experience with PicGo in Obsidian, it is usually achieved through community plugins: Install Plugin: Search for and install Image Auto Upload Plugin or PicGo Integration in Obsidian's "Community Plugins". Specify PicGo Executable Path: In the plugin's settings page, point the PicGo Path to the global executable path installed via npm in the previous step (e.g., /usr/bin/picgo or queried via which picgo). Operation Mechanism: When you paste a screenshot or image inside Obsidian, the plugin automatically calls the system's picgo command to push the image to GitHub cloud storage, and automatically replaces the local absolute path in Markdown with the remote image bed's CDN link, ensuring that when synchronizing notes across devices, images do not break due to being unfound.

documents.t: All commands are entered under Command Mode (Updated 2026-11-27: Strictly speaking, operations like i, a, o, dd, u, and p belong to Normal Mode, whereas colon-prefixed instructions like :w, :q, and :%s/... belong to Command-line Mode), and pressing the Esc key will return you to Normal Mode at any time. Command Effect Description :q Quit without saving (blocked if there are unsaved changes) :q! Force quit without saving (discard all unsaved modifications) :w Write and save current file :wq or ZZ Save and quit :wq! Force save and quit (applies to overriding when permissions allow)

Common shortcuts for switching from Normal Mode to Insert Mode or performing block operations: Command / Key Action Effect Description i Enter insert mode (Insert) at current cursor position a Enter insert mode after the cursor position o Open a blank line below the current line and enter insert mode dd Delete (cut) the entire line [number]dd Delete specified [number] of lines starting from the current line (e.g., 5dd) u Undo previous action p Paste (content buffered by dd or yy)
Utilize Ex commands in Command-line mode for powerful string searching and batch replacement.
documents.s: 3. Advanced Search and Global Replacement Commands

documents.t: Type / in Normal Mode followed by the keyword to search downwards (press n for next, N for previous).

Global replacement across the entire file: :%s/search_from/replace_to/g Interactive confirmation with user prior to each replacement: :%s/search_from/replace_to/gc (When prompted, press y to confirm replacement, n to skip, a to replace all, q to quit) Ignore English case differences: :%s/search_from/replace_to/gi Replace only on the "current line": :s/search_from/replace_to/g Specify a target line number range for replacement: :[start_line],[end_line]s/search_from/replace_to/gc (e.g., :10,50s/foo/bar/gc means perform confirmed replacement only between line 10 and line 50)

tip Ever since I started using Linux as my primary console, I began lavishly adopting Powerline everywhere. This article focuses on classic Vim in traditional and modern command-line interfaces, concentrating on how to build a high-aesthetic status bar via Powerline, combined with the Marker folding mechanism and efficient shortcuts, giving pure text editors an ultimate experience of both visual and structural management (Note: For modern Lua architecture of Neovim and NvChad, please refer to the companion article).
documents.s: Vim Terminal Customization and Advanced Folding Tips

documents.t: To ensure special icons and arrows render correctly in the status bar, ensure terminal fonts and packages are in place.
documents.s: I. Prerequisites: Powerline Fonts and Core Installation

documents.t: Arch Linux / Manjaro: sudo pacman -S powerline-fonts ttf-jetbrains-mono-nerd Debian / Ubuntu: sudo apt install fonts-powerline FreeBSD: sudo pkg install powerline-fonts (After installation, remember to switch your terminal emulator font setting to a font with Powerline support, such as JetBrainsMono Nerd Font)

Taking Arch Linux / Manjaro systems as an example: sudo pacman -S vim powerline python-powerline Updated 2026-11-27 The official Arch Linux repository has split the Vim integration plugin into vim-powerline (providing powerline-vim). It is recommended to install sudo pacman -S vim powerline vim-powerline. Once vim-powerline is installed, it is automatically mounted to the Vim runtime path; typically only set laststatus=2 needs to be configured without manually writing python3 load scripts.
Drive the dynamic status bar via embedded Python modules.

Copy the system-built-in Vim sample configuration to your home directory: cp /usr/share/vim/vim90/vimrc_example.vim ~/.vimrc (Note: Depending on the actual Vim version, vim90 in the path may be a version number like vim91)

Open ~/.vimrc with an editor and add the following configuration at the end: " Powerline status bar customization set laststatus=2 " Always show the bottom status bar " Load Powerline framework via embedded Python 3 python3 from powerline.vim import setup as powerline_setup python3 powerline_setup() python3 del powerline_setup
Faced with hundreds of lines of code, using Marker tags and foldmethod allows you to collapse temporarily ignored logic blocks effectively.
documents.s: III. Code Folding and Marker Configuration

documents.t: Add the following folding parameters to the same ~/.vimrc file: syntax on set foldmarker={{{,}}} set foldmethod=marker set foldlevel=0 " Collapse all blocks by default upon startup let php_folding = 1 " Additional dependent folding support for PHP syntax set foldnestmax=3 " Limit maximum nested folding levels to 3 layers

After configuration, add {{{ and }}} inside code comments to create folded blocks: // Database connection and initialization module {{{ function init_connection() { // Implementation details... } // }}}

Common shortcuts for operating folding states in Vim: Shortcut Command Effect and Description zi Enable / Disable file-wide folding functionality zo Open the folding block at the current cursor zc Close the folding block at the current cursor zO Recursively open all folding blocks at and below the current cursor level zC Recursively close all folding blocks at and below the current cursor level zm Decrement foldlevel by 1 (tighten overall folding level further) zM Set foldlevel to 0 (force all blocks folded) zr Increment foldlevel by 1 (loosen overall folding level further) zR Set foldlevel to maximum (fully expand all blocks) zx Update folding state (re-apply rules for all blocks except the one under the cursor) zf Select a range via Visual Mode to dynamically create start and end folding markers

documents.t: Powerline on Linux: An Integration Guide
It's just for show.

NeoVim offers high extensibility and asynchronous processing, and can be installed directly via native package managers across major Linux distributions: Arch Linux / Manjaro: sudo pacman -S neovim Debian / Ubuntu / Linux Mint: sudo apt install neovim Fedora / RHEL: sudo dnf install neovim Default configuration directory: ~/.config/nvim/
NvChad is a pre-configured, out-of-the-box Neovim distribution and theming setup written entirely in Lua. It maintains a lightweight footprint and a modular architecture.

Clone the official Starter repository to the user's .config/nvim directory using Git: git clone https://github.com/NvChad/starter ~/.config/nvim && nvim (Note: On first launch, Neovim will automatically trigger the plugin download and installation interface.)

NvChad's core design recommends placing all personal customizations inside ~/.config/nvim/lua/custom/. Since this directory is included in .gitignore by default, it is well-suited to being maintained as its own independent Git repository for cross-host synchronization: Full Override: Placing init.lua inside custom directly overrides and replaces NvChad's default behavior. Partial Override (Recommended): Placing chadrc.lua inside custom allows local overrides or extensions based on the structure of core/default_config.lua. Updated 2026-11-27 Starting from NvChad v2.5 (the NvChad/starter cloned above), the legacy v2.0 lua/custom/ directory and core/default_config.lua have been deprecated. The new structure maintains chadrc.lua, options.lua, mappings.lua, and plugins/init.lua directly under ~/.config/nvim/lua/ (with NvChad/NvChad itself loaded as a lazy.nvim plugin). The lua/custom/ examples in the sections below are kept only for understanding legacy v2.0 concepts.

All UI themes and custom module mounts are defined in this file: ---@type ChadrcConfig local M = {} -- 設定預設佈景主題 M.ui = { theme = "onedark", } -- 掛載自訂的程式碼摺疊模組 (對應 custom/folder.lua) M.folder = require "custom.folder" return M Module loading explanation: The syntax M.XXX = require "custom.XXX" loads the custom/XXX.lua file. Copying the corresponding file from the official core/ directory before editing offers the best compatibility.

-- 語法高亮（Neovim 預設開啟，若需強制執行可保留 vim.cmd） vim.cmd('syntax on') -- 使用 vim.opt 設定選項 (等同於 Vimscript 的 set) vim.opt.foldmethod = 'marker' vim.opt.foldmarker = '{{{,}}}' vim.opt.foldlevel = 0 vim.opt.foldnestmax = 3 -- 設定全域變數 (等同於 Vimscript 的 let，用來處理舊式外掛變數) vim.g.php_folding = 1 Core Mapping Principles:​ vim.opt: Dedicated to setting various Vim options (such as foldmethod, number, shiftwidth, etc.), supporting autocompletion and type handling. vim.g: Used to set global variables; for example, the traditional let php_folding = 1 must be mapped to vim.g.php_folding = 1. You can also call vim.cmd() from Lua to seamlessly carry over traditional .vimrc settings: vim.cmd('syntax on') vim.cmd('set foldmarker={{{,}}}') vim.cmd('set foldmethod=marker') vim.cmd('set foldlevel=0') vim.cmd('let php_folding = 1') vim.cmd('set foldnestmax=3') Common Keybindings for Managing Code Folding in Vim:​ Keybinding Effect & Description zi Toggle folding on/off for the entire file zo Open the folded block under the cursor zc Close the folded block under the cursor zO Recursively open all folded blocks under the current cursor level zC Recursively close all folded blocks under the current cursor level zm Decrease foldlevel by 1 (tighten overall folding level) zM Set foldlevel to 0 (force fold all blocks) zr Increase foldlevel by 1 (loosen overall folding level) zR Set foldlevel to maximum (fully expand all blocks) zx Update folds (reapply rules to all blocks except the one under the cursor) zf Dynamically create start and end fold markers for a visually selected range
Most NvChad keybindings start with the Leader Key. The default Leader Key is Space. Pressing it automatically brings up the keybinding hint menu (Which-Key).
documents.s: 4. NvChad Core Keybindings and Usage Guide (Key Mappings)

documents.t: Key Combination (Press Leader Space first) Function Description Notes Space + ch Open built-in Cheat Sheet Handy for viewing and searching all keybindings Space + th Theme Switcher Preview and switch color themes in real time Space + ff Find Files Fast fuzzy search across project files globally (not text inside files) Space + b Open New Buffer (Tab) Create a new blank buffer tab Space + x Close Current Buffer Close the active buffer tab (safer than :q!) Arrow keys or h/j/k/l Switch Active Buffers Quickly navigate between multiple open buffer tabs

Key Combination (Press Leader Space first) Function Description Notes Space + e Toggle Left File Tree Opens the tree and focuses it if not already open Space + q Close Left File Tree Simply collapses the sidebar :cd <路徑> Change Working Directory Switches the root directory of the file tree to the specified path (command) L (Uppercase) Jump to Right Text Pane Moves cursor focus from the file tree back to the code editor H (Uppercase) Jump Back to Left File Tree Moves cursor focus back to the file tree sidebar

In modern Neovim development environments, Mason.nvim is the core plugin for managing Language Servers (LSP), Debug Adapters (DAP), Linters, and Formatters. Through a unified graphical interface, developers can easily install and update development tools across major programming languages.
documents.s: 5. Mason Package Manager (LSP / DAP / Linters Management)

documents.t: Run the following Ex commands in NvChad or Neovim to invoke Mason: Command Effect Description Notes :Mason Open Mason Dashboard Displays an interactive UI where you can browse, install, or uninstall tools using arrow keys. :MasonInstall <package> Install Specific Tool Directly installs a specific Linter or LSP from the command line (e.g., :MasonInstall pyright, :MasonInstall typescript-language-server). :MasonUninstall <package> Remove Specific Tool Uninstalls language servers or formatters you no longer need. :MasonUpdate Update All Installed Tools Checks and upgrades all external binaries managed by Mason to their latest versions.

In NvChad, Mason is typically paired with mason-lspconfig.nvim to ensure language servers installed via Mason automatically integrate with Neovim's built-in LSP. If you need to customize or pre-install specific LSPs, extend the configuration in ~/.config/nvim/lua/custom/plugins.lua: -- 範例：透過 NvChad 的 plugins 覆寫機制擴充 Mason 自動安裝清單 local plugins = { { "williamboman/mason.nvim", opts = { ensure_installed = { "lua-language-server", "pyright", "typescript-language-server", "gopls", }, }, }, } return plugins Updated 2026-11-27 In NvChad v2.5 (NvChad/starter), the plugin override file has moved to ~/.config/nvim/lua/plugins/init.lua (instead of lua/custom/plugins.lua). You can also use M.mason = { pkgs = { ... } } in lua/chadrc.lua paired with :MasonInstallAll for batch installation. The upstream repository williamboman/mason.nvim has migrated to mason-org/mason.nvim (the old path still redirects, though mason-org/mason.nvim is recommended for new configurations).

Installing language servers through Mason equips Neovim with IDE-grade features such as autocompletion, syntax checking, Go to Definition, and real-time diagnostics. Below is a recommended list of LSP servers for major programming languages: Language / Technology Mason Package Name Core Features & Highlights Python pyright or basedpyright Powerful type-checking and autocompletion LSP developed by Microsoft, supporting real-time error diagnostics and code navigation. Lua lua-language-server Essential for writing Neovim custom configs and Lua scripts, with excellent support for Neovim's vim global variables. TypeScript / JavaScript typescript-language-server Core frontend development server providing type inference, refactoring, and autocompletion for TS/JS. HTML / CSS / JSON vscode-langservers-extracted Standard LSPs for the core web trio, delivering accurate tag and style completion. Go gopls The official LSP maintained by the Go team, offering top performance and the most complete feature set. Rust rust-analyzer An indispensable powerhouse for Rust development, offering strong macro expansion and type analysis. Bash / Shell bash-language-server Provides syntax checking and basic autocompletion for shell scripts. C / C++ clangd Based on LLVM/Clang, providing blazingly fast and accurate navigation and completion for C/C++ (generally preferred over ccls).

To have Mason automatically install these common LSPs at startup, add them directly to the ensure_installed array in ~/.config/nvim/lua/custom/plugins.lua (lua/plugins/init.lua in NvChad v2.5): ensure_installed = { "lua-language-server", "pyright", "typescript-language-server", "gopls", "clangd", "bash-language-server", }

In addition to handling syntax checking and navigation via LSP, Neovim is usually paired with dedicated Formatters to keep code formatting consistent across teams or personal projects. By installing them via Mason and hooking them up with conform.nvim or none-ls.nvim (the community-maintained fork after null-ls.nvim was archived), you can achieve automatic formatting on save. Language / Scope Mason Package Name Core Features & Highlights Python black or ruff black is the standard zero-config formatter in Python; ruff is a rapidly rising, ultra-fast Rust-based linter and formatter combo. JavaScript / TypeScript / JSON / HTML / CSS / Markdown prettier All-around frontend formatter that cleanly handles indentation and line wrapping across web and markup languages. Lua stylua A powerful formatter designed specifically for Lua (very common in the Neovim / NvChad ecosystem). Go gofmt or goimports Official standard Go formatters (typically bundled with gopls or the Go SDK itself, and also manageable via Mason). C / C++ / Java / Rust (and more) clang-format A powerful Clang-based formatter that strictly enforces layout rules via a .clang-format file in the project root. Shell Script shfmt The standard indentation tool dedicated to formatting Bash / Shell scripts.

Similarly, you can include commonly used Formatters in the ensure_installed array in ~/.config/nvim/lua/custom/plugins.lua (lua/plugins/init.lua in NvChad v2.5) to ensure they are automatically provisioned on every fresh setup: ensure_installed = { -- LSP "lua-language-server", "pyright", "typescript-language-server", "gopls", -- Formatter "prettier", "stylua", "black", "shfmt", }

documents.s: Disk Space Analysis and Management Guide (du / ncdu / duf / gdu)

documents.t: du is a POSIX-standard tool natively built into all Unix-like systems (Linux, FreeBSD, macOS). It calculates occupied space by sequentially reading filesystem metadata, making it ideal for standard shell script automation troubleshooting.
Support Status: Both (built-in natively on both Linux and FreeBSD).

Limit directory display depth (most commonly used for troubleshooting space): du -h --max-depth=1 # or abbreviated as du -h -d 1 Specify output in MB units and list the total sum of a specified directory: du -m -s /var/log/ Practical Classic: Find the top 5 largest subdirectories or files in the current directory du -m --max-depth=1 | sort -nr | head -n 5 Updated 2026-11-27 --max-depth=1 is a long parameter specific to GNU coreutils du (Linux); BSD du on FreeBSD and macOS does not support --max-depth. For cross-platform compatibility, use -d 1 instead (e.g., du -m -d 1 | sort -nr | head -n 5).

Created to overcome the shortcomings of plain-text du results being difficult to inspect layer by layer. It introduces an ncurses text user interface, allowing administrators to intuitively navigate directories in the terminal just like a file manager.
documents.s: 2. Terminal Interactive Pioneer: ncdu (NCurses Disk Usage)

documents.t: Support Status: Both (installable via each system's package repository).

Installation Command: # Linux (Ubuntu / Debian / RHEL) sudo apt install ncdu # FreeBSD (via pkg or Ports) sudo pkg install ncdu Launch and Interaction: # Scan current directory and enter interactive interface ncdu # Scan specified directory ncdu /var/log Interactive Shortcuts: Use up and down arrow keys to navigate, press Enter to enter a subdirectory, and press d directly on a target to delete space-hogging bulky files.

Although the name contains du, its core functionality focuses more on replacing the traditional df command, presenting the health status and remaining capacity of overall disk partitions (mount points) with excellent visual formatting.
documents.s: 3. Modern Disk Partition Viewer: duf (Disk Usage/Free Utility)

documents.t: Support Status: Both (cross-platform support).
Installation Command: # Install via package repository or binary sudo apt install duf # Some Linux distributions Execution: duf

A high-performance disk analysis tool written in Go, specifically optimized for modern SSD drives and multi-core CPU architectures, capable of fully utilizing hardware performance for parallel scanning.
documents.s: 4. Blazing-Fast Parallel Computation Rising Star: gdu (Go Disk Usage)

documents.t: Support Status: Both (cross-platform support).

Blazing Fast: Significantly faster than traditional du or ncdu when scanning directories containing millions of small files (such as node_modules). Common Operation Commands: # Interactive scan of current directory gdu # Display space status of all mount points only gdu -d # Start web server mode to remotely view scan results directly via browser gdu --web /path/to/scan

Tool Name Type Linux Support FreeBSD Support Core Advantages du CLI Tool Native Native Standard POSIX, ideal for script automation. ncdu Interactive TUI Supported (APT/Pkg) Supported (Pkg/Ports) Lightweight, supports keyboard interactive deletion. duf Disk Partition Viewer Supported Supported Colored progress bars, perfect mount point inspection interface. gdu High-Speed Parallel Analyzer Supported Supported Multi-threaded, ultra-fast scanning, Web UI support.

SNMP (Simple Network Management Protocol) is an application-layer protocol widely used for status monitoring and metric collection on networking equipment (such as routers, switches, firewalls) and servers (Linux / FreeBSD).
documents.s: SNMP (Simple Network Management Protocol) and System Monitoring Tools

documents.t: SNMP organizes monitoring metrics by maintaining a database called a MIB (Management Information Base), where each metric corresponds to a unique OID (Object Identifier). Operation Mechanism: GET / GETNEXT: The management system (NMS) actively queries monitored hosts (Agents) for values. TRAP / INFORM: When system anomalies occur (such as interface link-downs or hardware alerts), the monitored host proactively sends notifications outward. Major Version Differences: SNMPv1 / SNMPv2c: Uses plaintext Community Strings (such as public or private) for authentication, resulting in low security and high vulnerability to interception. SNMPv3: Introduces complete encryption and authentication mechanisms (supporting MD5/SHA authentication and DES/AES encryption (Updated 2026-11-27: MD5 and DES are insecure; modern practices should switch to SHA-256 / SHA-512 authentication and AES encryption)). It is strongly recommended to adopt this version in production environments.
documents.s: 1. SNMP Core Concepts and Operational Architecture

documents.t: Component / Tool Linux Support FreeBSD Support Core Purpose Net-SNMP (snmpd) Full Support (Native) Full Support (Native) Industry-standard SNMP Agent and testing toolkit. SNMPwalk / SNMPget Cross-platform Cross-platform Debugging commands used to manually query OID values. Prometheus SNMP Exporter Cross-platform Cross-platform Modern bridge converting SNMP data into time-series database metrics. LibreNMS / Cacti Cross-platform Cross-platform Visual network management and traffic graphing systems (NMS).
Servers must install and configure the SNMP Agent (snmpd) to respond to monitoring requests.
documents.s: 3. SNMP Server Deployment on Linux and FreeBSD (Net-SNMP)

documents.t: Linux (Ubuntu / Debian / RHEL): sudo apt install snmpd snmp # or RHEL/CentOS sudo dnf install net-snmp net-snmp-utils FreeBSD (via pkg): sudo pkg install net-snmp (On FreeBSD, add snmpd_enable="YES" to /etc/rc.conf and run sudo service snmpd start to start the service)

To ensure security, it is recommended to directly adopt SNMPv3 to configure accounts and passwords, avoiding plaintext communities: # Create an SNMPv3 dedicated read-only account (myuser) with authentication and encryption configured rouser myuser authPriv -V systemview # Set authPass and privPass passwords (passwords must be at least 8 characters long) createUser myuser SHA "MyAuthPassword123" AES "MyPrivPassword123" Updated 2026-11-27 FreeBSD configuration file path is /usr/local/etc/snmp/snmpd.conf (not /etc/snmp/snmpd.conf). createUser containing plaintext passwords should not remain in /etc/snmp/snmpd.conf long-term. The standard practice is to stop the snmpd service first, use the net-snmp-create-v3-user command, or write createUser to a persistent state file (commonly /var/lib/snmp/snmpd.conf on Linux and /var/net-snmp/snmpd.conf on FreeBSD). Upon startup, snmpd will automatically convert it into hashed usmUser entries and clear the plaintext passwords. Ensure systemview is defined in the configuration file for rouser ... -V systemview (Debian/Ubuntu defaults are typically systemonly), otherwise authorization errors will occur. It is also recommended to use SHA-256 and AES for authentication and encryption algorithms. Restart the service after configuration: # Linux sudo systemctl restart snmpd # FreeBSD sudo service snmpd restart

When monitoring systems fail to fetch data properly, you can use client tools provided by Net-SNMP in the terminal to troubleshoot: Use snmpwalk to scan the entire OID tree: # SNMPv3 test example snmpwalk -v3 -l authPriv -u myuser -A MyAuthPassword123 -X MyPrivPassword123 127.0.0.1 .1.3.6.1.2.1.1 Use snmpget to retrieve a single specific metric (e.g., system uptime sysUpTime): snmpget -v3 -l authPriv -u myuser -A MyAuthPassword123 -X MyPrivPassword123 127.0.0.1 .1.3.6.1.2.1.1.3.0
documents.s: 4. Common Manual Debugging and Testing Tools

documents.t: Traditional SNMP polling often encounters performance bottlenecks when dealing with large-scale infrastructures. Modern operations typically combine the following tools: Prometheus SNMP Exporter: Tailored for modern cloud-native architectures, it fetches SNMP data from traditional networking equipment via a dedicated exporter, converts it into Prometheus-compatible formats, and integrates with Grafana to render exquisite dashboards. LibreNMS / Zabbix: Full-featured network automatic discovery and performance monitoring systems with built-in massive device MIB databases, capable of automatically graphing switch port traffic and sending alerts.
Below is a summary of the core differences and practical operations of the three major cross-distribution Linux sandbox tools:
documents.s: Linux Cross-Distribution Package Format Guide: Flatpak, Snap, and AppImage

documents.t: Format Main Promoter Core Philosophy Runtime Mechanism Advantages Disadvantages / Pain Points Flatpak Red Hat / Community Focused on desktop GUI apps Shared Runtime dependency, Bubblewrap sandbox isolation Excellent permission control, decentralized repository (Flathub), fast startup speed Poor CLI tool support, mainly targets desktop applications Snap Canonical (Ubuntu) All-in-one (Desktop + Server) squashfs mount dependency, AppArmor sandbox isolation Supports server backend/Daemons, powerful automatic update mechanism Slightly slower cold boot, centralized (Canonical official store only), lsblk gets filled with loop devices AppImage Open Source Community (probono) Ultimate single file, portable "green" install-free Read-only image with built-in dependencies, executed directly via FUSE Run anywhere, no root required, completely non-polluting to the system Lacks official unified update mechanism, desktop integration (shortcuts/icons) must be handled manually
documents.s: I. Overview of Core Natures and Characteristics of the Three Formats

documents.t: Flatpak has become the de facto standard on the desktop for communities like Fedora, Arch, and Debian. Its packages are primarily centralized on Flathub, and its permission control is very strict (unable to read your home directory by default).
documents.s: II. Flatpak: The Preferred Choice for Modern Linux Desktop GUI Apps

documents.t: Most modern desktop distributions have it built-in. If your system does not have it pre-installed, you can install it manually: # Arch: sudo pacman -S flatpak # Debian/Ubuntu: sudo apt install flatpak # Add Flathub, the largest software repository currently (Required) flatpak remote-add --if-not-exists flathub https://dl.flathub.org/repo/flathub.flatpakrepo
documents.s: 1. Getting Started: Installing and Enabling the Flathub Repository

documents.t: Flatpak software typically uses Java-like "reverse domain name" naming conventions (e.g., org.mozilla.firefox, com.spotify.Client). # Search for software flatpak search <software_name> # Install software (can use full name or keyword to prompt selection) flatpak install flathub com.spotify.Client # Run software (application menu usually shows icons automatically; to run in terminal): flatpak run com.spotify.Client # Fully update all Flatpak software and runtimes flatpak update -y # Remove software flatpak uninstall com.spotify.Client

Clean up unused runtimes (free up disk space): After Flatpak upgrades, old runtimes (such as GNOME/KDE execution environments) often remain and occupy hard drive space: flatpak uninstall --unused Permission Modification Tool Flatseal: Because Flatpak has sandbox isolation by default, sometimes when you install an editor (like VSCode or GIMP), you might find it "cannot read folders on other hard drive partitions" or "cannot access a USB flash drive". Install Flatseal directly: flatpak install flathub com.github.tchx84.Flatseal Open this graphical tool to easily toggle whether a program can access the network, file system, camera, or Wayland/X11 display, just like on a mobile phone.
documents.s: 3. God-tier Cleanup and Permission Tuning (Must Learn)

documents.t: Snap is a technology built by Canonical. Beyond desktop software, its biggest feature is that it can package system daemons and server software directly (such as Nextcloud, Docker, Certbot).
documents.s: III. Snap: Ubuntu's Pride, Amphibious for Desktop and Server

documents.t: # Install software sudo snap install <software_name> # ⚠️ Critical parameter: Classic mode (--classic) # Some development tools that require deep system access (such as VSCode, Go, Node.js) need to be installed with sandbox mode disabled: sudo snap install code --classic # Search and info snap find <keyword> snap info <software_name> # Update software (Snap automatically updates in the background by default, but you can also trigger it manually) sudo snap refresh # Remove software sudo snap remove <software_name>

Snap retains "old versions" of each software by default in case upgrade rollbacks fail, but this causes /var/lib/snapd/snaps/ to consume a large amount of disk space. You can adjust the number of retained versions (default is 3, change to keep only 2): sudo snap set system refresh.retain=2
documents.s: 2. Space Slimming Skill (Clean up old snap versions)

documents.t: AppImage is like the install-free portable software (.exe) of the Windows era. It packages all code, libraries, and dependencies into a single .AppImage file.
documents.s: IV. AppImage: The True Single Executable "Portable Software"

documents.t: Download xxx.AppImage from GitHub Releases or the official website. Grant execution permissions: chmod +x xxx.AppImage Double-click to execute directly, or enter in the terminal: ./xxx.AppImage Want to get rid of it? Simply throw the file into the trash, and it is completely uninstalled with zero system library residue.

Many modern Linux distributions (such as Ubuntu 22.04+ or some minimalist systems) do not have older FUSE installed by default, causing AppImage execution to fail with the error: dlopen(): error loading libfuse.so.2. When encountering this issue, install the corresponding compatibility package: Ubuntu / Debian: sudo apt install libfuse2 (Updated 2026-11-27: Due to the t64 transition in Ubuntu 24.04+ and Debian 13+, the package name has changed to sudo apt install libfuse2t64) Arch: sudo pacman -S fuse2 Fedora: sudo dnf install fuse-libs

The biggest drawback of AppImage is that it is just a file; it does not automatically appear in your system application menu, nor does it have an icon. A community tool commonly used in the past is AppImageLauncher: After installation, whenever you double-click any new .AppImage file, it pops up a prompt asking: "Would you like to integrate it into the system?". Selecting "Yes" automatically archives the file to a centralized directory and creates a standard desktop shortcut and icon in the application menu, providing an experience close to native software. Updated 2026-11-27 AppImageLauncher upstream has not been actively maintained for years, and you may encounter installation or dependency issues on some newer distributions. If unavailable, modern desktop environments can instead use Gear Lever installed via Flatpak (flatpak install flathub it.mijorus.gearlever) to manage and integrate AppImages.
documents.s: 3. Advanced Tool: AppImageLauncher (Solving Desktop Shortcut Pain Points)

Traditionally Homebrew is a macOS staple, but its support for Linux (formerly Linuxbrew) is now very mature. The ultimate pain point solution: Servers without sudo privileges. When working on shared company or university servers (especially legacy CentOS 7 or older RHEL), system-provided packages are usually ancient, and you lack root privileges to run apt or yum to install newer software. Homebrew solves this problem perfectly—it installs all the latest CLI tools (such as git, python, node, fzf, ripgrep) entirely within your own home directory, without polluting or interfering with the underlying system.
documents.s: I. Foreword: Why use Homebrew on Linux?

documents.t: The official automated installation script defaults to attempting to use sudo to install the system in /home/linuxbrew/.linuxbrew. If you lack root privileges, the script automatically falls back to installing it under your home directory (typically ~/.linuxbrew). 1. Run the official installation script /bin/bash -c "$(curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Homebrew/install/HEAD/install.sh)" (If prompted for a sudo password during execution, you can press Enter to skip it; it will automatically fall back to local home directory installation) 2. Add Environment Variables (Extremely Important) Once installation is complete, Homebrew will not take effect automatically; you must add it to your environment variables. Follow the prompt at the end of the installation screen to add the following to your ~/.bashrc or ~/.zshrc: # Automatically load Homebrew environment variables upon system startup (using bash as an example) echo 'eval "$(/home/your_username/.linuxbrew/bin/brew shellenv)"' >> ~/.bashrc source ~/.bashrc 3. Verify Installation brew doctor If it displays Your system is ready to brew., it means you now have your very own high-level package manager!
documents.s: II. Getting Started: Installation Without Root Privileges

documents.t: Homebrew's syntax is extremely intuitive, and because it is installed in the user directory, all commands do not require sudo. 1. Software Installation and Removal # Search for packages brew search <keyword> # Install a package brew install <package_name> # Remove a package brew uninstall <package_name> # List all packages you "actively installed" (excludes dependencies, great for auditing your environment) brew leaves 2. System and Software Updates # Update Homebrew itself and remote package lists brew update # Upgrade all installed packages to the latest versions brew upgrade # Upgrade a specific package only brew upgrade <package_name>
documents.s: III. Basic Maintenance: Daily Package Management

documents.t: When compiling or downloading precompiled binary packages (Bottles), Homebrew caches files in ~/.cache/Homebrew, which can consume a significant amount of space over time. # Safe cleanup: remove old version caches, keeping the latest versions brew cleanup # Deep cleanup: delete all caches including the latest ones (-s = scrub) brew cleanup -s # Check how much disk space Homebrew is currently occupying brew info
documents.s: IV. Freeing Up Disk Space: Cache Cleanup

documents.t: On extremely old servers, after installing newer software via brew, you might encounter errors like lib64/libc.so.6: version 'GLIBC_2.28' not found when executing it. This means the underlying system's C library is too old. Homebrew's solution is aggressive and effective—it installs a modern version of gcc directly in your home directory! # Actively install a modern gcc via brew when encountering compilation or execution errors brew install gcc Once installed, software managed by Homebrew will automatically use this modern version of the library, no longer constrained by the underlying system.
documents.s: 1. Resolving C Library Dependency Issues on Legacy Systems (gcc / glibc)

documents.t: If you frequently switch between different servers or development machines, running brew install for dozens of tools every time is extremely painful. Homebrew has a built-in mechanism similar to requirements.txt or package.json, called Brewfile. Export current environment: # Dump a list of all currently installed packages into a file named Brewfile brew bundle dump Restore with one click on a new machine: Drop this Brewfile onto the new machine and run in the same directory: # Homebrew automatically reads the Brewfile and installs everything inside it brew bundle For developers without root privileges, this trick is the ultimate silver bullet for quickly replicating a familiar personal development environment (the Dotfiles philosophy).

documents.s: Node.js Modern Package and Environment Management Practical Notes

documents.t: In Linux (apt/dnf) or macOS, running sudo apt install nodejs or sudo npm install -g xxx directly is strictly discouraged. This leads to two severe consequences: Outdated Versions: System repositories usually lag behind by several major versions. Permission Hell: You will constantly encounter EACCES permission errors when installing global packages, forcing you to run npm with sudo, which is a major security and environment cleanliness faux pas. Modern Standard Practice: Use a Version Manager Classic Choice: NVM (Node Version Manager) Well-established and most popular. Installation command: curl -o- https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nvm-sh/nvm/v0.39.7/install.sh | bash Common commands: nvm install 20 # Install Node.js v20 (LTS) nvm use 20 # Switch to v20 nvm alias default 20 # Set default version nvm ls-remote # View all installable versions Blazing Fast Newcomer: fnm (Fast Node Manager) 🌟 Written in Rust, dozens of times faster than nvm, doesn't slow down terminal startup, and natively supports cross-platform. Highly recommended for new setups: # Install via script curl -fsSL https://fnm.vercel.app/install | bash # Common commands are almost identical to nvm fnm install 20 fnm default 20 Updated 2026-11-27 The NVM installation version (v0.39.7) and Node.js v20 referenced in the original text are outdated (Node.js 20 reached End-of-Life EOL in April 2026). In practice, check the official NVM GitHub Releases for the latest installation version, and prefer --lts (e.g., nvm install --lts, fnm install --lts) or current LTS versions (such as Node.js 22 / 24).
documents.s: I. Getting Started: Never Install Node.js Using System Native Commands

documents.t: Once you have Node.js, you face a choice of package managers: npm (Node Package Manager): Built-in default, standard and solid. Yarn: Developed by Facebook, once dominant due to speed and lockfiles, but confusion currently surrounds the v1 and v2+ generations. pnpm (Performant npm): 🌟 Strongly recommended for modern development! It utilizes a "Hard link" mechanism, storing identical packages only once on the entire disk. If your computer has 10 projects using React, npm duplicates them 10 times, whereas pnpm stores only 1 copy and links to it. Extremely disk-space efficient with lightning-fast installation speeds. Enabling/Installing pnpm: Newer Node.js versions have corepack built-in by default to manage these tools: # Enable corepack and prepare pnpm corepack enable pnpm Updated 2026-11-27 Starting from Node.js 25, official distributions no longer bundle corepack by default. If running corepack results in a command-not-found error, please use the official pnpm standalone installation script (curl -fsSL https://get.pnpm.io/install.sh | sh -), or install it first via npm install -g corepack before enabling. (Note: Basic commands below focus on the industry-standard npm, but parameter logic is mostly compatible with pnpm)
documents.s: II. The Three Pillars of Modern Package Managers: npm / yarn / pnpm

documents.t: In Node.js, packages are typically tied to project directories using package.json as the configuration file. 1. Initialization and Installation # Initialize a new project (generates package.json) npm init -y # Install all dependencies in batch based on package.json npm install # (For pnpm, simply run pnpm install or pnpm i) # Install a specific package and save to dependencies (required for production) npm install axios # Install a package and save to devDependencies (development only, e.g., eslint, typescript) npm install -D typescript 2. Removal and Updates # Remove a package and automatically update package.json npm uninstall axios # Check which packages in the current project are outdated npm outdated # Upgrade packages to the latest minor version allowed by package.json npm update
documents.s: III. Basic Maintenance: Project-Level Package Management

documents.t: In the past, we often installed command-line tools (such as Vue CLI, Create React App, TypeScript compiler) globally: npm install -g create-react-app (Not recommended) The modern standard practice is to use npx (Node Package Execute). It fetches and runs the latest CLI tools directly from the cloud on-demand without local installation, discarding them cleanly afterward: # Temporarily download and run the latest version of create-react-app, cleaning up after use npx create-react-app my-project # If typescript is already installed internally in your project (local package), you can invoke it directly with npx npx tsc --init Updated 2026-11-27 create-react-app was officially deprecated by the React team in February 2025. For new React projects, please use npm create vite@latest or modern frameworks recommended by the official team (such as Next.js or React Router).

The notorious node_modules is a disk space killer, consuming tens to hundreds of gigabytes over time. 1. Clean npm Global Cache Compressed archives downloaded each time remain in the cache; sometimes resolving package corruption issues (e.g., npm ERR! cb() never called) can also be achieved with this trick: npm cache clean --force 2. One-Click Removal of node_modules Across All Projects (Disk Savior) If you have a collection of legacy projects, you can use the open-source third-party tool npkill. It uses a super-fast text-based graphical interface to help you find all node_modules across your entire computer and wipe them with the spacebar. # Run on-demand via npx without polluting the environment npx npkill
documents.s: V. Space Cleanup: Rescuing Flooded Disks

documents.t: When writing Dockerfiles or setting up GitLab CI / GitHub Actions automated deployment, never use npm install. In production environments, you must ensure that installed versions match development 100%. npm install sometimes tries to be clever and stealthily upgrades minor versions. The Only Specified Production Command: npm ci Characteristics of npm ci (Clean Install): Strictly reads the locked versions in package-lock.json, guaranteeing 100% consistency. Forcefully deletes existing node_modules prior to execution, ensuring a clean environment. Throws an error and terminates if package.json and lock files mismatch, rather than silently modifying the lock file. Installation speed is typically twice as fast as npm install. Dockerfile Example: COPY package*.json ./ # npm ci is strongly recommended for production environments RUN npm ci --only=production COPY . . Updated 2026-11-27 --only=production has been marked as deprecated in newer npm versions; it is recommended to use RUN npm ci --omit=dev instead.
documents.s: VI. Advanced: Docker and CI/CD Best Practices (npm ci)

documents.t: One of the most terrifying disasters in Linux or macOS is running sudo pip install <package> directly. Polluting the System Core: The operating system itself (such as Ubuntu's apt or RHEL's dnf) heavily relies on specific Python packages at its core. Forcibly overriding and upgrading them with sudo pip can easily brick the system's package manager. PEP 668 Restrictions: Modern distributions (such as Debian 12, Ubuntu 23.04+) have banned global pip installation at the system level. If you do not use a virtual environment, the system will throw error: externally-managed-environment and refuse execution. Modern Standard Practice: Always use Virtual Environments or dedicated tools.
documents.s: I. First Step: Never, Ever Use sudo pip install

documents.t: This is the standard approach built into Python 3 without needing any third-party tools. Packages stay confined to the project directory without interfering with each other. 1. Creating and Activating a Virtual Environment # Inside your project folder, create a virtual environment named .venv python3 -m venv .venv # Activate the virtual environment (Linux / macOS) source .venv/bin/activate # (After activation, an (.venv) label will appear at the beginning of your terminal prompt) # Deactivate the virtual environment deactivate 2. Installing and Managing Packages (While Virtual Environment is Active) # Install packages (no sudo needed or allowed here) pip requests # Upgrade packages pip install --upgrade requests # Remove packages pip uninstall requests 3. Environment Codification: requirements.txt # Export installed packages and exact version numbers in the current environment to a list pip freeze > requirements.txt # On a new machine, restore and install all dependency packages with a single click pip install -r requirements.txt
documents.s: II. Basic Maintenance: Native venv and pip

documents.t: If you are not developing a project, but rather want to install global command-line tools (such as your commonly used ansible, docker-compose (Updated 2026-11-27: Docker Compose v1 Python package is deprecated; replaced by the native Docker Go plugin docker compose, no longer installed via pip/pipx), httpie, glances), using venv is too cumbersome, and sudo pip breaks the system. In this case, use pipx. pipx automatically creates a dedicated, isolated virtual environment in the background for each tool and links their executables to your global PATH. 1. Installing pipx # Ubuntu / Debian sudo apt install pipx pipx ensurepath 2. Installing Tools Using pipx # Safely install ansible globally without polluting the system's Python environment pipx install ansible # Run on demand (similar to npx), run a temporary tool and discard it pipx run cowsay "Hello Python!" # Upgrade tools installed via pipx pipx upgrade ansible # Upgrade all pipx upgrade-all
documents.s: III. The Ultimate Global CLI Tool: pipx (Python's brew/npx)

documents.t: When downloading and compiling packages, pip caches files in ~/.cache/pip, which can become a hard drive killer over time. # Check how much space the cache is occupying pip cache info # Clear all caches pip cache purge # Clear cache for a specific package pip cache remove requests
documents.s: IV. Space Cleanup and Cache Management

documents.t: Similar to Alpine's apk --no-cache, when packaging Docker containers, never let pip leave space-consuming cache files behind. Production Dockerfile Example: COPY requirements.txt . # Absolutely must add --no-cache-dir; this slims down your image by tens to hundreds of MBs RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt COPY . .

If you love the ultimate speed of Node.js tools like fnm or pnpm, you must meet the current rising star in the Python world: uv. It is a Python package and environment manager written in Rust by Astral. It is designed as a 1:1 drop-in replacement for pip and venv, but 10 to 100 times faster than pip, while supporting global caching (similar to pnpm, saving disk space). 1. Installing uv curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh | sh 2. Seamlessly Replacing Daily Commands You can directly replace your traditional pip habits with uv pip and experience blazing speed: # Create a virtual environment (dozens of times faster than python -m venv) uv venv # Activate environment source .venv/bin/activate # Lightning-fast package installation uv pip install requests # Lightning-fast installation from list uv pip install -r requirements.txt (For DevOps engineers who frequently build CI/CD pipelines or compile container images, switching to uv can significantly reduce waiting times.)

The basic command is ssh-keygen, where common parameters allow you to customize key length, algorithm, and output file name: # Basic from man ssh-keygen ssh-keygen [-q] [-a rounds] [-b bits] [-C comment] [-f output_keyfile] [-m format] [-N new_passphrase] [-O option] [-t dsa | ecdsa | ecdsa-sk | ed25519 | ed25519-sk | rsa] [-w provider] [-Z cipher] ssh-keygen -p [-a rounds] [-f keyfile] [-m format] [-N new_passphrase] [-P old_passphrase] [-Z cipher] ssh-keygen -i [-f input_keyfile] [-m key_format] ssh-keygen -e [-f input_keyfile] [-m key_format] ssh-keygen -y [-f input_keyfile] ssh-keygen -c [-a rounds] [-C comment] [-f keyfile] [-P passphrase] ssh-keygen -l [-v] [-E fingerprint_hash] [-f input_keyfile] ssh-keygen -B [-f input_keyfile] ssh-keygen -D pkcs11 ssh-keygen -F hostname [-lv] [-f known_hosts_file] ssh-keygen -H [-f known_hosts_file] ssh-keygen -K [-a rounds] [-w provider] ssh-keygen -R hostname [-f known_hosts_file] ssh-keygen -r hostname [-g] [-f input_keyfile] ssh-keygen -M generate [-O option] output_file ssh-keygen -M screen [-f input_file] [-O option] output_file ssh-keygen -I certificate_identity -s ca_key [-hU] [-D pkcs11_provider] [-n principals] [-O option] [-V validity_interval] [-z serial_number] file ... ssh-keygen -L [-f input_keyfile] ssh-keygen -A [-a rounds] [-f prefix_path] ssh-keygen -k -f krl_file [-u] [-s ca_public] [-z version_number] file ... ssh-keygen -Q [-l] -f krl_file file ... ssh-keygen -Y find-principals [-O option] -s signature_file -f allowed_signers_file ssh-keygen -Y check-novalidate [-O option] -n namespace -s signature_file ssh-keygen -Y sign -f key_file -n namespace file ... ssh-keygen -Y verify [-O option] -f allowed_signers_file -I signer_identity -n namespace -s signature_file [-r revocation_file] # Basically, only a few functions are commonly used: -b Defines encoding bit length; RSA defaults to 3072, which is generally sufficient. -t Encryption type: choices include dsa | ecdsa | ecdsa-sk | ed25519 | ed25519-sk | rsa. Most tutorials recommend rsa. -C Defines a corresponding email address in the comment. -f Defines the output key pair name. A common creation method is as follows: ssh-keygen -b 4096 -t rsa -f <server_or_service_name> Executing this generates two files inside ~/.ssh/: <server_or_service_name> (private key) and <server_or_service_name>.pub (public key). Updated 2026-11-27 dsa (-t dsa) has been disabled by default since OpenSSH 9.8 and was officially removed in OpenSSH 10.0 (2025). Please do not use it anymore. Modern practice generally recommends switching to ed25519 (e.g., ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -f <server_or_service_name>), which offers shorter keys, higher security, and faster computation. Fall back to 4096-bit rsa only when compatibility with extremely legacy OpenSSH servers is required.

documents.t: The process is basically the same: set the bit count and key type in the bottom right corner, then click Generate to create the Private Key and Public Key.

If you need to connect directly from a Linux desktop environment (such as Manjaro), installing putty on Manjaro includes puttygen out of the box. If using Ubuntu / Debian, an additional tool package is required: # Install PuTTY tools apt install putty-tools Once installed, you can convert .ppk to .pem format for OpenSSH usage: # Convert .ppk file to .pem file for direct use by ssh client puttygen yourkey.ppk -O private-openssh -o yourkey.pem After conversion, you can log in using the following command (ensure private key permissions are set to 600): # Log in using pem ssh -i /your/key/file user@hostname.or.ip
documents.s: Converting PPK to PEM in Linux Environment

documents.t: There are two common practices for deploying public keys to a remote server:

Directly paste the public key content into the target account's ~/.ssh/authorized_keys by editing with vi or appending via command: cat <server_or_service_name>.pub >> ~/.ssh/authorized_keys However, in practice, people often find manually uploading <server_or_service_name>.pub to the target host tedious, so this method is less frequently used. PuTTYgen Key Conversion (PEM to PPK)​ Since traditional PuTTY cannot directly read standard .pem private key files, if you want to connect to sshd from Windows via PuTTY, you can import and save as .ppk format: After loading the private key, you can set a protection passphrase: Enter your custom passphrase and click Save private key to save it as a .ppk file.

ssh-copy-id -i ~/.ssh/<server_or_service_name>.pub USER@HOST ssh-copy-id reads ~/.ssh/id_rsa.pub by default, so when using a custom file name, you must specify the public key path using -i. Once uploaded and passwordless login is confirmed, you can modify sshd_config on the server to disable password login.

In addition to client-side key preparation, the server's /etc/ssh/sshd_config usually needs tightened security settings as well: # Disallow root account to log in via ssh PermitRootLogin no # It is generally recommended to disable remote root login, but when using ansible, methods other than directly using the root account can feel cumbersome... choose carefully here. # Accept Public Key authentication method PubkeyAuthentication yes # Default Public Key location file name AuthorizedKeysFile .ssh/authorized_keys # This can actually be modified, but I generally leave it untouched. # Disable built-in password authentication system and empty passwords PasswordAuthentication no PermitEmptyPasswords no # Disable password authentication login ChallengeResponseAuthentication no UsePAM no # Specific User settings (this entire block must be placed at the very end of sshd_config) Match <User1>, <User2>, ... # Then define settings for these Users, e.g. PasswordAuthentication yes # This ensures only User1 and User2 can log in with passwords, while others cannot. Updated 2026-11-27 ChallengeResponseAuthentication has been deprecated since OpenSSH 8.7; newer versions should use KbdInteractiveAuthentication no instead. The Match block must specify a condition keyword and comma-separated lists must not contain spaces. The correct syntax is Match User user1,user2 (the original example Match <User1>, <User2> lacked the User keyword and contained spaces, leading to sshd configuration syntax errors). In modern Linux environments (such as those using systemd), it is recommended to keep UsePAM yes to ensure user sessions and resource limits function correctly, and simply turn off PasswordAuthentication no and KbdInteractiveAuthentication no to disable password logins.

The basic connection command is: ssh USER@HOST To specify a specific private key file, append the -i parameter: ssh -i /location/private_key USER@HOST Since SSH authentication relies on the private key, as long as you properly store the same private key on your frequently used client hosts and set the correct permissions, you can connect smoothly.

Generate a new key: ssh-keygen -t rsa -C "your@mail.for.github" Updated 2026-11-27 Since OpenSSH 8.8, legacy SHA-1 ssh-rsa signatures are disabled by default. GitHub also recommends prioritizing the more secure and concise Ed25519 key algorithm: ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "your@mail.for.github" Then paste the contents of id_rsa.pub (Updated 2026-11-27: or ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub if using Ed25519) into GitHub under Settings → SSH and GPG keys → New SSH key, and you are all set.

documents.t: vi /location/to/repo/.git/config # Change: url = https://github.com/<USER>/Repo.git # To: url = git@github.com:<USER>/Repo.git Updated 2026-11-27 In practice, you can also switch the remote URL directly inside the repository directory using Git commands without manually editing .git/config: git remote set-url origin git@github.com:<USER>/<Repo>.git Then you can connect happily.

Although ssh-add can be used to add the key for use, you often run into the issue of having to re-add it repeatedly; the fundamental solution is to keep the key filename as id_rsa so it can be used directly.... (Updated 2026-11-27: It is recommended to keep the default filename (such as id_ed25519), or configure IdentityFile and IdentitiesOnly yes for Host github.com in ~/.ssh/config, adding AddKeysToAgent yes as needed.)

documents.t: This is very simple and essentially relies on your system's package manager: # Arch Linux family sudo pacman -S zsh # or yay -S zsh # Yum family yum install zsh # FreeBSD pkg install zsh Updated 2026-11-27 Modern RHEL, Rocky Linux, AlmaLinux, and Fedora distributions have replaced yum with dnf; please use sudo dnf install zsh instead. On FreeBSD, execute sudo pkg install zsh (or as root).

Since manjaro-zsh-config is available in the AUR, installing this package automatically pulls in all related dependencies, so it's straightforward: # Arch Linux family # Since this is in the AUR: git clone https://aur.archlinux.org/manjaro-zsh-config.git cd manjaro-zsh-config && makepkg -si # Or simpler: yay -S manjaro-zsh-config Remember to copy /etc/zsh/zshrc-manjaro/.zshrc to ~/.zshrc for it to take effect (Updated 2026-11-27: The template provided by the AUR package manjaro-zsh-config is located at /etc/skel/.zshrc (which sources /usr/share/zsh/manjaro-zsh-config). If following the manual script copy method below, you should copy /etc/zsh/zshrc-manjaro as ~/.zshrc.)
zsh-completions zsh-autosuggestions zsh-history-substring-search zsh-syntax-highlighting zsh-theme-powerlevel10k ttf-noto-nerd (Noto Nerd Fonts)

# Arch Linux family sudo pacman -S zsh-theme-powerlevel10k # or yay -S zsh-theme-powerlevel10k # Other systems - Manual Installation sudo git clone --depth=1 https://github.com/romkatv/powerlevel10k.git /usr/share/ # The installation path is fixed to match Manjaro's configuration later. Updated 2026-11-27 Directly running git clone into an existing and non-empty /usr/share/ will fail. Manual installation requires specifying the target directory name: sudo git clone --depth=1 https://github.com/romkatv/powerlevel10k.git /usr/share/zsh-theme-powerlevel10k Also note that upstream romkatv/powerlevel10k has entered a limited maintenance state, with features mostly frozen but still fully functional.

sudo git clone --depth=1 https://github.com/romkatv/gitstatus.git /usr/share/zsh-theme-powerlevel10k/ # The installation path is fixed to match Manjaro's configuration later. Updated 2026-11-27 If the /usr/share/zsh-theme-powerlevel10k/ directory already exists, you must append the subdirectory name gitstatus (i.e., /usr/share/zsh-theme-powerlevel10k/gitstatus). Actually, powerlevel10k also automatically downloads the corresponding gitstatusd binary by default.

Since there is no directly installable package, please run the following script: git clone https://github.com/Chrysostomus/manjaro-zsh-config sudo cp -Rv manjaro-zsh-config/manjaro-zsh-prompt /usr/share/zsh/ sudo cp -Rv manjaro-zsh-config/zsh-maia-prompt /usr/share/zsh/ sudo cp -Rv manjaro-zsh-config/p10k.zsh /usr/share/zsh/ sudo cp -Rv manjaro-zsh-config/p10k-portable.zsh /usr/share/zsh/ sudo cp -Rv manjaro-zsh-config/command-not-found.zsh /usr/share/zsh/functions/ sudo cp -Rv manjaro-zsh-config/.zshrc /etc/zsh/zshrc-manjaro sudo cp -r manjaro-zsh-config/base16-shell /usr/share/zsh/scripts/ sudo chmod a+x /usr/share/zsh/scripts/base16-shell/ Updated 2026-11-27 The original GitHub repository Chrysostomus/manjaro-zsh-config has been migrated/archived; it is recommended to obtain it from official Manjaro repositories or the AUR. Additionally, before executing the copy commands above on non-Arch systems, you need to first create the target directories by running sudo mkdir -p /usr/share/zsh/functions /usr/share/zsh/scripts /etc/zsh. Then copy manjaro-zsh-config/.zshrc (or /etc/zsh/zshrc-manjaro) as ~/.zshrc and restart zsh.

Tool Name Platform Support Core Features Remarks screen Cross-platform (Linux/FreeBSD/macOS) A long-standing traditional standard tool built into almost all Unix-like systems. Relatively rudimentary features, phased out by most modern developers. tmux Cross-platform (Linux/FreeBSD/macOS) Industry standard and mainstream, featuring extremely strong extensibility and scripting support. Paired with oh-my-tmux, it achieves an out-of-the-box modern appearance. zellij Cross-platform (Written in Rust) A modern rising star based on WASM (Updated 2026-11-27: The core is written in Rust, supporting a plugin system via WASM), offering out-of-the-box mouse support and a rich UI. Excellent performance with an intuitive interface (similar to an IDE inside the terminal).

documents.t: List all running Sessions: tmux ls Reattach to a specified Session: tmux attach -t $number # or abbreviated tmux at -t 0 Smart startup command (combining auto-attachment and creation): tmux -u attach || tmux -u

Set Default Shell to zsh: Add the following to ~/.tmux.conf: set -g default-shell /usr/bin/zsh WSL Automatic Session Attachment: Add the following snippet to ~/.zshrc or ~/.bashrc. This is extremely useful in WSL environments: closing and reopening the terminal window will automatically reattach to the original Session: if command -v tmux &> /dev/null && [ -z "$TMUX" ]; then tmux attach-session -t default || tmux new-session -s default fi

documents.t: Although tmux has become mainstream, screen remains the best pre-installed rescue tool in many lightweight container images or legacy servers.

Start a new Session: screen -S mysession List background Screen Sessions: screen -ls Reattach to a specified Screen: screen -r mysession Keyboard Shortcuts: Detach (leave and send to background): Press Ctrl+a then d Create new window: Press Ctrl+a then c Switch windows: Press Ctrl+a then n (Next) or p (Previous)
zellij is a terminal multiplexer written in Rust. It simplifies layout concepts to the extreme, providing a bottom status bar and pane menu by default, with excellent mouse support.
documents.s: 4. Modern Rust Terminal Rising Star: zellij

documents.t: Arch Linux: sudo pacman -S zellij Cargo (Rust Package Manager): cargo install zellij

Start a new session: zellij List and manage Sessions: zellij list-sessions Reattach to a specified Session: zellij attach <SESSION_NAME> Core Operational Features: Upon startup, shortcut prompts (Shortcut Bar) are permanently stationed at the bottom of the screen. You can use arrow keys or the mouse for intuitive operation via Ctrl+p (control panel) and Ctrl+n (new pane) without needing to memorize complex Prefix combinations.

documents.t: Regardless of the operating system used, the primary step is to install general fonts capable of properly rendering Chinese, Japanese, and Korean characters: Arch Linux / Manjaro: sudo pacman -S noto-fonts-cjk Debian / Ubuntu / Linux Mint: sudo apt install fonts-noto-cjk RHEL / CentOS / Fedora: sudo dnf install google-noto-sans-cjk-fonts FreeBSD: sudo pkg install noto-fonts-cjk Updated 2026-11-27 The FreeBSD pkg repository does not contain a package named noto-fonts-cjk. Please install specific language fonts as needed (e.g., noto-tc for Traditional Chinese, noto-jp for Japanese) or the complete meta-port noto: for example, sudo pkg install noto-tc noto-jp.
It is strongly recommended to fully adopt the modern Fcitx5 family to achieve optimal performance, Wayland compatibility, and Japanese/Zhuyin candidate selection experience.

Also, official binary package repositories typically do not provide fcitx5-mozc directly; for Japanese input, you can install ja-fcitx5-anthy or compile Mozc via Ports.

documents.t: Under this combination, Fcitx5 offers extremely high integration, requiring almost no manual environment variable configuration: Ensure all aforementioned packages are installed, then re-login. The system will automatically launch fcitx5 in the background via XDG. Open KDE System Settings (Regional Settings -> Input Method), and add Chewing and Mozc to the list to start using them out-of-the-box.
documents.s: Scenario A: Modern Wayland + KDE Plasma (e.g., Arch Linux with Plasma 5.27/6)

documents.t: If you are not running Wayland + KDE, or if the system fails to load modules automatically, you need to configure environment variables manually: Global Environment Variables (/etc/environment): GTK_IM_MODULE=fcitx QT_IM_MODULE=fcitx XMODIFIERS=@im=fcitx SDL_IM_MODULE=fcitx GLFW_IM_MODULE=fcitx FreeBSD Environment Variables and Autostart: Add the following to your shell configuration file (~/.xprofile or ~/.bashrc): export GTK_IM_MODULE=fcitx5 export QT_IM_MODULE=fcitx5 export XMODIFIERS=@im=fcitx5 Updated 2026-11-27 For compatibility, Fcitx5's GTK/Qt IM module and XIM identifier names remain fcitx (not fcitx5). The correct settings should be export GTK_IM_MODULE=fcitx, export QT_IM_MODULE=fcitx, and export XMODIFIERS=@im=fcitx. Add the background startup command to your window manager startup script (~/.xinitrc): fcitx5 -d &

This is a multi-user independent concurrent game streaming architecture based on Windows 11 and hardware virtualization technology. Traditional streaming solutions (such as standard Sunshine) can only capture the current single foreground desktop and cannot support simultaneous multi-user operation. This solution leverages Duo paired with virtual graphics cards and virtual gamepad drivers to achieve simultaneous output of 2 completely independent 1080p 60fps game streams on a single physical host—without requiring a virtual machine (VM)—with zero input focus conflicts.
documents.s: Duo Stream (Moonlight + Sunshine) Multiplayer Gaming Streaming Solution

documents.t: Item Recommended Specs (Based on Dual-User 1080p 60fps Streaming) Notes & Bottlenecks Operating System Windows 11 (22H2 / 23H2 (Updated 2026-11-27: 22H2 and 23H2 Home/Pro have reached end of support; version 24H2 or higher is recommended) Pro or higher) Windows is required. Linux compatibility for single-card multi-X-Server / Wayland multi-seat gamepad passthrough is extremely poor. Processor (CPU) 6 Cores / 12 Threads or higher (e.g., Intel Core i7-8750H / AMD Ryzen 3600 or higher) Must simultaneously handle logic calculations for 2 games and background service scheduling. Memory (RAM) 16 GB or higher (32 GB dual-channel recommended) Prevents memory exhaustion when running dual mid-range games and loading texture packs. Graphics Card (GPU) NVIDIA RTX 2060 6GB or higher (or equivalent) VRAM and encoder are major bottlenecks: Dual-stream splits approximately 2.5–3GB VRAM per session; requires NVENC supporting multi-session hardware encoding (Turing / Ampere architecture or higher). 4GB GPUs (like RTX A400) can only handle 2D or light games. Network Environment All-Wired Gigabit (1GbE / 2.5GbE) The host must be plugged into an Ethernet cable and reside within the same Layer 2 broadcast domain (L2 Switching) as clients, avoiding Layer 3 software routing forwarding and NAT latency. Client Devices Living room Shield TV Pro, Android TV box, lightweight work laptop, or tablet Running Moonlight Client, equipped with Bluetooth or 2.4G gamepads.

Main Programs: Duo (Multi-user Sunshine Fork) (https://www.google.com/search?q=https://github.com/giggio/duo (Updated 2026-11-27: The original link was a search redirect pointing to the wrong repository; corrected to the official DuoStream/Duo repository)): Core scheduling manager specifically designed to assign multiple Windows accounts, virtual screens, and virtual input devices. Sunshine: Open-source low-latency game streaming host. Moonlight: Streaming client receiver (supports Windows / macOS / Linux / Android / iOS / tvOS). Underlying Dependent Drivers: IddSampleDriver (Virtual Display Driver): Windows virtual graphics card driver that generates extended virtual screens without requiring a physical HDMI dummy plug. ViGEmBus (Virtual Gamepad Emulation Bus): Virtual gamepad driver responsible for isolating gamepad signals from each client and injecting them into the designated Session. Peripheral Management (Optional): EmuDeck for Windows: Retro emulator integration suite. RomM: Centralized game ROM / BIOS management platform (mounted via NFS/SMB provided by a NAS or backend server).

Install Clean Drivers: Install the latest NVIDIA GeForce Game Ready or Studio drivers. Install ViGEmBus: Download and install the latest ViGEmBus driver to provide virtual gamepad support. Configure IddSampleDriver (Virtual Screen): After installing the virtual display driver, go to system Display settings to confirm a new virtual screen (Display) has been added. Set the virtual screen resolution to 1920x1080 and refresh rate to 60Hz (can be set to 120Hz if streaming to high-refresh devices). Set display mode to "Extend these displays".
documents.s: Step A: Basic Environment and Driver Configuration

documents.t: To prevent multi-user connections from fighting over keyboard, mouse, and active window focus, independent user environments must be established in Windows: Create two local standard user accounts (e.g., Player1 and Player2). Configure auto-login or ensure both accounts possess background Session execution permissions.
documents.s: Step B: Create Isolated User Accounts

documents.t: Install Duo: Run the Duo setup wizard; it will automatically detect and bind the Sunshine executable and IddSampleDriver. Create two "Seats" in the Duo configuration panel: Seat 1: Bind user Player1, associate virtual screen Display 1, assign virtual gamepad 1. Seat 2: Bind user Player2, associate virtual screen Display 2, assign virtual gamepad 2. Sunshine Encoder Tuning: Open Sunshine WebUI (https://localhost:47990). Configuration ➔ Audio/Video: Encoder: Force-specify NVENC. NVENC Preset: Set to P1 or P2 (Performance, minimizing encoding latency). Capture Method: Select Desktop Duplication API (DXGI). Moonlight Pairing: Client A (e.g., Living room TV Shield TV) opens Moonlight, pairs with Duo's Seat 1 port. Client B (e.g., Laptop/room device) opens Moonlight, pairs with Duo's Seat 2 port.
documents.s: Step C: Duo and Sunshine Configuration

documents.t: Shutdown Prevention: When the living room Moonlight client clicks "Quit / Turn Off PC" in the menu, it may trigger a physical Windows shutdown by default. Solution: Press Win + R, type gpedit.msc (Local Group Editor) ➔ Navigate to Computer Configuration ➔ Windows Settings ➔ Security Settings ➔ Local Policies ➔ User Rights Assignment ➔ Edit "Shut down the system", remove the standard Users group, and leave only Administrators to prevent remote players from accidentally shutting down the system. Wake-on-LAN Troubleshooting Optimization: Windows 11 enables "Fast Startup" by default, which cuts off network card standby power, preventing it from receiving Magic Packages. Go to Power Options and turn off "Turn on fast startup"; in Device Manager network card properties, set "Shutdown Wake-On-Lan" to Enabled and "Energy Efficient Ethernet" to Disabled. Local Save Data Isolation, Centralized ROM / BIOS Sharing: If paired with EmuDeck or emulators, game ROMs and BIOS should be centrally mounted from a NAS via SMB network shares; however, game saves (Saves / States) must remain local under each user's %APPDATA% or respective Windows user directory. This prevents file lock issues or save data overwriting when Duo runs the same game concurrently. Laptop Battery Care: If using a gaming laptop as the Duo host, keeping it plugged in long-term at high temperatures will easily cause lithium batteries to swell. Be sure to use manufacturer control software (such as MSI Center / Dragon Center) to lock the charge limit to 50%–60%, or physically disconnect the internal battery and run solely on AC power. Same-Subnet L2 Direct Routing to Relieve Gateway Burden: Dual 1080p 60fps streams can reach instantaneous bandwidths of 80–100 Mbps. Ensure the streaming host and main clients (such as Shield TV) are plugged into the same network switch (same VLAN/subnet), allowing packets to route entirely via hardware line-speed switching and avoiding unnecessary routing through software routers which causes latency and jitter.
